text_kjv: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God,

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 40:1 opens the second major division of Isaiah's prophecy—chapters 40–66, often called the Book of Consolation. After 39 chapters dominated by judgment, exile, and the consequences of covenant-breaking, God now commands the heavens to comfort His people. The doubled imperative 'comfort, comfort' is not gentle reassurance; it is urgent, prophetic speech at its most intense. God does not ask the heavenly council—He commands them. The shift is seismic: Israel has paid the price of exile, and now restoration begins. This verse is not about what Israel deserves, but about what God intends to do.

The opening word nachamú (comfort) carries weight in Hebrew that the English word barely captures. It means far more than sympathy; it implies restoration to dignity, removal of shame, the reversal of what has been broken. When God says 'comfort my people,' He is announcing that the machinery of judgment has run its course and the machinery of redemption is now engaged. The phrase 'your God' (Eloheikem) in the mouth of the exiled community would have sounded like a father's voice to children who feared they had been abandoned.

word_study.meaning: To comfort, console, show compassion; related to נִחוּם (nichuem), meaning repentance or comfort. The root implies both the physical act of consolation and the deeper emotional restoration of dignity and hope.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that this doubled imperative carries divine urgency—not a gentle suggestion but a command. The repetition is characteristic of prophetic speech at its most intense and signals the tonal turning point of the entire book. In Hebrew rhetoric, doubling an imperative emphasizes both the seriousness and the reality of what is commanded—it is not conditional or tentative.

word_study.meaning: My people; covenant community. The possessive 'my' binds the speaker (God) to the community in relationship, not transaction.
word_study.significance: Even in exile, Israel remains God's people. This covenant relationship is not severed by judgment; it is the foundation upon which restoration is built. The exile was punishment, but not rejection.

cross_references.connection: Extends the theme of comfort: 'Sing, O heavens... the LORD hath comforted his people,' showing comfort as a sustained divine action throughout these chapters.
Paul identifies God as 'the God of all comfort' and connects Isaiah's consolation to Christ's redemptive work, showing how comfort flows from the atonement.
The previous book ends with Jerusalem weeping and having no comforter—Isaiah 40:1 announces the arrival of that very comforter.
Joseph Smith's prayer in Liberty Jail echoes the exilic despair that Isaiah 40:1 is meant to address, showing how this verse speaks to covenant people in all dispensations.

commentary.historical_context: The historical setting of Isaiah 40–66 is the Babylonian exile (586–538 BCE). Jerusalem has fallen; the temple is destroyed; the covenant community sits in captivity. Nearly 50 years have passed since the first wave of exiles were taken to Babylon. The community is losing faith—has God abandoned them? Is exile permanent? Is the covenant broken? Into this psychological and spiritual darkness, Isaiah 40:1 speaks. The command to comfort is not abstract theology; it is the answer to a community's cry of abandonment. The prophet is addressing both the exilic community (who need to hear restoration is coming) and the heavenly council (who are commanded to proclaim it). Ancient Near Eastern kings customarily issued proclamations of restoration and amnesty after military conquest; Isaiah reframes this political reality as a redemptive act of the divine king.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:17-19 presents Alma in spiritual exile, in despair over sin, until Christ's voice brings comfort and redemption—a microcosm of what Isaiah 40 announces for all Israel.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:104, 110:8—the phrase 'your God' appears repeatedly in Doctrine and Covenants as the Lord binds Himself to His covenant people, echoing Isaiah's own language of intimacy despite distance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The comfort announced in Isaiah 40 is inseparable from the rebuilding of the temple (chapters 44–45). Comfort and temple are linked because God's presence—and thus His relationship with His people—is renewed in the temple.

commentary.christological_typology: The command to 'comfort my people' points forward to Christ's incarnation. In the theology of Isaiah 40–66, God's comfort comes through a Servant who suffers and bears the sins of many (Isaiah 53). Comfort is not cheap reassurance; it comes through the work of redemption performed by the Messiah. The doubled imperative also recalls Jesus's dual nature: divine and human, both fully present to suffer with and save His people.
commentary.application: This verse invites modern Latter-day Saints to recognize that covenant people experience seasons of judgment and seasons of consolation. When we feel spiritually distant from God—in our own 'exile'—Isaiah 40:1 reminds us that God's voice is commanding angels and prophets to comfort us. The comfort is not earned; it is a divine decision made on behalf of a covenant community. In times of spiritual darkness, doubt, or disappointment, this verse says: God has not abandoned you. Your God has spoken, and comfort is coming.

text_kjv: Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned: for she hath received of the LORD's hand double for all her sins.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 2 unpacks the comfort announced in verse 1 with four interconnected messages for Jerusalem. First, the prophets are to 'speak to the heart' (al-lev) of Jerusalem—an idiom meaning to speak tenderly, persuasively, in a way that reaches the core of her being. She has been broken by exile; she needs the voice of restoration to penetrate her despair. Second, she is told that her 'warfare is accomplished.' The Hebrew tseva'ah carries both military and covenantal dimensions—not just military conflict, but the spiritual warfare of living under covenant judgment. That warfare has ended. Third, her iniquity is pardoned (nasa'—literally 'lifted' or 'carried away'). This is not a mild absolution; it is the removal of a burden. Fourth, and perhaps most difficult for modern ears: she has received from God's hand 'double for all her sins.'

That final clause requires careful reading. It does not mean God punished excessively or that Israel suffered more than she deserved. In Hebrew financial language, 'double' refers to full, complete payment—the debt is settled in full. When a thief paid 'double,' he paid what was owed completely and without remainder (Exodus 22:4-7). So Jerusalem's exilic suffering was not extra punishment for extra sin; it was the full measure of covenant justice executed completely. Now that justice is satisfied, restoration can begin. The message is radical: You have paid. The account is closed. Your God calls you home.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'speak to the heart'; an idiom for tender, persuasive speech that reaches the inner core of a person's being. 'Comfortably' is a weakened translation.
word_study.significance: The phrase assumes Jerusalem is broken, grieved, and hardened. The prophets are not to speak doctrine or argument; they are to speak directly to the wounded heart. This is the language of healing speech.

word_study.meaning: Warfare, military service, or more broadly, any kind of service or hard labor. In covenantal contexts, it refers to the spiritual struggle of exile and judgment.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering renders this 'warfare' to capture both the military and covenantal dimensions of Israel's suffering. She has been in spiritual and physical combat against the consequences of covenant-breaking. That warfare—that service—is now accomplished.

word_study.meaning: Forgiven, accepted, atoned for. Related to ratzon (will, favor). When iniquity is nirtzah, it is brought into alignment with God's will and accepted by Him.
word_study.significance: This is not mere cancellation; it is restoration to divine favor. The iniquity is not erased from history; it is accepted and absorbed by God's covenant mercy.

word_study.meaning: Double; twofold. In financial contexts, it indicates full payment without remainder (cf. Exodus 22:4). Not 'excessive' but 'complete.'
word_study.significance: A misreading of this word has led to the idea that God punished Israel excessively. The Hebrew meaning is the opposite: the debt is paid in full. Justice is satisfied completely, and grace can now flow.

cross_references.connection: Uses kiflayim ('double') in the context of restitution—when a debt is paid kiflayim, it is paid in full and completely satisfies the obligation.
God's covenant curses are structured in escalating stages; Isaiah 40:2 announces that Israel has now passed through the final stage and restoration begins.
Jeremiah prophesies the end of exile and the new covenant; Isaiah 40:2 announces its fulfillment: the debt is paid, the covenant people are restored.
Peter applies Isaiah's language of sin-bearing and payment to Christ: 'Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree,' extending Isaiah's pattern to the atonement.
The Lord promises forgiveness when transgressions are forsaken: 'I, the Lord, forgive sins unto those who confess their sins before me'—the same covenant pattern as Isaiah 40:2.

commentary.historical_context: By the time of Cyrus's decree (538 BCE), allowing exiles to return, Babylon itself was becoming unstable. The Neo-Babylonian Empire was weakening before the Persian advance. Politically, exile was ending not because Babylon chose mercy but because the geopolitical order was shifting. But the prophet reframes this political reality theologically: it is not Cyrus who is freeing Israel; it is God who is fulfilling His covenant. The 'double payment' language reflects the legal frameworks of the ancient Near East. When a contract was fulfilled, payment was made 'double'—once to the creditor and once to seal the agreement. So Jerusalem's payment of exilic suffering was not punitive excess; it was the legal satisfaction of a broken covenant, after which relationship could be renewed.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 3:11-12 presents the same pattern: sin demands a price, but the Savior 'taketh upon him their transgressions' and 'suffereth himself to be afflicted.' The payment is made in full by the Redeemer.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:34-35—'Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth his brother his trespasses... even so must ye forgive.' The principle of full, final forgiveness is tied to the Atonement's logic.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The restoration of Jerusalem in Isaiah 40:2 is incomplete without the rebuilding of the temple (Isaiah 44:26-28). The temple is where the payment has been symbolically made and where covenant renewal is enacted.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 40:2 prefigures the atonement. The 'double payment' language finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ, who takes upon Himself the full measure of humanity's covenant debt. His suffering in Gethsemane and on the cross is the 'double payment' that satisfies divine justice completely, so that grace and restoration can flow to all who covenant with Him. The idea that payment must be made in full before restoration can begin is central to Latter-day Saint understanding of the atonement.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, Isaiah 40:2 offers profound reassurance in seasons of spiritual reckoning. When you have repented and made restitution for sin, this verse testifies that your iniquity is not held over you eternally. God does not keep a record of past transgression once you have entered into a covenant of repentance and endurance. The 'double payment' has been made—either through your own suffering and growth or through Christ's atonement. The path forward is not perpetual guilt; it is restoration to covenant standing.

text_kjv: The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 40:3 is one of the most densely prophetic verses in all of Scripture. All four Gospel writers—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—identified this verse as the mission of John the Baptist. But understanding the verse requires wrestling with a text-critical question: where does the 'voice' belong? The Masoretic Text (MT) accentuation connects 'in the wilderness' with 'prepare'—'A voice cries: In the wilderness prepare the way.' The Septuagint and all four Gospels read it differently: 'A voice cries in the wilderness'—making the wilderness the location of the crying voice, not the location of the preparation. The Dead Sea Scrolls' paragraph spacing suggests the Gospel reading was available in the pre-Christian period. Both readings are legitimate Hebrew, and both are theologically rich.

Under either reading, the meaning is clear: someone will come before the Lord, preparing the way. The imagery is of ancient road-building for a royal procession—servants go ahead and level the terrain, fill the valleys, lower the mountains, straighten the crooked paths. All barriers to the king's passage are removed. In the context of Isaiah 40, this is simultaneously literal (the return from exile requires a literal journey through the desert) and spiritual (obstacles to encountering God must be removed). The 'voice' is not the Messiah; it is the forerunner. In Jewish tradition, such a figure was expected to prepare for the Messiah's arrival. When John the Baptist emerged in the wilderness, baptizing and calling Israel to repentance, all four Gospel writers recognized in him the fulfillment of Isaiah 40:3.

word_study.meaning: Voice, sound, cry. In prophetic contexts, it can refer to a divine proclamation or the call of a prophet. The voice carries authority.
word_study.significance: Qol is not just sound; it is a vehicle of meaning and power. When Isaiah hears the qol, it is not background noise—it is a prophetic utterance demanding response.

word_study.meaning: One who calls or cries out; an active voice demanding attention and obedience. Related to qara (to call, to proclaim).
word_study.significance: The qore' is not passive or introspective; he is actively summoning Israel to action. This is a prophetic call in its most urgent form.

word_study.meaning: Wilderness, desert; in biblical thought, often a place of testing, preparation, and encounter with God. Israel spent 40 years in the midbar; prophets encountered God there.
word_study.significance: The wilderness is not merely geography; it is a spiritual space. John's ministry in the wilderness echoes Israel's own wilderness wanderings and recalls how God met His people in the desert.

word_study.meaning: Way, path, journey. Also can mean 'manner' or 'conduct.' In covenantal theology, one's derekh is one's pattern of obedience or disobedience.
word_study.significance: Preparing the 'way of the LORD' means both clearing a literal path and preparing a people whose 'way' (conduct and covenant obedience) is aligned with God's purposes.

word_study.meaning: Highway, elevated path, causeway. An engineered road elevated above surrounding terrain, built for rapid travel. Used for royal routes and military campaigns.
word_study.significance: The mesillah is not a natural path; it is constructed by human labor for a specific purpose. Preparing God's way requires intentional work—repentance, baptism, covenant commitment.

cross_references.connection: All four Gospel accounts explicitly identify John the Baptist's wilderness ministry as the fulfillment of Isaiah 40:3, making this verse the scriptural anchor for understanding John's role as forerunner.
Malachi also prophesies a messenger who will prepare the way before the Lord, tying Isaiah 40:3 to broader messianic expectation in the final book of the Old Testament.
God led Israel through the wilderness with a pillar of cloud and fire; Isaiah 40:3 echoes this by calling for preparation of a way through the wilderness, suggesting a new exodus.
The Lord identifies Sidney Rigdon as one who will prepare the way, using Isaiah 40:3's language to describe the role of forerunners in the latter-day restoration.
Nephite prophets apply Isaiah 40:3 to the signs preceding Christ's birth in America, showing the verse's enduring application to Christ's various comings.

commentary.historical_context: The historical return from Babylonian exile (538 BCE) was not a casual journey. The journey from Babylon to Judea was roughly 500 miles through desert and hostile territory. Ancient Near Eastern practice involved sending advance parties to prepare routes, establish way stations, and ensure safe passage for the king or dignitary traveling behind them. Isaiah's language of leveling valleys and lowering mountains reflects both this literal requirement and the metaphorical idea that obstacles to restoration must be removed. The 'voice crying in the wilderness' became the archetypal prophetic image in Jewish tradition—a solitary figure in the desert calling Israel to repentance and preparation. When John the Baptist emerged in the same wilderness (Judea's eastern desert), at the Jordan River, baptizing and preaching repentance, every educated Jew would have recognized Isaiah 40:3 echoing in his work.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 10:8-10 applies Isaiah 40:3 to John the Baptist's role in preparing for Christ's ministry in the New World setting. The phrase 'the way of the Lord' is central to Book of Mormon theology—the straight and narrow path.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:67 and surrounding context describe the preparation of the way for the Second Coming using similar imagery of leveling and straightening—showing how Isaiah's pattern applies to all of Christ's coming, not just his first advent.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the ultimate 'way of the LORD.' Isaiah 40:3 calls for preparation of a way that leads to encounter with God; in Latter-day Saint theology, temples are the sacred space where such encounter occurs. The work of forerunners (prophets, forerunners like John) is to prepare people spiritually to enter these sacred spaces.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 40:3 prophesies a forerunner figure, and John the Baptist is his fulfillment. But the verse's ultimate significance is Christological because it prepares the way not for an intermediary but for the Lord Himself. The 'way of the LORD' is a path that leads to encounter with God in person. In Christian theology, Jesus is both the way (John 14:6—'I am the way') and the destination. The verse simultaneously announces John the Baptist's role and Jesus's identity as the destination of all preparation and forerunning.
commentary.application: Isaiah 40:3 invites modern Latter-day Saints to reflect on the role of forerunners in spiritual preparation. John the Baptist's ministry was not about him; it was about preparing Israel for encounter with Christ. Similarly, modern prophets and the restored gospel are forerunners preparing the world for Christ's second coming. On a personal level, the verse challenges us: Are we removing obstacles in our own hearts that prevent us from 'seeing' God? Repentance, covenant, and endurance are the work of leveling the way—preparing ourselves spiritually to encounter the Lord.

text_kjv: Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain:

commentary.narrative:
Verse 4 is the expansion and application of verse 3. The abstract command to 'prepare the way' becomes concrete: every topographical obstacle is removed. Valleys are lifted up (exalted); mountains and hills are brought down (made low); crooked paths become straight; rough, broken ground becomes smooth. The imagery is vivid because it reflects actual ancient road-building practices. When a royal procession was expected, servants would level terrain, fill ravines, and remove rocks to create a passable highway. But the language also carries spiritual weight: in the leveling of terrain, we see the leveling of inequalities, the removal of barriers, the creation of a path that the humblest person can walk.

The Hebrew verbs are worth noting. 'Exalted' (yissabe') is often used of spiritual elevation. 'Made low' (yishlalu) has a tone of humbling. The pairing suggests a reversal of status—what is lowly is lifted up, what is proud is brought down. This echoes the Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55), where Mary sings that God 'hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.' The way of the Lord is a way where the proud are humbled and the humble are exalted. In the context of exile and return, this means that Babylon's power (the 'mountain' of empire) is brought low, and Israel's humiliation (the 'valley' of exile) is lifted up. But it also means that in the spiritual preparation for encounter with God, all human pride and pretension must be stripped away.

word_study.meaning: To be lifted up, exalted, raised in status. Related to nasa (to bear, to lift, to forgive). Can refer to both physical elevation and spiritual status.
word_study.significance: The same root is used in Isaiah 53:12 ('he shall be exalted') and in covenantal language of being lifted from shame. Every valley being exalted means every lowly place and every lowly person is restored to dignity.

word_study.meaning: To be made low, brought down, humbled. Related to shaphal (low, beneath). The opposite of exaltation.
word_study.significance: Mountains and hills (symbols of power, kingdoms, pride) are brought down. In biblical geography, mountains often represent nations or powers (cf. Zechariah 4:7, where the 'mountain' of opposition to the temple is leveled).

word_study.meaning: Crooked, twisted, deceitful. Related to Jacob (Ya'aqov), though that name's etymology is debated. The word suggests both literal crookedness and moral or spiritual deviousness.
word_study.significance: Making the crooked straight is not merely engineering; it is moral and spiritual realignment. Crookedness suggests deception; straightness suggests truth and integrity.

word_study.meaning: Rough places, uneven ground, rocky terrain. The word emphasizes the harshness and difficulty of the landscape.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering renders this 'rough places' to emphasize not just unevenness but the difficulty and pain of the journey. Making rough places plain means removing obstacles and suffering from the path.

cross_references.connection: Mary's Magnificat echoes Isaiah 40:4's pattern: 'He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree,' showing how Isaiah's reversal becomes the pattern of Christ's coming.
Luke's Gospel explicitly quotes Isaiah 40:3-4 (including verse 4's topographical language) as fulfilled in John the Baptist's ministry, adding verse 5 ('all flesh shall see the salvation of God').
The 'mountain' of opposition to the rebuilding of the temple is promised to become a plain—using Isaiah's language to describe spiritual obstacles removed by God's Spirit, not human might.
The Kirtland Temple dedication prayer and other Doctrine and Covenants passages invoke the language of removing obstacles and preparing ways for God's work in the latter days.
Abinadi prophesies that the Savior will 'come down from heaven,' and Alma interprets Isaiah 40:3-4's preparation language in terms of spiritual leveling before Christ's appearance.

commentary.historical_context: The topographical details in Isaiah 40:4 would have been viscerally real to both the exiled community and to anyone familiar with desert travel. The Judean desert is notoriously difficult—narrow wadis (valleys), sudden escarpments, large boulders, and rocky outcroppings make travel treacherous. The journey from Babylon through the desert to Judea was genuinely dangerous. The 'crooked' paths refer to the necessity of winding around geographical obstacles; the 'rough places' refer to the rocky terrain. Isaiah is not using merely abstract language; he is promising that the return journey will be transformed—made smooth, direct, safe. Ancient Near Eastern royal inscriptions frequently celebrate the construction of roads and the conquest of difficult terrain as signs of imperial power. Isaiah appropriates this language but redirects it: it is not the human king but the divine King whose power creates the way. The later rabbis would see in verse 4 a promise that God would work miracles to make the return journey possible, just as He had parted the Red Sea for the original exodus.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 8's vision of the tree of life features a 'strait and narrow path'—a way that is made clear and direct, with barriers removed (represented by the mist of darkness and the river). Isaiah 40:4's straightening and leveling is the preparation for accessing that path.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 84:100, 136:32—references to the 'straight course' and the preparation of ways reflect Isaiah 40:4's language, showing how nineteenth-century Latter-day Saints understood their own westward journey as a 'preparation of the way' in Isaianic terms.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temples stand at the end of prepared ways. Isaiah's topographical leveling is the spiritual and physical preparation that makes possible the building and operation of temples where God's presence dwells.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 4 describes the literal removal of obstacles for the king's passage, but in Christological terms, it describes the work of grace that removes the obstacles between humanity and God. Sin, pride, self-deception, and spiritual hardness are the mountains, valleys, and crooked places in the human heart. The atonement is the power that levels them. In this sense, John the Baptist's call to repentance (the removal of barriers) is inseparable from Christ's atoning work (the power that effects that removal).
commentary.application: For modern readers, Isaiah 40:4 speaks to the removal of obstacles between ourselves and the Lord. What 'mountains' of pride, unbelief, or self-reliance stand in your way? What 'valleys' of despair or shame need to be lifted? What 'crooked' paths of deception (self-deception or others' deceptions) need to be straightened? The verse promises that God can and will remove these obstacles for those who prepare themselves—through repentance, baptism, covenant, and endurance. The 'way of the LORD' is the straight path through the gospel of Jesus Christ.

text_kjv: And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together: for the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 5 is the culmination and goal of the preparation work described in verses 3-4. The way is being prepared not for its own sake but so that the glory of the LORD can be revealed and witnessed by all humanity. 'The glory of the LORD' (kevod YHWH) is a technical term in Hebrew Bible theology—it refers to the manifest, visible presence of God, the divine radiance and majesty that becomes perceptible to human senses. This is not abstract or metaphorical; it is God's presence becoming tangible, visible, accessible. In Exodus, God's glory filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34); in 1 Kings, it filled the temple (1 Kings 8:11). Isaiah himself encountered the glory in the temple vision of chapter 6 ('I saw the LORD sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up... and the whole earth is full of his glory'—Isaiah 6:1, 3). Now Isaiah 40:5 promises a revelation of that glory on a cosmic scale: 'all flesh shall see it together.'

The phrase 'all flesh' (kol-basar) is crucial. It does not mean only Israel or the righteous; it means all humanity. This is a promise of universal revelation—a time when all people, everywhere, will perceive God's presence and power simultaneously. The statement is so sweeping that it can only refer to either a future messianic age or Christ's return in glory. Luke's Gospel (3:4-6) emphasizes this universality by quoting Isaiah 40:5 in full, including 'all flesh shall see the salvation of God.' The final clause—'for the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it'—is a prophetic authentication formula. This is not human speculation; it is God's own word, and therefore it will certainly come to pass.

word_study.meaning: Glory, radiance, majesty, presence, weight (literally and figuratively). In theological contexts, kevod YHWH refers to the manifest presence of God made visible and perceptible. The root may relate to 'heavy' or 'weighty,' suggesting substance and authority.
word_study.significance: Kevod is not merely reputation or honor (though it includes these); it is the actual, visible manifestation of God's presence and power. When God's kevod appears, reality shifts. Barriers between heaven and earth become permeable.

word_study.meaning: To be revealed, uncovered, made manifest. Literally, to remove a covering so that what is hidden becomes visible. Also used for divine self-disclosure.
word_study.significance: The glory of the LORD is not created at that moment; it is revealed—it was always there, but a veil is removed. In covenantal terms, God's glory is always present to those who seek it; the revelation is the removal of scales from human eyes.

word_study.meaning: All flesh, all humanity, all mortal beings. 'Flesh' (basar) emphasizes the physical, embodied nature of humans—not just their spirits, but their whole selves.
word_study.significance: The universalism here is striking. Not 'all Israel,' not 'all the righteous,' but 'all flesh'—every human being, in their physical bodies. This universalizes the promise of salvation and revelation.

word_study.meaning: Together, at the same time, in unison. The word emphasizes simultaneity and unity.
word_study.significance: The revelation will not be private or gradual but public and instantaneous. All humanity will perceive the glory at once, eliminating the excuse of ignorance. In Luke 3:6, 'all flesh shall see the salvation of God' echoes this promise of simultaneous, universal revelation.

word_study.meaning: The mouth of the LORD; a metonymy for God's word or command. What proceeds from God's mouth has creative and binding power.
word_study.significance: This is a prophetic authentication formula. It links the spoken word to divine authority and power. What God says will come to pass because His word is backed by His power.

cross_references.connection: Luke's Gospel quotes Isaiah 40:3-5 in full to show that John the Baptist's ministry was the beginning of a larger pattern: the preparation of the way culminates in the universal revelation of God's salvation.
Isaiah's temple vision declares that 'the whole earth is full of his glory'—a promise that the glory which filled the temple will ultimately fill all the earth, as Isaiah 40:5 promises.

The Lord tells the members of the Church, 'I have set before you life and death... and all things are before me, and all things are mine' — emphasizing that God's glory and knowledge encompass all things.
John's Revelation promises that Christ will come 'with clouds; and every eye shall see him,' fulfilling Isaiah 40:5's promise of universal, simultaneous revelation.
Habakkuk prophecies that 'the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea'—a parallel promise to Isaiah 40:5 of universal revelation.

commentary.historical_context: In the context of the Babylonian exile, Isaiah 40:5 would have sounded almost impossibly grand. Israel sits in captivity in Babylon; Babylon's gods seem ascendant; God's temple lies in ruins. Yet the prophet promises that God's glory will be revealed to all flesh. This is an act of prophetic faith—not based on current circumstances but on covenant promises and the nature of God. In the ancient Near East, the glory (or radiance) of a god was believed to manifest in the god's temple and through the god's chosen king. Isaiah expands this: the glory will not be confined to temple or king but will be universally revealed. This was a scandal to Babylonian religious thought, which believed that gods were bound to particular temples and peoples. Isaiah's universalism is radical.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 3 Nephi 8:11-25 describes the glory of the resurrected Christ appearing to the Nephites—a partial fulfillment of Isaiah 40:5's promise, foreshadowing the universal revelation at Christ's second coming.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:12, 88:88, 110:4—Doctrine and Covenants passages describe the revelation of God's glory in visions and at key moments in Church history, showing how Isaiah 40:5's promise is being fulfilled progressively.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where God's glory is revealed to covenant people. Isaiah 40:5's ultimate promise is that what is now confined to temples will eventually fill all the earth—no more 'veil' separating God from humanity.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 5 looks forward to the revelation of Christ's glory. In John 1:14, 'the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.' Christ's incarnation is a revelation of the divine glory in human form. But more completely, Christ's return in glory (Revelation 1:7; Matthew 24:30) is the fulfillment of Isaiah 40:5—when all flesh shall see His glory simultaneously. The cross and resurrection are the lens through which the glory is revealed and the basis upon which universal salvation becomes possible.
commentary.application: Isaiah 40:5 calls modern Latter-day Saints to anticipate and prepare for the revelation of God's glory. This is not idle speculation but covenant preparation. The phrase 'all flesh shall see it together' reminds us that at Christ's coming, ignorance will be impossible—every person will know the truth. This should motivate us to seek personal revelation now, to develop the eyes and ears to perceive God's glory in the scriptures, in the temple, and in personal revelation. The promise also humbles us: God's glory cannot be confined or controlled by human institutions or preferences. It will be revealed on God's timeline and in God's way.

text_kjv: The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field:

commentary.narrative:
Verse 6 shifts the perspective dramatically. After five verses of expansion and promise (preparation of the way, revelation of glory, universal salvation), the prophet is abruptly confronted with a command: 'Cry!' The prophet responds with bewilderment: 'What shall I cry?' What message could possibly match the grandeur of verse 5? And the answer is stark and humbling: the very opposite of expansion and exaltation. The answer is about human transience and frailty. 'All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field.' In a single verse, we move from the eternal glory of God to the radical impermanence of human life. This is not pessimism; it is the necessary counterpoint to the promise of God's glory. The glory can be truly glorious only against the backdrop of human frailty. The salvation announced in verses 1-5 is necessary precisely because human strength and righteousness are as temporary as grass.

The textual variant here is significant. The Dead Sea Scrolls read 've'amar' ('and he said'—third person) where the Masoretic Text reads 'va'omar' ('and I said'—first person). If the DSS reading is original, then an unidentified voice gives the response, making it more obviously a divine voice speaking through the prophet. If the MT reading is original, then the prophet himself is speaking, his bewilderment and the answer both proceeding from his own realization. Either way, the message is clear: human achievements, beauty, strength, and righteousness are ephemeral. This is the message the prophet must cry—not to depress, but to redirect hope away from human strength toward God's eternal power and mercy.

word_study.meaning: To cry out, call, proclaim. In prophetic contexts, it means to make a proclamation with urgency and authority.
word_study.significance: The command to 'cry' is a commission. The prophet is not to whisper or suggest but to proclaim loudly and clearly. What he is commissioned to cry is immediately the question: What message is urgent enough to warrant this emphasis?

word_study.meaning: Grass, hay, herbage. In Hebrew poetry, grass is the standard metaphor for human frailty and the brevity of life. Grass grows quickly but withers even more quickly, especially in the arid climate of the Levant.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that the metaphor is vivid because the grass of the Judean hills literally withers quickly in the hot, dry summers. Isaiah is using imagery that his audience would have seen daily—the contrast between the lush green of spring and the brown, dead stalks of summer.

word_study.meaning: Beauty, comeliness, grace, or (in other contexts) steadfast love. The word is polysemous, but in this context clearly refers to aesthetic beauty or outward charm.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that chassed here means 'beauty' or 'comeliness' rather than the more common meaning 'steadfast love.' Human beauty and charm—what we take pride in—are as temporary as grass. Even our best qualities fade.

word_study.meaning: The flower of the field, wild flowers, blooms. The word tzitz suggests bright, striking appearance—flowers are beautiful and visible, yet temporary.
word_study.significance: If grass is the general metaphor for transience, the flower is the particular emphasis on how quickly beauty passes. A flower is beautiful in its moment but fades within days. All human splendor follows this pattern.

cross_references.connection: This psalm directly echoes Isaiah 40:6: 'As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth. For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone.' Showing this metaphor is central to biblical anthropology.

Peter quotes Isaiah 40:6-8 directly: 'All flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of the grass... But the word of the Lord endureth for ever,' contrasting human transience with God's eternal word.
James applies the grass metaphor to the rich: 'as the flower of the grass he shall pass away,' showing how human wealth and status are as temporary as grass in the face of eternity.
The wise understand that riches and beauty do not last; therefore they prepare for eternity—a theme that undergirds Isaiah 40:6's realism about human nature.
The Lord's description of the condition of the world before His return echoes the grass metaphor—all human works and pride shall be brought low, but God's word remains.

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah's 'cry' about human transience would have resonated powerfully with the exilic community. They had watched their city fall, their temple destroyed, their leaders carried away into captivity. Everything they trusted in—human strength, national power, architectural achievement—had proven temporary. Even the greatest empires (Babylon's, for example) were ultimately fleeting. Yet this is not a counsel of despair but of reorientation: if human strength and glory are temporary, then hope cannot rest on these things. Hope must rest on the eternal God and His covenant word. The metaphor of grass was already proverbial in ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature, but Isaiah gives it new prophetic weight. The Mesopotamian exiles would have known that the great temples and palaces of Babylon would eventually crumble, just as Jerusalem's had. But God's word, revealed through the prophet, abides forever.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 13:16 (Nephi's quotation of Isaiah 3:16) applies similar language to human vanity: 'Because the daughters of Zion are haughty.' The recognition of human frailty is the precondition for genuine repentance and covenant obedience.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:33-34, 48:26-27—The Lord promises that when He comes in glory, human pride and pretension shall be brought low, but 'the righteous shall sit down upon my throne, and shall partake of the glory of my kingdom.' The contrast mirrors Isaiah: human grass withers, but God's kingdom endures.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches the transience of mortal life (hence the emphasis on death and resurrection in temple ordinances) and the eternal nature of God's covenant. Isaiah 40:6 is the prophetic grounding for this temple doctrine: we are grass, but God's covenant is eternal.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 40:6 sets up the theological framework for the Servant passages (Isaiah 42, 49, 50, 52-53) that follow later in this section. The Servant, too, will be described as 'despised and rejected,' as one with 'no form nor comeliness' (Isaiah 53:2)—taking on the very frailty that verse 6 describes. But the Servant's voluntary embrace of human transience becomes the means of eternal salvation for all who believe. Christ's incarnation means God Himself enters into the very grass-ness of human existence, but through His resurrection, grass becomes eternal.
commentary.application: Isaiah 40:6 invites modern Latter-day Saints to an honest reckoning with human frailty. In a culture that emphasizes self-improvement, human achievement, and personal strength, this verse speaks truth: all our earthly glory is temporary. This is not meant to paralyze but to liberate. When we truly understand that we are 'grass'—that our beauty, strength, and accomplishments are temporary—we become free to seek what is eternal. This verse calls us to release our grip on the things of this world and to lay hold on the covenant promises of God, which alone endure forever. It is the necessary humility that precedes the exaltation described in verses 1-5.

text_kjv: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah shifts from the theme of comfort (verse 1-6) to the fundamental human condition that makes comfort necessary. The verse paints a vivid image of the Judean desert: grass that springs green after rain withers rapidly when the hot sirocco wind blows across the land. The prophet uses this natural phenomenon as a metaphor for human fragility and mortality. The word translated 'spirit' here is ruach, which in this context means 'breath' or 'wind'—the hot, desiccating desert wind that kills vegetation overnight. This is not the Holy Spirit but the meteorological reality of the ancient Near East. The verse establishes a parallel: just as grass cannot withstand the Lord's breath, neither can human beings resist His will or escape the brevity of mortal life.

The genius of Isaiah's metaphor lies in its universality. In ancient Judah, every person understood this image intimately. They had watched vegetation flourish and die with the seasons. They knew that all human achievement, beauty, and strength were equally fragile. The prophet is not being pessimistic; rather, he is establishing the necessary foundation for the promise that follows in verse 8—that while humans and their works fade like grass, the word of God stands forever. This contrast between human mortality and divine permanence runs throughout Isaiah 40 and becomes the basis for trusting in God's redemptive promises to exile Israel.

word_study.meaning: Grass, pasture, or vegetation. The root suggests something that is easily trampled or destroyed. In Hebrew poetry, it frequently represents the fragile, temporary nature of human life.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes this term carries the weight of transience. Unlike 'plant' or 'herb,' chatsir emphasizes vulnerability—grass is useful but disposable. This word choice primes the reader for the sharp contrast with God's enduring word in verse 8.

word_study.meaning: To dry up, wither, or become barren. The root conveys complete desiccation, not merely fading color but the loss of all vitality and substance.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests an irreversible process. Once grass yavesh, it cannot be revived. This underscores the finality of human mortality and the irreversibility of God's judgments.

word_study.meaning: To wither, fade, or droop. Often used of flowers losing their beauty and form. The root emphasizes aesthetic loss—the visible beauty disappears.
word_study.significance: Where yavesh emphasizes complete drying, navel emphasizes the loss of beauty and glory. Together, these verbs create a complete picture of deterioration: first the loss of beauty (navel), then total desiccation (yavesh).

word_study.meaning: Wind, breath, or spirit. The semantic range is broad: it can mean the Holy Spirit of God, human breath, wind, or the hot desert wind (sirocco). Context determines meaning.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering correctly identifies this as 'breath' (meteorological wind) rather than 'Spirit.' This is crucial: Isaiah is describing a natural phenomenon, not divine judgment. Yet the juxtaposition—'the breath of the LORD blows upon it'—suggests that even nature's destructive forces operate under God's sovereignty. The sirocco becomes a symbol of divine power to dissolve all that seems solid.

word_study.meaning: People, nation, or kinship group. In Isaiah, often refers specifically to the covenant people of Israel.
word_study.significance: The final clause 'surely the people is grass' applies the vegetation metaphor to humanity at large, and especially to Israel. No amount of political power, military strength, or national pride exempts them from the condition of grass. This humbling truth prepares exiled Israel to receive grace rather than rely on their own strength.

cross_references.connection: Peter quotes Isaiah 40:6-8 directly, applying it to the transience of human flesh and the permanence of God's word—the same contrast Isaiah draws here.
The psalmist uses identical imagery: 'As for man, his days are as grass... the wind passeth over it, and it is gone.' Both passages express the same theological truth about human fragility.
Job describes human life as 'fleeting and full of trouble,' comparing it to grass that withers. The same metaphor conveys the brevity of mortal existence.
In the Book of Mormon's version of Isaiah 3:1, the same vocabulary of judgment and frailty appears, showing how the Nephites understood human weakness before God.
The Lord describes how all things pass away unless they are quickened by His Spirit, echoing Isaiah's contrast between mortal decay and divine permanence.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Levant, the sirocco (khamsin in Arabic) was a well-known meteorological phenomenon—a hot, dry wind that could destroy crops in a matter of hours. Vegetation that flourished after winter or spring rains could be completely desiccated by a single day's exposure to this wind. For an exiled Judahite audience in Babylon, the sirocco would have been a memory of home, a symbol of both nature's power and human vulnerability. The image would have resonated with their experience of exile itself: they were like grass torn from their soil, transplanted to foreign ground, vulnerable to forces beyond their control. The Babylonian audience may also have been familiar with similar desert wind phenomena (the Sharav), making this a universally intelligible metaphor for transience. Archaeological evidence and ancient texts confirm that grain and vegetable crops in the Levantine region were subject to rapid destruction by heat and wind, making this a realistic rather than merely poetic comparison.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon employs similar language about human frailty and divine permanence. In Alma 32:21, Alma teaches about faith in things not seen but yet believed—a doctrine rooted in the recognition that temporal things fade but eternal truths remain firm. The constant Book of Mormon theme that all earthly kingdoms must fall (see Helaman 6:37) echoes Isaiah's insistence that human power is grass.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:24-25 contains a paraphrase of this very concept: 'All things are created by me, and all things are sustained by the power of my word... And again, verily I say unto you, all things are created of me, and all things are sustained of me; wherefore, all things must needs be done in mine own way.' The restoration clarifies that divine permanence operates through God's word—a concept that Isaiah 40:8 fully develops.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment drama teaches members that all earthly powers and principalities—represented by the fallen world—pass away, while those who accept the covenants enter into God's eternal order. Isaiah 40:7 establishes the theological premise that makes covenantal eternity precious: without the knowledge that all flesh fades like grass, the promise of eternal life in God's presence loses its meaning.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 7 foreshadows Christ's mortality. Though Jesus was divine, He entered human flesh and experienced human limitation. He too would face the 'breath' of judgment—not the natural wind but the weight of human sin. Yet unlike the grass, which merely withers, Jesus' death leads to resurrection and eternal life. The verse thus prepares for the Messianic promise that follows: it shows why the Messiah must come—not to strengthen human grass but to transcend it through divine power.
commentary.application: Modern Latter-day Saints are surrounded by cultural messages that equate human value with physical beauty, youth, wealth, and power. Isaiah 40:7 cuts through this with a single image: grass. The verse invites us to release attachment to temporal measures of worth and status. If we are grass—beautiful, useful, but ultimately temporary—then our true identity must lie elsewhere: in our divine heritage, in our covenants with God, in our role in His eternal work. This should free us from the exhausting project of self-aggrandizement. It should also cultivate compassion: if we are all grass, then we understand our common vulnerability and recognize that our neighbors face the same forces of decay and loss that we do. The verse suggests that true strength comes not from resisting our mortality but from aligning ourselves with what endures—God's word and His purposes.

text_kjv: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.

commentary.narrative: The prophet now completes the contrast he began in verse 7. The repetition of the first clause—'the grass withereth, the flower fadeth'—drives home the universal nature of transience. Nothing human or natural escapes the cycle of growth and decay. But then comes the conjunction that transforms everything: 'but.' This single word, in Hebrew 'vav' (and) followed by the negation of impermanence, shifts from description to affirmation. God's word will stand forever—yaqum le'olam. The phrase suggests not mere existence but an active standing, a rising up, an establishment that will never be shaken. For an exiled Israel, this is not abstract theology; it is living promise. While their temple lies in ruins and they themselves are rootless in a foreign land, God's word—His covenants, His purposes, His prophecies—remains unmoved. The verse is quoted in 1 Peter 1:25 and appears in the Book of Mormon (1 Nephi 19:24), indicating its centrality to New Testament and Restoration understanding of divine constancy.

word_study.meaning: Word, matter, thing, or event. In Hebrew thought, a word is not merely sound but an agent of reality—words accomplish what they declare. God's davar is creative and effective.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that 'davar Elohenu' (the word of our God) is set in deliberate contrast to the withering chatsir. In Isaiah 55:10-11, davar appears again with the same emphasis on its efficacy: God's word does not return empty but accomplishes His purposes. For exiled Israel, God's davar—His covenant promise, His redemptive plan—is the only certainty.

word_study.meaning: To stand, rise up, or be established. The root suggests both physical uprightness and stable establishment. In legal or covenantal contexts, it means to endure as valid or binding.
word_study.significance: This verb is dynamic, not merely passive. God's word does not merely exist—it stands firm, rises up, proves itself valid. The Covenant Rendering's 'will stand forever' captures the sense of permanent, unshakeable establishment. Yaqum appears again in verse 10 when the Lord 'comes,' and the same root indicates His active arrival and power.

word_study.meaning: Forever, eternity, or the age to come. Can mean perpetual duration or the future age of restoration.
word_study.significance: This term appears frequently in Isaiah 40-66 (the Book of Consolation), emphasizing eternal restoration. For the exiles, le'olam was not merely philosophical—it was the promise of return, restoration, and God's unending fidelity. The phrase 'yaqum le'olam' (will stand forever) thus encompasses both timespan and quality: God's word is permanent and eternal.

cross_references.connection: Peter quotes Isaiah 40:6-8 exactly, applying it to the transience of mortal flesh and the permanence of the gospel word that endures forever—the same contrast Isaiah draws here and the same theological point about God's word sustaining faith.
Nephi quotes Isaiah 40:8 in the Book of Mormon, testifying that God's word endures. This verse becomes a lens through which Nephi interprets the permanence of God's covenant with the house of Israel.

Isaiah returns to this theme: God's word is like rain that accomplishes its purpose and does not return empty. The same davar (word) that stands forever in 40:8 is here shown to be actively creative and effective.

The Lord declares that His word is sure and His purposes will be accomplished: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the prophecies and promises which are in them shall all be fulfilled... Whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.'
The psalmist affirms that God's word is settled in heaven forever—the same eternal permanence Isaiah 40:8 promises. Both passages contrast God's constancy with human transience.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient world, empires rose and fell. Babylon, which held Israel captive, seemed permanent and invincible. Kings built monuments to their glory and inscribed their deeds on stone, yet within centuries those empires crumbled. For an exiled Israelite, the promise that God's word alone endures forever would have been countercultural. Babylon's word—its decrees, its propaganda, its power—seemed absolute. But Isaiah announces that behind and beyond all earthly powers stands God's davar, His word, which will outlast all human kingdoms. The historical setting of the exile (586 BCE onwards) makes this verse not merely comforting but radical. It asserts that Israel's God is more real, more powerful, and more enduring than the Babylonian pantheon and the Babylonian state. The Dead Sea Scroll 1QIsaᵃ preserves this verse without significant variant, indicating that this affirmation was stable and central in the Jewish tradition from at least the 2nd century BCE.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Throughout the Book of Mormon, this principle recurs: God's word, covenant, and purposes stand forever while earthly kingdoms fall. Helaman 12:2 teaches that 'all these things are done in the sight of the Lord; and this people observed to do his commandments.' The implicit contrast is that God's commandments and covenants, not human power, determine the course of history. Moroni 10:34 caps the Book of Mormon with the promise that God's word shall endure forever.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:37-38 and D&C 21:4-6 declare the constancy of God's word and the permanence of His revelations. Joseph Smith's revelation that the Lord's word will 'all be fulfilled' directly parallels Isaiah's assertion that God's davar stands forever. This becomes the foundation for the Restoration's authority: Joseph Smith taught that the word of the Lord, once given, cannot fail.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony teaches that God's covenants and purposes are eternal. In contrast to the temporary, external ordinances of the law of Moses, the higher covenants of the temple are described as 'everlasting.' Isaiah 40:8 provides scriptural foundation for this principle: if God's word stands forever, then the covenants made in His name—especially in the temple—are eternal and unbreakable.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is 'the Word made flesh' (John 1:1, 14). Isaiah 40:8 thus prefigures the incarnation: God's eternal davar takes human form in Jesus. Moreover, the permanence of God's word is ultimately fulfilled in Christ's resurrection. While all other things—including His mortal body—would be subject to death, His word (His teaching, His covenant, His promise of redemption) stands forever because it is rooted in His divine nature. The verse also points to the new covenant established by Christ's atonement: this word 'will stand for ever,' never to be revoked or superseded.
commentary.application: In a world of constant change and uncertainty, Isaiah 40:8 offers a steady anchor. For Latter-day Saints, this verse affirms the reliability of God's word as mediated through living prophets and restored scripture. While human institutions—including church organizations, political systems, and even popular interpretations of faith—may shift and evolve, the fundamental davar of God remains unmoved. This should strengthen our commitment to scripture study and to listening to the voice of the Lord through His servants. It should also humble us: we are grass, but we are held within God's eternal purposes. Our personal struggles, failures, and disappointments, while real and deserving of compassion, are not the final word on our lives. God's word about us—that we are His children, that we can repent and be redeemed, that we can return to Him—stands forever. This should free us to release perfectionism and embrace the long view of covenant belonging.

text_kjv: O Zion, that bringest good tidings, get thee up into the high mountain; O Jerusalem, that bringest good tidings, lift up thy voice with strength; lift it up, be not afraid; say unto the cities of Judah, Behold your God!

commentary.narrative: Isaiah's focus shifts from theological principle to concrete address. The prophet now speaks directly to Zion and Jerusalem—personified as feminine figures, heralds of good news. The command is urgent and physical: ascend the high mountain, lift up your voice, do not be afraid. The verb mevasseret (herald of good news) is a feminine participle suggesting that Zion herself is the messenger, not merely the recipient of good news. This is theologically significant: after exile, Zion will not be a passive victim awaiting rescue but an active herald announcing God's restoration. The command to ascend a high mountain places this proclamation in public view—a herald does not whisper but cries aloud from an elevated place where all can hear. The repetition of 'lift up thy voice with strength' emphasizes urgency and confidence. Zion is not to make a timid announcement but to proclaim with full authority and power. The closing command, 'say unto the cities of Judah, Behold your God!' is the heart of the verse: after decades of exile, the exiles are being called to announce that their God has not abandoned them, that He is returning, that He will reign. The feminine voice of Zion—often in Hebrew poetry representing the city or nation itself—becomes the instrument through which God's redemptive purpose is proclaimed.

word_study.meaning: One who brings good news or announces good tidings. Feminine participle of the root b-s-r. In later usage, this root becomes the basis of the Greek euangelion (gospel).
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that the grammar makes Zion herself the herald: she is the one who brings good news, not one to whom it is brought. This is a crucial reversal: Zion, who has been silent and grieving in exile (cf. Isaiah 51:17-23), now becomes the proclaimer. Her very restoration is itself the good news. The connection to 'gospel' (from Greek euangelion, which derives from this Hebrew root) is profound: the root b-s-r contains the seed of the New Testament concept of the gospel. Zion becomes, in effect, a gospel messenger.

word_study.meaning: Go up, ascend. An imperative commanding movement upward or forward.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests not just movement but elevation and advancement. Zion is called to rise, literally to climb to a high place, symbolically to assume dignity and authority. After exile's humiliation, Zion is commanded to ascend.

word_study.meaning: A high, elevated mountain. In biblical imagery, mountains are places of revelation, covenant, and divine presence.
word_study.significance: Zion is commanded to take her stand on a high mountain—a symbol of unshakeable foundation and proximity to God. Mountains in Hebrew scripture are places where God reveals Himself (Sinai, Zion itself) and where His word is proclaimed authoritatively.

word_study.meaning: To lift up, raise, or exalt. An imperative form emphasizing elevation.
word_study.significance: Repeated twice in this verse ('lift up thy voice' and the imperative 'lift it up'), the verb creates urgency and emphasis. Zion is not to be modest or hesitant. She is to raise her voice—and by extension, to raise herself—with full authority.

word_study.meaning: Voice, sound, or cry. In biblical rhetoric, a raised voice signals authority, urgency, and power.
word_study.significance: The command to lift up one's qol (voice) with strength is the command to speak truth with authority. In a patriarchal ancient world, women were often required to be silent; here a feminine figure—Zion—is commanded to raise her voice loudly.

word_study.meaning: Strength, power, or ability. The root suggests capacity and capability.
word_study.significance: Zion is not to speak timidly or apologetically. She is to proclaim with koach—with all the strength and power at her disposal. This is not a whispered rumor but a bold proclamation.

word_study.meaning: Behold, see, or look. A demonstrative interjection calling attention to what follows.
word_study.significance: The word 'Behold' summons attention and focus. It is often used in prophetic contexts to announce the arrival or presence of something momentous. Here, Zion is to proclaim 'Behold your God!'—a dramatic announcement that God is present, returning, and ruling.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah returns to the image of the herald proclaiming good news on the mountains: 'How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings.' This verse completes the vision begun in 40:9, showing the herald's journey and the beauty of the proclamation.

Paul quotes Isaiah 52:7 and applies it to the preaching of the gospel, rooting Christian evangelism in this Isaianic image of the herald proclaiming God's redemptive purposes. The connection between Isaiah 40:9 and the New Testament gospel message is thus explicit.

Nephi sees the mother of Jesus and testifies of her, connecting the vision of God coming to His people (40:9-10) with the incarnation. Zion's proclamation that God comes is fulfilled in Mary's role as the mother of Jesus.

The Lord commands His servants to lift up their voices as a trump: 'Hearken to the voice of the Lord your God, while I speak unto you.' The command to 'lift up thy voice' echoes Isaiah's charge to Zion.
John's revelation also emphasizes the proclamation and unveiling of Jesus Christ. Like Zion's command to proclaim 'Behold your God,' Revelation announces Christ's arrival to the churches.

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah's command to Zion to ascend a high mountain and proclaim good news would have been heard by exiled Judahites who had not seen their homeland for decades. Jerusalem lay in ruins; the temple was destroyed. The command to Zion to 'lift up thy voice' is therefore not merely poetic—it is a command to a conquered, silenced people to reclaim their voice and proclaim their faith. In the ancient Near Eastern context, heralds (sometimes called 'criers') were official messengers who stood in public places and announced decrees. By positioning Zion as a herald, Isaiah elevates the nation from victim status to the role of messenger of the divine will. The Dead Sea Scroll 1QIsaᵃ preserves this verse without significant variant, and some early manuscripts include a paragraph break after 'wilderness' in verse 3, supporting the Synoptic reading of that verse as a herald's proclamation. The archeological evidence suggests that post-exilic Judea was indeed rebuilt by those who had heard such proclamations of hope.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon portrays Nephi and his descendants as heralds who proclaim God's word to their people, taking on a role analogous to Zion's. Mosiah 12:21 describes the proclamation of good tidings in language echoing Isaiah 52:7. The entire Book of Mormon—as Moroni's introduction states—is itself a herald's proclamation announcing the Savior's coming and God's restoration of His covenant with Israel.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 21:4-5 and D&C 29:2 command modern disciples to 'lift up their voices' in proclaiming the gospel. The same verb that commands Zion to raise her voice commands the Restoration to do the same. Section 33:9 promises that the Lord's servants will lift up their voices and declare repentance and faith. The Restoration extends Isaiah's vision: modern Zion (the Church) is called to be a herald of good news.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In Latter-day Saint theology, Zion represents the covenant people, the house of God. The temple is the place where God's presence is manifest. Isaiah 40:9 thus points to the temple as the place from which God's word is proclaimed. Modern temple worship can be understood as part of Zion's proclamation: those who enter the temple covenant are, in effect, part of the herald's message to the world.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 9 points to the incarnation and to the messianic coming. Jesus Christ is 'the God' whom Zion is commanded to proclaim. He is the ultimate good news (gospel) that the heralds announce. Moreover, the command to Zion to proclaim and not be afraid foreshadows the post-resurrection commission to the disciples: 'Go ye and preach the gospel' (D&C 68:1). The timid disciples, fearful after the crucifixion, are commanded to 'lift up thy voice' and proclaim the resurrection. Zion's role as herald is thus fulfilled ultimately in the Church's role as proclaimer of Christ.
commentary.application: Modern Latter-day Saints can reflect on what it means to be part of Zion and to proclaim good news in a skeptical age. The verse invites us to reclaim our voices after a culture that often requires silence on matters of faith. 'Be not afraid' becomes directly applicable: the command is to speak the message of God's presence and power without apologizing for our faith. This does not mean being aggressive or disrespectful, but it does mean being clear and confident. The verse also reminds us that our role as members of the Church is not passive. We are not merely recipients of good news; we are bearers and proclaimers of it. Every conversation where we mention faith, every teaching moment, every example of living covenants is part of Zion's proclamation: 'Behold your God!' The command to ascend a high mountain can be understood as a call to perspective—to see our lives and our message from a higher vantage point, not from the limited perspective of current opposition or doubt. From that elevated place, the proclamation becomes clear and audible.

text_kjv: Behold, the Lord GOD will come with strong hand, and his arm shall rule for him: behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him.

commentary.narrative: The verse shifts focus from Zion's proclamation to the reality she announces: the arrival of God Himself. The double 'behold' (hinneh) creates dramatic emphasis and anticipation. The image is of a mighty warrior approaching with strength to establish His reign. 'The Lord GOD' uses both Adonai and YHWH—the covenant name joined with the title of sovereignty. God does not come in weakness or condescension but with 'strong hand' and a 'ruling arm.' This is not the image of a distant deity but of one who actively governs and subdues. However, the verse immediately shifts to something unexpected: with this mighty arm comes not judgment but 'reward.' The word carries the sense of recompense, wages earned, or the fruit of labor. In context, this refers to the redeemed people themselves—those whom God has preserved through exile and whom He now retrieves and restores. The final clause, 'his work before him,' indicates that God's redemptive work is visible, accomplished, and ready to be displayed. For exiled Israel, this verse would have carried immense weight: the God who seemed distant and silent in Babylon is announcing His return as an active, powerful ruler who brings salvation with Him.

word_study.meaning: The double designation combines Adonai ('Lord,' the title of sovereignty) with YHWH (the covenant name of God). This combination emphasizes both God's absolute power and His covenant fidelity.
word_study.significance: The use of both titles together is significant. YHWH alone would emphasize God's transcendence and covenant character; Adonai alone would emphasize sovereignty. Together, they proclaim God as both sovereign ruler and faithful covenant-keeper.

word_study.meaning: With strength, with might, or with a strong hand. The root chazaq conveys the idea of firmness, power, and unshakeable strength.
word_study.significance: The phrase suggests not merely power but purposeful, unmovable power. God comes not tentatively but with full strength. The Dead Sea Scroll 1QIsaᵃ reads 'be-chozaq' (with a vav as mater lectionis), but the meaning is identical. This power is not arbitrary but redemptive: it establishes God's rule and brings restoration.

word_study.meaning: Arm, might, or power. In Hebrew poetry, the arm is the symbol of action and strength. God's arm accomplishes His will.
word_study.significance: The arm appears frequently in Isaiah 40-66 as the symbol of God's redemptive power. In verse 11 (immediately following), the same zerou'a gathers lambs with tenderness. The contrast—the arm that rules with might (v. 10) and the arm that gathers lambs gently (v. 11)—reveals the full character of God: both warrior and shepherd.

word_study.meaning: To rule, govern, or have dominion. The root suggests the exercise of sovereign authority.
word_study.significance: God's arm 'shall rule for him'—indicating that His governance is exercised through His power. This is not distant decree but active rule. In the context of exile, this means that God actively governs the affairs of Judah and the nations, not that He is powerless or absent.

word_study.meaning: Reward, wages, or recompense. The term can refer to payment for labor or the fruit of one's work.
word_study.significance: In this context, the 'reward' refers to the people themselves—the redemptive harvest of God's covenantal labor. God's reward is not treasure or conquest but the restoration and salvation of His people. This reframes the image of the returning warrior: He does not come to plunder but to gather what is precious to Him.

word_study.meaning: Work, deed, or accomplishment. The term refers to completed labor and its visible results.
word_study.significance: God's peulat—His redemptive work—is 'before him' in the sense that it is ready to be displayed and accomplished. The work of salvation is not future and uncertain but present and prepared. God comes not to begin His work but to complete and reveal it.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah again uses the same image of God's coming with His reward: 'Say to the daughter of Zion, Behold, thy salvation cometh; behold, his reward is with him.' The reward motif—the redeemed people as the fruit of God's labor—recurs throughout the Book of Consolation.

In John's final vision, Jesus declares 'My reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be.' This directly applies Isaiah's language to the final coming of Christ, establishing Christ as the fulfillment of Isaiah's God who comes with reward.
Isaiah describes the return from exile using similar language: God's arm raised up to bring back the remnant. Both passages use the arm-metaphor for God's redemptive power in restoring Israel.

The Lord describes His coming to reign over the earth with glory and power, directly echoing Isaiah's imagery of the sovereign God arriving with might to establish His rule. The same redemptive purpose is announced.
Alma describes the strength of God's arm in preserving His people through trials, using language that echoes Isaiah 40:10's portrayal of the powerful divine arm that both rules and redeems.

commentary.historical_context: In the context of the Babylonian exile, the image of God arriving with strong hand would have been revolutionary. Babylon's kings were portrayed in official inscriptions as all-powerful and victorious. The Jewish exiles, by contrast, appeared powerless and defeated. The prophecy that Israel's God would come with a 'strong hand' asserts that the God of Israel—not the gods of Babylon—possesses true power and authority. Historically, the Persian conquest of Babylon and Cyrus's decree allowing the Jewish return would have been experienced as the fulfillment of this vision: power shifted, and the exiles were restored. Archaeologically, the Cyrus Cylinder (discovered in 1879) documents Cyrus's policy of repatriating conquered peoples, which aligns with the historical context of Isaiah 40's proclamation. For the exiles, seeing Babylon's power crumble and experiencing the possibility of return would have confirmed the prophet's assertion that God's arm is mighty and effective.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly portrays God's arm as extended in power to preserve His covenant people. Nephi's vision in 1 Nephi 14 shows that God's people are gathered in the last days through the power of His arm. The restoration of the gospel in the latter days is portrayed as God's arm being stretched out again (3 Nephi 16:15-20) to gather Israel and bring about redemption. The concept of the 'arm of the Lord' becomes a central metaphor for divine intervention in the last days.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 35:24 and D&C 38:21 describe the Lord coming in 'red apparel' (the imagery of a warrior bringing judgment and redemption). D&C 45:48-53 speaks of the Lord's arm stretched out to deliver His people. The Restoration teaches that Jesus Christ is the 'arm of the Lord' made manifest (see D&C 76:107 for 'the arm of the Lord'). The prophecy of Isaiah 40:10 is fulfilled in Christ's coming—both His first advent (humble but with power to redeem) and His second advent (with evident power and glory).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple terminology, God's 'arm' extended in power to protect and redeem the covenant people is a recurring theme. The temple represents the meeting place where God's power is manifest to establish covenant with His people. Isaiah 40:10—the God who comes with strong hand and ruling arm—foreshadows the Lord's declaration in the temple of His desire to gather and bless His people.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 10 points to Jesus Christ in both His first and second comings. In the first advent, Christ came with the 'arm of the Lord' to accomplish redemption through His atoning sacrifice. His 'reward'—the souls He came to save—He carries back to the Father. In the second advent, Christ will come 'with strong hand' and 'his arm shall rule for him,' explicitly fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy. The verse thus encompasses both the humble power of the incarnation and the visible power of the final judgment and reign. The balance between 'strong hand' and 'reward'—between might and mercy—characterizes both comings: Christ rules with absolute authority yet gathers His people with compassionate strength.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, Isaiah 40:10 offers profound assurance during times of powerlessness or despair. When personal circumstances feel overwhelmed by forces beyond our control, when the world seems to be governed by principles opposed to righteousness, this verse affirms that God's arm is strong and rules over all. His 'reward' is not wealth or status but the redeemed people—ourselves included if we remain in covenant. This should reduce our anxiety about worldly outcomes and increase our focus on the eternal economy in which God's rule is absolute. The verse also teaches us about God's character: He is not arbitrary or capricious but purposeful and redemptive. He comes with might, but the purpose of that might is to gather, preserve, and restore His people. For those in the covenant, this should produce both confidence and gratitude. The 'strong hand' that rules over all creation is the same hand that carries us homeward with our reward.

text_kjv: He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young.

commentary.narrative: The verse reveals the unexpected intimacy of God's rule. The God who arrives with a strong hand and ruling arm (verse 10) now appears as a shepherd gathering lambs. This is one of Scripture's most powerful reversals: raw power employed for tenderness. The shepherd metaphor is one of the most evocative in Hebrew poetry, suggesting intimate knowledge, care, and personal attention. The verb 'feed' (yir'eh) carries the sense of pasturing, guiding to food, and tending. The phrase 'his flock' emphasizes possession and protection—these sheep belong to the shepherd and are under his watch. The central image—gathering lambs in his arm and carrying them 'in his bosom' (becheiqo)—suggests physical closeness and warmth. The lamb is the most vulnerable member of the flock; its inclusion in the shepherd's protective care indicates that none is too small or weak to receive attention. The final clause, 'shall gently lead those that are with young,' speaks to ewes carrying lambs, requiring special care that does not push them beyond their strength. The shepherd does not drive the nursing mothers but guides them gently, at a pace they can sustain. For exiled Israel—scattered, weakened, bearing the trauma of displacement—this image would have been deeply moving. The mighty God of verse 10 is the same God who knows each of His people intimately and cares for them as a shepherd tends vulnerable lambs.
