The phrase 'so impoverished that he hath no oblation' suggests a man who lacks resources for even a proper temple offering—the bare minimum of religious participation in his context. Yet even this man will scrape together resources for an idol. He 'chooseth a tree that will not rot,' a careful selection for durability. He 'seeketh unto him a cunning workman'—the same charash of verse 19, the skilled laborer whose services cost money. All of this effort and expense for what? 'That shall not be moved'—so the idol will not fall over. The irony is suffocating: a man with nothing pursues the creation of something that cannot even fall. He invests his scarcity in ensuring the stability of a worthless object. Isaiah is indicting not merely idolatry as theological error but as a poverty-inducing obsession, a perversion of human priorities that locks the poor in cycles of futile expenditure.

word_study.meaning: One who is made needy, diminished, or pressed into want. The root sak conveys the idea of being narrow, confined, or reduced in circumstances. The passive participle emphasizes a state of deprivation.
word_study.significance: The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this word with plene spelling (mesukkhan), confirming the original sense. Isaiah's choice of this term establishes the man not merely as poor but as actively, progressively impoverished—ground down by his commitment to idolatry even as it drains his resources.

word_study.meaning: An offering lifted up or separated unto the Lord. In the Torah, terumah refers to the priestly contribution set apart from firstfruits and other products. It is the donation of the willing heart, given as homage to God.
word_study.significance: By saying the man 'hath no terumah,' Isaiah means he cannot afford even the basic religious donation. Yet this same man will somehow find resources for the idol. The juxtaposition is damning: authentic worship is beyond his means, but false worship commands his entire economy.

word_study.meaning: To choose, select, or prefer. The verb implies active deliberation and preference—picking one thing over another.
word_study.significance: The poor man is not coerced into idol-making; he *chooses* it. This agency is crucial to Isaiah's indictment. He has agency enough to select durable wood; he has will enough to hire a craftsman. Yet he directs all this choice and will toward the worship of nothing. The Dead Sea Scrolls manuscript preserves identical language, confirming the original text's emphasis on deliberate choice.

word_study.meaning: Wood resistant to decay. The verb rakav means to rot, decay, or become soft. The poor man's selection of incorruptible wood reflects practical concern with durability—the idol must last, must endure, must not crumble.
word_study.significance: Even the poor man's idol-making aims at permanence. This contrasts sharply with the grass and flower of verses 6-8, which fade and wither. There is an ironic inversion: the man prioritizes the permanence of his idol over the permanence of God's word, which alone endures forever (verse 8).

word_study.meaning: Wise, skillful, or expert. In craft contexts, it refers to technical expertise and mastery. The term elevates the artisan's status as someone of considerable talent.
word_study.significance: Isaiah's use of 'wise craftsman' (charash chakham) is laden with irony. The man hires wisdom—skill, expertise, knowledge—and directs it toward making an idol. The wisdom of human hands serves vanity. This echoes throughout Isaiah's polemic: human wisdom, when divorced from knowledge of God, becomes foolishness.

word_study.meaning: Will not totter, slip, or shift. The verb mot refers to motion, wavering, or instability. The negation indicates a state of fixed stillness.
word_study.significance: The idol's supreme achievement is immobility. It will not fall. It will not move. This is the summit of its 'power'—absolute, dead, static fixity. The irony is withering: the poor man has labored and spent to create something that *cannot act*, cannot move, cannot help, cannot speak. It is frozen in place, and that is victory.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah expands this verse into an extended mockery, describing the carpenter who 'taketh the pine tree, and the cypress, and maketh himself a god.' The same poor-man logic appears: even those with least resources dedicate them to idolatry.

The prophet describes idol-making as a cooperative community effort: 'They helped every one his neighbour; and every one said to his brother, Be of good courage.' Even in poverty, communities pool resources for idols—a damning communal choice.

Moses warns Israel that in exile they will 'serve gods, the work of men's hands, wood and stone, which neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.' Isaiah's poor man is fulfilling precisely this curse of disobedience.

Solomon teaches that 'the thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want.' The poor man of Isaiah 40:20 exemplifies this: his diligent effort in idol-making leads not to plenteousness but to want.

Paul instructs: 'having food and raiment let us be therewith content.' This stands as a New Testament counterweight to Isaiah's poor man, who lacks even a proper offering yet squanders scarcity on an idol.

commentary.historical_context: Archaeological evidence from the Levantine region shows that wooden idols were indeed the poor man's alternative to the gold and silver statuary of the wealthy and temples. Excavations have uncovered remnants of wooden deity figures, some with careful construction and durable-wood selection. In the ancient Near East, particularly during periods of economic hardship (as Judah faced during exile), idol-making among the poor was a reality, often encouraged by religious syncretism and anxiety about securing divine favor on the cheap. Isaiah's observation is socially acute: poverty often drives people toward magical or idolatrous thinking, as if they can control divine blessing through the manufacture of tangible objects.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob in the Book of Mormon (Jacob 4:8) observes that 'despising the words of plainness, and the easiness of the way' leads people into complex and destructive practices. The poor man of Isaiah 40:20 despises the simplicity of God's word and invests his poverty in the hardness of idol-making.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 76:104 teaches that those who 'love and made a lie' will be cast out. The idol-maker is making a lie—a false representation of divinity—and the poor man compounds the lie by staking his scarcity on it. D&C 121:37 affirms that 'when we undertake to cover our sins...by the device of men, our activity becomes as salt which has lost its savor.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The true temple requires no chains, no rotting wood, no skilled carving to secure it. God's house stands by covenant, not craftsmanship. For the poor, the temple offers access to covenant blessing without the expense of creating false gods. The Poor among the Latter-day Saints are explicitly invited to the temple without financial barrier—a direct fulfillment of Isaiah's implicit critique.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus contrasts Himself with the idols of human making when He says, 'I am the living bread which came down from heaven' (John 6:51). He does not need to be carved, chained, or selected for durability; He is eternally alive, eternally present, eternally available. He is the opposite of the dead idol—not a creation of human hands but the Creator in human form. Where the idol must be 'chosen' and 'sought out,' Christ offers Himself freely to all, especially the poor.
commentary.application: Modern idols seduce the poor with particular force. Consumer culture, debt, status-chasing, comparison—these are the 'trees that will not rot' of our age. A person scraping by financially may convince himself that the right purchase, the right image, the right credential will finally secure his place or worth. Isaiah invites us to see that dynamic with clarity: we are spending our scarcity on things that cannot move, cannot help, cannot give what they promise. For covenant members, the application is stark: we must audit our financial choices ruthlessly. Are we investing scarce resources in authentic worship and covenant community, or in the idols of security and status? The poor man of verse 20 would challenge us: 'What are you willing to spend your scarcity on?'

text_kjv: Have ye not known? have ye not heard? hath it not been told you from the beginning? have ye not understood from the foundations of the earth?

commentary.narrative: Isaiah shifts from satire to interrogation. Four hammering rhetorical questions demand that his audience acknowledge what should already be obvious: the knowledge of God's supremacy is not new, not obscure, not requiring special revelation. It is ancient, foundational, universally available. 'Have ye not known?' appeals to personal experience. 'Have ye not heard?' appeals to communal memory and teaching. 'Hath it not been told you from the beginning?' reaches back to the oldest traditions and the primordial history itself. 'Have ye not understood from the foundations of the earth?' grounds the knowledge in creation itself—as if the very structure of the world testifies to God's character. The exiled Judeans to whom Isaiah speaks have no excuse for ignorance. They have been told, they have heard, they should know. The implication is clear: any return to idolatry is not because God's truth is unavailable; it is because they have chosen not to remember it, chosen not to listen, chosen not to understand. This verse functions as a hinge: it moves from the mockery of idols (vv. 19-20) to the cosmic demonstration of God's power (vv. 22-24), but it does so by insisting that this knowledge should not require new evidence. The audience already knows better.

word_study.meaning: The interrogative particle halo introduces a question expecting affirmation ('Is it not...?'). The verb yada means to know through experience, relationship, or intimacy. It is not mere information but relational knowing.
word_study.significance: Isaiah does not ask, 'Have you not been told facts?' but rather 'Have you not known?' The difference is crucial. Yada implies a personal, experiential knowledge. God's power is not abstract doctrine; it is the living reality they have witnessed or should have witnessed.

word_study.meaning: The verb shama means to hear with understanding and often with the implication of obedience. It is not passive hearing but active listening that produces response.
word_study.significance: 'Hearing' in biblical idiom is not merely auditory but obedient. Have they not heard—and heeded—what was proclaimed? The question implies that the problem is not God's silence but humanity's refusal to listen and act on what has been heard.

word_study.meaning: Hugad is the passive 'was told' or 'was declared' (Hofal of nagad, to make known). Merosh means 'from the beginning,' from the primordium, from the headwaters of time.
word_study.significance: This is not recent revelation but ancient witness. From Israel's earliest stories—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the Exodus, Sinai—the character of God has been made known. The tradition stretches back without break.

word_study.term_english: understood from the foundations of the earth
word_study.term_original: הֲלוֹא הֲבִינוֹתֶם מוֹסְדוֹת הָאָרֶץ (halo habinhotem mosedot ha'aretz)
word_study.meaning: Habin means to discern, perceive, or understand through observation. Mosedot (plural of musdah) means foundations, base structures. Ha'aretz is the earth. Together, 'foundations of the earth' refers both to the primordial act of creation and to the observable structures of the cosmos.
word_study.significance: The TCR translation note captures the double sense perfectly: 'from the very structure of creation.' God's power is readable in creation itself—not just in historical tradition but in the ongoing, observable cosmos. The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1). This is visible knowledge, embedded in the structure of reality itself. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse identically, confirming the original's emphasis on the universality of this knowledge.

cross_references.connection: Paul writes that God's 'invisible things...are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.' Isaiah's insistence that the knowledge is 'from the foundations of the earth' finds full articulation in Paul's natural revelation argument.

The psalmist declares, 'The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.' This is the same knowledge Isaiah says should be understood 'from the foundations of the earth'—the cosmos itself speaks.

Moses commands Israel to teach the Shema from generation to generation: 'Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD.' Isaiah's question 'have ye not heard?' echoes this foundational command of Torah. The knowledge should have been transmitted.

In the book's opening, Isaiah says, 'I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me.' The audience's ignorance is willful, not innocent. They *have* been told from the beginning.

Alma teaches that those who 'do not believe the word...do not receive the word of God...because they will not seek.' Isaiah's four questions in verse 21 pinpoint exactly this: the people refuse to know, refuse to hear, refuse to understand what is freely available.

commentary.historical_context: Exiled in Babylon (sixth century BCE), Judean captives were surrounded by a cosmology utterly different from their own. Babylonian astronomy was advanced; Babylonian theology was sophisticated; Babylonian religious structures were visible and powerful. Yet Isaiah insists that their own ancestral knowledge—from Abraham through Moses and the prophets—contains the truth that supersedes all Babylonian claims. The question 'Have ye not known...from the beginning?' is a return to older, deeper roots. It is also a claim about the universal accessibility of monotheistic knowledge: one need not be a Babylonian scholar or a priest with secret knowledge. The foundations of the earth themselves testify. This was a radical epistemological claim in a polytheistic context.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi in 1 Nephi 15:8 speaks of 'the spirit of the Lord [working] upon' him to understand the mysteries of God, but he first had to 'seek earnestly' and listen to the words his father had already taught him. Isaiah's question presupposes that the knowledge has been made available; the problem is refusing to 'know' and 'hear' it.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:40 teaches that 'the light shineth in darkness' and that 'the darkness comprehendeth it not.' But this implies that the light *is* available, shining. Those who do not comprehend it are those who refuse to look. D&C 21:4-5 promises that 'the Lord's voice crieth unto all men' and that all should 'hear my voice and know that I am he.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where ancient knowledge—from the foundations of the world—meets present revelation. The endowment teaches themes that echo from creation itself, relayed through prophets 'from the beginning' to the present day. A covenant member entering the temple should recognize the continuation of knowledge 'told...from the beginning.'

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus embodies this principle when He says to Nicodemus, 'If I have told you earthly things, and ye believe not, how shall ye believe, if I tell you of heavenly things?' (John 3:12). The knowledge of God has been available since the foundations of the world; refusing it is not ignorance but willful blindness. Christ is the Word 'from the beginning' (John 1:1-3)—the knowledge of God made incarnate, accessible, present. His incarnation is not the introduction of alien truth but the fulfillment of truth that has always been testified to 'from the foundations of the earth.'
commentary.application: For contemporary covenant members, this verse is a call to ruthless honesty about what we know. We have the standard works. We have had prophets. We have the restored gospel. We have walked the temple. The plea 'Have ye not known?' is Isaiah asking us: What are you doing with what you already know? Are you choosing ignorance despite available truth? Are you hearing but not heeding? Are you understanding but not acting? The verse disallows excuses. It forbids us from claiming that if we only knew better, we would do better. We know. The question is whether we will *become* what the knowledge demands. This is particularly sharp in an age of information overload: we suffer not from scarcity of knowledge but from scarcity of will to act on the knowledge we possess.

text_kjv: It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in:

commentary.narrative: Having insisted that the knowledge of God should be universally available, Isaiah now delivers the vision that should command belief. The portrait is staggering in its scale. God 'sitteth upon the circle of the earth'—enthroned above the entire sphere of visible creation, observing it from a vantage point of absolute dominion. From this throne, humanity appears not as the measure of all things but as grasshoppers—infinitesimal, insignificant, seen as insects are seen. The image is not meant to comfort but to humble. The second clause amplifies the vastness: God 'stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain.' The verb natah (stretch) suggests ease, effortlessness—the heavens are not labored over but simply drawn out, like fabric unrolled. He 'spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in'—the cosmos itself is God's dwelling, His shelter, His domain. For exiled Judeans in Babylon, this vision would have reoriented their entire perspective. The great Babylonian temples and ziggurats, impressive as they were, existed within a universe already fully claimed and stretched out by the God of Israel. Their god had no temple building it needed; His residence was the cosmos itself. The idols of Babylon, chained down and dependant on human artisans, belonged to a provincial deity imagining itself great. The God of Isaiah dwelt in the vastness itself.

word_study.meaning: To sit, dwell, or be enthroned. In royal and divine contexts, yoshev indicates the secure, permanent occupation of a throne. The present tense suggests ongoing, eternal occupation.
word_study.significance: Yoshev is not temporary perching but secure habitation. God is not visiting the throne of the earth; He is sitting upon it as His rightful, permanent place. This stands in contrast to the idols of verse 19, which must be kept from toppling.

word_study.meaning: The circle or vault of the earth. Chug denotes a circular or dome-like form—the horizon-circle where sky meets earth, visible to any observer. Ha'aretz is the earth or land. The phrase describes the entire visible sphere of creation.
word_study.significance: The TCR translator note explains: 'circle, sphere, or vault...the visible horizon where sky meets earth.' This is not scientific cosmology (the ancient mind did not think in terms of a spherical planet) but rather the visual horizon—what is visible from any standing point on earth. God sits above all that is visible and knowable. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this word identically, confirming the original's emphasis on the encompassing dome of sky.

word_study.meaning: Grasshoppers or locusts. Small insects visible to the human eye but insignificant in scale. Used metaphorically for their absolute littleness and powerlessness.
word_study.significance: This is the radical scale-reversal. In Babylonian thought, humanity (especially the king) was the measure of cosmic importance. Isaiah inverts that completely. From God's vantage point, all humanity is proportionally as grasshoppers to us. The image is meant to be unsettling, humbling, clarifying. It denies human centrality and asserts divine centrality. Elsewhere in Isaiah (33:4), the same word describes the plundering of spoil—grasshoppers gathering what falls. Here, humans are themselves the insects.

word_study.meaning: To extend, stretch, or spread out. The verb suggests an action of pulling, drawing, or spreading fabric. It conveys both action and ease.
word_study.significance: Noteh implies that the heavens are extended by divine effort but without strain. This is not like human metal-working (as in verse 19), which requires labor and multiple artisans. God stretches out the heavens the way one might unfurl a cloth. The ease of the action heightens the contrast with the laborious process of idol-making.

word_study.meaning: Thin fabric, membrane, or curtain. The comparison suggests something filmy, translucent, malleable—easily spread and hung.
word_study.significance: Curtains in ancient tents and temples were precious, durable materials, yet the metaphor emphasizes their thinness and the ease with which they can be arranged. The heavens, vast and apparently solid, are compared to something as insubstantial as a curtain in God's hand. This further diminishes human perception of the cosmos's independence.

word_study.term_english: spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in
word_study.meaning: Spread or stretched (like a tent) to dwell or sit in. Mitach means to stretch or spread. Ohel is a tent—the portable dwelling of a nomad. Shavet means to dwell, sit, or inhabit.
word_study.significance: The heavens are not a permanent structure that took eons to build but a tent—a temporary-looking, nomadic dwelling that can be pitched and struck by God's hand. This is the ultimate expression of divine ease and cosmic subordination. What appears to us as the fixed, eternal dome of the sky is, to God, as provisional as a nomad's tent. This imagery would have resonated powerfully with Israelite memory: their ancestors were tent-dwellers, nomads under God's protection. The paradox is that the heavens—apparently eternal—are actually more temporary in form than even the tents that sheltered Israel's history.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist writes, 'He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision.' The image of God seated and observing from above echoes Isaiah's throne, though the psalmist emphasizes God's mockery of earthly rebellion.

The psalmist praises: 'Who coverest thyself with light as with a garment: who stretchest out the heavens like a curtain.' This is nearly identical language to Isaiah 40:22, affirming the image's scriptural rootedness.

Job declares, 'Which alone spreadeth out the heavens, and treadeth upon the waves of the sea.' The spreading of heavens is attributed solely to God, making human achievement (including idol-making) proportionally insignificant.

The New Testament applies Isaiah 40:26 and related language directly to Christ: 'Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth; and the heavens are the works of thine hands.' Christ is revealed as the One who stretches out heavens.

John's vision in the Doctrine and Covenants describes God's glory: 'the light and the Redeemer of the world...his throne is in the heavens.' This echoes Isaiah's vision of God enthroned above all creation.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient Near Eastern cosmologies typically understood the sky as a solid vault (the 'firmament' or raqia of Genesis 1:6-8), usually held aloft by pillars or by a god's physical effort. The Egyptian sky-goddess Nut was depicted as arching over the earth. Mesopotamian texts describe the heavens as a firm, structural dome. Isaiah's image of the heavens as a mere curtain or tent would have been shocking—suggesting that what appeared permanent and substantial was actually as malleable, from God's perspective, as fabric. For exiled Judeans in Babylon, where the great ziggurat of Marduk dominated the skyline and Babylonian astronomy was highly developed, Isaiah's reduction of the visible cosmos to a 'tent' would have been intellectually and spiritually liberating. The most 'permanent' things the Babylonians could imagine—the fixed stars, the ordained heavens—were actually provisional in God's hand.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi in 1 Nephi 17:30 teaches that God's 'tender mercies' sustain even the cosmos: 'I know that he loveth his children; nevertheless, I do not know the meaning of all things.' This echoes Isaiah's vision of a God who stretches out heavens so casually that they are like tents. The ordinary love with which God sustains us is the same ease with which He sustains the cosmos.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:32 teaches that God 'compounded the elements—the same that taketh up room in the heavens, the same that the earth is composed of.' This reflects Isaiah's understanding: God is the sovereign composer of both the vast (the heavens) and the intimate (the earthly elements).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the heavens and the earth are explicitly represented and brought into covenant relationship. The veil separating the terrestrial from the celestial is itself a kind of 'curtain' (parochet in Hebrew), echoing Isaiah's language. God's 'tent' is, in temple theology, where God dwells with His people.

commentary.christological_typology: In John 1:1-3, Christ is the Word 'by whom all things were made,' and 'without him was not any thing made.' The One who 'sits upon the circle of the earth' and stretches out the heavens as a tent is revealed in the Restoration as Jesus Christ. Colossians 1:16-17 affirms that in Christ 'all things...were created...and in him all things consist.' The stretching out of the heavens is His work, and He holds it all together by the word of His power.
commentary.application: This verse operates on contemporary readers with particular power in an age of anthropocentric anxiety. We worry about our significance, our impact, our legacy—will the world remember us? Isaiah invites a radical reorientation. From the vantage point of the One who sits above the circle of the earth and stretches out the heavens as a tent, our anxiety about smallness is inverted. We are small, yes—like grasshoppers. But we are the grasshoppers He chose to covenant with, to speak to, to redeem. For modern members, the application is liberation: Stop trying to prove your cosmic significance. God already knows you. Accept your smallness as a gift. From that acceptance flows freedom. You are not the center of creation, and that is the most liberating truth you can embrace. Only from that humility can authentic discipleship begin.

text_kjv: That bringeth the princes to nothing; he maketh the judges of the earth as vanity.
text_kjv_alt: That bringeth the princes to nothing; he maketh the judges of the earth as vanity.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah now draws the political implication from the cosmic vision. If God sits enthroned above the circle of the earth with all humanity appearing as grasshoppers, then the most powerful human rulers—princes and judges—stand in the same diminished relationship to His power. 'He bringeth the princes to nothing'—not that they cease to exist, but that their power and significance are brought to nothing (ayin). Those whom the world honors as great are, in relation to God's sovereignty, nullified. The second clause intensifies this: 'he maketh the judges of the earth as vanity' (tohu). Tohu is the same term used in Genesis 1:2 to describe the earth before creation—formless, empty, void. It is not merely that earthly rulers are small; they are reduced to a pre-creation state of nothingness. For the exiled Judeans, hearing this prophecy in Babylon, the relevance would have been electrifying. Babylon's king—represented in the Hebrew Bible as Nebuchadnezzar—presented himself as the apex of earthly power. Isaiah's declaration that all earthly princes are 'nothing' in relation to God is a direct theological challenge to Babylonian political theology. The verse also echoes verse 17, where the prophet said God 'maketh the nations...as nothing, and as things of nought.' The vocabulary circles back: princes, judges, nations—all human power structures—are tohu, ayin, empty, null.

word_study.meaning: Gives or brings to 'ayin (nothing). The verb natan means to give or place. Ayin literally means 'nothing,' 'non-being,' or 'zero.' Together, the phrase indicates a reduction to nullity, an absolute negation of status or power.
word_study.significance: Ayin is not merely poverty or diminishment; it is nothingness itself. Isaiah does not say princes are weakened or diminished but that they are brought to ayin—to a state where they possess no substance. This is radical political theology: human power has no independent substantiality in relation to God.

word_study.meaning: Nobles, chieftains, or princes. The word refers to those of high birth and authority, the ruling elite. In the ancient Near Eastern context, rozenim denotes the administrative and military aristocracy.
word_study.significance: By singling out rozenim, Isaiah targets the very top of human power structures. It is not street beggars brought to nothing but the elite, the ones who wielded real military and political authority. The radicality increases: those with the most power in the human sphere are nullified in relation to God's authority. In context, this may include explicit reference to Babylonian princes and officials who held power over the exile community.

word_study.meaning: To make, do, or fashion. Asah is the verb used throughout Genesis 1 for creation ('God made the heavens and the earth'). Here, it indicates God's active formative power over human rulers.
word_study.significance: By using asah—the creation verb—Isaiah suggests that God 'makes' rulers into vanity with the same power He uses to create. Their transformation into nothingness is not an accident but a deliberate divine act. Just as God 'made' the heavens, He 'makes' the judges to be tohu.

word_study.meaning: Judges, rulers, or administrators of the earth/land. Shofet refers to those who govern, arbitrate disputes, and exercise judicial-political authority. Eretz is the earth or land.
word_study.significance: Shofetim were a traditional authority structure in Israel (the judges of the book of Judges) and in all ancient Near Eastern societies. By invoking this term, Isaiah identifies the universal political structure and pronounces it relativized before God. Whether Babylonian officials, Egyptian pharaohs, or Israelite judges, all fall under the same judgment: they are tohu in God's sight.

word_study.meaning: Like the void, formless emptiness, or chaos. Tohu (from which tohu comes) appears in Genesis 1:2 ('the earth was...tohu') to describe pre-creation chaos. It signifies a state of non-being, absence of form, absolute nullity.
word_study.significance: The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse identically. By comparing earthly judges to tohu, Isaiah equates their power with pre-creation non-being. They have the substance of a void. This is not metaphorical diminishment but ontological negation. Earthly power has no more reality, in the final reckoning, than the formless void that preceded creation. The echo of Genesis 1:2 may be intentional: what humanity creates in the form of kingdoms and rulers is, like the pre-creation chaos, destined for overturning.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah prophesies that nations 'rush like the rushing of many waters' but God 'rebuketh them, and they flee far off...and lo, at eventide trouble...and before the morning he is not.' The princes and judges brought to nothing in verse 23 are the same ones who are here scattered like chaff.

Earlier in Isaiah, the prophet declares, 'The lofty looks of man shall be humbled...In that day a man shall cast his idols...to the moles and to the bats,' reducing human pride and human-made power to nothing. Verse 23 is the theological principle underlying this prophecy.

The psalmist warns earthly rulers: 'Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth. Serve the LORD with fear.' This is the pastoral application of Isaiah's principle: because princes are brought to nothing in relation to God, they must bow before Him.
Daniel declares, 'He removeth kings, and setteth up kings.' This is exactly Isaiah's principle in action: God brings princes to nothing and raises them according to His will, not their own.

The Lord declares concerning the American Civil War, 'For behold, the anger of the Lord is kindled against the nations.' The verse shows God's sovereignty over political upheaval, consistent with Isaiah's principle that judges of the earth are made as vanity.

commentary.historical_context: In the sixth century BCE, when Isaiah was likely composed in its current form, Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar II had conquered the Near East and was the undisputed superpower. The Babylonian king presented himself in theological terms—as the deputy of Marduk, the chief god of the Babylonian pantheon. The royal inscriptions made explicit claims to divine support and cosmic authority. An Israelite priest or prophet making the bold claim that Babylonian princes were 'nothing' and 'vanity' was directly confronting the imperial ideology that dominated the world as the exiles knew it. This prophecy offered a counter-narrative to imperial power: Yes, Babylon is mighty. Yes, Nebuchadnezzar is great by earthly standards. But in relation to the God of Israel, all earthly princes are void. This theological move would have been spiritually sustaining for the exiled community, preventing total despair at their political impotence.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 37:16-17 teaches that the righteous are 'instruments in the hands of God to bring about his eternal purposes' while the proud are brought to nothing. Isaiah's principle is repeatedly enacted in the Book of Mormon: proud rulers (Lamoni's father, Noah, Amalickiah) are brought to judgment, while humble servants are exalted.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 127:8 affirms that 'the same sociality which exists among us here will exist among us there [in heaven].' This appears to validate human relationships and position. Yet D&C 76:52-56 clarifies that in the celestial kingdom, all are equal—relativizing all earthly status. Isaiah's principle is fundamental: judges of the earth are made as vanity because only covenant relationship with God determines ultimate significance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, all are equal before God—prince and pauper wear the same garments. The leveling of status that happens in the temple is a living enactment of Isaiah's truth. One of the temple's prophetic functions is to declare that earthly judges and rulers, however great, are tohu before the God whose house this is.

commentary.christological_typology: In Revelation 19:19-21, the kings and armies of the earth gather for battle against Christ, and they are utterly defeated: 'The beast was taken, and with him the false prophet...these both were cast alive into a lake of fire.' Christ is revealed as the One before whom all earthly princes and judges are brought to nothing. Matthew 28:18 records the risen Christ's claim: 'All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth.' This is Isaiah's prophecy fulfilled—the Judge of all judges, the Prince of princes, is revealed as alone possessing real authority.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members in democratic societies, this verse challenges the idolatry of political power. We are not exiles under an alien king as the original hearers were, yet we inhabit a world saturated with political messaging, power-seeking, and the valorization of leaders. Isaiah invites a radical reorientation: these judges of the earth, however powerful they seem, are tohu—void, formless, empty of ultimate significance. This does not justify neglect of political duty or indifference to justice. Rather, it frees us from the spiritual trap of believing that earthly political power is ultimate. We can engage civically without investing our souls in princes. We can vote, advocate, and participate while remaining clear-eyed: these officials, wise or foolish, are brought to nothing in relation to God's eternal purposes. This is liberation from political despair and from political idolatry simultaneously.

text_kjv: Yea, they shall not be planted; yea, they shall not be sown: yea, their stock shall not take root in the earth: and he shall also blow upon them, and they shall wither, and the whirlwind shall take them away as stubble.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah extends the vision of verse 23 into a prophecy of judgment. The princes and judges of verse 23 now appear as vegetation—planted, sown, rooted—but vegetation that never takes hold. The repetition of 'yea...yea...yea' creates a breathless, inevitable rhythm: scarcely are they planted before they are not planted; scarcely sown before they are not sown; scarcely rooted before they find no root. The tense is crucial: Isaiah is not describing something that will happen in the future but something that is already happening or is inherent in the nature of earthly power. Then the climax: God 'shall also blow upon them, and they shall wither.' The 'blowing' (nashaf) recalls the breath of God from verse 7—'the grass withereth, the flower fadeth, because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it.' The princes of the earth follow the same law as grass: they exist in a realm subject to God's breath, and that breath withers them. Finally, 'the whirlwind shall take them away as stubble'—what remains of them after withering is scattered and blown away like the chaff of grain after threshing. The image crescendos from planted growth to withering to complete dispersal. For the exiled community, this would have offered profound consolation: Yes, Babylon seems established, rooted, permanent. But it is actually as unstable as grass, as vulnerable to divine breath as any plant, destined for the dispersal that comes to all things without God's sustaining covenant.

word_study.meaning: Scarcely planted; barely sown; hardly...when (af bal construct a breathless temporal sequence). Nittau is the passive Niphal of nata, meaning to be planted. The phrase emphasizes the rapidity with which planting gives way to non-planting.
word_study.significance: The TCR translator captures this perfectly: 'Scarcely are they planted.' The af bal construction (appearing three times in this verse) creates a sense of immediacy and inevitability—no sooner does one thing happen than it is undone. This is not patience waiting for judgment; it is judgment inherent in the nature of the thing itself. Earthly rulers are planted, yes, but their planting is itself the beginning of their unplanting.

word_study.meaning: The trunk, stalk, or root-stock of a plant. Gizeah refers to the substantial base from which a plant grows and draws life. It is the difference between a passing shoot and a plant with deep roots.
word_study.significance: By referring to the 'stock' of the rulers, Isaiah emphasizes that their power lacks foundation. The root stock is the symbol of established, deep-rooted authority. That these have no root stock (or no rooting of their stock) means their power is superficial, not genuinely established.

word_study.meaning: Root in the earth. Shoresh is the root of a plant—the organ that draws water and nutrients from the soil and anchors the plant. To take root is to become established, stable, and self-sustaining.
word_study.significance: Earthly power is imagined as vegetation that cannot root. The earth itself (eretz) is, in Isaiah's vision, unable or unwilling to receive the roots of tyrannical rulers. There is something providential about this—the very medium into which they seek to plant themselves refuses to anchor them. In the context of Israel's covenant with God, it is God who controls whether a ruler will be established or not.

word_study.meaning: And also He blew/breathed upon them. Nashaf means to blow, breathe upon, or sweep. The verb is used of divine action—God's breath or wind causing devastation. The added 'also' (gam) suggests that this blow from God is just one more inevitable element in the pattern.
word_study.significance: Nashaf echoes verse 7, where God's breath causes the grass to wither and the flower to fade. The same divine breath that sustains creation (verse 26-31) can also wither it. Human rulers are subject to the same breath of God as vegetation. This is not special judgment but subjection to the ordinary law of creation: all things depend on God's sustaining breath.

word_study.meaning: And they dried up; withered; became desiccated. Yabach refers to loss of moisture and vitality. It is the natural fate of vegetation when separated from water and the sustaining elements of soil.
word_study.significance: Withering is not external punishment but the natural consequence of being severed from the source of life. The rulers wither because they attempt to draw life from the earth alone—from human power, from political structures, from Babylonian ideology—rather than from covenant with God. They wither because their roots cannot take hold in that soil.

word_study.term_english: whirlwind shall take them away as stubble
word_study.meaning: The storm/whirlwind (seara) carries them away like straw or stubble (qash). Tisa is the Qal verb 'to lift, carry, or bear away.' The comparison is between the rulers (now reduced to withered chaff) and the lightest, least substantial remnants of grain after harvest.
word_study.significance: The final image completes the destruction: not only do the rulers wither, but what remains of them is so insubstantial that a storm can scatter them entirely. Qash (stubble) is proverbial for worthlessness—the left-over chaff that has no value after the grain is extracted. The whirlwind that carries them away is not depicted as extraordinary or punitive but as the ordinary natural wind that sweeps away light things. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse with minor orthographic variants (af bal written with vav: bul) but identical meaning. The prophet depicts destruction as utterly natural, inevitable, and complete. There is a note of resigned finality: of course the whirlwind takes them as stubble. What else would happen to withered straw?

cross_references.connection: Isaiah prophesies, 'their root shall be as rottenness, and their blossom shall go up as dust: because they have cast away the law of the LORD.' The withering of verse 24 is the judgment for rejecting God's word—exactly what the princes and judges of verse 24 exemplify.

Isaiah describes the Assyrian army as 'as the grass of the field, and as the green herb, as the grass on the housetops, and as corn blighted before it be grown up.' This is the inverse situation—invaders are destroyed like withered grass—but using the same agricultural imagery.

The psalmist counsels, 'Fret not thyself...For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb.' This is Isaiah's principle applied: the wicked and the mighty, like grass, wither before God.

Job cries out to God, 'Wilt thou break a leaf driven to and fro? and wilt thou pursue the dry stubble?' Job compares himself to chaff, the worthless remnant—echoing Isaiah's image of rulers scattered as stubble.

Peter quotes Isaiah 40:6-8 directly: 'All flesh is as grass...but the word of the Lord endureth for ever.' This verse's contrast between withering rulers and enduring God reflects the same principle Isaiah articulates throughout chapter 40.

commentary.historical_context: The agricultural imagery of planting, rooting, withering, and dispersal would have resonated powerfully with ancient Israelites and Judeans, who were primarily an agrarian people. They understood viscerally what it meant for crops to fail to take root, for plants to wither, for wind to scatter seed. But in the context of exile, this imagery also had political application: the hope was that Babylon—mighty as it seemed—would not 'take root' in its dominion but would wither and be scattered. The prophet was offering an agricultural metaphor for political collapse. Historically, within a generation or two of the likely composition of Isaiah 40-55, Babylon did indeed fall to the Persians (539 BCE), vindicating Isaiah's prophecy. The city that seemed so established proved unable to root itself securely.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma describes the fall of wicked rulers with similar imagery. In Alma 62:40, following military defeat, Amalickiah's armies are 'scattered and taken captive...as the leaves of a tree...are blown away by the wind.' The Book of Mormon enacts Isaiah's prophecy repeatedly: pride leads to withering, and the whirlwind of judgment disperses the wicked.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:8 teaches that God 'sent forth the fulness of [His] gospel by the hands of [His] servants.' This is the counterpoint to verse 24: while earthly rulers wither and are scattered, the gospel—the word of God—is sent forth and endures. D&C 88:40 also affirms that 'the light shineth in darkness' and cannot be taken away by any whirlwind of opposition.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment presents the eternal covenant that enables a people to 'take root' spiritually in the earth. Those who make and keep covenants in the temple have a root that the whirlwind cannot scatter. This stands in direct contrast to the rulers of verse 24 who lack covenant foundation.

commentary.christological_typology: Matthew 3:12 describes Christ's coming judgment: 'He will thoroughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.' This applies Isaiah's image of scattering as chaff directly to Christ's role as judge. Those who do not root themselves in Him—the true foundation—will be scattered like the stubble of verse 24. Conversely, those who are 'in Christ' are rooted in bedrock (Matthew 7:25: 'the house [built on rock] fell not'). Christ is the only secure root, the only firm foundation that cannot be withered or scattered by the whirlwind of judgment.
commentary.application: For contemporary members of the Latter-day Saint Church, this verse contains a sober warning about the futility of rooting ourselves in earthly power, wealth, status, or ideology. These things wither; the whirlwind scatters them. This is not cynicism but realism. The powerful nations of history, the billionaires of our age, the celebrities who command attention—all are destined for the fate of stubble. Yet the application is not paralyzing despair but liberating clarity. If we stop investing our ultimate hope in things that wither, we are free to invest in what endures: covenant relationship with God, spiritual development, service, love. Practically, this means scrutinizing our own 'roots.' Where are we trying to take root? In career advancement? In consumer status? In ideological correctness? In family legacy? All of these can be good, but they cannot be ultimate. Only a root in the God of the covenant, sustained by His breath, provides a foundation that cannot be scattered. The verse invites personal inventory: What are you rooting yourself in? When the whirlwind comes—and it will—will that root hold?

text_kjv: To whom then will ye liken me, or shall I be equal? saith the Holy One.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah shifts from addressing the exiles directly to rendering God's own voice. The Prophet poses the central theological question of this entire section: who is comparable to the God of Israel? This is not a rhetorical flourish but the foundation of the exiles' confidence. If God is incomparable—utterly transcendent—then the circumstances of their captivity cannot diminish His power or redefine His nature. The double interrogative ("to whom... or shall I be equal") leaves no room for equivalence. In the ancient world, comparing gods was dangerous theology; here Isaiah claims not just superiority but radical incomparability.

The speaker identifies Himself as "the Holy One"—without the appositional "of Israel" found elsewhere in the chapter. This nakedness of the title emphasizes God's absolute otherness rather than His covenant relationship. The Hebrew *qadosh* (holy) means fundamentally "set apart" or "separate." God is not just morally pure or religiously significant; He exists in a category entirely distinct from creation. The exiles, listening to these words in Babylon—surrounded by Nebuchadnezzar's propaganda, the visual evidence of defeated gods and conquered peoples—needed to hear that their God stands in no comparison with the idols of their captors.

word_study.meaning: to be like, to resemble, to compare. The root suggests making something alike or finding equivalence. In context, the verb demands a search for a proper comparison—and the answer is: there is none.
word_study.significance: This verb establishes the rhetorical structure of Isaiah 40. The entire chapter's argument against idolatry depends on the logical impossibility embedded in this question. To *damah* God to an idol is to commit category error.

word_study.meaning: set apart, separate, holy. The term denotes fundamental otherness—not moral quality alone but ontological difference. In Hebrew, holiness is primarily about separation from the profane, not virtue per se.
word_study.significance: By standing alone without 'of Israel,' the divine epithet emphasizes transcendence over covenant. The exiles need to know that God's power and nature are not dependent on their circumstances but rooted in His absolute distinctness from all creation. The Covenant Rendering's isolation of this title underscores the theological point.

cross_references.connection: A parallel rhetorical question: 'To whom will ye liken me, and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be like?' The repetition of this challenge throughout Isaiah 40–46 becomes the refrain of the entire consolation section.

Moses' song at the Red Sea: 'Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?' The ancient assertion of God's incomparability is reclaimed for the exiles.
Nephi describes the power of the gentile nations, yet they ultimately remain subject to God's greater power. The comparison motif—what can be likened to God—carries through the Book of Mormon.

In the vision of the Father and Son, the revelation emphasizes that all things are subject to God's governance. The incomparability claimed in Isaiah finds fuller expression in latter-day revelation about the divine hierarchy.

commentary.historical_context: The exiles in Babylon circa 540 BCE would have been surrounded by Mesopotamian temple art, processional statues, and public theology asserting the power of Marduk and other Babylonian deities. Nebuchadnezzar's propaganda explicitly claimed that the gods of the conquered nations had been overcome by Babylon's gods. Asking "to whom will you liken me?" in this context is a direct theological challenge to the entire Babylonian religious apparatus. The form of the question—an interrogative that expects no answer—was a known rhetorical device in ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature, especially in contexts of theodicy and divine exoneration.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 11:5–6, Nephi describes a vision where he sees God speaking, and the voice asks: 'Believest thou the words of thy brother?' The pattern of God's voice posing foundational questions to direct human belief and alignment appears throughout Book of Mormon theophany.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:41–50 teaches that all things are governed by law and that God's power sustains all creation. The incomparability affirmed in Isaiah 40:25 is the foundation for understanding the unified governance described in D&C 88.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the question of God's nature and our relationship to Him is central. The incomparability of God is what makes covenant possible—we approach not an equal but One who condescends to make promises with us. The veil between worlds reflects the separation (*qadosh*) that Isaiah asserts here.

commentary.christological_typology: While this verse emphasizes God's transcendent nature, the full gospel understanding requires that God's incomparability is not distant: it is precisely the God who is incomparable who condescends in Jesus Christ. Christ's incarnation does not diminish God's holiness but reveals its deepest meaning—a God so utterly other that He can become fully human without ceasing to be God. The answer to 'who is like God?' is answered in the Atonement: God alone is like God, and only God could accomplish what Christ accomplished.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse asks: Do we truly believe that God is incomparable to the circumstances of our lives? When we face trials, loss, or uncertainty, do we reduce God to a scale where He competes with earthly powers? Isaiah 40:25 invites us to step back from the immediacy of our situation and ask: To what have I compared God lately? Have I made Him equal to my fear, my doubt, or the world's apparent power? The exiles' freedom began when they refused to liken their God to Babylon's gods. Our freedom begins when we stop sizing God down to fit our present anxieties.

text_kjv: Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things, that bringeth out their host by number: he calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might, for that he is strong in power; not one faileth.

commentary.narrative:
The Prophet now calls the exiles to look upward—literally and theologically. The "eyes on high" point to the stars, which in the ancient world were considered eternal and divine. If God created and personally names every star—literally calling them forth into visibility by their individual names—then His knowledge is intimate and comprehensive. The image is of a military commander at roll call, speaking each soldier's name to confirm their presence. No star is missing; not one fails to appear when called. The theological argument is devastatingly simple: if God knows every star by name, surely He has not forgotten Israel. The exiles can see the stars nightly; they are a visible, nightly demonstration of God's intimate knowledge and comprehensive power.

The Covenant Rendering's emphasis on "not one is missing" (rather than KJV's "not one faileth") makes the argument even more direct. In Hebrew, the original language carries the sense of a master call, where each entity responds to its name. This is the opposite of the exiles' fear (expressed in verse 27) that their cause has been "hidden" or "disregarded." God hides nothing—He names all. The stars become a kind of visual theology: if you doubt God's knowledge of your situation, look at the night sky and see how many things He knows by name.

word_study.meaning: to create, especially to create from nothing without preexisting material. This is the word used in Genesis 1:1 for God's initial creation act. It denotes creative power that requires no material substrate.
word_study.significance: By using *bara*, Isaiah claims for God the kind of creative power that is absolutely unique and unrepeatable. No human craftsman or idol-maker can *bara*; they can only reshape existing materials. God's incomparability (verse 25) is grounded in His singular creative capacity.

word_study.meaning: army, host, multitude. Often used for heavenly armies or the vast array of created things organized under God's command. The word carries a sense of military organization and obedience.
word_study.significance: The stars are not random scattering but an organized *tzava*—a host under command. This military imagery reinforces the exilic context: just as a general knows the disposition of his troops, God knows the arrangement and status of all creation. The exiles' captors may control Jerusalem, but God commands the cosmos.

word_study.meaning: by count, by enumeration. Suggests not just observation but systematic accounting and knowledge. Every star is counted; not one is omitted from God's enumeration.
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes exhaustive knowledge. God does not roughly estimate the stars; He counts them. The ancient world considered this impossible—how could anyone count the stars? Yet Isaiah asserts that God does exactly this, and does so while calling each by name.

word_study.meaning: to call by name; to speak forth into existence or recognition. The verb *qara* carries both the sense of naming and summoning. When God "calls" a star by name, He simultaneously knows it and brings it into active existence.
word_study.significance: In Hebrew thought, to know something's name is to have power over it and intimate knowledge of it. When God calls Israel by name (Isaiah 43:1), He is claiming them with the same comprehensive knowledge and power He exercises over the stars. The parallelism is intentional: God knows the stars by name, therefore God knows Israel by name.

word_study.meaning: not one is absent, not one is lacking, not one fails to appear. The root *adar* suggests absence or deficiency. The negative double-assertion (not one) emphasizes completeness.
word_study.significance: This is the emotional anchor of the verse. Against the exiles' fear that they have been forgotten (verse 27), Isaiah says: Look at the stars. Every single one appears. Every single one is known and called forth. This is how God operates. Do you really believe He has forgotten you when He has not forgotten a single star?

cross_references.connection: He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names.' This Psalm directly parallels Isaiah 40:26, making the star-naming claim a recurring motif in Hebrew wisdom about God's comprehensive knowledge.
I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine.' The promise given to Israel directly echoes the pattern established in verse 26: God calls things and people by name with intimate knowledge and claim.

The LORD hath appeared of old unto me, saying, Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love.' The same era of prophecy (exilic period) reassures Israel that God's attention and love have not ceased, parallel to Isaiah's argument about the stars.

There is no such thing as immaterial matter. All spirit is matter... The revealed understanding of creation in D&C expands on the comprehensive divine knowledge asserted here: God's knowledge extends to all substance, spiritual and temporal.

Lehi's vision of God seated upon His throne surrounded by countless angels reflects the same picture of comprehensive divine presence and knowledge that Isaiah describes through the stars—a heavenly host organized and known.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the stars were often considered divine or the dwelling places of gods. Mesopotamian astronomy was highly advanced; the Babylonians had cataloged visible stars and created the zodiac. However, the theological claim that a single God could *know* all stars by name was unique to Israel's monotheism. The exiles would have heard Babylonian priests claim knowledge of the stars for divination purposes, but Isaiah inverts this: it is not that stars reveal the future to humans; rather, God's perfect knowledge of the stars is *evidence* of His comprehensive care for all creation, including Israel. The night sky, visible to the exiles every evening, becomes a nightly sermon on God's attentiveness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Jacob 4:8–9, Jacob teaches that God knows all things, past, present, and future: 'But behold, the Jews were a stiffnecked people; and they despised the words of plainness, and killed the prophets, and sought for things that they could not understand. Wherefore, because of their blindness, which blindness came upon them by the looking beyond the mark, they must needs fall.' The pattern of comprehensive divine knowledge enabling covenant faithfulness appears throughout the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:6–13 teaches that the light of Christ enlightens all things and that God's knowledge is comprehensive and immediate. The principle established in Isaiah 40:26—that God knows all things—is foundational to D&C theology about God's omniscience and the nature of divine light.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge is central to the covenant. God does not covenant with a people generally; He knows and claims each individual member by name. The veil represents the barrier between this comprehensive divine knowledge and human understanding, which is progressively removed through ordinances.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the Word by whom all things were created (John 1:3), and He is the One who calls His sheep by name (John 10:3). The stars created and called forth by God in Isaiah 40:26 are called forth by Christ in His capacity as Creator. When the exiles heard this promise that God names all the stars, they foreshadowed the Gospel promise that the Savior calls His covenant people by name individually, knowing each one completely.
commentary.application: In our modern context, we live under an incomprehensibly vast cosmos—more stars visible to us through telescopes than were visible to the ancients. Isaiah's promise becomes even more extraordinary: God knows by name not just the visible stars but all of them. When we feel invisible, forgotten, or lost in the crowd, Isaiah 40:26 offers a radical counter-narrative: the God who numbers and names the stars knows you specifically. He has not forgotten your name, your circumstances, or your faith. The question for us is not whether God knows us but whether we truly believe He does. Modern disciples are invited to look at the night sky not as an illustration of our cosmic insignificance but as evidence of God's intimate, comprehensive care.

text_kjv: Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, My way is hid from the LORD, and my judgment is passed over from my God?

commentary.narrative:
Now Isaiah names the doubt directly. The double address—"Jacob" and "Israel"—encompasses the entire covenant community without distinction. Both names (the patriarch and the nation he fathered) are invoked to show that this is not a temporary complaint but a deep theological despair rooted in the covenant identity itself. The exiles are not just sad or anxious; they are making a claim about God's nature and His relationship to them. They say: "My way is hidden from the LORD." In other words, God does not see what is happening to us. He is blind to our condition. More than that, they claim: "My judgment is passed over." The Hebrew *mishpati* (my right, my judgment, my justice) refers to their rightful claim on God's covenant obligation. The exiles feel that God has overlooked His own promise to vindicate them.

This complaint must be understood in its historical depth. The exiles have been in Babylon for roughly fifty years (if dated to 540 BCE). A generation born in captivity has known nothing else. The temple is destroyed; the Davidic monarchy is gone; Jerusalem is a city under foreign occupation. From a purely earthly perspective, the complaint makes sense. Where is God's vindication? Where is the deliverance promised through covenant? Isaiah does not ridicule this despair; rather, he shows it to be a logical error given what verse 26 has just claimed about God's comprehensive knowledge. If God knows every star by name, then by definition, He cannot have missed Israel. The complaint rests on the false assumption that Israel has become so insignificant that God's attention has wandered from them.

word_study.meaning: path, way, journey, conduct, manner of life. Can denote both the literal path one walks and the figurative course of one's life or circumstances.
word_study.significance: The exiles claim their *derek* is hidden from God—that is, their entire situation, their path of suffering, is unobserved. But in Hebrew thought, one's *derek* is transparent to God. The complaint reveals a foundational misunderstanding about God's nature.

word_study.meaning: hidden, concealed, obscured from view. The passive voice suggests that something has been hidden from the observer, not intentionally hidden but simply out of sight.
word_study.significance: The exiles feel that God's attention has been diverted or that their situation has become invisible to Him. This is presented as the psychological root of their despair—not wickedness, but a collapse of confidence in God's attentiveness.

word_study.meaning: judgment, justice, right, claim, vindication. In a covenant context, it denotes the rightful obligation God has toward His people and their rightful claim on His justice.
word_study.significance: The exiles are not simply complaining about personal hardship; they are asserting that God has not fulfilled His covenant obligation to vindicate them. They feel entitled to *mishpat* by covenant, and God has not delivered it. This is a covenant claim, not mere complaint.

word_study.meaning: to pass by, to pass over, to go beyond, to transgress. Can mean both physical passage and the idea of overlooking or neglecting.
word_study.significance: The exiles claim God has *abar*—passed over—their justice. The same root is used in Exodus 12 for the Passover, when God passes over the homes of the faithful. Here, the exiles feel that God has passed them by without stopping to deliver them.

cross_references.connection: Why hast thou forgotten me? Why go I mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?' The complaint in Isaiah 40:27 echoes a pattern of psalmist despair that God has forgotten His people, which is answered throughout the Psalms by recourse to God's remembered covenant.

We have transgressed and have rebelled: thou hast not pardoned. Thou hast covered thyself with anger, and persecuted us.' Lamentation articulates the same sense that God has turned His face away and hidden His response. Isaiah 40:27 captures the emotional and theological crisis of the exilic period.

I will hide my face from them, and they shall be devoured... This covenant curse articulates the inverse of what the exiles fear in verse 27. They fear they have become the cursed ones from whom God hides His face.

Zion said, The LORD hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me. Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.' Later in Isaiah, the same complaint is answered with a direct divine promise not to forget.
Alma describes the moment when he cried out to Christ despite his despair, and was answered. The pattern of covenant doubt followed by covenant reassurance appears throughout the Book of Mormon.

commentary.historical_context: The exilic period (586–539 BCE) was a profound theological and psychological crisis for Judah. The destruction of the temple was interpreted not just as military defeat but as potential evidence that God had abandoned His people or been defeated by Babylon's gods. The Babylonian "New Year" festival celebrated Marduk's victory over chaos; exiled Judeans witnessed annual public theology asserting Babylon's divine triumph. In this context, Isaiah's challenge to the exiles' despair is not sentimental but radical: he is claiming that Israel's God has not been defeated, has not turned away, and has not forgotten. The complaint articulated in verse 27 would have been the constant ambient despair of the exile. Some scholars suggest that parts of the Book of Lamentations, which express similar despair, were composed during or immediately after the fall of Jerusalem, making Isaiah 40's answer to that despair theologically crucial.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 15:4–11, Laman and Lemuel despair that God has hidden His face from Israel and that their wilderness journey is abandoned. Nephi responds by teaching them the very principle Isaiah establishes here: God has not forgotten; they have not understood covenant. The pattern of covenant doubt answered by covenant reaffirmation runs throughout the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–3 records Joseph Smith's anguished cry in Liberty Jail: 'O God, where art thou? And where is the pavilion that covereth thy hiding place?' The language of divine hiddenness and human despair echoes Isaiah 40:27. D&C 121:7–9 provides the answer: the Lord has not forsaken Joseph, though his situation seems hidden from divine attention. This is a latter-day Isaian moment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the place where God's hiddenness is answered by presence. The veil separates the hidden from the revealed, and temple ordinances progressively remove that barrier. In the context of exile, the temple's destruction meant the loss of the primary physical space where God's presence was ordinarily manifest. Isaiah's consolation promises that God's presence is not localized to the destroyed temple but extends to all creation and to Israel herself.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ, in His passion, cried out with language echoing verse 27: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46, quoting Psalm 22:1). Christ experienced what the exiles feared—a moment when God's face seemed hidden. Yet Christ's Atonement is precisely the answer to the exiles' complaint: God has not abandoned His people but has provided the ultimate vindication through the sacrifice of His Son. The *mishpat* (justice, vindication) that the exiles felt was denied them is fulfilled in Christ's resurrection and in the promise of universal resurrection and judgment.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members recognize verse 27 in their own moments of despair. When prayers seem unanswered, when circumstances seem unjust, when the course of our lives feels hidden from God's view, we are tempted to the same complaint. Isaiah invites us to a different perspective: What if your circumstance is not hidden from God but rather you have forgotten that God sees all? What if your *mishpat*—your rightful claim on God's covenant promises—has not been overlooked but is being kept in God's eternal record? The exiles' recovery came not through their situation changing (they still faced the journey back to Judah) but through their understanding of who God is. Modern application requires the same reframing: Do I believe that God sees, even when I cannot see His action? Can I trust His covenant when His vindication is delayed?

text_kjv: Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah now answers the exiles' despair with a direct assertion about God's nature. The double interrogative—"Hast thou not known? Hast thou not heard?"—appeals to knowledge that should be foundational and obvious. This is not new revelation but a call to remember what has always been true. God is *Elohei olam*, the everlasting God, the God who exists beyond time itself. The appellation comes from Genesis 21:33, where Abraham calls on this very name, grounding the exiles' confidence in the deepest wells of their patriarchal tradition. This God does not faint (*ya'af*) or grow weary (*yiga'*) as humans do. The exiles might fear that God's attention has wandered because they themselves are exhausted; they might assume that if they are weary, God must be too. Isaiah categorically denies this assumption.

The statement "there is no searching of his understanding" (or as The Covenant Rendering puts it, "His understanding is unsearchable") introduces a final note of mystery. God is not just powerful but inscrutable. His ways cannot be computed or fully grasped by human reason. This is not a barrier to faith but its foundation. If God's understanding could be fully searched and measured by human minds, then God would be smaller than human comprehension—and therefore not truly God. The exiles' confusion about why they suffer is rooted in the illusion that God's plan should be comprehensible to them. Isaiah offers a more mature faith: God's understanding is beyond searching, therefore trust is not based on understanding but on the character of the One whom we cannot fully understand.

word_study.meaning: God of eternity, the everlasting God, God who exists beyond all time. *Olam* denotes the distant past and distant future, time without visible boundaries. This is the God who never began and never ends.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that this title emphasizes God's existence beyond time. For exiles who live in the moment-by-moment despair of captivity, this title is revolutionary. God is not caught in the present crisis; He stands outside of time itself. What appears to be abandonment to time-bound humans is invisible to the eternal God who sees past and future simultaneously.

word_study.meaning: does not faint, does not weaken, does not grow exhausted. *Ya'af* is the opposite of strength and alertness; it describes the collapse of energy and attention.
word_study.significance: The same verb will be used in verse 30 to describe youths who *do* faint and grow weary. Isaiah is setting up a contrast: God never experiences what humanity inevitably experiences. The exiles' exhaustion is real, but it is not God's condition. God does not tire of watching over them.

word_study.meaning: does not grow weary, does not become tired. *Yiga'* describes the wear and tear of effort, the accumulated fatigue that even the strongest eventually experience.
word_study.significance: This verb also reappears in verse 30 in reference to young men. The repetition creates a powerful contrast between God's nature (never tiring) and human nature (inevitably tiring). Even the strongest humans eventually weary; God never does.

word_study.meaning: searching out, investigation, inquiry. The root suggests a systematic effort to discover hidden things. To *cheqer* something is to investigate it thoroughly until it is understood.
word_study.significance: By saying there is no *cheqer* of God's understanding, Isaiah is claiming that God's mind cannot be exhaustively investigated or comprehended. This is not about God hiding information but about the fundamental gap between divine omniscience and human limited cognition. It is an epistemological statement: some things about God cannot be found out by searching.

word_study.meaning: understanding, discernment, wisdom, intelligence. The term denotes both the capacity to understand and the actual knowledge possessed. God's *tevunah* is His comprehensive perception and wisdom.
word_study.significance: The exiles' despair is rooted in their inability to understand God's plan. Isaiah affirms that this inability is not a defect in them but a reflection of the infinite nature of God's *tevunah*. Some mysteries are meant to remain mysteries, and faith does not require their resolution.

cross_references.connection: Abraham called there on the name of the LORD, the everlasting God.' This is the original source of the *Elohei olam* title, grounding the exiles in their patriarchal heritage and showing that the God of Abraham is the same God who sustains them now.

Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.' The same title and the same assertion of God's eternal nature appear in the Psalms, suggesting this was central to Hebrew theology.

For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen... even his eternal power and Godhead.' Paul grounds knowledge of God's eternality and power in creation itself, parallel to Isaiah's use of the stars in verse 26.

Hearken to the voice of the Lord your God, while I speak unto you; for the hour is nigh, and the day soon at hand when the earth is ripe; nevertheless, my word shall all be fulfilled. The revelation announces that God's word and understanding transcend human time; what appears unfulfilled in the moment will be fulfilled in God's eternal economy.

And I knew that the Lord God was with me, therefore I could not be overpowered... Nephi exhibits the faith that verse 28 calls for: trust in God's eternal nature and power even when circumstances suggest otherwise.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the gods were typically portrayed as powerful but finite. They struggled against chaos, faced rivals, and required human support (through sacrifice and worship) to maintain their strength. The biblical God is radically different: eternal, never tiring, beyond human comprehension. For Babylonian exiles surrounded by temple theology that depicted gods as needing human support and facing rivals, Isaiah's portrait of the everlasting God who never faints or grows weary would have been countercultural and reassuring. It asserts that Israel's God is fundamentally different from the gods of the empire. The exiles' exhaustion was real; Isaiah acknowledges human limitation while denying that God shares it.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 26:35, Ammon declares: 'And I trust that when they shall be raised from the dead they will be redeemed, and be exalted by the resurrection of Christ unto a state of never-ending happiness.' The Book of Mormon affirms the eternal nature of God's plan and the impossibility of His failing, even when circumstances seem to suggest otherwise. The exiles' doubt is answered by the same appeal to God's eternal character.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 38:1–2 directly echoes verse 28: 'Hearken, O ye people of my church, saith the voice of him whose eyes are upon all men, and whose ear is open unto the cries of the righteous, saith Jesus Christ your Redeemer, the eternal God.' The eternal nature of God is affirmed in modern revelation with explicit connection to God's attentiveness—the very thing the exiles doubt in verse 27.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ordinance represents a covenant made with a God who is eternal, unchanging, and forever. The veil symbolizes the boundary between time and eternity. Temple worship is the place where mortals encounter the eternal God; in that encounter, the limitation of time-bound understanding is momentarily transcended.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is described in Revelation 1:8 as "the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the ending." This is Christ's claim to the very eternality (*Elohei olam*) that Isaiah asserts. Moreover, in Hebrews 7:24–25, Christ is portrayed as having an unchanging priesthood because He ever lives: "But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood; wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them." Christ's eternal nature is the ground of His power to save. The exiles' salvation depends on the eternality of God that verse 28 asserts.
commentary.application: For modern disciples, verse 28 confronts us with a crucial question: Do we truly believe that God never tires of caring for us?
