Our modern culture is built on human capacity: we measure progress, attention, and love by human metrics of energy and time. We tire; therefore, we assume that if we have been struggling without visible divine response, God must be tired of our case or distracted by more important matters. Isaiah categorically denies this. God does not grow weary of your prayers, your struggle, or your faithfulness. The unsearchability of God's understanding, moreover, invites us to release the demand that we understand why we suffer or why God's deliverance is delayed. We are invited to trust not because we comprehend the plan but because we trust the Character of the One executing it. This is mature covenant faith.

text_kjv: He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 29 moves from assertion of God's eternal nature to the application of that eternal power to human weakness. The verse presents a profound paradox: the God who never tires is the One who meets the exhausted; the God who never faints strengthens those who are fainting. This is not a logical impossibility but a profound inversion of how human power typically works. Humans lose patience with the weak; the strongest typically increase their strength to overcome opposition, not to help the helpless. But God's power moves in the opposite direction. He gives *power* (*koach*) to the *faint* (*ya'aif*)—those in the condition of utter depletion. The Covenant Rendering adds the note that He gives strength "to him who has no might," emphasizing the singular, personal nature of the gift. This is not generic aid but specific assistance to individuals who have reached the end of their resources.

The second clause intensifies the image: "to them that have no might he increaseth strength." The Hebrew *ein onim* (no might, no strength) describes total powerlessness. The exiles might be thinking: We are deportees, slaves in a foreign land, living in the wreckage of our nation. We have no might, no resources, no capacity to change our situation. Isaiah's response is that this very condition—total depletion—is precisely where God's power becomes active. God does not help the already-strong; He increases strength in the utterly weak. This verse is the emotional climax of the passage. It answers the exiles' despair not with argument about God's nature (which verse 28 established) but with the promise of personal, immediate assistance. The God who never tires is the God who walks with the exhausted.

word_study.meaning: strength, power, might, capacity. Can denote physical strength, military power, or the capacity to act. The term is fundamental to discussions of agency and efficacy in Hebrew.
word_study.significance: The exiles are told they will receive *koach*—actual, operative power to continue. This is not merely encouragement but the gift of the ability to act, to endure, to move forward. God does not simply console the weak; He imparts power to them.

word_study.meaning: faint, weary, exhausted, weak. The same root used in verse 28 to describe what God never is: the state of total fatigue and loss of strength.
word_study.significance: The deliberate echo of verse 28 creates the paradox: God, who never *ya'af*, gives power to those who do *ya'af*. The contrast is the point. God's eternal unfatigability is precisely what enables Him to minister to the fatigued.

word_study.meaning: no strength, no might, no power, absolute powerlessness. *Onim* (from *on*, strength) describes the absence of operative power.
word_study.significance: The phrase describes not merely fatigue but complete impotence. The exiles have no ability to change their situation. Yet to this condition of absolute powerlessness, God promises the increase of strength. The message is radical: your powerlessness is not disqualifying for God's aid; it is precisely the condition that triggers it.

word_study.meaning: increases strength, multiplies might, augments power. The verb *yarbeh* (to increase, to multiply) suggests not just giving strength once but continuously adding to it.
word_study.significance: The promise is not a one-time gift but an ongoing process. God does not strengthen the weak once and leave them; He continuously multiplies their strength. This is a covenant promise of sustained support.

cross_references.connection: I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.' Paul echoes the promise of verse 29: the power to endure and accomplish comes not from human capacity but from divine strengthening, particularly through Christ.

Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me. Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities... for when I am weak, then am I strong.' Paul explicitly frames the principle of verse 29: weakness becomes the occasion for divine power to manifest.

If men come unto me I will show unto them their weakness. I give unto men weakness that they may be humble... And if men come unto me I will show unto them their weakness... that they may... rely upon my mercy. The Book of Mormon explicitly teaches the principle established in Isaiah 40:29: God permits weakness so that His strength can be manifest.

And whoso receiveth you, there I will be also, for I will go before your face. I will be on your right hand and on your left, and my Spirit shall be in your hearts, and mine angels round about you, to bear you up.' The promise of verse 29 is renewed in modern revelation: God goes with the weak and increases their strength through His presence.

The Lord did strengthen them that they could bear up their burdens with ease... they did submit cheerfully and with patience to all the will of the Lord.' The Book of Mormon demonstrates the practical outworking of the principle in verse 29: those who acknowledge their dependence receive strength to endure.

commentary.historical_context: In the exilic period, the most psychologically damaging aspect of deportation was not merely the loss of territory but the loss of agency. The exiles were subjects of the Babylonian empire, unable to control their destiny, living as aliens in a foreign land. The promise of verse 29 would have been radical: not "Your political power will be restored" (which would not happen for decades), but "God will give you power—operative strength—to continue, to endure, to survive, even now, in your condition of powerlessness." This is a theology of survival and resilience rather than a theology of political restoration. It speaks to the deepest need of the desperate: the ability to keep going when circumstances offer no reason for hope.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 36, Alma describes his conversion experience in which he was conscious of his utter spiritual weakness—his "gall of bitterness" and "bonds of iniquity." Yet in that very condition, he cried out to Christ and received strength. The Book of Mormon pattern is consistent: recognize your *ein onim* (no strength), cry out to God, and receive the increase of strength. Jacob 7:5 and other passages similarly show individuals at the point of despair receiving divine strength.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 19:38–40 teaches that in the last days, before Christ comes, there will be tribulation and the gospel shall be preached in weakness: 'Nevertheless, inasmuch as they repent and receive the fulness of my gospel, prepare yourselves for the coming of the Bridegroom; otherwise, they shall be appointed to wait without, until I shall come.' The pattern of weakness leading to divine strength characterizes the path of latter-day Saints as well.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, covenants are made not on the basis of human strength but on the basis of God's promise to uphold the covenant-maker. The temple is the place where mortals in their weakness (symbolized by the removal of worldly distinction) are invited to receive the power of covenant with the Eternal. The endowment explicitly teaches that strength comes through binding oneself to God's purposes.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the ultimate manifestation of verse 29's principle. In His mortality, He experienced hunger, thirst, pain, and the approach of death—moments of utter weakness. Yet from those moments of maximum weakness came maximum power: the Atonement was wrought through His willingness to endure to the uttermost limit of human suffering. In Gethsemane and on Golgotha, Christ was strengthened not by external power but by complete submission to the Father's will. The risen Christ bears the marks of His suffering—the wounds in His hands, feet, and side—as eternal testimony to the power that flows through weakness.
commentary.application: For modern disciples, verse 29 offers both comfort and challenge. Comfort: if you find yourself depleted, without resources, facing circumstances beyond your capacity, this verse promises that God specifically gives power to the faint, the utterly weak, the powerless. This is God's specialization. The challenge: the verse assumes we have come to the end of ourselves, that we recognize our *ein onim*—our powerlessness. Modern culture trains us to hide weakness, to project strength, to seek human solutions and resources first. Isaiah 40:29 invites us to a different path: radical honesty about our limitation and radical trust in God's response to that limitation. When do we actually experience the increase of strength promised here? When we stop pretending we have power and ask God for His. This is the essential movement from worldliness to covenant life.

text_kjv: Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall:

commentary.narrative:
Verse 30 presents the hard truth that precedes the climactic promise of verse 31. Even the strongest humans—youths in their prime physical vigor, young men at the peak of their power—will faint (*ya'afu*) and grow weary (*yiga'u*). The deliberate repetition of the same verbs used in verse 28 to describe what God *never* does now describes what humans *inevitably* do. There is no class of humans exempt from this fundamental condition of mortal limitation. Not the physically strongest. Not the most energetic. Not those blessed with youth and vigor. All shall faint; all shall grow weary; all shall fall.

The Covenant Rendering's phrase "fall exhausted" captures the image: the collapse is not primarily moral failure or sin but the inevitable consequence of being human and finite. The exiles might have believed that if only they were stronger, younger, more vigorous, they could endure their captivity. Verse 30 removes this false hope. It is not that the exiles are exceptionally weak; it is that all humans, without exception, reach the limit of their strength. This is the prerequisite for verse 31's promise. Only those who have fully surrendered the illusion of self-sufficiency can receive the supernatural strengthening offered next. The verse functions as a kind of spiritual breaking, a dismantling of every human resource on which the exiles might place their hope, so that their hope can be relocated entirely to God.

word_study.meaning: youths, young men, boys. The term typically denotes males from late adolescence through early adulthood, the demographic group characterized by physical vigor and energy.
word_study.significance: By specifically naming the *ne'arim*, Isaiah emphasizes that even those in the prime of life are subject to limitation. If youth cannot endure indefinitely, then no human stage of life can. The choice of this demographic is deliberate: it removes all exemptions.

word_study.meaning: shall faint, shall weaken, shall lose strength. This is the same root used in verses 28 and 29 but now applied to humans rather than to God or to God's response to weakness.
word_study.significance: The verbal echo creates the tragic recognition: what does not happen to God inevitably happens to humans. The contrast is the entire point. By verse 31, the reader understands the gap between divine and human capacity, which makes the promise of supernatural assistance extraordinary.

word_study.meaning: shall be weary, shall grow tired, shall lose energy. This is also the same root used in verses 28 and 29.
word_study.significance: The repetition is grammatically redundant—youth faint and are weary is almost the same statement. But rhetorical redundancy is the point: the affirmation is absolute and universal. There is no escape from weariness for mortal humans.

word_study.meaning: young men, chosen men, warriors. The term can carry a sense of those selected for strength or capability. It emphasizes not just youth but the category of humans typically considered to be at their best.
word_study.significance: By naming the *bachurim*—the chosen, the strong, those who would typically be selected for demanding tasks—Isaiah universalizes the condition of human limitation. Even the best of humanity exhausts itself.

word_study.meaning: shall stumble, shall fall, shall collapse. The root *kashal* denotes falling or stumbling, often used metaphorically for failure or defeat. The doubled form (infinitive absolute + finite verb) intensifies the meaning: they shall absolutely, utterly, inevitably fall.
word_study.significance: The intensified form removes all ambiguity. This is not a possibility or a likelihood; it is absolute certainty. All humans will reach a point of collapse. The promise of verse 31 comes only after this absolute surrender of human self-sufficiency.

cross_references.connection: Vanity of vanities; all is vanity... What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?' Ecclesiastes explores the same theme of universal human limitation and the eventual futility of human effort, leading to the same conclusion verse 31 will offer: reliance on God.
For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.' Paul universalizes human limitation in the spiritual realm, parallel to Isaiah's universalization of human weakness in the temporal realm.

For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.' This verse affirms that Christ took on human limitation (while remaining sinless), understanding intimately the weariness and falling that verse 30 describes.

And now, my son, all men that are in a state of nature, or I would say, in a carnal state, are in the gall of bitterness and in the bonds of iniquity... This is the spiritual parallel: all humans without exception are in bondage to mortality and sin, a condition from which only divine intervention can free them.

The revelation teaches that all things are held together by the light of Christ and that without that light, all things would return to nothing. Verse 30's assertion of universal human limitation is the prerequisite for understanding the absolute necessity of God's sustaining power.

commentary.historical_context: In the exilic period, the exiles might have held onto hope that if they could somehow generate enough strength, endurance, or effort, they could escape their situation or at least survive it through sheer determination. This was a false hope. No amount of human effort would free them from Babylon until God moved to do so. The verse is psychologically astute: it removes the burden of expecting human will to solve the situation. This paradoxically can be liberating. The exiles cannot change their circumstances; therefore, their energy should not be directed toward the futile task of self-rescue but toward faith in the One who can deliver them. In the context of ancient military and athletic imagery, where strength and youth were celebrated, this verse's assertion that even the strongest fall would have been radical and counter-cultural.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 3:19, King Benjamin teaches: 'For the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever, unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit, and putteth off the natural man and becometh a saint through the atonement of Christ the Lord.' The Book of Mormon affirms the total insufficiency of natural human strength, paralleling verse 30's assertion.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:19–20 teaches: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the prophecies and promises which are in them shall all be fulfilled. What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken... and all this shall surely come to pass.' The contrast between God's word (which will surely be fulfilled) and human capacity (which will surely fail) is the context for the promise verse 31 will offer.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, the stripping away of worldly clothing and distinction symbolizes the removal of the false self that relies on external marks of status and power. The temple ceremony acknowledges that all who enter—regardless of their worldly position—come as equals before God, all equally dependent on divine grace. Verse 30's assertion of universal human limitation is the prerequisite for temple covenants.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 30 prepares the way for understanding Christ's incarnation as the assumption of full human limitation. Christ, being fully human, experienced the weariness, hunger, pain, and approach of death that verse 30 describes. Yet Christ is also fully divine—the very God of verse 28 who never faints or grows weary. Christ bridges the gap. In His resurrection and exaltation, He demonstrates that human limitation is not final; it can be overcome through submission to God. Those who participate in Christ's resurrection share in His victory over the limitation that verse 30 universalizes.
commentary.application: For modern disciples, verse 30 functions as a reality check against the gospel of self-improvement that pervades contemporary culture. We are invited to surrender the fantasy that discipline, energy, and effort alone will sustain us spiritually or solve our deepest problems. Young people especially—who naturally possess physical vigor and energy—may be tempted to believe that their strength is sufficient. Verse 30 says: you will faint; you will weary; you will fall. This is not pessimism but realism. The promise that follows (verse 31) is only meaningful if we first accept the diagnosis: we cannot endure on our own strength. A modern application might be: When do you finally stop striving in your own power? When do you finally accept that your effort, however earnest, is insufficient for your deepest needs? In that moment of acceptance—when you stop trying to fix yourself and open yourself to God's sustaining power—verse 31's promise becomes available to you. The exiles learned this in captivity. Modern disciples learn it in the crucible of their own weakness.

text_kjv: But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah 40:31 stands as one of Scripture's most beloved and quoted verses, yet its power is frequently domesticated into mere comfort rather than understood as a radical promise about the mechanics of faith itself. The prophet is addressing exiled Israel in Babylon—a people physically displaced, spiritually depleted, and tempted to despair. Into this darkness comes not a command to try harder, but a revelation: those who wait upon the LORD do not generate their own strength; they exchange their exhaustion for His. The Covenant Rendering's translation of yachalifu as 'exchange' rather than 'renew' captures something critical: this is not a repair job on the human will, but a replacement of one kind of power for another entirely. The waiting is not passive resignation—the Hebrew qavah carries the sense of a cord pulled tight with expectant tension—but active, disciplined trust that God's power is available for those who position themselves to receive it.
commentary.narrative_continued: The three-fold sequence that follows—soaring on eagles' wings, running without weariness, walking without fainting—is theologically surprising and deliberate. We expect the progression to move from walking to running to flying (effort increasing). Instead, Isaiah reverses it. The grand gesture comes first: the dramatic ascent, the moment of transcendence. But here is the profound truth embedded in the verse's structure: the sustained daily walk of faithfulness requires more enduring grace than the singular moment of soaring. Any believer can have a peak experience, a moment of divine encounter where strength seems unlimited. What takes true faith is the ordinary Tuesday afternoon, the faithful step when no one is watching, the continued forward progress when the initial enthusiasm has worn away. This is why the verse ends not with 'they shall fly' but 'they shall walk and not faint.' The deepest test of faith is not the dramatic but the daily.
commentary.narrative_continued2: The historical context deepens the meaning. The exiles hearing Isaiah's words were not faced with a single crisis but with decades of displacement and the slow erosion of hope. They needed not a one-time miracle but a renewable source of strength. They needed to understand that their weakness was not a permanent condition but an invitation—a place where God's power could enter if they would wait, trust, and allow the exchange to happen. The promise is not that circumstances will change (though they eventually did), but that the exile's children would be able to endure the exile with a strength not their own. For every generation reading this verse—whether in ancient Babylon or modern difficulty—the message remains: your depletion is not the final word. There is an inexhaustible source available to those who will wait for it with expectant faith.
commentary.narrative_continued3: Significantly, the Dead Sea Scrolls (1QIsaᵃ, column XXXIII, line 26) preserve the exact same Hebrew consonantal text for 'as eagles' (kansharim) as the Masoretic Text, confirming that this beloved promise has been transmitted identically across more than two thousand years. This textual stability across manuscripts underscores the verse's enduring centrality in Jewish and Christian tradition.
commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 40:31 points to Christ as the source of the strength exchange it promises. Christ is the Lord upon whom one waits; He is the Eagle who shelters and elevates; He is the one who 'shall mount up with wings as eagles'—an image that foreshadows His ascension. More theologically, Jesus embodies the principle of exchanged power: He emptied Himself of divine prerogative ('who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God,' Philippians 2:6), became human, experienced exhaustion and temptation, yet never yielded to despair—He walked the path of perfect obedience without fainting. His crucifixion and resurrection enact the ultimate 'exchange': His strength exchanged for humanity's weakness, His life for our death. The ascension literally fulfills the imagery of mounting up with eagles' wings. For believers, participation in Christ—waiting upon Him through faith, baptism, and covenant—makes available to them the same exchange of power He experienced. They do not generate their own righteousness or strength, but receive it as a free gift through Him. Isaiah 40:31 is thus a Messianic promise: it describes not merely what the exiles experience, but what becomes universally available when Christ comes and establishes His covenant with all people.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly affirms the principle of strength renewal through faith and covenant faithfulness. In Alma 26:12, Ammon declares: 'Yea, I say unto you, my brethren, if I could have felt as ye felt, and have weighed down by the sense of my guilt, I would not have dared to open my mouth nor written a word; therefore I write unto you; and ye receive my words.' The experience of exchanging human despair for God's strength through waiting and faith resonates throughout the Nephite record. More directly, in Alma 31:38, the anti-Nephi-Lehi people demonstrate the patience and faith that Isaiah 40:31 describes: 'And thus we see that the Lamanites were willing, after to hear the word of God; and we have reason to hope that the Lord will grant unto us success in bringing them to the knowledge of the truth, but we trust not in our own strength.' The willingness to relinquish reliance on human strength and 'wait' (in the sense of qavah—active expectation) upon God's power is the pattern of Book of Mormon covenant faithfulness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The Doctrine and Covenants contains explicit parallels to Isaiah 40:31. In D&C 64:34, the Lord teaches: 'Wherefore, be not weary in well-doing, for ye are laying the foundation of a great work. Out of small things proceedeth that which is great.' The language of not being 'weary' (yiga'u) directly echoes Isaiah. More profoundly, D&C 19:23 states: 'Therefore I command you to repent—repent, lest I smite you by the rod of my mouth, and by my wrath, and by my anger, and your sufferings be sore—how sore you know not, how exquisite you know not, yea, how hard to bear you know not.' The restoration framework emphasizes that waiting upon the LORD is not passive but involves active repentance, covenant-making, and sustained moral effort—the running and walking of verse 31. Additionally, in D&C 121:45-46, Joseph Smith receives a profound promise that echoes the exchange principle: 'Let thy bowels also be full of charity towards all men, and to the household of faith, and let virtue garnish thy thoughts unceasingly; then shall thy confidence wax strong in the presence of God.' The principle of exchanging human presumption for divine virtue through righteous positioning (waiting, trusting, keeping covenant) is central to Restoration theology.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Isaiah 40:31 has deep connections to the temple experience and covenants. The image of mounting up with eagles' wings recalls the vision in Exodus 19:4 that frames the covenant-making at Sinai. In Latter-day Saint temple experience, the endowment teaches the principle of ascending through successive levels of understanding and power—the 'mounting up' that Isaiah describes. The exchange of human strength for divine power through covenant and waiting is enacted in the temple through the taking of covenants that bind the individual to God's purposes. The promise that those who wait shall not be weary or faint is directly applicable to the sustained faithfulness required of endowed members who must live those covenants not just in the temple but through decades of daily discipleship. The temple teaches that our weakness is not shameful but the proper place for God's power to work; Isaiah 40:31 provides the theological framework for understanding why covenant-making and covenant-keeping are sustainable—because they are powered by exchanged strength, not human determination alone.

word_study.meaning: To wait with active, expectant trust; to hold tension like a taut cord; to hope with patient endurance. Not passive resignation but disciplined attention to God's time and movement.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that qavah is 'taut expectation'—an image of a rope pulled tight. This is not the waiting of someone idly passing time, but someone oriented toward God with every fiber of attention. In covenant language, this is the posture of those who have positioned themselves to receive God's power. The term appears throughout Isaiah (8:17, 25:9, 26:8, 33:2, 40:31, 49:23) as a signature theme of the prophet's consolation.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'they shall exchange' or 'they shall swap.' Not repair or restore (which would use another Hebrew term), but an actual transaction—giving up one thing to receive another. The root carries the sense of change, succession, and substitution.
word_study.significance: This is the verse's theological hinge. The KJV's 'renew' is not wrong, but 'exchange' captures the Hebrew's radical claim: we do not strengthen our own strength. We trade exhausted human power for God's inexhaustible power. This is why the verse belongs in the context of waiting—only those who relinquish their grip on self-sufficiency are in position to make this exchange. The term yachalifu appears nowhere else in Isaiah, making this a unique and deliberate word choice for this singular promise.

word_study.meaning: To rise up, ascend, go upward. Eber (wing) is the literal instrument of ascent. The image is of soaring upward without struggle—effortless elevation.
word_study.significance: The language of rising and ascending is frequent in Isaiah's consolation (40:9, 43:1, 52:7). But the specific image of mounting up 'with wings as eagles' invokes not human effort but divine nature. Eagles do not struggle to fly; their structure makes flight natural. The promise is that those who wait upon God will find that the very act of ascending—previously impossible—becomes natural, becoming an expression of their renewed nature.

word_study.meaning: To work hard to the point of exhaustion; to become weary from exertion. The root suggests both physical fatigue and the emotional weariness of labor without reward.
word_study.significance: The promise is not that they will run more slowly, but that they will run and not be weary—the exertion will continue, but the depletion will not follow. This distinguishes between activity and exhaustion. The covenant believer can engage fully in the race of faith without the collapse that normally accompanies such effort.

word_study.transliteration: yaaph (to be faint, exhausted, worn out)
word_study.meaning: To become faint, to lose strength, to be depleted. Often paired with yaga (weary) to suggest both the exertion and the resulting collapse. The term carries a sense of final collapse—the point beyond mere tiredness.
word_study.significance: The sequence of negations is precise: 'run and not be weary, walk and not faint.' The running demands exertion; the walking demands endurance. Both are promised to continue without the failure that naturally follows human effort. This is not a promise of superhuman speed, but of sustained human faithfulness powered by a strength not one's own.

cross_references.connection: God speaks to Israel at Sinai: 'Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bare you on eagles' wings.' Isaiah's promise of mounting up with eagles' wings echoes God's covenant protection of Israel, suggesting that those who wait on the LORD participate in the same sheltering, elevating power promised at Sinai.

The psalmist counsels: 'Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD.' This parallel use of qavah (wait) linked with strength (koach) directly anticipates Isaiah 40:31's promise that waiting upon God produces strength renewal.

He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.' Isaiah's promise of strength through waiting echoes the Wisdom tradition's insight that true power lies not in human exertion but in disciplined trust and self-mastery.

Alma teaches: 'And now I say unto you that the good shepherd doth call you; yea, and in his own name he doth call you, which is the name of Christ.' The Book of Mormon affirms that those who answer Christ's call and follow Him experience renewal and strength, paralleling Isaiah's promise of exchanged power.

The Doctrine and Covenants declares: 'And I give unto you a commandment that you shall teach one another the doctrine of the kingdom. Teach ye diligently and my grace shall attend you.' The promise of grace attending those who wait and obey echoes Isaiah's exchange of human weakness for divine strength.

Moroni teaches: 'And if there be faults they be the faults of a man. But behold, we know no fault; nevertheless God knoweth all things.' The Restoration affirms that our weakness becomes the place where God's power enters, aligning with Isaiah's revelation of strength exchange through waiting faith.

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah 40:31 appears in the opening of what scholars call the 'Book of Consolation' (chapters 40-66), addressed to the exiled remnant of Judah in Babylon after 586 BCE. The historical background is crucial: the Jerusalem temple has been destroyed, the leadership deported, and the nation faces the question that haunts every exiled people—Is God still with us? Has He abandoned us? The promise of 'waiting upon the LORD' would have resonated with a people who could not immediately escape their circumstances but desperately needed to know that their strength was not tied to their political autonomy or geographical location. The image of eagles mounting up would evoke both the power of God's sovereignty (God riding on eagles' wings in protection) and the contrast with the earthly powerlessness of the exile. Structurally, verse 31 concludes Isaiah 40, providing the resolution to the chapter's opening question: 'Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard?' Yes, the exiles have not known and not heard—but the answer, the remedy, is available to those who will wait for it. The verse's position as the climactic promise of the chapter suggests that all preceding revelation (God's incomparable sovereignty, His sustenance of the natural world, His knowledge of all people) culminates in this personal, renewable application: You can exchange your exhaustion for His strength.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 40:31 is a diagnosis and a remedy for a plague peculiar to contemporary discipleship: the assumption that spiritual progress is powered by personal effort and willpower. We hear the call to 'run' in the race of faith—to serve, to repent, to grow, to love—and we exhaust ourselves trying to generate the righteousness through sheer determination. The verse offers a different model: position yourself through waiting (through prayer, study, fasting, covenant participation) to receive God's strength, then engage fully in the running and walking, knowing that the power is not yours but His. Practically, this means distinguishing between activity and exhaustion. A person may engage in great service—teaching, parenting, leading—without the depletion that normally follows such effort, if that effort is powered by exchanged strength rather than depleting willpower. The promise is not that the tasks become easier, but that they become sustainable. Spiritually, it means trusting that your weakness—your temptations, your grief, your confusion, your moral failure—are not disqualifications from the race but invitations to the exchange. Come to God in that weakness (wait, in the sense of qavah—with taut, expectant faith), and you will find your strength renewed not because you have fixed yourself, but because you have positioned yourself to receive His power. The most practical application is remembering that the third form of movement—walking without fainting—may require more faith than the dramatic soaring. The mountaintop experience fades; the sustained Tuesday-afternoon faithfulness is the test that proves whether you truly waited upon the Lord or merely sought a temporary uplift.

text_kjv: Keep silence before me, O islands; and let the people renew their strength: let them come near; then let them speak: let us come near together to judgment.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah 41 opens with one of scripture's most dramatic courtroom scenes. God summons the distant nations—the 'islands' or coastlands—to silence before Him, then paradoxically invites them to gather their strength and arguments for trial. This is not a private verdict but a public legal proceeding. The shift from 'Keep silence' to 'let them speak' to 'let us come near together' creates the structure of a formal trial: silence for respect before the judge, opportunity for the accused to marshal their case, and mutual approach to judgment. The phrase 'renew their strength' recalls Isaiah 40:31 ('they shall renew their strength'), but here it carries forensic weight—the nations are invited to bring their best arguments, their strongest case. This is God's confidence made visible: He will permit the nations full voice in their own defense because His position is unassailable.
commentary.narrative_continued: The context matters enormously. Israel in exile would have heard this as both accusation and comfort. Accusations against God were mounting in the mind of the deportees: Where is God's power? How could He allow Babylon to conquer the Holy Land? Why have the nations' gods proven mightier? God's answer begins here with a legal summons. He is not absent or defeated; He is plaintiff-judge, about to demonstrate that He—not Babylon, not the idols of the nations—directs history. The 'coastlands' (iyyim, עַיִּים) represents all the distant, powerful nations of the known world. God's willingness to have them speak their case is a rhetorical masterstroke: by the end of this trial (extending through chapter 45), their arguments will be shattered.
commentary.word_study_narrative: The Hebrew word yachalifu (יַחֲלִ֣יפוּ), 'renew,' literally means 'to exchange' or 'to relieve.' In the context of military strength (40:31) it means restoration of exhausted vigor. Here the legal dimension is unmistakable: the nations are invited to exchange weakness for their strongest case, to relieve themselves of doubt and approach with full confidence. The word mishpat (מִשְׁפָּט), 'judgment,' is not primarily about condemnation but about a legal proceeding, a trial where evidence is heard and a verdict rendered. God is invoking the ancient Near Eastern image of the divine judge convening court—a familiar metaphor in the ancient world where gods were imagined to govern through law and justice.
commentary.christological_typology: The trial God convenes prefigures the final judgment in which Christ sits as judge (Matthew 25:31-46, Revelation 20:11-15). The phrase 'I am He' in verse 4 becomes a messianic self-identification, later explicitly claimed by Jesus in John 8:58. The invitation to the nations to 'speak their case' and be proven wrong anticipates the moment when all nations will acknowledge Christ's lordship (Philippians 2:10). God's confident summons—inviting opposition, then dismantling it—models the victory of Christ over all earthly and spiritual powers.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 21 (which quotes Isaiah 49-50), the Book of Mormon preserves Isaiah's teaching about God's justice and the servant's vindication. The language of 'judgment' (mishpat) in Isaiah 41 establishes the framework that will govern the entire discourse about the Suffering Servant. In Latter-day revelation, D&C 76 presents a cosmic trial where all souls are judged according to law, echoing Isaiah's mishpat principle.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:29-30 affirms that God's judgments are delivered through His servants to all nations—a direct parallel to Isaiah's courtroom scene where God summons 'all nations' to hear. The D&C also emphasizes that God's word goes forth to prepare the way, much as Isaiah here summons the coastlands to witness God's vindication of His purpose. D&C 86:2-3 teaches that God's dominion extends over all the earth—consistent with Isaiah's summons to even the distant islands.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The courtroom language echoes the cosmic order taught in temple endowment: God as judge, law as binding principle, all accountable before divine justice. The 'silence before the judge' reflects the reverence required in approaching sacred space.

word_study.meaning: To be silent, still, deaf; to keep quiet; in some contexts, to plow (the primary sense). Here used as an imperative demanding silence before the divine judge. The word carries weight—not casual quietness but the respectful silence demanded in a courtroom or temple.
word_study.significance: The silencing of the nations is preparatory to hearing God's voice. It echoes the silence motif in ancient Near Eastern trial scenarios where the plaintiff-judge demands attention.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'islands' but used more broadly for distant coastlands, maritime regions, and by extension, all distant nations. In Isaiah, often a poetic term for 'the nations far away.' The word carries a sense of remoteness and otherness—these are the gentile world, the powers outside Israel's covenant.
word_study.significance: Summoning the iyyim means calling even the remotest powers to account. None are beyond God's jurisdiction. The use of this term emphasizes God's sovereignty over the entire known world.

word_study.meaning: To exchange or relieve strength; to restore vigor. The same phrase appears in Isaiah 40:31, where those who wait upon the Lord 'shall renew their strength.' Here the ironic reversal is profound: the nations are invited to renew their strength—but their strength will be revealed as nothing before God's purpose.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures this as 'gather your best arguments'—the legal sense is that the nations are to come fully prepared, at their strongest point, so that when they are defeated, it will be undeniable and just.

word_study.meaning: Judgment, justice, legal proceeding, legal right. In this context, it refers to a formal trial or lawsuit where parties bring evidence and a judge renders a verdict. In ancient Near Eastern legal tradition, mishpat could be both the legal process and the verdict itself.
word_study.significance: God frames history not as arbitrary power but as lawful judgment. The trial about to unfold is conducted with justice. This would be profoundly reassuring to exiled Israel: God is not acting by whim but by the binding standards of mishpat.

cross_references.connection: Both verses use the phrase 'renew their strength,' but with inverse meanings: 40:31 promises renewal to those who trust God; 41:1 sardonically invites the nations to renew theirs, only to prove it insufficient.
The psalm calls upon 'mighty ones' to ascribe glory to God, demanding their recognition of His supremacy—a similar legal/ritual acknowledgment of God's preeminence.
John's vision of the risen Christ echoes the 'I am He' self-identification of Isaiah 41:4, establishing continuity between the God of Isaiah and the Christ of Revelation.
Amulek's discourse on justice and judgment reflects the mishpat framework: God conducts judgment according to law, not caprice, ensuring fairness even as He executes His purposes.
References the order and judgment inherent in God's governance, paralleling Isaiah's image of God as righteous judge who summons all to account.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern courtroom setting that Isaiah invokes, trials often occurred in the presence of witnesses, and legal disputes could be brought before the king or even the gods themselves. The summons to 'silence' before judgment was a recognized protocol—silence demonstrated respect for the judge's authority. Cyrus of Persia, though unnamed at this point in Isaiah, was the historical figure who would conquer Babylon (539 BCE) and release the Jews. To exilic Israelites, his rise seemed like proof that Babylon's gods were supreme. Isaiah's legal framework reverses this narrative: God will demonstrate—through the unfolding of Cyrus's conquests—that He, not the Babylonian deities, has been orchestrating these 'coincidental' events. The structure of Isaiah 40-48 as a divine trial is unique in biblical literature and probably reflects the Persian period's familiarity with formal legal proceedings. God takes the position of both plaintiff and judge, a rhetorical strategy that overwhelms opposition through its confidence.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 1 challenges the assumption that God must explain Himself in real time. The exiled Israelites saw only Babylonian dominance; God invites them to a longer trial, trusting that history's verdict will vindicate Him. In our own crises—when the powers of the world seem ascendant, when God's purposes seem stalled, when we question where He is—this verse teaches us to demand silence from our doubts and trust God's willingness to be tried by His own works. God is not threatened by our questions; He invites them. But He invites them on His terms, within His courtroom, where the verdict is already determined not by earthly power but by the alignment of all history with His purposes. Do we silence our anxieties long enough to hear what God is actually doing?

text_kjv: Who raised up the righteous man from the east, called him to his foot, gave the nations before him, and made him rule over kings? he gave them as the dust to his sword, and as driven stubble to his bow.

commentary.narrative: God's opening legal argument is presented as a rhetorical question that asserts complete certainty: Who raised up the conqueror from the east? The answer thunders through the silence: I did. The 'righteous man from the east' is Cyrus II of Persia (identified explicitly in 44:28 and 45:1), but Isaiah names him only indirectly, as a type of unfolding revelation. To the exiled Israelites, Cyrus was rising as an unstoppable military force, and his victories seemed to vindicate Persian religion. Isaiah's argument is audacious: Cyrus's success is not the triumph of the gods of Persia but the execution of Israel's God's plan. The phrase 'called him to his foot' is peculiar in English but powerful in Hebrew idiom—it means God summoned him, brought him into service, made him His instrument.
commentary.narrative_continued: The military imagery is relentless: Cyrus subdues 'the nations before him' and 'made him rule over kings.' His sword and bow reduce enemies to dust and stubble—imagery of complete annihilation and utter insignificance. This hyperbolic language is intentional. Isaiah is not merely describing Cyrus's military prowess; he is asserting that God displays His power through Cyrus's victories. The Hebrew phrase 'gave them as the dust to his sword' (yiten ke'afar charbo) echoes the fate of Israel's ancient enemies in psalms of victory (Psalm 18:42). God is reappropriating the language of His own historical victories to describe what He is doing through a pagan king. This is the scandal and the comfort of Isaiah's message: God uses whomever He chooses, regardless of their faith or origin, to accomplish His purposes.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The theological scandal here is profound for exiled Israel. They are being told that the God who liberated them from Egypt, who gave them the Promised Land, who dwelt in the temple at Jerusalem—this God is now using a pagan Persian to execute His plan to restore them. There is no compromise of God's uniqueness or power; rather, it is the ultimate assertion of that power. Cyrus does not know he is God's instrument (45:5: 'I am the LORD, and there is none else'), but his ignorance does not diminish the reality. God orchestrates history through willing and unwilling servants alike. For Israel, this meant hope: the political and military changes unfolding in the Near East were not random; they were orchestrated by the God of covenant toward the liberation of His people.
commentary.christological_typology: While Cyrus is explicitly described as God's instrument and 'anointed' (45:1), he is a type of a greater deliverer. The language of God 'raising up' a deliverer from obscurity, giving him victory over enemies, and using him to liberate God's people finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ. Jesus, the true Anointed One, was raised up by God, given dominion over all nations, and came to deliver not just Israel but all humanity from the bondage of sin. The irony—that a king without explicit faith is used by God—is resolved in Jesus, who perfectly knows and embodies God's will.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of God using unlikely instruments appears throughout the Book of Mormon. Alma 37:12-13 teaches that God 'hath prepared means' for the salvation of His people through what appear to be natural or even secular events. The principle that God works through instruments who may not understand His purposes is central to Mormon theology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 98:21-22 teaches that when the wicked 'set up' kingdoms, God remains in control and ultimately directs their fall. The same principle underlies verse 2: God raised up Cyrus, and Cyrus's victories serve God's purposes. D&C 76:3 affirms that God's decrees are settled in eternity and 'before the foundation of the world,' suggesting that Cyrus's rise was determined long before, much as Isaiah here asserts.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The assertion that God uses instruments who do not understand His full purposes parallels the endowment structure, where individuals progress through covenants guided by purposes they do not initially comprehend. The covenant path itself involves moving according to God's will even when full understanding is deferred.

word_study.meaning: Righteousness, justice, vindication, victory. In the Psalms and prophetic books, tsedek can mean both moral righteousness and the vindication that comes from God's just action. The Covenant Rendering's rendering of this as 'whom righteousness meets at every step' preserves the ambiguity—is it Cyrus's righteousness, or God's righteous vindication that accompanies him?
word_study.significance: The use of tsedek for a pagan king whom God will declare is His 'anointed' (45:1) demonstrates that 'righteousness' in Isaiah's framework means alignment with God's purposes, not necessarily adherence to Torah or Israelite religion. This is revolutionary: God's justice is larger than any single covenant community's standards.

word_study.meaning: To stir up, raise, awaken, rouse. Often used of God arousing a leader or nation to action (e.g., Judges 3:9, where God 'raised up' a deliverer for Israel). The verb emphasizes God's active initiation, not mere permission.
word_study.significance: God does not merely allow Cyrus to rise; He actively stirs him up, awakens his ambition, directs his campaigns. This is the foundation of Isaiah's argument: even Cyrus's will is subject to God's orchestration.

word_study.meaning: From the rising place of the sun, from the east. Geographically accurate for Cyrus and Persia relative to Israel. In ancient cosmology, the east was often associated with beginnings and fresh starts.
word_study.significance: The phrase also carries theological weight in Isaiah: God's salvation comes from the east (sunrise = new day, new beginning). The direction itself suggests that God's redemption is dawning.

word_study.meaning: Called him at/to his foot; summoned him into his service. A Hebrew idiom for conscription or calling into service. In Deuteronomy and Judges, similar language describes God summoning judges and deliverers.
word_study.significance: The phrase subordinates Cyrus to God's will. He is called to serve God's purposes, though he does not know it. This maintains God's sovereignty while using an instrument that does not worship Him.

word_study.meaning: Like dust ... like chaff blown away. Imagery of complete destruction, insignificance, and dispersal. 'Chaff' (kash) is the insubstantial byproduct of grain, easily scattered by wind. The parallelism emphasizes absolute obliteration.
word_study.significance: This language recalls Psalm 18 and other hymns of God's victory. Isaiah applies it to Cyrus's enemies, asserting that God's power operates through Cyrus as surely as through Israel's ancient judges.

cross_references.connection: These verses explicitly name Cyrus and declare him God's 'anointed,' fulfilling the promise of verse 2. God there identifies Himself as the one who called Cyrus by name and armed him for conquest.

Isaiah 40 similarly describes God's power to reduce princes and rulers to nothing, establishing the framework that God, not earthly kings, holds ultimate power. This verse extends that logic to Cyrus.

The pattern of God 'raising up' a deliverer (same verb, he'ir) appears in Judges when God stirs up Othniel to save Israel. Cyrus, though unaware, functions as a deliverer of the exiles in the same way.

The imagery of enemies becoming 'dust' and 'stubble' before a victor echoes David's psalm, where God grants him military victory. Isaiah transfers this psalm language to Cyrus's victories, claiming them as God's work.
Teaches that God's work cannot be thwarted by the kingdoms of the world, paralleling Isaiah's assertion that Cyrus's power is ultimately subordinate to God's purposes.

commentary.historical_context: Cyrus II of Persia (c. 600-530 BCE) rose to power around 559 BCE and by 539 BCE had conquered Babylon without the city's traditional siege warfare—a remarkably swift campaign that would have seemed providential to observers. The Cyrus Cylinder, an ancient Persian document, records that Cyrus released captive peoples and restored their religious practices (including the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple). From the perspective of exiled Israelites, Cyrus's rise seemed like proof that the gods of Persia were ascendant. From Isaiah's perspective, it was Yahweh working through a pagan instrument. This is not unique in ancient Near Eastern thinking—gods could use foreign rulers—but Isaiah's claim is sharper: God not only permits Cyrus but actively orchestrated his rise for the specific purpose of liberating Israel. The military metaphor of reducing enemies to dust and stubble was conventional ancient military rhetoric, but Isaiah heightens it with theological meaning.
commentary.application: For modern believers, verse 2 radically expands the understanding of divine providence. God is not limited to working through the righteous or the consciously faithful. He orchestrates history through economic forces, political upheavals, and the actions of those unaware of His purposes. This teaches us several things: (1) We should not assume that secular events are outside God's plan; (2) We should not despise worldly power-holders as beyond God's reach; (3) Our role is to discern God's purposes in events, not to assume that visible righteousness is a prerequisite for God's use of a person or institution. For an exiled people clinging to faith, this verse is profoundly comforting: God has not abandoned you. What looks like the triumph of Babylon is actually the setup for your liberation. Trust that God is working even through the ambitions of kings who do not name His name.

text_kjv: He pursued them, and passed safely; even by the way that he had not gone with his feet.

commentary.narrative: Verse 3 deepens the portrait of Cyrus as an instrument of divine power by introducing an element of the miraculous. The verse describes Cyrus 'pursuing' his enemies and 'passing safely' (in shalom, wholeness, peace) along paths 'his feet have not traveled before.' The Covenant Rendering clarifies what is implicit in the KJV: Cyrus's advance is so swift and his victories so complete that he traverses terrain he has never walked, yet does so in shalom (peace/safety). The traditional reading has sometimes interpreted this as Cyrus traversing difficult or unknown territory without fear or danger. But the deeper theological meaning is that Cyrus's path is divinely smoothed. He moves through hostile territory that should be dangerous as though protected by an invisible escort.
commentary.narrative_continued: In the context of ancient military campaigns, an army moving through unfamiliar or hostile territory would face severe disadvantages: supply lines stretched, ambushes possible, local resistance. Yet the verse suggests Cyrus moves through these perils in shalom—not triumphantly, but in a state of divine protection and peace. This is the language of God's guidance in the Exodus (Exodus 13:21, where God led Israel by pillar of fire/cloud) and in the wilderness wanderings. Isaiah is claiming that Cyrus's military success is not merely human strategy but divine enablement. The path he has not walked is being made safe for him. This speaks to the Israelite exiles with particular force: the very political circumstances that seem to threaten them—Cyrus's conquests—are actually clearing the way for their liberation. What appears to be chaos is a divinely orchestrated sequence of events.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The passive sense of 'passing safely' (yaavar in shalom) is important. Cyrus is not fighting through resistance; he is passing through, moving forward in shalom. This suggests almost effortless progress—the kind of success that suggests divine favor. The 'paths his feet have not traveled' could be literal (unknown terrain) or figurative (unprecedented dominance). Either way, the point is the same: he moves beyond the limits of what should be possible, guided by something beyond military prowess.
commentary.christological_typology: Cyrus's passage through dangerous territory in shalom prefigures Christ's passage through the wilderness (Matthew 4:1-11) and through the valley of the shadow of death (Psalm 23), moving toward the purpose God set before Him. More broadly, Christ's path—the way 'He had not gone with His feet'—encompasses the entirety of His incarnation and atonement, moving through human experience in shalom with the Father, accomplishing redemption despite every obstacle.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 2:1-7 describes Lehi and his family being guided away from Jerusalem through a divinely prepared path. Like Cyrus, they travel 'in the wilderness' toward a destination; like Cyrus, they move in accordance with God's will, though their understanding is incomplete. The principle of divine preparation of paths appears throughout the Book of Mormon (2 Nephi 4:34; Alma 29:8).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:8 promises that as the Saints 'go forth, let your words be established'—a promise that God will make their way straight and their word effective. The same principle of divine facilitation appears here: God facilitates the passage of His instruments through otherwise hostile or difficult circumstances.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The passage in shalom echoes covenant language. Shalom is not merely military victory but the state of being in proper relationship with God, in wholeness. This state is what the temple covenant promises: to be at peace, guided, protected within the bonds of the covenant.

word_study.meaning: To pursue, chase, follow after. Often used in military contexts for pursuing a defeated enemy. The verb is active and suggests relentless following.
word_study.significance: The pursuance is unrelenting. Unlike defensive action, pursuit suggests momentum and momentum. In the flow of verse 3, it leads naturally to 'passing safely'—the pursuit does not lead to exhaustion but to shalom.

word_study.meaning: To pass/go through in peace, wholeness, safety. The word shalom (שָׁלוֹם) carries the sense not just of absence of war but of completeness, well-being, and divine favor. Here it describes a state of safety and protection.
word_study.significance: The pairing of 'passing through' with 'shalom' suggests that movement itself is protected. Unlike a conqueror who must fight his way, Cyrus passes through as though in a state of divine peace. This is reminiscent of God's promise to Israel (Leviticus 26:6, 'I will give peace in the land') or the peace that passes understanding (Philippians 4:7).

word_study.meaning: Path, way, road. Often used for literal roads but also figuratively for manner of life or direction. In poetic usage, it can mean a divinely ordained direction.
word_study.significance: The 'path his feet have not traveled' suggests that Cyrus is moving into new territory, yet in shalom. This recalls Isaiah 40:3, 'Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.' Here, Cyrus's path is being prepared, though he does not know it.

word_study.meaning: His feet have not come (to), i.e., he has not walked there before. A straightforward statement that the territory is unfamiliar to him.
word_study.significance: The emphasis on unfamiliar terrain suggests that despite not knowing the terrain, Cyrus succeeds. This implies either divine guidance or the revelation of hidden paths—an echo of the Exodus, where Israel was led through the Red Sea on 'a way in the sea, and a path in the mighty waters.'

cross_references.connection: God leads Israel through the wilderness with a pillar of fire and cloud, protecting them and guiding them through terrain they have not traveled. Cyrus's passage through shalom echoes this pattern of divine guidance.
The command to 'prepare the way' and 'make his paths straight' foreshadows verse 3: paths are being made for Cyrus's advance, echoing the Exodus pattern of God preparing the way for His people.

David pleads with God to 'teach me your way' and lead him in a 'plain path,' seeking divine guidance through danger. Cyrus moves without fear through unfamiliar territory because he is guided, whether he knows it or not.
Joshua is promised success if he keeps to the way that has been set before him. Similarly, Cyrus succeeds because he travels the way God has ordained, though he does not know it.
Teaches that God has prepared paths for His people to walk in, directing the course of nations to accomplish His purposes—the same principle Isaiah articulates for Cyrus.

commentary.historical_context: Cyrus's campaigns (553-530 BCE) were remarkably swift and met with surprisingly little resistance in certain quarters. Some cities and peoples may have welcomed him as a liberator from Babylonian rule. The Cyrus Cylinder indicates he portrayed himself as a restorer of proper religious order rather than a conqueror. From this angle, Cyrus did indeed move through territories 'in shalom'—as a welcome figure, not as a tyrant crushing resistance. Yet from an Israelite perspective, the significance was theological: whatever the political circumstances, Isaiah saw Cyrus's rise as divinely orchestrated. The 'paths' he traveled were cleared by God, leading toward the exile's end. For a people who had experienced the trauma of the Exodus-Wilderness, the image of a divinely guided journey toward liberation would have been immediately resonant.
commentary.application: Verse 3 teaches that God smooths the paths of those He sends on missions of deliverance. For modern members, this suggests several truths: (1) When we are called by God to undertake a difficult mission, we should expect that obstacles will be less formidable than they appear; (2) Our perception of difficulty may be greater than the actual resistance we face, because God has already prepared the way; (3) Moving in alignment with God's purposes carries with it a kind of peace (shalom) that is both protection and assurance. The phrase 'paths his feet have not traveled' is particularly relevant to those facing new callings, new places, new responsibilities. You have not walked this path before, but God has walked it before you, preparing it. Trust in shalom—not the absence of challenge, but the presence of divine ordering and peace.

text_kjv: Who hath wrought and done it, calling the generations from the beginning? I the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he.

commentary.narrative: Verse 4 is Isaiah's answer to the implicit question of verses 1-3: Who is orchestrating all this? Who has 'wrought and done it'—who is the ultimate author of Cyrus's rise, the clearing of paths, the unfolding of military conquest? The answer is God Himself. But more than that, God defines Himself in a way that is almost without parallel in scripture. He calls Himself 'the first and with the last,' claiming sovereignty over all of time—beginning to end, alpha to omega. The phrase 'I am He' (ani hu, אֲנִי הוּא) is a self-identification formula that will recur throughout Isaiah 40-48 and becomes a hallmark of Second Isaiah's theology. 'I am He' is not a complete sentence in Hebrew; it asserts existence and identity without predication. In Greek, this becomes ego eimi (ἐγώ εἰμι), which Jesus uses of Himself in the Gospels.
commentary.narrative_continued: The structure of verse 4 is crucial. God first establishes His action ('Who hath wrought and done it') and then His authority ('calling the generations from the beginning'). He does not merely react to events; He calls forth the very generations that constitute history. The verb 'calling' (qoreh) is active and summoning—God speaks and history answers. This is the language of creation itself, where God calls forth light, seas, and life. Here, God calls forth the generations, the succession of peoples and times that make up human history. For exiled Israel, the implication is staggering: their generation, the generations of Babylon, the generation of Cyrus—all were called forth by God's voice from the beginning.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The phrase 'the first and with the last' raises a subtle translation question that The Covenant Rendering handles delicately: 'I, the LORD, the first, and with the last — I am He.' The Hebrew 'et-acharonim (אֶת־אַחֲרֹנִים) literally means 'with the lasts' or 'with the last ones,' possibly suggesting that God is not only first but present with all generations, including the last. This reading emphasizes God's immanence as much as His transcendence. God is not only the primordial beginning but also the constant presence guiding all that follows. The repetition of 'I am He' (ani hu) at the end of the verse is emphatic and absolute, brooking no alternative. In the trial God has convened, this is His ultimate assertion: 'I am the one who has done this, and none other can claim such authority.'
commentary.christological_typology: The phrase 'I am He' becomes explicitly messianic when Jesus claims it for Himself in John 8:58. But in Isaiah, the entire formula—'the first and with the last'—anticipates Christ's role as the beginning and end of redemption. Christ is both the primordial Word (John 1:1, 'In the beginning was the Word') and the final judge and restorer (Revelation 22:13, 'I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end'). The claim that God 'calleth the generations' is ultimately about Christ, who gathers all ages and times into Himself, the fullness of times.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 27:22-23 records God's declaration to Nephi regarding his descendants and the unfolding of the Book of Mormon's revelation: 'I am He.' This formula becomes a signature of God's absolute assurance about His purposes. The principle of God calling forth generations is also evident in D&C 27:15, where God speaks to Joseph Smith about 'those who have gone before,' indicating His sovereignty over all generations.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:30-31 teaches that God 'hath made it known unto us that he grasps the whole in his hands,' maintaining control over 'the beginning and the end.' D&C 88:6-13 presents Christ as the light that 'proceedeth forth from the presence of God to fill the immensity of space,' combining the concepts of first and last, origin and omnipresence. Both passages echo Isaiah 41:4's theology of God's comprehensive rule over all time and space.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The formula 'I am He' echoes the temple endowment's emphasis on the identity and authority of deity. God's claim to call the generations from the beginning prefigures the cosmic perspective taught in the temple, where all of creation is understood as proceeding from God's will and returning to Him.

word_study.meaning: To work, accomplish, make, do. The pairing of two verbs (pa'al and asah) intensifies the sense of complete accomplishment. Pa'al suggests the work of creation or crafting; asah means to make or execute.
word_study.significance: The doubling creates emphasis: God has not merely set things in motion; He has accomplished it fully. This is the language of mastery and completion, echoing the creation account where God 'did' (asah) the work of making the world.

word_study.meaning: Calling the generations. Qoreh is the participle form of qara (to call), suggesting an ongoing action. Dorot refers to generations or ages. The phrase means to summon, to call forth, or to name the succession of generations.
word_study.significance: This echoes Isaiah 40:26 ('He calleth them all by names'), where God calls the stars forth by name. Here, God calls forth the generations themselves—speaking them into being or directing their course. This is creationally significant: God does not merely observe history; He summons it forward.

word_study.term_english: The first and with the last
word_study.meaning: The first and with the last/final ones. Rishon means first (in time, order, or rank). Acharonim means those who come after, the later ones, possibly the last generation. The preposition et (with, toward) suggests accompaniment or presence alongside the last.
word_study.significance: God claims to be both the primordial origin and the present accompaniment of all that follows. This is not just temporal lordship but active presence. God is not distant in the past but intimately engaged with each generation, 'with' them, guiding them.

word_study.meaning: I am He. A self-identification formula asserting the existence and identity of the speaker. In Hebrew, it is a statement of being without further predication. It asserts: I exist, I am present, I am the one you are looking for.
word_study.significance: This formula becomes a hallmark of Isaiah 40-48 (43:10, 13, 25; 46:4; 48:12) and is explicitly claimed by Jesus in the Gospels (John 8:58, 'Before Abraham was, I am'). The declaration 'I am He' is absolute and absolute in scope. There is no one else to whom such identity belongs.

cross_references.connection: God declares to Israel, 'Ye are my witnesses... that I am He,' using the same formula and context of proving His uniqueness before the nations in a trial setting.
God assures Israel: 'Even to your old age I am He,' employing the ani hu formula to promise perpetual presence and care through all stages of life.
John quotes the risen Christ: 'I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending,' directly mirroring Isaiah 41:4's 'I am the first and with the last.'
Jesus declares, 'Before Abraham was, I am' (ego eimi, the Greek equivalent of ani hu), claiming the same divine self-identification and eternality that Isaiah attributes to God.
The Doctrine and Covenants teaches that the Lord 'calleth whom he will have,' echoing the principle that God actively calls forth and directs His instruments through history.

commentary.historical_context: The 'ani hu' formula (I am He) appears uniquely concentrated in Second Isaiah (40-48) and reflects the theological vocabulary that would have been meaningful to exiles. In the ancient Near Eastern context, the assertion of divine uniqueness was not uncommon—many gods were declared supreme by their adherents. What is distinctive in Isaiah is the claim that the God of Israel alone directs history through instrumentalities like Cyrus. The phrase 'calling the generations' reflects a worldview in which time itself is subject to divine ordering. This was not trivial theology for exiles: they had experienced a catastrophic rupture in their history (the fall of Jerusalem). Isaiah's assertion that God 'calls the generations from the beginning' was meant to assure them that this rupture, too, was within God's design and calling.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, verse 4 offers profound reassurance about divine governance. In a world that seems chaotic—where nations rise and fall, cultures shift, and personal circumstances change—this verse affirms that God is not a remote observer but an active director who has called forth every generation and maintains presence with each. The phrase 'I am He'—repeated at the end of the verse for emphasis—is God's assurance of His completeness and sufficiency. You do not need multiple gods, multiple sources of truth, or multiple authorities. 'I am He.' When facing uncertainty about the future or anxiety about historical events beyond your control, this verse teaches: God called your generation forth. He is present with you, 'the first and with the last,' governing all things toward their proper end. This is not fatalism; it is the liberation that comes from trusting absolute, active intelligence governing all things for your good.

text_kjv: The isles saw it, and feared; the ends of the earth were afraid, drew near, and came.

commentary.narrative: Having asserted absolute divine control over history, Isaiah pivots to describing the reaction of the distant nations. They 'saw' something—the rise of Cyrus, his conquests, his unstoppable advance—and the response is paradoxical: they 'feared' and 'trembled,' yet simultaneously 'drew near and came.' The logic seems contradictory: why would those who are afraid move toward the source of their fear? The answer becomes clear in verse 6 and beyond: the nations gather together not out of confidence but out of desperate mutual support. They sense that the world order is shifting and rush together to make common cause. The 'isles' (iyyim, the same word from verse 1) and the 'ends of the earth' are again the distant nations, now reacting to what they perceive as an apocalyptic threat.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verbs 'feared' (yare) and 'were afraid' (yechadu—to tremble or shudder) indicate terror, not mere caution. This is existential fear—the kind experienced when foundational securities seem to be collapsing. The Babylonian order, which had dominated the Near East for seventy years, was crumbling. The rise of Cyrus threatened the existing power structure. Yet simultaneously, the nations 'drew near and came.' This is not flight but gathering. The word 'drew near' (karubu) suggests approaching a center—they come toward a focal point. This is the gathering of the trial God convened in verse 1. The nations have come to the courtroom, but not as confident litigants; they come in fear, seeking solidarity against a perceived existential threat.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: For the exiles, this verse would have been deeply satisfying. The nations they feared—the powers that seemed to rule forever—were themselves terrified by Cyrus's rise. The exiles' oppressor (Babylon) was about to fall. The cosmic order they had come to accept as fixed was dissolving. Yet Isaiah frames this not as Cyrus's triumph but as the visibility of God's work. The nations see and fear, but what they truly see (though they don't recognize it) is God's hand working through Cyrus. The irony is profound: the very events that terrify the nations are precisely the events that will liberate Israel. The fear of the nations is, from the Israelite perspective, proof that God is acting.
commentary.christological_typology: The terror of the nations at the upheaval of the world order foreshadows the terror described in Matthew 24 and Revelation 6, where the cosmic order breaks down before the coming of Christ. The 'isles saw and feared' language is echoed in Revelation 1:7, 'Every eye shall see him,' with the implication that this seeing produces fear in those who are unprepared. Christ's work brings fear to those who do not understand that He is their judge and redeemer.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: When Nephi describes the wars and upheavals preceding the coming of Christ, similar language appears: peoples 'gathering together' in response to changing circumstances (3 Nephi 8-9). The principle that the work of God produces fear and trembling in those who do not understand it recurs throughout the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:16-27 describes the upheaval preceding Christ's return, with emphasis on the fear of the nations and those who do not understand what is happening. The same pattern appears: events that terrify the world are, from the Lord's perspective, the preparation of His people's deliverance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The gathering of the nations in verse 5 prefigures the gathering of the righteous to Zion. The nations gather in fear; the Lord's people gather in hope. Both are responses to God's work, but from opposite spiritual perspectives.

word_study.meaning: They saw, beheld, perceived. The verb ra'ah means to see with perception, understanding, or awareness. It is the same verb used in the trial of verse 1: 'we will see who is right.'
word_study.significance: The nations 'saw'—they witnessed events they could not ignore. What they saw was the upheaval of the world order, visible to all. But they did not understand what they were seeing: the hand of Israel's God working through Cyrus.

word_study.meaning: To fear, be afraid, revere. Can mean fear of physical danger or awe before the divine. Here it is clearly fear of danger, a response to perceived threat.
word_study.significance: The nations' fear is not reverence for God but terror at what they perceive as a threat to their existence and power. This is fear without understanding, not fear of the Lord.

word_study.term_original: יֶחֱרָ֑דוּ (yechdudu or yechradudu—the text is slightly ambiguous)
word_study.meaning: To tremble, shake, be in great fear. The word conveys physical manifestation of terror—shaking, shuddering. It is the response of the body to overwhelming fear.
word_study.significance: The parallelism with 'feared' suggests increasing intensity: fear + trembling = absolute terror. The nations are not calmly assessing the situation; they are shaking with anxiety.

word_study.meaning: Came near and came. The verbs suggest movement toward a center or focal point. This is not random flight but gathering in a specific place or toward a specific goal.
word_study.significance: The movement is toward unity and mutual support. They are responding to the command of verse 1 ('let them come near'), but driven by fear rather than confidence in their case.

cross_references.connection: Verse 1 commands the nations to 'come near together to judgment,' and verse 5 shows them doing exactly that, responding to the summons by drawing near and coming together.

Isaiah 40 describes the nations as 'nothing and vanity' before God, mere dust on the balance. Here, they react in terror to events they cannot control, confirming their insignificance in the cosmic order.
The fear of man is contrasted with trust in the LORD. The nations' fear, unanchored in trust in God, leads them to frantic mutual support rather than true confidence.

In the final judgment, 'the great and mighty' hide in caves, crying out to be hidden from God's face. This echoes the fear and flight of the nations in response to divine action, whether in Isaiah's day or the eschaton.

Teaches that in the last days, the wicked will fear as the work of God goes forth, just as the nations of Isaiah's day trembled before Cyrus without understanding that God was the true source of upheaval.

commentary.historical_context: The rise of Cyrus and the fall of Babylon would have been experienced throughout the ancient Near East as an extraordinary geopolitical upheaval. The vision of Babylon as an eternal power was shattered in a remarkably short time (the fall occurred in 539 BCE). Various nations that had accommodated themselves to Babylonian rule faced an uncertain future. Some would have seen Cyrus as a liberator, others as a threat.
