When members ask authentic questions about faith, morality, and doctrine, the Church responds—imperfectly, perhaps, but responsively. In contrast, purely secular worldviews, material atheism, or false religious systems often cannot answer the deepest human questions about meaning and purpose. Additionally, the verse teaches personal responsibility: when God asks—when conscience, scripture, and prophecy speak to you—do you respond, or do you remain silent in hardness of heart? A responsive heart to God's inquiry is the foundation of discipleship.

text_kjv: Behold, they are all vanity; their works are nothing: their molten images are wind and confusion.

commentary.narrative: Verse 29 delivers the final, annihilating verdict on idolatry: the idols and their works are summarily declared to be 'aven (delusion/wickedness), 'efes (nothing/zero), and their cast metal images are 'wind and tohu' (emptiness and primordial chaos). This is not a tentative conclusion but a definitive pronouncement. The chapter has built a case: God raised up Cyrus (v. 25), announced it in advance (vv. 26-27), searched for any counselor among the idols (v. 28), and now renders final judgment. The verdict is on all counts: the idols are delusion, their works accomplish nothing, and their physical representations are empty wind. The theological audacity is complete: the great idols of Babylon—Marduk, Ishtar, Nabu, whose statues towered over the city, whose temples consumed resources—are reduced to wind and chaos. They have no substance, no power, no reality.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Covenant Rendering notes that 'tohu' (chaos/emptiness) echoes Genesis 1:2, where the earth was 'tohu va-bohu' (chaos and void) before creation. By describing the idols as 'tohu,' Isaiah suggests they are not merely powerless but primordial, anti-creation, unformed. They lack the coherent reality of God's created order. This is the deepest condemnation: idols are not simply false but fundamentally unreal, not participants in God's cosmos but representatives of the formless void. For the exiled Judah, this would be theologically liberating: the powers that held them captive—the great idols, the religious systems, the imperial might—are unveiled as illusion. They appear mighty and real, but they are wind. Only God is real, only God's covenant is real, only God's purposes endure. The trial of Isaiah 41 closes with this pronouncement: case dismissed. The idols stand condemned to non-existence.

word_study.meaning: vanity, delusion, wickedness, iniquity—refers to emptiness, futility, and moral corruption. Root 'wn suggests bending, distortion, falsehood.
word_study.significance: Aven is more than mere non-existence; it suggests active deception. The idols are not simply absent but present as lies. They seduce people into false worship and false hope. In Isaiah, aven is used repeatedly for idolatry (1:13, 'your new moons and your appointed feasts are a burden unto me; I am weary to bear them') and for false security (59:4, 'they conceive mischief, and bring forth iniquity').

word_study.meaning: nothing, zero, end—the absolute negation of being. Efes means not just 'little' or 'insignificant' but the complete absence of substance.
word_study.significance: Isaiah uses 'efes' to describe the nothingness of idols and human strength before God (40:17, 'all nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity'). The works of the idols are 'efes—they produce zero results, zero salvation, zero power.

word_study.meaning: cast images, molten images—from root n-s-k (to pour, cast metal). These are the physical idols poured from molten metal, the objects of worship in Babylonian temples.
word_study.significance: Isaiah deliberately mentions the physical form of the idols: they are real objects made of metal, real things worshiped in real temples. Yet despite their material substance, their spiritual reality is zero. The contrast is striking—material reality does not guarantee spiritual reality. A golden statue is 'wind and tohu.'

word_study.meaning: wind, breath, spirit—the fundamental principle of life and movement in Hebrew thought. Ruach is also 'spirit' in the sense of non-material reality.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'wind and tohu' (ruach va-tohu) is a masterful paradox. Ruach usually means 'breath' or 'spirit'—the life principle. But here it means merely wind, formless and directionless. The idols are not even empty spirits; they are empty wind—movement without power, appearance without substance. In ecclesiastical terms, they are 'wind and vanity' (Ecclesiastes 2:11).

word_study.meaning: desolation, chaos, formlessness, void—the primordial chaos before creation in Genesis 1:2. Used metaphorically for confusion, confusion, meaninglessness.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes the resonance with Genesis 1:2: 'the earth was without form (tohu) and void.' By saying the idols are 'tohu,' Isaiah places them not in the created order (which God called 'good') but in the realm of pre-creation chaos. They belong to nothingness, not to being. This is the deepest condemnation of all.

cross_references.connection: All nations before God 'are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity'—the same verdict applied to human nations and their idols.
Qoheleth's pronouncement: 'Vanity of vanities; all is vanity'—an existential reflection that echoes Isaiah's judgment on idolatry and false pursuits.
The earth was 'without form (tohu) and void'—primordial chaos before God's creative word. Idols are reduced to this pre-creation state, the opposite of creation.
Paul applies Isaiah's logic to NT Christian context: 'We know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one'—directly echoing Isaiah's verdict.

Alma challenges the Zoramites: 'Can ye think of being saved when you have yielded yourselves to become subjects of the devil?' False religion and idolatry lead to subjection and loss of agency, the ultimate 'nothingness' of spiritual emptiness.

commentary.historical_context: The great idols of Babylon—massive statues of Marduk and other deities in the temple Esagila—were indeed made of precious metals and housed in the most impressive architectural structures of the ancient world. Nebuchadnezzar II decorated Babylon with unparalleled religious monuments. Yet within one generation (by 539 BCE), Cyrus conquered Babylon and reportedly dismantled many of these idols or removed them (though the historical record is complex). From a Babylonian perspective, the idols had failed: they did not protect Babylon from conquest. From Isaiah's perspective, this was inevitable—the idols were always 'wind and tohu.' The archaeological and historical record shows that Babylonian religion, for all its material grandeur, could not answer the deepest questions or prevent historical catastrophe. The temple structures survive (in ruins) in modern Iraq, but they are shells, hollow monuments—exactly as Isaiah describes them.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Helaman 13:29-31 describes the fate of secret combinations and idolatry in the Nephite nation: 'O that ye would awake; awake from a deep sleep, yea, even from the sleep of hell, and shake off the awful chains by which ye are bound...Your destruction is made sure.' False gods and false systems of belief lead to destruction. Jacob 4:13-14 teaches that 'we search the prophets, and we have many revelations and the spirit of prophecy; wherefore, we believe in the Son of God.' In contrast to the silent idols, God's word through prophets is living and powerful.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:38 affirms that God's word, not the philosophies of men, carries lasting authority: 'What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken; I excuse not myself; and though the heavens and the earth pass away, my word shall not pass away.' The restoration teaches an absolute contrast between God's eternal word and the vain philosophies of the world (D&C 88:118, 'seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom'—implies discernment from the worthless).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The greatest contrast to Babylonian idols is the temple of God. Latter-day Saint temples are not made primarily of precious metals and stone (though they are beautiful) but are places of covenantal truth and enduring spiritual substance. The temple endowment teaches that what is real is what is spiritual and eternal; what is material and temporal without spiritual substance is 'wind and confusion.' The temple clothes us in covenantal reality; idolatry dresses us in illusion.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the antithesis of 'aven and 'efes. He is absolute Being ('I AM,' John 8:58), not non-being. He is absolute Word (logos), not silence. His kingdom is described as eternal, unchanging, and unshakeable (Daniel 2:44, 'a kingdom which shall never be destroyed'). Where idols crumble to dust, Christ rises to eternity. The trial that condemns the idols in Isaiah 41 foreshadows the trial that condemns the world's false systems through Christ's resurrection. Christ is the ultimate answer to idolatry: not a God of wind and chaos, but the God of order, creation, and redemptive purpose.
commentary.application: This verse is a call to ruthless spiritual inventory. What have you made into an idol? What do you serve with more devotion than God? Is it wealth, success, status, romantic love, political ideology, or even a warped version of religion itself? This verse asks: Is your focus on wind and tohu—things that have no ultimate substance? Idolatry in modern context is not necessarily wooden statues but anything that commands your ultimate allegiance and promises you what only God can deliver. Money promises security but delivers anxiety. Status promises dignity but delivers emptiness. Relationships, however beautiful, promise ultimate meaning but cannot deliver it. All these 'molten images'—shiny, attractive, apparently real—are, by Isaiah's reckoning, wind and chaos. For Latter-day Saints, this verse invites reflection on whether we are truly centered on covenantal discipleship (the real, eternal, substantial) or distracted by the glittering illusions of the world. It calls for courage: to name the idols for what they are, to cease serving them, and to redirect our worship toward the God who is actual, who speaks, who acts, and whose word endures forever. The verdict is clear: the idols stand condemned. The question is: will you stand with them, or will you stand with God?

text_kjv: To open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah 42:7 defines the Servant's concrete mission in language that Jesus Himself would later apply to His own ministry. The verse articulates three interconnected liberations: opening blind eyes, releasing prisoners, and freeing those trapped in darkness. These are not merely metaphorical—they describe both the physical healings that characterized Jesus's public ministry and the deeper spiritual blindness and bondage that sin creates. The repetition of 'prison' (Hebrew: assir and beit-kela) emphasizes the totality of captivity: both the dungeon itself and the house/structure of imprisonment. This creates a parallelism where spiritual darkness equals confinement, and light equals freedom. The Servant's work is thus fundamentally liberatory, undoing the consequences of sin and ignorance that bind humanity.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Dead Sea Scrolls confirm the MT reading here without significant variant, showing this text was preserved with remarkable consistency across a thousand years. In the context of Isaiah 40–49, this verse responds directly to the exiles' condition: they are blind to God's promised deliverance, imprisoned by despair and foreign rule, sitting in the darkness of displacement. Yet the Servant's mission transcends their particular historical moment. When Jesus reads from Isaiah 61:1-2 in Luke 4:18-19 (a passage with identical language and parallel commission), He identifies Himself as the fulfillment of this Servant role. The irony that Isaiah later describes Israel itself as 'blind' and 'deaf' (42:19) suggests that the Servant's liberation extends even to those who fail to recognize it—a foreshadowing of Jesus's ministry to a spiritually resistant people.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The triple mission—eyes opened, prisoners freed, darkness dispelled—operates on multiple registers simultaneously. Physically, Jesus healed the blind, cast out demons (spiritual imprisonment), and brought light to those in spiritual darkness. Soteriologically, His atonement removes the blindness of ignorance, breaks the chains of sin and death, and dispels the darkness of separation from God. Communally, the Servant's work restores sight to those who cannot see the kingdom, releases those held captive by false systems, and illuminates the path for all nations. The verse thus anchors the entire servant theology of Isaiah in concrete, tangible acts of liberation that reflect God's character: He does not leave humanity in bondage but actively works to set the captive free.
commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 42:7 is one of the most explicit prefigurations of Christ's redemptive work in the Old Testament. The Servant who opens blind eyes, releases prisoners, and dispels darkness is Jesus Christ fulfilling His role as Savior. The three liberations map onto the three dimensions of His atonement: (1) opening blind eyes = illuminating truth and dispelling ignorance through His teachings and revelation; (2) releasing prisoners = breaking the chains of sin and death through His sacrifice; (3) freeing those in darkness = restoring relationship with God the Father and enabling spiritual progression. In typological terms, the Servant stands as the antitype to Israel's captivity: where Israel was exiled, blinded, and imprisoned, Christ becomes the means of universal liberation. His resurrection becomes the ultimate 'opening' of the prison house of death.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 27, Nephi sees the sealed book and describes those who are 'blind' and 'deaf' in terms closely paralleling Isaiah 42:7. The Book of Mormon emphasizes that spiritual blindness afflicts even those with the scriptures, reinforcing Isaiah's insight that opening eyes requires divine action, not merely human effort. Additionally, Alma 26:3 uses the language of spiritual bondage and liberation in describing missionary work, applying the Servant's mission to the Lord's restored work in bringing souls from spiritual darkness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:6-13 teaches that Christ is 'the light and the Redeemer of the world' who breaks the bands of death and opens the prison of hell. Section 93 emphasizes that Christ is 'the light' that 'shineth in darkness' (D&C 93:2), directly applying the Servant's liberatory function to post-Restoration theology. The Doctrine and Covenants consistently portrays redemption in the Servant's language of opening eyes, removing chains, and dispelling darkness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment portrays progression from spiritual darkness (the telestial room) through increasing light to the celestial room—a narrative arc directly paralleling Isaiah 42:7's sequence of opening eyes, releasing from bondage, and moving from darkness into light. The garment itself can be understood as marking covenant membership in the Servant's liberatory work.

word_study.meaning: Blindness; those who are blind. The root עוור (awer) means to be blind. The feminine plural form emphasizes not blindness as an abstraction but the concrete state of those who cannot see.
word_study.significance: In Isaiah's theology, blindness represents both physical disability and spiritual imperception—inability to see God's work, recognize His revelation, or understand His purposes. The Servant's opening of blind eyes thus restores both literal sight and spiritual perception. The Covenant Rendering's 'eyes that are blind' preserves this concrete quality.

word_study.meaning: Prisoner, captive. From the root אסר (asar), 'to bind' or 'to imprison.' The word emphasizes bondage and restraint, not mere detention.
word_study.significance: The prisoner is one bound by force, unable to move freely. In the servant theology, this describes those bound by sin, false religion, ignorance, or oppressive systems. The Servant breaks these bonds. In Jewish tradition, this verse became a prooftext for the Messiah's liberation of Israel; in Christian theology, it foreshadows Christ's breaking of death's chains.

word_study.meaning: Darkness, obscurity, gloom. Used throughout Scripture for both literal darkness and spiritual blindness, divine judgment, or separation from God's light.
word_study.significance: In Isaiah, darkness often symbolizes alienation from God (8:22, 9:2, 29:18, 42:16, 59:9-10). Those 'who sit in darkness' are trapped in ignorance or despair. The Servant brings light—literal illumination and spiritual awakening. The parallel in John 1:4-5 and 8:12 applies this explicitly to Jesus.

word_study.meaning: 'House of confinement' or 'prison.' Kela (כלא) means confinement; beit (בית) means house or structure. The phrase emphasizes the totality and permanence of captivity.
word_study.significance: The redundancy of 'prisoners from prison' and 'darkness out of the prison house' is intentional. It stresses that bondage is comprehensive and systemic. The Servant's work is not partial release but complete liberation. For early Christians, this applied to Jesus's harrowing of hell and the resurrection of the dead.

cross_references.connection: Jesus Himself reads Isaiah 61:1-2 in the synagogue and claims its fulfillment in His ministry, using nearly identical language about opening blind eyes, releasing captives, and proclaiming liberty—directly identifying Himself as this Servant.

Jesus declares 'I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life'—directly fulfilling the Servant's role of liberating those in darkness through His presence and teaching.

Paul describes his apostolic commission using Servant language: 'to open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light'—showing how the Servant's mission extended through the apostolic ministry.

The parallel servant passage that Jesus cited in Luke 4, sharing identical themes of sight-giving, prisoner-release, and light-bringing, confirming that Isaiah consistently portrays the Servant as liberator.

President Joseph F. Smith's vision describes the Savior's work among the righteous dead in the spirit world, freeing them from captivity and opening their eyes to gospel light—a latter-day application of the Servant's liberatory mission.

commentary.historical_context: In the exilic context (sixth century BCE), these verses spoke directly to Judean prisoners held in Babylon. They experienced literal imprisonment, displacement, and spiritual darkness—disconnection from temple, land, and familiar worship. The language of opening blind eyes and releasing prisoners would have resonated powerfully with captives who had lost hope of return. Historically, Cyrus II (Persian king) would become the agent of physical liberation in 538 BCE, but Isaiah envisions a deeper, spiritual liberation through the Servant that transcends any single historical figure. The prisoner imagery also connects to ancient Near Eastern practices of mass deportation used by imperial powers (Assyria, Babylon) to control conquered peoples. Isaiah's radical claim is that a figure anointed by God will reverse this subjugation and restore sight, freedom, and dignity to those whom empires had rendered blind and powerless.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 42:7 reframes our understanding of discipleship and the gospel. We are called to participate in the Servant's work of opening blind eyes—testifying to those blinded by materialism, false doctrine, or worldly deception; releasing prisoners—advocating for the captive, imprisoned, or spiritually bound; and dispelling darkness—bringing light through teaching, service, and faithful example. On a personal level, the verse invites us to recognize where we remain blind, imprisoned, or darkened—areas where sin, unbelief, or ignorance hold us—and to invite Christ's liberating power. The verse also reminds us that salvation is not passive reception but active liberation: Christ does not merely offer escapes; He actively breaks chains and opens eyes. Our covenants bind us to participate in this work in our families, communities, and the world.

text_kjv: I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah 42:8 pivots from describing the Servant's liberatory work to anchoring that work in God's exclusive divine identity and sovereignty. The verse opens with the foundational formula 'I am the LORD' (ani YHWH)—a declaration that appears repeatedly throughout Isaiah 40–49 (40:28, 41:4, 43:3, 43:11, 44:6, 45:5, 45:6, 45:18, 48:12) as the bedrock of all monotheistic faith and action. This is not merely a name but an assertion of unshared divinity and power. The phrase 'that is my name' emphasizes the permanence and absoluteness of this identity—YHWH (Yahweh) is not one deity among many, but THE name, the name that encompasses all reality. The verse then establishes the corollary: God will not share His glory (kavod, weight, honor, majesty) with any other being or image. This statement appears in the immediate aftermath of verses describing the Servant's work, making clear that the Servant's power to liberate flows not from autonomous authority but entirely from participation in God's exclusive glory.
commentary.narrative_continued: The second half of verse 8 adds a sharp polemic: 'neither my praise to graven images.' This directly addresses the idolatry pervasive in both the Babylonian context of the exiles and the ancient Near Eastern religious environment generally. Carved idols were believed by their worshippers to be repositories of divine presence and power. Isaiah's declaration strips away this claim: God's praise—the acknowledgment of His glory and power—belongs to Him alone and can never transfer to human-made images. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse without textual variant, indicating that this radical monotheistic statement was transmitted with complete fidelity across centuries. In the context of Isaiah 40–49, this verse serves as the authoritative foundation for everything that follows: the Servant can accomplish liberation because He serves the one God whose glory none can diminish or share. This stands in stark contrast to Babylonian theology, which posited a pantheon of competing deities and cosmic powers.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: For Christian readers, verse 8 takes on additional force when read in light of New Testament Christology. Jesus Christ, the incarnate Servant, receives the worship and glory that God declares He alone will accept (John 1:1-3, Philippians 2:6-11, Revelation 5:11-14). This is not a violation of monotheism but its vindication: Jesus's receipt of glory is possible only because He is eternally one with the Father in nature and power. The verse thus becomes a lens through which to understand the radical claim of Christian faith: the Servant whose work is described in verse 7 receives divine honor not as a separate power but as the very embodiment of God's glory among humanity. The exclusivity principle—'my glory I give to no other'—remains intact, but the Servant's identity is so thoroughly one with God that He cannot be 'another' in any ultimate sense.
commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 42:8 establishes the theological foundation for understanding Christ as the Servant. If God will not share His glory with graven images or false deities, then the Servant's receipt of divine honor (Isaiah 42:1, 49:3-4) must mean that the Servant shares God's essential nature—not as a creature elevated to divine status but as the eternal Son who is one with the Father. In Christian theology, the incarnation does not violate verse 8 because Christ is not 'another' god but the second person of the Godhead, eternally God. The Servant's power to open blind eyes and break chains derives entirely from identification with God's exclusive glory. Revelation 21:23 describes the heavenly city where 'the Lamb is the light thereof'—indicating that Christ's glorification is not separate from but the manifestation of God's ultimate glory.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon directly applies Isaiah's monotheistic insistence throughout its pages. In 2 Nephi 31:2-3, Nephi teaches that 'we talk of Christ, we rejoice in Christ, we preach of Christ'—but always as the means of glorifying God the Father, never allowing the Savior to eclipse God's exclusive glory. Alma 34:14-15 emphasizes that Christ's atonement works through and in harmony with God's purposes, not in competition with them. The Book of Mormon's consistent Christology preserves Isaiah's monotheistic framework: the Servant glorifies the Father; He does not diminish or displace God's unique honor.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:22-24 reveals that the Father and the Son are distinct personages but united in glory, power, and purpose: 'And now after the many testimonies which have been given of him, this is the testimony, last of all, which we give of him: That he lives! For we saw him, even on the right hand of God.' The Doctrine and Covenants clarifies what Isaiah 42:8 holds in tension: God will share His work and presence with the Servant (Christ and later the faithful), but His ultimate glory and exclusive divinity remain intact. D&C 84:35-39 explicitly teaches that the glory of God is the light by which all things move and exist, and that sharing in this glory comes through covenant relationship, never through idolatry or displacement of God's supremacy.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment presents the celestial room as the ultimate manifestation of God's glory (kavod)—a space of radiant light and peace that represents God's presence without any carved image or material representation. The progression from the telestial through terrestrial to celestial rooms reflects the principle of verse 8: true worship leads not to material idols but to the presence of God Himself. The temple's absence of graven images, despite housing sacred ordinances, embodies Isaiah's principle that God's glory cannot be captured in human craft.

word_study.meaning: 'I am Yahweh.' Ani (אני) is the first-person singular pronoun 'I'; YHWH (יהוה) is the ineffable name of God, traditionally pronounced Adonai ('Lord') in Jewish practice. The formula 'ani YHWH' asserts personal identity with the divine name—not 'I serve YHWH' or 'I speak for YHWH,' but 'I AM YHWH.'
word_study.significance: This formula appears 12 times in Isaiah 40–48 alone, functioning as a refrain anchoring monotheistic faith. It echoes God's self-revelation to Moses at the burning bush ('I AM THAT I AM,' Exodus 3:14). In the Servant Song context, it establishes that the Servant's work derives entirely from identification with the one true God. For Latter-day Saints, it resonates with D&C 29:1, where Christ declares 'I am Jesus Christ, the Son of God,' claiming personal identity with divine purpose.

word_study.meaning: Glory, honor, weight, majesty, brightness. The root kabad (כבד) means 'heavy' or 'weighty,' so kavod originally denoted the weightiness or substance of something—metaphorically, its importance, honor, and visible manifestation of power. In Isaiah, God's kavod is His visible presence and overwhelming majesty (40:5, 60:1).
word_study.significance: Kavod is not something God possesses casually but His essential attribute—the divine weight and honor that commands worship and obedience. That God 'will not give' this to another means it is utterly nontransferable. Yet in Isaiah 40:5, 'the glory of the LORD shall be revealed'—suggesting that the Servant's work makes God's kavod visible and known to all flesh. For Christians, the incarnation is the ultimate revelation of God's glory in human form (John 1:14).

word_study.meaning: Praise, song of praise, hymn. From the root halal (הלל), meaning 'to shine' or 'to boast,' tehillah is the acknowledgment and celebration of another's greatness. It appears in the title 'Psalms' (Tehillim) and denotes the worship response of creation to God.
word_study.significance: God's praise cannot be given to carved images because they have no being or power worthy of celebration. Only the living God, who acts in history and saves, deserves tehillah. In the context of Isaiah 42, the Servant's work (opening eyes, freeing prisoners) generates praise to God—creation recognizes His power through the Servant's acts. Verses 10-12 will extend this theme universally.

word_study.meaning: Carved idols, graven images. From the root pasal (פסל), 'to carve' or 'to sculpt.' Pesilim are human-made religious images—statues or reliefs representing deities.
word_study.significance: The polemic against pesilim runs throughout Isaiah 40–46, emphasizing the absurdity of worshipping objects made by human hands. Isaiah 40:19-20 satirizes the craftsman who selects fine wood and hires a skilled artisan to make a steady idol. In contrast, God is uncreated, eternal, and incomparable. The Servant's work demonstrates God's power to act in history; no carved image can claim such reality.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah establishes the incomparability of God: 'To whom then will ye liken me, or shall I be equal? saith the Holy One. Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things.' Verse 8 reiterates this incomparability and exclusivity.

God reveals Himself to Moses as 'I AM THAT I AM,' the same formula of self-identity that echoes through 'I am the LORD' in Isaiah 42:8, establishing continuity of divine identity across the Hebrew Bible.

Moses declares to Israel: 'Unto thee it was shewed, that thou mightest know that the LORD he is God; there is none else beside him'—the foundational principle that Isaiah 42:8 reasserts in the exilic context.

Jesus prays to the Father: 'And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was'—claiming participation in God's unique glory and demonstrating how Christ fulfills Isaiah 42:8 without violating monotheism.

The Lord declares to Oliver Cowdery: 'Seek not for riches but for wisdom; and behold, the mysteries of God shall be unfolded unto you, and then shall you be made rich'—emphasizing that God's glory and honor cannot be displaced by material wealth or false idols.

commentary.historical_context: In the Babylonian exile (sixth century BCE), Judean captives were surrounded by polytheistic religious practice and grand temple iconography. Babylonian temples housed massive carved idols representing Marduk, Nisaba, and other deities. These were not merely decorative but believed to be conduits of divine presence and power. Exiled Judeans would have faced constant pressure to participate in this religious framework or at minimum to acknowledge its legitimacy. Isaiah's polemic in verse 8 directly confronts this environment: the God of Israel is not one deity among many, nor does He reside in carved images. This distinction was not merely theological but survival-necessary for maintaining Jewish identity and faith during captivity. The exclusivity principle—'my glory will I not give to another'—became a rallying point for monotheistic resistance and the foundation of Jewish identity that would outlast Babylonian empire and cultural dominance.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, Isaiah 42:8 challenges us to distinguish between genuine worship of God and subtle idolatry. We may not worship carved images, but we can subtly give our ultimate loyalty and praise to money, status, career advancement, social media presence, or political ideology—graven images of modern culture. The verse calls us to jealously guard God's exclusive place in our hearts and to ensure that our praise, honor, and ultimate devotion flow to Him alone. It also teaches us to be humble servants who, like the Servant described in verse 7, accomplish God's liberatory work without seeking personal glory. As members of the Church, we participate in the Servant's mission—opening eyes to spiritual truth, releasing those bound by sin, dispelling spiritual darkness—but always as instruments of God's glory, never as independent powers. The verse reminds us that in temple and family, in teaching and service, we point always toward God, never toward ourselves or our accomplishments.

text_kjv: Behold, the former things are come to pass, and new things do I declare: before they spring forth I tell you of them.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah 42:9 presents God's mastery over time and history as proof of His divinity and the unique legitimacy of His word. The verse divides into three temporal movements: (1) 'the former things are come to pass'—what God predicted previously has been fulfilled; (2) 'new things do I declare'—God announces future events not yet realized; (3) 'before they spring forth I tell you'—God speaks of what will happen before it manifests in history. This temporal sequence establishes a pattern that distinguishes the true God from idols and false prophets. The 'former things' (rishonot) likely refers to earlier prophecies in Isaiah 40–41 that have begun fulfillment, or to the history of God's dealings with Israel that confirm His faithfulness. More broadly, it encompasses the entire arc of Old Testament prophecy: Abraham's call, the exodus, the covenant at Sinai, the establishment of David's throne. All these have occurred, demonstrating that God's word is reliable. The 'new things' (chadashot) point toward the imminent future: the return from exile, the rise of Cyrus, the universal revelation of God's salvation through the Servant.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve verse 9 identically to the Masoretic Text, with the consonantal text חדשות (chadashot, 'new things') unchanged. This textual stability underscores the ancient and reliable transmission of Isaiah's witness. The verse responds directly to Isaiah 41:22-23, where God had challenged the idols: 'Let them bring them forth, and shew us what shall happen: let them shew the former things, what they be; that we may consider them, and know the latter end of them; or declare us things for to come. Shew the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that ye are gods.' The idols cannot do this; they cannot predict or control history. God, by contrast, announces both retrospectively (former things fulfilled) and prospectively (new things to come), demonstrating that history moves according to His purposes. This claims for God what modern philosophy and science often reserve for impersonal forces or natural laws: intelligence, intentionality, and causative power.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: For the exiles in Babylon, verse 9 would have been profoundly reassuring. They had witnessed the fulfillment of Isaiah's earlier prophecies: the fall of the northern kingdom, the siege and exile of Judah, the dominance of Babylon. These 'former things' were not primarily comforting—they were judgments. But their fulfillment proved Isaiah's prophetic credibility. Now, Isaiah declares 'new things': you will return; your oppressor will be overthrown; the servant will accomplish a worldwide mission of liberation and revelation. Because God proved faithful in judgment, His promise of restoration could be trusted. The verse thus encodes both the logic of the Exodus (God rescued Israel from Egypt as a type of future, greater deliverance) and the logic of prophecy itself (fulfilled word builds faith in unfulfilled promise). For readers throughout history, the verse invites this reasoning: Where has God proven faithful in the past? Where can you trust His promises for the future?
commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 42:9 foreshadows Christ's dual role as revealer of past truth and announcer of future kingdom. Jesus Himself demonstrated this in His ministry: He revealed the true meaning of Torah and prophets ('thus it is written,' Matthew 26:54), fulfilling 'former things,' while also announcing new covenants and future events (the resurrection, the second coming). The incarnation itself is the supreme 'new thing' that Isaiah announces—not predicted by name in specific detail but initiated by God as an unprecedented act in history. Revelation 19:10 states that 'the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy,' meaning that all prophecy points toward and flows from Christ. Thus, when God declares 'new things' through Isaiah, the ultimate 'new thing' is the Servant Himself—the incarnate Son who fulfills all previous prophecy while opening entirely new chapters of God's redemptive work.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon applies Isaiah's principle of fulfilled prophecy throughout. Nephi's fulfillment of Isaiah prophecies (1 Nephi 21:1-26, citing Isaiah 49) demonstrates how 'former things' become markers of credibility for 'new things' to come. 3 Nephi 15:1-8 shows the risen Jesus explaining why certain prophecies had been and would be fulfilled differently than expected, affirming both God's control of history and His freedom to announce 'new things' beyond human prediction. The entire Book of Mormon is structured as an announcement of 'new things'—the coming forth of additional scripture in the latter days (2 Nephi 29).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:28-33 teaches that the Lord's work 'must increase and abound more and more' and that He 'comprehendeth all things,' past and future. This echoes Isaiah 42:9's claim that God holds all time in view and announces both what has been and what will be. D&C 29:11 declares 'All things unto me are spiritual,' emphasizing that God's relationship to history is not passive but active and purposeful. Section 68:3-4 similarly establishes that God's words are 'scripture' precisely because they 'are true' and 'shall be fulfilled.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment presents a cosmological narrative—from creation through Fall through redemption—that demonstrates God's control over the great movements of history toward salvation. The endowment itself enacts Isaiah's principle: it reveals the 'former things' (the plan of salvation enacted in Eden and through Abraham) and points toward 'new things' (exaltation and eternal increase). Covenants made in the temple bind us to participate in God's ongoing work of redemption.

word_study.meaning: 'The former things' or 'the first things.' From the root rishon (ראשון), meaning 'first' in time or order. The definite article (ha-) indicates these are specific, known events—not abstract past, but concrete historical facts already witnessed.
word_study.significance: In Isaiah's rhetorical strategy, 'former things' serves as proof of God's prophetic accuracy and power. Every fulfilled prediction demonstrates that God controls history and speaks truth. This becomes the foundation for faith in 'new things' not yet manifest. The term carries the weight of verifiable history.

word_study.meaning: 'New things' or 'new matters.' From the root chadash (חדש), meaning 'new,' 'fresh,' 'renewed.' The Covenant Rendering notes that shir chadash ('new song,' verse 10) marks each significant act of God in history.
word_study.significance: Chadashot emphasizes that God's work is not merely repetition of the past but continual novelty—new acts, fresh revelations, unprecedented mercies. This breaks fatalism (the exile might seem permanent) and opens possibility (God will do something unexpected). It echoes the tradition of God's 'new thing' in Jeremiah 31:22 ('A new thing in the earth') and Revelation 21:5 ('Behold, I make all things new').

word_study.meaning: 'I declare,' 'I announce,' 'I make known.' From the root nagad (נגד), meaning 'to tell,' 'to report,' 'to reveal.' The hiphil form (maggid) emphasizes the active, deliberate disclosure of information.
word_study.significance: The term underscores God's role as revealer and communicator. God does not merely know the future; He announces it, brings it to light, shares it with humanity. This connects to prophecy itself—the prophet's role is to be God's mouthpiece, declaring (maggid) what God has revealed. Isaiah positions himself as the vehicle through which God's declarations flow.

word_study.meaning: 'They will spring forth,' 'they will grow,' 'they will emerge.' From the root tzamach (צמח), meaning 'to grow,' 'to sprout,' 'to shoot up' (as plants from the ground).
word_study.significance: The metaphor is agricultural and organic: the new things will grow naturally from the soil of God's purposes, not artificially forced. This suggests inevitability and life—the new things are as certain as spring's growth. It also suggests gradual unfolding: first the word, then the reality. The verb tense (imperfect) indicates future, ongoing action.

cross_references.connection: God challenges the idols directly: 'Produce your cause, saith the LORD; bring forth your strong reasons... Let them bring them forth, and shew us what shall happen.' Verse 9 answers this challenge by demonstrating that God alone can predict and fulfill history.

Jeremiah similarly promises 'a new thing in the earth'—a new covenant and new way of relationship. Isaiah 42:9's 'new things' connect to this theme of God's continual renewal and redemptive innovation.

The Lord teaches that all things are 'spiritual unto me' and unfold 'according to the power of my Spirit' in 'their time,' emphasizing God's sovereign control over history and revelation that Isaiah 42:9 expresses.
'Behold, I make all things new'—the ultimate fulfillment of Isaiah's 'new things' at the eschaton, showing how God's novelty and renewal continue to the end of time.

The Lord declares through Mormon that His 'arm is stretched out still' and He will continue to reveal according to the needs of the time, echoing Isaiah's conviction that God announces new things as history unfolds.

commentary.historical_context: In the exilic period (early sixth century BCE), the reliability of Isaiah's earlier prophecies would have been tested by the brutal facts of exile. Isaiah had predicted the fall of northern Israel (722 BCE) and the Assyrian threat; these had come to pass. He had predicted Judean exile and destruction (fulfilled 586 BCE); these were happening around and within his audience. For an exiled community, the question was existential: Can we trust this same prophet's announcement of restoration and return? Verse 9 addresses this by building faith on fulfilled prediction. The 'former things' were prophecies that had proven true, even when they were hard to believe beforehand. This precedent should embolden faith in the 'new things'—promises of return, restoration, and universal salvation through the Servant. Historically, Cyrus II of Persia would rise in the 550s BCE, overthrowing Babylon and releasing prisoners of war (including Judeans) to return home—fulfilling yet more of Isaiah's predictions and validating his prophetic word. The verse encodes the ancient Near Eastern understanding of prophecy as distinctive to Israel's God: whereas Babylonian divination (hepatomancy, augury) sought to read omens in entrails or stars, Israel's prophets claimed direct revelation and announcement of God's future purpose.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, Isaiah 42:9 invites deep reflection on how we evaluate spiritual claims and build faith. The verse teaches us to look at fulfilled prophecy as evidence of God's faithfulness. Where has the Lord proven true in your life? Where have your patriarchal blessings, priesthood blessings, or priesthood leadership's counsel come to pass? These 'former things' become the foundation for trusting the 'new things' God is announcing today—whether personal revelation about your future, the Church's ongoing doctrinal development (as in recent temple changes), or prophetic declarations about latter-day events. The verse also calls us to remain spiritually alive and attentive: God is always announcing 'new things.' We must listen for them. This resists spiritual complacency (assuming the past fully contains God's purposes) and opens us to the ongoing revelatory relationship that defines Latter-day Saint faith. Are we expecting God to do new things? Are we listening for His voice? Are we prepared to be surprised by what He accomplishes?

text_kjv: Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise from the end of the earth, ye that go down to the sea, and all that is therein; the isles, and the inhabitants thereof.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah 42:10 marks a dramatic turn from proclamation to doxology: the announcement of God's work in verses 1-9 now elicits responsive praise. The verse opens with an imperative—'Sing unto the LORD'—that extends to an ever-widening circle of worshippers. The command begins with seafarers (those who go down to the sea), extends to all marine life and sea creatures ('all that is therein'), and reaches to 'the isles, and the inhabitants thereof'—coastlands and island peoples. This geographical specificity is not random; it reflects the known world from an ancient Levantine perspective. The Mediterranean coastlands, Phoenician and Greek territories, Cyprus, distant islands—all become witnesses called to sing. The 'new song' (shir chadash) responds to God's 'new things' announced in verse 9. As the Covenant Rendering notes, a new song marks each significant divine act in history. The newness is not musical novelty but historical event: God has done something unprecedented, something worthy of fresh praise that old songs cannot adequately express. The imperative form ('sing') is not polite request but authoritative summons. The entire created order, especially humanity spread across the earth, is called to acknowledge God's work.
commentary.narrative_continued: The universality of this call is striking. In Isaiah 40–49, the scope repeatedly expands from Israel to humanity to all creation. Here, verse 10 announces that coastland peoples and island nations—those geographically and often politically most distant from Judah—should join the chorus. This is not mere political fantasy but theological vision: the Servant's work (verse 7) liberates all who sit in darkness, opens eyes to all the blind, breaks chains throughout the world. Therefore, universal praise is not sentimental exaggeration but logical consequence. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse without variant, confirming the stability and consistency of this radical universalism across centuries of Jewish tradition. For exiled Judeans, verse 10 would have offered both comfort and challenge. Comfort: the entire world will eventually recognize and praise the God of Israel, vindicating Jewish faith even in exile. Challenge: how could this be? The exiles themselves were captive; the visible world was under Babylonian imperial control. Yet verse 10 envisions a future where this reality is flipped—the hidden God is publicly praised, and all nations acknowledge His work.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The verse's structure moves from 'sing unto the LORD' (imperative) to 'his praise from the end of the earth' (participial construction). This movement from command to description emphasizes inevitability: the praise will flow from the earth's uttermost reaches not merely because God commands it but because the reality of His work compels it. The parallel in verse 12 will intensify this: 'Let them give glory to the LORD and declare His praise in the coastlands.' The repetition reinforces the vision that God's glory, which He refuses to share (verse 8), will be publicly known, seen, and celebrated worldwide. For Christian readers, verse 10 prefigures the eschatological vision of Revelation 5:9-10, where all nations, tribes, peoples, and languages sing praises to the Lamb—the servant whose work has ransomed people for God. The 'new song' of Isaiah 42:10 becomes the song of the 144,000 in Revelation 14:3, indicating continuity between Isaiah's vision and Christian apocalypse.
commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is both the subject and, in typological terms, the fulfillment of Isaiah 42:10's vision. As the Servant whose work is described in verse 7, Christ is the agent who opens eyes and frees prisoners—thus inspiring the 'new song.' Additionally, as the object of the worship, Christ—when recognized and known—evokes universal praise. Revelation 5:11-12 depicts the Lamb surrounded by 'ten thousand times ten thousand and thousands of thousands' singing 'Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing.' The incarnation is itself the 'new song' that creation erupts into—a wholly unprecedented divine action that demands fresh praise. In typological terms, every new song in Scripture points toward this ultimate song: the recognition that God has acted in history through Jesus Christ, breaking every chain and opening every eye.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon extends Isaiah's vision of universal praise. 2 Nephi 25:10-12 teaches that 'all the House of Israel' will eventually be gathered and that the Gentiles will be partakers of the blessings of Israel and the covenants of God. Alma 5:50-51 describes how the righteous will 'sing the song of redeeming love.' More broadly, the entire missionary thrust of the Book of Mormon—bringing the gospel to all nations—enacts Isaiah's vision of universal praise. Nephite and Lamanite cultures, both removed from Jerusalem's temple worship, eventually unite in acknowledging Christ. This literalizes Isaiah's vision: peoples from distant lands joining in one song of praise.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:11 teaches that 'All things are the Lord's; and he is in all things.' D&C 65:5-6 declares that the kingdom of God will 'fill the whole earth' and 'many people shall go and say, Come ye, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Jacob.' This directly fulfills Isaiah's vision of universal praise flowing from every land. D&C 76:82-88 describes the celestial kingdom in terms suggesting an eternal community of praise—all nations, kindreds, and peoples acknowledging God's glory.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the house of God where praise occurs in its most focused and covenant form. But Isaiah 42:10 suggests that the entire earth becomes a temple—all creation a sanctuary of praise. Modern temple work, particularly the work for the dead, extends this vision: generations from every nation and era are brought into covenant relationship and included in the eternal circle of praise. The eschatological temple of Revelation 21:22-26 makes this explicit: the entire New Jerusalem becomes a place of worship where 'the nations...shall walk in the light of it.'

word_study.meaning: 'A new song.' Shir (שיר) means 'song,' 'music,' 'singing.' Chadash (חדש) means 'new,' 'fresh,' 'recent.' Together, shir chadash denotes a song composed in response to a new divine action.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that 'new song' (shir chadash) appears also in Psalms 33, 40, 96, 98, 144, 149 as a standard formula for liturgical praise of God's recent or upcoming acts. Revelation 5:9 and 14:3 employ the same concept in the Christian apocalyptic tradition. The newness is not stylistic but historical—the song expresses gratitude for what God has newly done. The term signals that praise must keep pace with God's acts; stale hymns cannot capture fresh mercies.

word_study.meaning: 'Praise,' 'song of praise,' 'hymn.' From halal (הלל), 'to praise,' 'to shine,' 'to glory in.' Tehillah is the joyful acknowledgment of God's greatness and goodness.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'his praise from the end of the earth' (tehillato miktzeh ha-aretz) indicates that praise flows from the uttermost places—there is no location beyond God's reach or awareness. The entire earth becomes a choir, and every distant place contributes its voice to the universal acknowledgment of God.

word_study.meaning: 'Those who go down to the sea,' 'seafarers,' 'mariners.' Yordei (יורדי) is the masculine plural participle of yarad (ירד), 'to go down,' 'to descend.' Yam (יָם) is 'sea.' The phrase denotes merchants, sailors, fishermen—all who traverse the waters.
word_study.significance: In the ancient world, seafarers represented the farthest reach of commerce and communication. They were connected to distant lands, foreign peoples, and international exchange. By summoning seafarers to praise, Isaiah signals that even the most cosmopolitan, secular, business-driven elements of society are called to acknowledge God.

word_study.meaning: 'Isles,' 'islands,' 'coastlands,' 'distant lands.' From an Akkadian loanword (ayya) meaning 'island.' In Isaiah, iyim often refers to lands across the sea, including coastal civilizations like Phoenicia, Cyprus, Greece, and places beyond.
word_study.significance: Iyim represents geographical and cultural distance. By calling the isles to praise, Isaiah extends the circle of worship to peoples who might have no direct contact with Israel or its traditions. The universalism is radical: even those most distant are summoned to acknowledge God's work.

cross_references.connection: 'Sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth... For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised.' This psalm encapsulates the same imperative of universal, new-song praise that Isaiah 42:10 demands.

'And they sung a new song, saying, Thou art worthy... and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation.' The New Testament's vision directly echoes and fulfills Isaiah's call to universal praise centered on redemptive work.

Later in Isaiah, the returning exiles are called to 'Go ye forth from Babylon, flee ye from the Chaldeans, with a voice of singing'—showing how the 'new song' of verse 10 is enacted in the exiles' own liberation experience.

The Lord promises that in the latter days, 'every coronal shall hear the voice of the Lord' and 'all things are theirs, whether life or death.' This evokes the universal scope of praise in Isaiah 42:10—all creation acknowledging God's work.
Nephi teaches that the risen Jesus will appear to the Nephites as well as the Jews, extending salvation's reach globally—a fulfillment of the universal praise Isaiah 42:10 anticipates.

commentary.historical_context: In the exilic period, the command to sing a new song—especially from the ends of the earth—would have seemed almost absurd to captive Judeans. They were not singing; they were mourning (Psalm 137:1-4: 'By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept'). The isles and distant lands were not acknowledging Israel's God but worshipping their own pantheons under their own rulers. Yet Isaiah's vision transcends contemporary realities. From the ancient Near Eastern perspective, coastlands were centers of Phoenician and Greek commerce and influence—powerful, independent, prosperous. The idea that these sophisticated maritime peoples would abandon their gods to praise Israel's God was not realism but eschatological vision—a declaration of what WILL be, not what IS. The new song thus becomes an act of prophetic imagination and faith: in the face of exile's silence, Isaiah insists that God's work will eventually evoke praise from every corner of the earth. This was not unusual in prophetic tradition; the prophets regularly announced futures that contradicted present realities, calling faith into being before circumstances changed.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, Isaiah 42:10 extends an invitation and a challenge. First, it invites us to participate in the great universal chorus of praise. No matter how isolated we feel, how marginalized our faith seems in a secular world, we are part of an eternal community singing the new song of redemption. The gospel's worldwide expansion—with missionaries and members in 190+ countries—literalizes Isaiah's vision of praise rising 'from the end of the earth.' We are witnesses and participants. Second, the verse challenges us to examine what we are singing. Are our hymns, prayers, and testimonies responsive to what God is actually doing in history—His new work? Or are we trapped in repetition of old songs, unable to perceive or celebrate God's fresh mercies? Third, verse 10 reminds us that when we sing praises, we join not just our local ward community but the entire company of the faithful across all times and places. Our voices matter in the cosmic chorus. Finally, the verse calls us outward: Are we helping others hear and join this 'new song'? The missionary work of the Church is essentially an invitation to sing—to recognize God's work and add your voice to the praise.

text_kjv: Let the wilderness and the cities thereof lift up their voice, the villages that Kedar doth inhabit: let the inhabitants of the rock sing, let them shout from the top of the mountains.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah 42:11 continues and intensifies the call to universal praise initiated in verse 10, now explicitly naming specific geographical and cultural regions. The verse moves geographically from maritime regions (verse 10) to terrestrial ones: wilderness and cities, desert villages, rocky fortresses, and mountain peaks. The geographical specificity reveals Isaiah's vision of truly universal praise—not merely abstract but concretely encompassing every inhabited zone and every form of human settlement. 'Kedar' refers to the Arabian desert tribes, descendants of Ishmael (Genesis 25:13), historically known as Bedouin nomads who ranged across the Syrian and Arabian deserts. Their inclusion in the call to praise is significant: they were geographically distant from Jerusalem, often in tension or conflict with Judean interests, and not part of the covenant community. Yet Isaiah summons even Kedar to 'lift up their voice.' 'Sela' (the 'rock') likely refers to Petra, the great Nabatean city carved into red rock, or more broadly to any rocky settlement in the southern regions. The call ascends from settlements to mountaintops—progressively higher, more dramatic, more difficult to reach. Each location, from wilderness to peak, becomes a choir in this cosmic chorus of praise.
commentary.narrative_continued: The progression from verse 10 to verse 11 moves outward in ever-widening circles: first, the distant seas and isles; now, the distant deserts, rocks, and mountains. The pattern suggests that no terrain is too remote, no people too foreign, to be summoned to praise. The wilderness (midbar) was often imagined in ancient Near Eastern thought as chaotic, dangerous, and godless—yet even there, creation is called to acknowledge God. Cities, by contrast, represent civilization, commerce, and political power—centers of human agency. By calling both wilderness and cities to sing together, Isaiah suggests that all domains of human experience and settlement find their ultimate meaning in praising God. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse without significant variant, confirming the stability of this radical universalism. The Dead Sea Scrolls' scribe at 1QIsaᵃ would have read these same words without deviation, preserving for centuries afterward the vision that even Arabian Bedouins and mountain dwellers would someday acknowledge Israel's God.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: Theologically, verse 11 challenges any notion of God as the God of Jerusalem alone, or of Israel alone. The Servant's work (verse 7) has universal scope, and therefore the praise responding to that work must also be universal. The verse implicitly rebukes the theology of imperial confinement: God is not contained in a temple, not limited to a people, not restricted by geography or political boundaries. The shout from the mountaintops (v. 11b) echoes with exultation: not quiet confession but loud proclamation, not shameful hiding but bold declaration. This exultation will appear again in Isaiah 44:23, 48:20, and especially in the New Testament apocalypse (Revelation 19:1-8), where 'a great voice of much people in heaven' cries out in celebration. For a people in exile, silenced by captivity, this promise of ultimate, universal, triumphant voice would have been both sustaining and revolutionary. It answered the deep question: Does my God still have a voice? Will my silence be permanent? The answer is no: one day, the entire world will cry out in praise.
commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the agent whose work inspires this universal praise. Isaiah 42:1-4 established the Servant as the one bringing forth justice to the Gentiles; verse 11 shows the Gentiles' response—they sing and shout. Typologically, Christ's incarnation, death, and resurrection are the 'new thing' (verse 9) that eventually evokes praise from every nation and people. Revelation 5:9-13 explicitly portrays this: the Lamb is surrounded by praise from 'every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation.' The Cross becomes the pivot point: the scandal of crucifixion is transformed into the victory of resurrection, and what appeared to be defeat becomes the moment that summons all creation to acknowledgment. In Christological terms, every person—from Kedar to Petra to the ends of the earth—is invited into relationship with God through Christ, and that relationship finds its expression in worship and praise.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records Nephi's vision of all nations coming to Jerusalem (1 Nephi 21:22-23), which directly parallels Isaiah 42:10-11's vision of universal praise. Additionally, Helaman 5:47-49 describes the Lamanites hearing the voice of the Son of God in a miraculous way, showing how even those most distant from Jerusalem and least likely candidates (in Nephite estimation) are brought into God's fold. The overall thrust of the Book of Mormon—a record of peoples in the Americas—itself enacts Isaiah's vision: distant lands acknowledging God's work.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:58-59 teaches that 'the righteous shall be gathered on my right hand unto eternal life; and the wicked on my left hand will I be ashamed to own before the Father.' This suggests a universal gathering of all peoples to stand before the Lord—the ultimate fulfillment of Isaiah's vision of all creation praising God. D&C 110:11 speaks of the Church being 'established, never to be thrown down, neither moved out of its place,' suggesting an eternal, universal nature that transcends geographical boundaries. D&C 65 teaches of the kingdom rolling forth in all the earth 'in the midst of the thick darkness covering the earth.'

word_study.meaning: 'Wilderness,' 'desert,' 'pastureland.' From the root davar (דבר), possibly related to 'to speak' (davar), midbar denotes unsettled, sparsely populated regions—in Palestine, the Negev and Trans-Jordanian steppes.
word_study.significance: In biblical imagery, the wilderness is simultaneously a place of danger and testing (where Israel wandered 40 years) and a place of divine encounter and purification (where God refines His people). By calling the wilderness to sing, Isaiah universalizes praise beyond the realm of civilization and established religion. The wilderness becomes a worshipping community—paradoxically, a spiritual center.

word_study.meaning: Hatzeirim (חצרים) are enclosures, villages, or pastoral settlements (from hatzar, 'to enclose'). Kedar (קדר), etymologically related to 'dark' or 'black,' was the designation for the northern Arabian desert peoples, Bedouin descendants of Ishmael. Teshe (תשב) means 'dwell' or 'inhabit.'
word_study.significance: Kedar appears frequently in Isaiah (21:16, 60:7) as a symbol of distant, foreign, non-Israelite peoples. By name-checking Kedar, Isaiah explicitly includes those most culturally and religiously alien to Jerusalem. This is radical inclusivity. Kedar's inclusion signals that no tradition, no people, no region is exempt from God's summons to praise.

word_study.meaning: Sela (סלע) means 'rock' or 'crag.' In biblical geography, it often refers to Petra, the great Nabatean carved-rock city southeast of the Dead Sea, or more broadly to any fortified settlement in rocky terrain. Yashvei (יושבי) means 'inhabitants' or 'those who sit,' suggesting residents, settlers, and dwellers.
word_study.significance: Rocky settlements in arid regions were strongholds—defensive, secure, but also remote and isolated. The call for them to 'sing for joy' suggests that even the most fortified, self-contained communities cannot escape or ignore God's work. They too must join the universal chorus.

word_study.term_english: shout from the top of the mountains
word_study.meaning: Rosh (ראש) means 'head' or 'top'; harim (הרים) is 'mountains.' Yitzvachu (יצוחו) is 'let them shout,' 'let them cry out' (from tzavach, צוח, meaning 'to cry,' 'to shout,' 'to make a sound').
word_study.significance: Mountains in ancient Near Eastern cosmology often represented the realm of the gods or the heights from which divine voice carries farthest. The shout from mountaintops is not whispered prayer but bold proclamation. The verb tzavach emphasizes a loud, piercing, undeniable voice. The praise cannot be contained or silenced.

cross_references.connection: The genealogy of Ishmael lists Kedar among his twelve sons and their settlement regions, establishing Kedar as a historical Arabian people. Isaiah's inclusion of Kedar in verse 11 specifically targets this people in their remote settlements for inclusion in God's praise.

'Let the sea roar, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein. Let the floods clap their hands: let the hills be joyful together. Before the LORD; for he cometh to judge the earth.' The psalm uses nearly identical language and scope as Isaiah 42:10-11, suggesting this is a common prophetic/liturgical theme.

'For ye shall go out with joy, and be led forth with peace: the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing... Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree.' Later Isaiah extends the vision of universal, creation-wide praise and transformation.

'And I beheld, and I heard the voice of many angels... And every creature which is in heaven, and on the earth, and under the earth... I heard saying, Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, be unto him.' This echoes and fulfills the universal cosmic praise Isaiah anticipates.
'Where God and Christ are the judge of all... and all the Holy Angels,' showing how the Restoration retains the vision of universal, eternal praise and judgment centered on God's and Christ's glory.

commentary.historical_context: In the sixth century BCE, the Arabian desert peoples (Kedar) and the Nabatean rock-dwelling peoples (residents of Sela/Petra) were indeed distant from Jerusalem in every sense: geographically, culturally, politically, and religiously. Kedar maintained its own polytheistic traditions and nomadic lifestyle. Petra would not become a major city until the Nabatean period (centuries after Isaiah), but the archaeological and textual evidence suggests rocky settlements existed in the region. From a realistic, political standpoint, expecting desert nomads and distant rockland dwellers to join in praise of Israel's God would have seemed fantastical to exiles in Babylon. Yet Isaiah's point is theological, not political: history moves according to God's purposes, and all peoples will eventually recognize His work. The verse reflects a distinctly Jewish theological confidence in God's eventual universal recognition despite present exile and silence. This confidence would sustain Jewish communities through centuries of diaspora, grounding faith not in political power (which they lacked) but in theological vision (that God's purposes transcend empires).
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, Isaiah 42:11 offers a vision of the Church's ultimate scope and destiny. We are a restoration movement claiming truth for all people, in all lands, across all cultures. The Church's missionary work and global expansion enact Isaiah's vision: the gospel is preached to Kindgdoms and nations, calling each to recognize God's hand and join the eternal choir of praise. On a personal level, the verse invites us to recognize that praise is not optional but a response to God's work. When we see divine providence in our lives, in our families, in our communities, we are called to 'lift up our voice,' to 'sing,' to 'shout' boldly—not in embarrassment or whispered qualification, but with full hearts. The verse also reminds us that no one is too distant, too different, too foreign to be included in God's purposes. In a Church that is increasingly culturally diverse, with members from every nation and background, we live Isaiah's vision. Every culture, every language, every people brings its unique voice to the praise of God. Are we honoring and celebrating that diversity? Are we recognizing God's work not only in expected places but in the wilderness, the rocks, the mountaintops—the unexpected quarters where His Spirit moves? Are we ourselves singing boldly, or have we been silenced by the world's mockery? The verse calls us to courageous, joyful, public praise.

text_kjv: Let them give glory unto the LORD, and declare his praise in the islands.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah 42:12 concludes the call to universal praise that began in verse 10, bringing the vision to its final, focused crescendo. The verse employs two verbs of declaration—'give glory' and 'declare praise'—both in the imperative, commanding the 'islands' (iyim, the distant coastlands) to consciously, deliberately, and publicly acknowledge God's work. This verse echoes verse 8, where God insisted 'my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images.' Now the circle closes: God's glory, which He refuses to share with idols, is precisely what the islands and distant peoples are commanded to give to Him. The parallelism is deliberate and theologically profound. In verse 8, God asserts exclusive claim to glory (kavod) and praise (tehillah); in verse 12, that same glory and praise flow from the ends of the earth in responsive worship. The verb 'give glory' (yashimu kavod) is literally 'let them set' or 'place' glory—suggesting that these distant peoples actively contribute their honor and acknowledgment to God's account. 'Declare praise' (yagidu tehillah) means to announce, proclaim, make known the celebration of God's greatness. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse without significant variant, confirming that this vision of global divine praise has been faithfully transmitted through centuries.
commentary.narrative_continued: The specific mention of 'islands' (iyim) at the verse's conclusion circles back to verse 10's similar phrasing. This repetition is not mere stylistic habit but theological emphasis. Islands and coastlands represent the farthest reaches of the known world—places that would seem least likely to acknowledge Israel's God. Yet these are precisely the regions summoned to give glory and declare praise. The verse thus carries an implicit universalism: if even the islands, the most distant lands, give glory to God, then truly all creation has been brought into His worship. This creates an inclusivity that transcends national, ethnic, and geographical boundaries. For the exiled community reading or hearing these words, the verse would have been both humbling and exalting. Humbling: Judah itself, in exile, was not currently in a position to give glory loudly—their temple was destroyed, their political independence lost, their voice silenced by captivity. Exalting: yet the promise assures that one day, the entire world will give the glory that Judah is temporarily unable to give, and that restoration will include Judah itself as both giver and channel of this universal praise.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The doxological structure of verses 10-12 moves from invitation to summons to command to assertion. Verse 10 opens 'Sing unto the LORD a new song'—invitation. Verse 11 extends this with 'Let the wilderness...lift up their voice...let the inhabitants...sing'—summons to specific peoples. Verse 12 concludes 'Let them give glory unto the LORD'—a final, authoritative command that all these voices must ultimately be offering glory and praise to God, not to themselves or to idols. This progression from invitation to command reflects the increasing universality and inevitability of God's purposes. The entire arc of Isaiah 42:1-12 thus moves from God's agent (the Servant, verses 1-4) through God's sovereignty (verses 5-8) through God's prophetic reliability (verse 9) through the world's responsive praise (verses 10-12). The theology is coherent: because God is sovereign, His Servant will accomplish liberation; because that liberation will be real and visible, all creation will respond with authentic praise.
commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the focal point of all this universal praise. Isaiah 42:1-7 describes the Servant who accomplishes liberation; verses 10-12 show the world's response. Typologically, Christ's redemptive work—His incarnation, atoning death, and resurrection—is the ultimate act of God that compels all creation to acknowledge His glory. Revelation 5:9-14 crystallizes this: the Lamb who was slain receives the praise of 'every creature which is in heaven, and on the earth, and under the earth, and such as are in the sea' (Revelation 5:13). The islands and distant lands of Isaiah 42:12 find their ultimate destination in kneeling before the throne of God and the Lamb (Revelation 21:3-4). Every voice in the cosmos—whether from civilized centers or remote islands—ultimately glorifies God through Christ.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon itself is presented as evidence of the principle Isaiah 42:12 embodies: that God's word will be made known 'from the east to the west.' 2 Nephi 29:11-12 teaches that God will 'do a marvelous work among the children of men' through the coming forth of the Book of Mormon, and that eventually 'all the righteous shall be righteous still' and 'all the wicked shall be wicked still.' The Americas (the 'islands' of the Western Hemisphere) are summoned to acknowledge God's work through this record. Similarly, Alma 37:19 uses the image of trusting God's word to reach far and wide, fulfilling Isaiah's vision globally.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 65:5-7 teaches that 'the kingdom of God will roll forth as the stone which is cut out of the mountain without hands' and will 'fill the whole earth.' This directly applies Isaiah's vision to the latter-day work: the gospel (the proclamation of God's glory and praise) will eventually reach every nation, kindred, tongue, and people (D&C 77:8). D&C 1:14 declares that the Lord speaks to the Church 'with a voice of calamity by the way; and also the voice of calamity by the way for all people.' The principle that all peoples will hear and have opportunity to acknowledge God's glory is foundational to Restoration theology.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Salt Lake Temple, when completed in 1893, was announced to the world as a sign that God's house was established on the earth and would draw all nations. The temple's universality—its ordinances applicable to all people of all times—embodies Isaiah's vision: eventually, all people will have opportunity to participate in God's work and give glory to His name. Baptism for the dead ensures that even those from 'the islands'—remote generations and cultures—can be brought into covenant relationship and added to the chorus of praise. The temple is the house where all nations gather, metaphorically and literally, to acknowledge God.

word_study.meaning: 'Let them give' or 'let them place/set glory.' Yashimu (ישימו) is the hiphil imperfect of sima (שים), meaning 'to place,' 'to set,' 'to put.' Kavod (כבוד) is 'glory,' 'honor,' 'weight,' 'majesty.'
word_study.significance: The verb 'place' or 'set' suggests an active, deliberate act. Worshippers are not passively receiving glory from God but actively placing it, offering it, setting their acknowledgment before Him. This is the fundamental posture of worship: the creature intentionally directing honor toward the Creator. The Covenant Rendering's 'Let them give glory to the LORD' captures this sense of active, volitional offering.

word_study.meaning: 'They shall declare,' 'they shall announce,' 'they shall make known.' From nagad (נגד), meaning 'to tell,' 'to declare,' 'to report.' The hiphil form (yagidu) emphasizes active, vocal proclamation.
word_study.significance: Declaration is public, audible, and intentional. To 'declare praise' (yagidu tehillah) is not merely to think gratefully but to speak it, broadcast it, make it known to others. The term is used for prophetic announcement (Isaiah 41:22-23, 'declare...what shall happen') and for witness testimony. Worshippers become proclaimers, spreading the knowledge of God's glory throughout the earth.

word_study.meaning: 'Praise,' 'song of praise,' 'hymn.' From halal (הלל), 'to praise,' 'to shine,' 'to boast in.' Tehillah is the joyful, public celebration of another's greatness.
word_study.significance: The concept of tehillah is central to biblical worship. The book of Psalms is titled Tehillim (Psalms, literally 'Praises'). Tehillah encompasses all forms of worship expression: singing, shouting, testifying, celebrating. To 'declare praise in the islands' means to make God's greatness known wherever people gather, no matter how distant or foreign.

word_study.meaning: 'Islands,' 'coastlands,' 'distant lands.' From an Akkadian loanword (ayya), 'island.' In biblical usage, iyim often refers to seafaring, trading peoples on the Mediterranean and beyond—Phoenicians, Greeks, peoples of Cyprus, and distant maritime regions.
word_study.significance: As in verse 10, iyim represents the geographical and cultural extremity—the farthest reaches of the known world. By insisting that even the islands will declare God's praise, Isaiah establishes that no place is beyond God's sovereignty or excluded from His worship. The term has eschatological force: when the ends of the earth acknowledge God, His kingdom is fully established.

cross_references.connection: Verse 8 declares 'my glory will I not give to another,' and verse 12 completes the thought: that glory flows instead to God from all the islands and nations, fulfilling His exclusive claim to honor.

'Sing unto the LORD a new song... Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people... Say among the heathen that the LORD reigneth.' The psalm parallels Isaiah's structure of universal, public declaration of God's glory and kingship.
Later Isaiah envisions God gathering 'all nations and tongues,' and they 'shall come and see [His] glory.' Verse 12 anticipates this eschatological gathering where all peoples declare God's praise.
