In the New Jerusalem, 'the nations of them which are saved shall walk in the light of it: and the kings of the earth do bring their glory and honour into it.' The ultimate fulfillment of Isaiah's vision that the islands and distant lands will give their glory to God.

'And as all have not faith, seek ye diligently and teach one another words of wisdom... that ye may be perfect in your understanding of a truth.' The principle that all truth will eventually be known globally resonates with Isaiah's vision that all lands will declare God's praise.

commentary.historical_context: The historical moment of Isaiah's exilic community was one of profound silence and marginalization. The temple had been destroyed; public worship was impossible; the people were captives in a foreign land whose gods dominated the religious landscape. In this context, verse 12's command that the islands 'declare His praise' would have been both radical hope and subversive claim. The exiles were claiming that despite their present political and religious powerlessness, the entire world would eventually acknowledge their God. This was not naive optimism but theological conviction based on God's demonstrated faithfulness (the fulfilled 'former things' of verse 9) and God's sovereignty over all nations. Historically, the return from exile in 538 BCE under Cyrus the Persian would validate Isaiah's confident expectation of restoration, though the full universal acknowledgment remained eschatological (future). For later Christian readers, the phrase 'declare his praise in the islands' would evoke the missionary expansion of Christianity throughout Mediterranean and trans-Mediterranean regions—an apparent fulfillment of Isaiah's vision that the gospel message would reach distant lands.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, Isaiah 42:12 calls us to become declarers of God's praise, wherever we are and wherever we go. We are commissioned to take the gospel to 'all nations' (Matthew 24:14), making known in every island, every land, every people the glory and praise of God's work through Christ. On a personal level, the verse challenges us to ask: Am I actively declaring God's praise, or am I passive in my faith? Do I publicly acknowledge God's hand in my life, in my family, in my community? Or do I confine my gratitude to private moments? The verse's emphasis on declaration suggests that authentic praise is not silent but vocal, not hidden but public. We are called to be witnesses—to 'declare His praise' in whatever sphere of influence God has given us. Additionally, verse 12 reminds us that we participate in something cosmic and eternal: our individual testimonies and praise-givings join the universal chorus that will eventually encompass all creation. A seemingly small act—a testimony in Sunday School, a conversation with a friend about divine providence, a heartfelt prayer of gratitude—contributes to the fulfillment of Isaiah's vision. No voice is too small, no island too remote, no praise too quiet. All of it matters. All of it adds to the great chorus that will eventually 'declare His praise in the islands.'

text_kjv: The LORD shall go forth as a mighty man, he shall stir up jealousy like a man of war: he shall cry, yea, roar; he shall prevail against his enemies.

commentary.narrative: After the portrait of the gentle Servant in verses 1-4, Isaiah suddenly shifts to the warrior God. This verse marks a dramatic tonal pivot: the Servant works quietly, but the LORD Himself enters the fray with unstoppable force. The imagery is deliberately visceral—God 'cries out' and 'roars' like a warrior in battle. This is not mere metaphor; it reflects ancient Near Eastern divine warrior theology, where God acts as Israel's defender and judge. The mention of 'jealousy' (Hebrew qin'ah) is crucial: this is not petty envy but God's fierce, protective zeal for His people and His own glory. It is the passionate intensity of a God who will not tolerate the abuse of His servants or the mockery of idolatry.
commentary.narrative_continued: The context matters profoundly. Israel is in exile, watching their enemies prosper and their God seemingly silent. This verse assures them that God's restraint is not indifference—it is purposeful. Like a warrior preparing for battle, God has been gathering His strength. The 'enemies' here are both the oppressive nations and the idolatrous systems that blind Israel to their redemption. When God 'prevails,' He does so completely, as befits divine omnipotence. This sets up the paradox of the chapter: the gentle Servant and the mighty Warrior are both expressions of God's redemptive plan.

word_study.meaning: A warrior, strong one, champion. In Hebrew tradition, a gibor combines physical strength with divine commission. The term carries overtones of proven power and righteous purpose.
word_study.significance: God is not merely strong; He is a proven warrior whose strength is always in service of justice. This echoes Exodus 15:3, 'The LORD is a man of war,' establishing God's identity as defender of His covenant people.

word_study.meaning: Zealous passion, protective fervor, fierce devotion. The root suggests both jealous protection of what is one's own and righteous indignation against violation. In biblical theology, God's qin'ah is always motivated by covenant love, never by petty emotion.
word_study.significance: This reframes divine 'jealousy' as passionate protection rather than wounded pride. God's zeal is aroused because His people and His glory are being desecrated. The Covenant Rendering's translation of qin'ah as 'zeal' (rather than mere 'jealousy') captures this protective dimension more accurately.

word_study.meaning: To cry out, shout aloud, roar. These terms are onomatopoetic, mimicking the sounds of battle. Yaria can denote a war cry or shout of triumph; yatsriach conveys shouting with intensity and urgency.
word_study.significance: The repetition of vocal imagery—crying out, roaring—emphasizes the active, vocal nature of God's intervention. This is not silent intervention but a public declaration that breaks through exile's oppressive silence. It directly contrasts with the Servant's silence in verse 2.

cross_references.connection: The Song of the Sea explicitly identifies the LORD as 'a man of war' (ish milchamot), establishing the divine warrior tradition that Isaiah 42:13 invokes. Both passages celebrate God's victory over oppressive powers.
The psalmist describes the LORD extending His mighty scepter and ruling among enemies, echoing the warrior God who 'prevails against his enemies' in verse 13.

Later in Isaiah, God is described as putting on righteousness as armor and the garments of vengeance—another portrait of God as divine warrior rising up against injustice, parallel to this verse's martial imagery.
Nahum describes God's jealous wrath against enemies and the force of His anger, using the same theological framework of divine qin'ah (zeal) as an instrument of justice and protection.

Modern revelation affirms that God's power is expressed both in gentle ways and through judgment against those who reject His purposes—reflecting the dual portrayal of Servant and Warrior in Isaiah 42.

commentary.historical_context: The divine warrior motif was widespread in ancient Near Eastern religion and literature. The Ugaritic Baal, the Egyptian Re, and Mesopotamian deities all had warrior aspects. However, Israel's war-god theology was distinctive: Yahweh's battles were always on behalf of the covenant people and rooted in justice, not capricious aggression. The 'man of war' imagery would have resonated powerfully with exiled Israelites, reminding them that their God was not diminished by Babylonian power but was gathering strength for their deliverance. The shift from the Servant's quiet work (vv. 1-4) to God's battle cry reflects a both/and theology: redemption comes through humble suffering and through divine judgment against oppression.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 26:15, Ammon describes the 'arm of the Lord' stretched out in power, using warrior imagery to explain God's strength in defending the faithful. This parallels Isaiah's portrayal of God as a mighty warrior aroused to action. The Book of Mormon repeatedly affirms that God's power is active and manifest, not distant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 133:46-51 uses similar imagery of God's righteous indignation and His triumph over His enemies. The revelation confirms that God's zeal is always directed toward the triumph of His kingdom and the deliverance of His people—the theological core of Isaiah 42:13.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment teaches that God's power is manifest in both subtle and dramatic ways. The Servant's quiet consecration (vv. 1-4) and the Warrior's decisive action (v. 13) together reflect the balance of spiritual work: internal transformation and external triumph are both necessary for full redemption.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus embodies both aspects shown in this passage. As the Servant, He was silent before His accusers (Matthew 27:12-14). As the returning King, He will come with power and glory to judge the nations (Revelation 19:11-15). The passage prefigures Christ's two advents: His first coming as the gentle, suffering Servant; His second coming as the conquering warrior whose 'zeal' (qin'ah) will consume all opposition to God's kingdom.
commentary.application: Modern disciples live between these two poles: we are called to serve quietly and faithfully like the Servant, but we trust in a God whose zeal and power will ultimately vindicate righteousness. In moments when justice seems delayed and evil prospers, Isaiah 42:13 is a covenant assurance that God has not forgotten His people. We can do our quiet work of service knowing that the Almighty God is gathering His strength to make all things right. Our role is faithful obedience in the small, humble tasks; God's role is to ensure that His purposes triumph. This transforms our covenant service from a burden into an act of trust in God's invincible power.

text_kjv: I have long time holden my peace; I have been still, and refrained myself: now will I cry like a travailing woman; I will destroy and devour at once.

commentary.narrative: God now explains His apparent silence during the exile. For generations, He has 'held His peace'—a deliberate, purposeful restraint. This is not passivity or absence but chosen reserve, like a warrior who waits for the moment to strike. The image of a woman in labor is one of the most visceral in Scripture: it combines pain, urgency, intensity, and the inevitability of birth. Labor is unstoppable once it begins; similarly, God's intervention, when it comes, will be unstoppable. The movement from restraint to action is total and irreversible. The final phrase—'I will destroy and devour at once'—conveys the swift, comprehensive nature of God's judgment against those who have oppressed His people and resisted His purposes.
commentary.narrative_continued: For an exiled Israel, this verse would have provided immense psychological relief. The silence they experienced was not abandonment but strategy. God was not impotent; He was restraining Himself—like a coiled spring. The woman-in-labor metaphor is particularly powerful because labor is productive suffering. It is pain with purpose, pain that brings life. So too will God's judgment bring redemption. The verse announces that the waiting period is over. What was impossible to discern during the exile—that God was present and purposeful—will become undeniable. The shift from 'peace' (silence) to vocal intensity ('cry,' 'roar,' 'destroy') completes the picture: God's intervention is total, sudden, and inevitable.

word_study.meaning: To be silent, to keep silence, to refrain from speaking or acting. The perfect tense conveys completed action in the past. This is not involuntary muteness but deliberate restraint.
word_study.significance: God's silence was an act of will, not circumstance. This reframes the exile experience: what felt like divine absence was actually divine reserve. The covenantal God chooses when to speak and when to act—and His restraint is as purposeful as His action.

word_study.meaning: To restrain oneself, to hold back, to control oneself. The reflexive form emphasizes self-control and deliberate resistance. This suggests internal struggle—the difficulty of restraint.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests that restraint cost something. It was not easy for God to 'hold back' from intervening. This dignity of restraint adds theological weight to His eventual action: when God acts, it will be because waiting has become impossible, because the moment of transformation has arrived.

word_study.meaning: Yoledah means 'a woman giving birth,' emphasizing the bodily intensity of labor. Ef'eh means 'I will cry out' or 'I will scream,' capturing the involuntary vocalization of intense pain and effort.
word_study.significance: This is perhaps the most startling image in the passage. God's intervention is compared to the physical intensity and vocal urgency of childbirth. It signals that what is about to happen is productive—it will bring something new to life—but also that it cannot be controlled or delayed once it begins. The Covenant Rendering's 'I will gasp and pant' captures the anatomical reality: the sounds are involuntary, urgent, physical.

word_study.meaning: Shom can mean 'to desolate' or 'to lay waste'; sh'af means 'to pant' or 'to pant heavily' but in context carries overtones of consuming or devouring completely. Together they convey total obliteration.
word_study.significance: The pairing creates an image of relentless consumption. What stands against God's purposes will be entirely consumed. The physical imagery—panting, devouring—maintains the visceral tone throughout the verse, emphasizing that God's action is total and unstoppable.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist implores God not to remain silent but to 'awake' and 'arise' for justice, reflecting the same theology that God's silence is chosen and must be broken for righteousness to be established.

Jeremiah describes waiting patiently for God's salvation despite His apparent silence, affirming that restraint precedes restoration—parallel to Isaiah's understanding of the exile as purposeful waiting.
God struggles with the tension between justice and mercy, between abandoning Israel and redeeming them, capturing the internal 'restraint' that Isaiah 42:14 describes—the cost of God's patience.

The dedicatory prayer of the Kirtland Temple asks God to not hide His face from His people but to manifest His power and glory. This echoes Isaiah's theology: God's manifest action is the fulfillment of the covenant when the time is right.
Later in Isaiah, the prophet pleads with God not to hold His peace but to act, showing that the theology of divine restraint and its breaking is a consistent theme throughout the prophecy.

commentary.historical_context: The image of the woman in labor would have resonated across ancient Near Eastern cultures as a symbol of inevitable, unstoppable natural process. However, for exiled Israel, it carried additional weight: the exile itself was often described as a time of travail and birth pangs (cf. Isaiah 26:17-18). Isaiah transforms this metaphor: Israel's suffering is not productive; it is God's travail that will bring forth redemption. The woman-in-labor image also invokes the creation accounts where birth is the ultimate act of producing something new from within—suggesting that God's intervention will not merely restore the past but will bring about unprecedented renewal. The rhetoric would have provided both comfort (God has a plan) and warning (resistance is futile).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:26-27 describes Alma's spiritual breakthrough after intense suffering, using language of birth and new life coming from travail—the same theology of productive suffering that Isaiah employs. The Book of Mormon teaches repeatedly that redemption comes through intensified divine action that transforms those who are willing.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 101:1-5 addresses the Saints during a period of intense persecution, affirming that God has permitted trials but will act decisively to vindicate His people. The revelation embodies the same logic as Isaiah 42:14: divine restraint precedes overwhelming intervention.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the candidate experiences a symbolic death and rebirth. The birth imagery in Isaiah 42:14 connects to that transformative experience: redemption is not instantaneous enlightenment but a process of travail that produces fundamental transformation. God's 'crying out like a travailing woman' is an act of creation, bringing forth the redeemed.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus in Gethsemane experienced the travail described in this verse. In Luke 22:44, His sweat 'was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground'—a physical, visceral expression of intense internal struggle. Jesus' cries of anguish on the cross ('My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?') are the 'cries' of verse 14. Yet this travail was productive: it brought forth redemption for all humanity. Christ embodies both the silence of the exiled people and the anguished cry of God's intervention.
commentary.application: In seasons when God seems silent, Isaiah 42:14 teaches that restraint is neither absence nor indifference. For modern disciples facing delayed answers to prayers or prolonged difficult circumstances, this verse offers perspective: we may be in a period of purposeful divine reserve. However, the verse also promises that this restraint will not last forever. When God acts, it will be decisive and comprehensive. Our task is to maintain faith during the silence, trusting that the delay has purpose. Additionally, the verse teaches us about patience and timing in our own discipleship: sometimes we must restrain ourselves from acting prematurely, trusting that God's timing will make our eventual action effective and productive. The woman in labor does not force the birth; she works with the process. Similarly, disciples work with God's timeline, not against it.

text_kjv: I will make waste mountains and hills, and dry up all their herbs; and I will make the rivers islands, and I will dry up the pools.

commentary.narrative: The manifestation of God's zeal takes visible, cosmic form. Mountains—symbols of permanence and stability—will be made waste. Herbs will wither. Rivers will be redirected so completely that they become islands. Pools will dry up. This is not localized destruction but a comprehensive reshaping of creation itself. For an exiled Israel, these images would have echoed the Exodus narrative: the waters of the Red Sea parted, revealing dry ground; mountains and natural obstacles were irrelevant to God's saving power. Isaiah portrays God as possessing not just military power but creative power—the same power that made the mountains now can unmake them. This is the language of cosmological reversal, of God reasserting sovereignty over a creation that has been twisted by human rebellion and idolatry.
commentary.narrative_continued: The specific imagery matters. Mountains represent obstacles; herbs represent abundance and livelihood; rivers represent barriers and boundaries. By drying them up or transforming them, God removes every impediment to His people's redemption. The vision is one of total environmental transformation in service of divine redemptive purposes. This connects Isaiah 42:15 to the earlier command in Isaiah 40:3-4: 'Make straight in the desert a highway for our God. Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low.' The reshaping of the landscape is not random destruction but purposeful preparation for God's people to return. It is creation itself being mobilized for redemption.

word_study.meaning: To make desolate, to lay waste, to render barren. The word conveys complete deprivation of fertility and life. It is the opposite of the blessing that creation was meant to be.
word_study.significance: While the destruction of obstacles is necessary for redemption, the verb itself carries weight: God does not take lightly the desolation He inflicts. Yet it is done in service of a higher purpose—clearing away what impedes salvation.

word_study.meaning: To cause to wither, to desiccate, to drain of moisture. The word suggests the removal of the vital moisture that sustains life and fertility.
word_study.significance: In the context of ancient Near Eastern fertility theology, drying up is a sign of divine curse or judgment. However, here it is redemptive: the drying up of obstacles is the preparation for the pathway of salvation. The language is deliberately ambiguous, mirroring the paradox that judgment and salvation are intertwined in God's plan.

word_study.meaning: To convert rivers into islands—an act of radical geographic inversion. Rivers are typically barriers; islands are typically surrounded by them. Here, the transformation reverses the natural order.
word_study.significance: This image suggests that what was once a dividing force becomes a rallying point. The rivers that separated people groups will be transformed. For Israel's return, this means even the greatest natural barriers (like the Euphrates) become passable. The Covenant Rendering's 'turn the rivers into islands' captures the inversion more clearly than 'make the rivers islands.'

cross_references.connection: The earlier command to prepare the way is here shown to be accomplished by God's own power: mountains are made low, valleys are exalted—the same transformations described in 42:15.

The parting of the Red Sea, where waters were divided and the seabed became dry ground for Israel's passage, is the historical precedent for Isaiah's vision. God's power over water is demonstrated in both passages.
Jeremiah prophesies that God will dry up Babylon's sea (the Euphrates), using the same imagery of drying up waters as an act of judgment and liberation—parallel to Isaiah's vision.
The psalmist describes God turning rivers into deserts and deserts into water sources—God's power to reshape geography for His purposes, matching Isaiah's vision of cosmic transformation.
Modern revelation teaches that God controls all the elements and uses them in service of His purposes, affirming that the reshaping of nature is within God's dominion.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thought, control over nature was a divine prerogative. Baal was supposedly lord of rain and vegetation; Re controlled the sun; the sea was often portrayed as a chaotic force that only the gods could master. Isaiah's vision invokes these elements precisely to show that Yahweh surpasses all other gods in power. The drying up of water sources, the destruction of mountains, the transformation of geography—these demonstrate divine omnipotence. For exiled Israel, such language would have been deeply encouraging: the God who created these features could unmake them for His purposes. The imagery also echoes the Mesopotamian creation mythology (Enuma Elish), where the god Marduk defeats the chaos-waters and reshapes creation. Isaiah appropriates this imagery for Yahweh, asserting Israelite theological superiority.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's vision in 1 Nephi 11-14 includes cosmic imagery where the natural elements respond to God's will. The principle that nature is subject to God's command, not His servant, appears throughout the Book of Mormon, especially in accounts of God's judgments (e.g., Alma 40:24-26 regarding the resurrection).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:14-16 teaches that God will command the elements, and they shall obey. The vision in Isaiah 42:15 is an expression of this dominion. Modern revelation confirms that reshaping creation is within God's power and purpose.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the candidate views representations of creation and God's dominion over it. The principle that God can reshape creation according to His will is foundational to the temple theology of redemption and exaltation. The reshaping of the landscape in Isaiah 42:15 is a sign that creation itself participates in redemption.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus demonstrated power over nature—calming storms, walking on water, turning water into wine—foreshadowing His ultimate power at the resurrection and in the creation of a new heavens and new earth. In Revelation 21:1-4, when Jesus returns, 'the former things are passed away' and He creates 'a new heaven and a new earth,' fulfilling Isaiah's vision of cosmic transformation. The reshaping of geography in Isaiah 42:15 points to the ultimate transformation of all creation in Christ.
commentary.application: For modern disciples, Isaiah 42:15 teaches that obstacles—whether personal, institutional, or circumstantial—are not insurmountable in God's hands. When we face seemingly immovable barriers (mountains of debt, valleys of despair, rivers of division), we can trust that God's power extends to reshaping our circumstances. However, the verse also teaches patience: the reshaping of geography takes time. We must not expect instantaneous transformation but rather trust that God is working across time and circumstance to clear the path. Additionally, the verse invites us to participate in God's redemptive work: just as the physical landscape must be transformed for God's people to return, our own hearts must be transformed, our priorities reshuffled, our boundaries reset. We are both the beneficiaries of cosmic transformation and agents in smaller transformations around us.

text_kjv: And I will bring the blind by a way that they knew not; I will lead them in paths that they have not known: I will make darkness light before them, and crooked things straight. These things will I do unto them, and not forsake them.

commentary.narrative: The verse shifts focus from cosmic destruction to personal redemption. The 'blind' are Israel—spiritually blind during the exile, unable to perceive God's purposes or pathway home. God will guide them through unfamiliar territory by routes they cannot see, yet He will not lose them. The transformation is total: darkness becomes light, crooked paths become straight, and the promise 'I will not forsake them' anchors everything in covenant fidelity. This verse answers the deepest fear of the exile—that God has abandoned His people. The structure of the verse emphasizes God's active role: 'I will bring,' 'I will lead,' 'I will make,' 'I will do'—five divine actions that bracket the covenant promise of non-abandonment. For Israel, these are not metaphorical concessions but literal salvation.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verse echoes Isaiah 40:3-4 and 42:15, tying together the cosmic and personal dimensions of redemption. God reshapes geography (v. 15) so that He can guide the blind (v. 16). The preparation of the way is not abstract; it is practical—roads cleared, obstacles removed, pathways made plain. Yet the paradox remains: the blind are being guided through a way they 'know not.' This suggests that redemption requires trust beyond sight. Israel cannot navigate by their own understanding; they must follow God's guidance even when the path is unfamiliar. The promise is not that they will understand the way but that God will not forsake them—covenant presence rather than human comprehension. The final phrase clinches the theology: abandonment is not an option. God's covenant holds even when understanding fails.

word_study.meaning: Blind ones, those without sight. In Isaiah, blindness is both literal disability and metaphor for spiritual inability to perceive God's purposes.
word_study.significance: In Isaiah 42:18-19, Israel is explicitly called blind and deaf—unable to perceive the Servant's mission or God's redemptive work. Verse 16 shows God personally guiding these spiritually blind people, demonstrating that blindness is not permanent. God's guidance is effectual despite human inability to see.

word_study.meaning: A path/way they have not known. The phrase emphasizes the gap between God's knowledge and human knowledge, between divine planning and human perception.
word_study.significance: This is not a path that should have been known but wasn't. It is a path that is genuinely new—perhaps the exilic return route, perhaps the spiritual journey to restoration. The gap between known and unknown is bridged only by trust.

word_study.term_original: אָשִׂים מַחְשָׁךְ לִפְנֵיהֶם לָאוֹר (asim machshak lifneihem la'or)
word_study.meaning: To set/place darkness before them as light. The transformation is total: what was obscure becomes illuminated. Darkness (machshak) can mean both physical darkness and the darkness of ignorance or judgment.
word_study.significance: The inversion is radical: God transforms the very obstacles into aids. Darkness, which typically obscures, becomes light that guides. This suggests that God does not remove all darkness but transforms its meaning and effect. The Covenant Rendering's phrasing emphasizes the transformation: 'I will turn the darkness before them into light.'

word_study.meaning: Twisted, crooked things are made straight/level. Ma'akashim carries overtones of deception and wrongness; mishor means straightness and correctness, both literally and morally.
word_study.significance: This echoes Isaiah 40:4 and introduces a moral dimension: God not only makes the physical path straight but straightens what is morally twisted. The redemption is comprehensive—physical, spiritual, and ethical.

word_study.meaning: I will not abandon/leave them. The verb 'azav' means to leave, to abandon, to forsake. The negation makes this an absolute covenant promise.
word_study.significance: This phrase directly addresses exile's greatest psychological trauma—the fear of permanent abandonment. The covenant God does not forsake His people. This is not conditional promise but absolute commitment. The phrase appears in Deuteronomy 31:6 and becomes a recurring motif in Isaiah (41:10, 46:28), anchoring redemption in covenantal fidelity.

cross_references.connection: The preparation of the highway, with valleys exalted and mountains made low, is the concrete expression of the path preparation promised in verse 16. God makes the way straight by reshaping the landscape.
Moses' farewell promise—'He will not forsake thee'—becomes God's promise in Isaiah 42:16. Both passages anchor covenant people in the certainty of God's presence despite fearful circumstances.

The psalmist trusts that God will lead him in right paths and that even in darkness, God's presence ensures no fear of evil—parallel to Isaiah's vision of darkness transformed into light through God's guidance.

Nephi declares that the Lord gives no commandments save He provides a way to accomplish them, echoing Isaiah's principle that God guides the blind through unknown ways because He has prepared the path.
Modern revelation teaches that the Lord will provide all things and 'lead [His people] in all righteousness,' matching Isaiah's vision of divine guidance for the spiritually blind.

commentary.historical_context: For exiled Babylonians, the journey home was dangerous and unfamiliar. Some Jews had been born in Babylon and had never seen Palestine. The return route would have been disorienting—a different geography from anything in their collective memory. Isaiah addresses this literal situation through spiritual metaphor: Israel is blind because it has lost its bearings spiritually, not understanding God's purposes or perceiving how restoration is possible. God's promise to guide them 'in a way they know not' is both literal (the route home) and spiritual (the path to restored relationship with God). The blindness language also reflects a theological claim: the gods of Babylon cannot see (they are carved idols); but Israel's God has vision and will guide His people despite their blindness. This is a declaration of theological superiority and spiritual superiority.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 37:43-45, Alma describes the Liahona as a guide for those who trust in the Lord, even when the path is unknown—a literal embodiment of Isaiah 42:16's principle. Nephi's experiences crossing the wilderness (1 Nephi 16) show a people being guided through an unknown path by divine means, foreshadowing the return from exile.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 6:7-9 teaches that the Holy Ghost will guide the faithful, 'enlighten your mind' and 'inspire your heart.' This is the modern expression of Isaiah's promise: spiritual blindness is cured not by human wisdom but by divine guidance through the Spirit.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the candidate is led through sacred space following a path that is new and unfamiliar, guided by those who have walked it before. The temple thus enacts Isaiah 42:16: the candidate is 'brought by a way' he or she 'knows not,' trusting guides who understand the covenant pathway. The temple experience is a microcosm of the journey through mortality toward exaltation.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus is presented in John 8:12 as 'the light of the world'—the fulfillment of Isaiah's promise that God will make darkness into light. More profoundly, Jesus is the guide who leads us through unknown terrain: He tells His disciples, 'I am the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6). His declaration echoes Isaiah 42:16: the path to the Father is unknown to us, but Jesus is both the path and the guide. In John 10:3-4, Jesus describes Himself as the good shepherd who leads the sheep: they follow 'for they know his voice'—again, the relationship between blind follower and seeing guide, which Isaiah 42:16 establishes.
commentary.application: Modern disciples often find themselves on paths they did not anticipate and cannot fully understand. Career changes, health crises, family disruptions, calls to service in unfamiliar places—these stretch our faith because we cannot see the destination. Isaiah 42:16 teaches that this is precisely the condition in which God expects us to walk. Our task is not to understand the path but to trust the Guide. The verse also teaches a principle about spiritual darkness: we are all spiritually blind to some degree, unable to perceive God's full purposes. The cure is not human enlightenment but divine guidance. We must cultivate the willingness to be led by God even when we cannot see the path ahead. The final promise—'I will not forsake you'—is the foundation that makes such trust possible. We can walk in darkness because we trust that we are not walking alone. This is the essence of covenant discipleship: not understanding everything but trusting the One who does.

text_kjv: They shall be turned back, they shall be greatly ashamed, that trust in graven images, that say to the molten images, Ye are our gods.

commentary.narrative: The verse provides sharp contrast to verse 16: while God guides the blind forward, those who trust in idols are 'turned back' (nasogu achor)—the opposite direction. The shame is profound and inevitable. The idolaters are explicitly identified: those who 'say to the molten images, Ye are our gods.' This is not abstract idolatry but the concrete worship of Babylonian deities—the false gods that the exile's propaganda claimed had defeated Israel's God. Isaiah exposes this claim as delusion. Those who trust in these powerless images will be 'greatly ashamed' (yeboshshu boshet)—a phrase that conveys complete humiliation and confusion. The turning back is not a neutral reversal but a reversal away from salvation, while shame is not merely embarrassment but the realization of fundamental error.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verse addresses a critical moment in exile theology: some Israelites had begun to accommodate themselves to Babylonian religion, perhaps concluding that Babylon's gods had proved superior. Others had syncretized, blending Yahweh worship with Babylonian imagery and practice. Isaiah cuts through this compromise with stark clarity: there is a dividing line. Those who walk forward with God (v. 16) and those who turn back to idols (v. 17) are on utterly different trajectories. The shame of the idolaters will be public and visible—a sign to all of the folly of trusting false gods. For faithful Israelites under pressure to abandon their God, this verse would have been both warning and assurance: warning against accommodation, assurance that faith in the true God would be vindicated while idolatry would be exposed as folly.

word_study.meaning: They retreat, they draw back, they reverse direction. The verb nasogu conveys movement away from something; achor means backward or behind. Together they depict not just movement but deliberate reversal.
word_study.significance: This is the opposite trajectory from the forward movement promised to the faithful in verse 16. While God leads the blind forward on an unknown path, the idolaters move backward—away from God's purposes. The contrast is directional, cosmic even: forward toward redemption or backward toward destruction.

word_study.meaning: They are ashamed with shame—an emphatic construction. Boshet means shame, confusion, disgrace. The doubling of the root intensifies the emotion and certainty.
word_study.significance: Shame in Hebrew thought is not mere embarrassment but a sign of fundamental error and being exposed as a fool. The certainty conveyed ('they shall be ashamed') suggests this is not a possibility but an inevitability—the discovery of error is written into the very nature of idolatry.

word_study.meaning: Pesel: an image carved or sculptured, typically from wood or stone. Massekah: a molten or cast image, typically made from metal by pouring molten material into a mold. Both denote physically created representations of deity.
word_study.significance: The pairing emphasizes the material nature of idols—they are made things, products of human craft. This contrast is intentional: God is spirit and cannot be represented by material objects. The commandment against graven images (Exodus 20:4) is rooted in the theology that God is not reducible to physical form. Isaiah uses precise terminology to emphasize this difference.

word_study.meaning: You are our gods. The direct speech—recorded as something the idolaters actually say—emphasizes the audacity and absurdity of the claim. Elohim (gods) denotes divine power and authority.
word_study.significance: By recording these words verbatim, Isaiah invites the reader to hear the emptiness of the claim. Inanimate objects are addressed as divine. The very absurdity is the point: how can carved wood or cast metal be god? The verse thus functions as both condemnation and reductio ad absurdum.

cross_references.connection: The commandment against making graven images is the foundational basis for Isaiah's condemnation of idol worship. God explicitly forbids the creation and worship of idols because they misrepresent His nature.

Later in Isaiah, a more extended satire on idol-making shows the absurdity of worship carved from the same wood used for fuel. Isaiah 42:17 and 44:9-20 together form a comprehensive theological critique of idolatry.
Jeremiah similarly mocks idols as powerless—they cannot speak, walk, or harm, yet people bow down to them. The theological critique of idolatry is consistent across prophetic books.
The psalmist declares that those who serve graven images are ashamed—matching Isaiah's promise that idolatry inevitably leads to shame and exposure.

In Lehi's dream, those in the great and spacious building mock those who follow God's way. These mockers represent the idolatrous orientation that Isaiah condemns—trust in human wisdom and material things rather than in God.

commentary.historical_context: Babylon was renowned for its idolatry and its theological claim that the gods of Babylon had triumphed over the gods of defeated nations. The major Babylonian gods—Marduk, Ishtar, Enuma Elish—were represented by elaborate statues in temples. For exiled Israelites surrounded by this religious culture, the temptation to conclude that Babylonian gods were real and powerful would have been significant. Archaeological evidence shows that some Judeans did adopt Babylonian religious practices during the exile. Isaiah's stark language is designed to counteract this assimilation: the gods of Babylon are not real; they are mere crafted objects without power or knowledge. The shame Isaiah promises is public shame—the recognition by all nations that trust in idols was folly. This would have been meant to steel the faith of Israelites tempted by accommodation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 13, Nephi sees a vision of Babylonian captivity and its spiritual paralysis. The people's inability to distinguish truth from false religious systems is treated as spiritual blindness—parallel to Isaiah's claim that idolaters are unable to see the truth. The Book of Mormon emphasizes repeatedly that trust in 'arm of flesh' and in false systems leads to confusion and shame (2 Nephi 28:31; Jacob 4:14).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 76:96-112 describes those who serve false gods and systems in the celestial kingdom's absence. Modern revelation affirms that trust in false spiritual authorities and systems has cosmic consequences—not merely social embarrassment but fundamental disconnection from salvation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that God is not represented by material images but is encountered through covenant and spirit. The temple's prohibition on photography and recording reflects the principle underlying Isaiah's critique: God is not reducible to representation. The temple is the house of God, not because it contains His image but because it is the place where covenant relationship is enacted.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus is the true image of God—not in the sense of a carved representation but in the sense of incarnate reality (Hebrews 1:3, Colossians 1:15). The false gods that Isaiah condemns are powerless imitations; Jesus is the fullness of deity in bodily form. Additionally, those who reject Jesus (the true God) and embrace false religious systems will be 'turned back' from salvation, experiencing shame at the revelation of their error—the fate Isaiah promises to idolaters. The contrast between the faithful who are guided forward (v. 16) and the idolaters turned backward (v. 17) foreshadows the final judgment where sheep and goats are divided (Matthew 25:32-46).
commentary.application: For modern disciples, Isaiah 42:17 warns against subtle idolatry: not necessarily carved images but false sources of trust and authority. Modern idols might include: trust in wealth and financial security rather than God's provision; trust in human expertise and systems rather than divine guidance; trust in charismatic leaders or institutions rather than God; trust in social status, appearance, or accomplishment as sources of ultimate meaning. The verse teaches that these alternatives ultimately fail and bring shame—not petty embarrassment but fundamental error exposed. More positively, the verse invites alignment with verse 16's trajectory: forward movement with God rather than backward retreat into false securities. This requires regular examination: Where am I trusting? Who or what am I following? Is my trajectory forward with the living God or backward toward something lesser? The shame Isaiah promises is not punishment from without but the internal realization of fundamental error—the fruit of choosing false gods. The remedy is redirection toward the true God who guides, sustains, and does not forsake.

text_kjv: Hear, ye deaf; and look, ye blind, that ye may see.

commentary.narrative: The verse pivots sharply from indictment of idolaters (v. 17) to direct address of Israel. The tone becomes urgent and paradoxical. God commands the deaf to hear and the blind to see—commands that seem impossible. Yet the very impossibility of the command is the point: only God can make the deaf hear and the blind see. This verse applies the language of verses 16-17 specifically to Israel: the people are spiritually deaf and blind. They should be hearing the Servant's message (v. 2) and perceiving God's purposes, but they cannot. The verse thus functions as both indictment and appeal. Israel is indicted for spiritual insensitivity, yet the appeal assumes they can change if they will respond to God's voice. The repeated imperative—'Hear,' 'Look'—suggests urgency. This is not a gentle invitation but a command that demands response.
commentary.narrative_continued: The paradox deepens when we realize that this verse comes after the Servant Song (vv. 1-4), where the Servant is described as having eyes that open the blind and ears that free captives. If the Servant is meant to accomplish this spiritual transformation, why does God still command Israel to hear and see? The answer lies in the logic of covenant: God provides the means of salvation (the Servant), but individuals must respond. The Servant's mission is not coercive; it requires receptivity. Israel is spiritually blind and deaf—but not by nature, only by will. The command 'hear' and 'look' is an appeal to willingness, to the turning around that alone can restore sight and hearing. The verse thus stands as a threshold: on one side, the offer of guidance and restoration; on the other, the alternative of continued blindness and deafness. The choice remains with Israel. The urgency of the imperative suggests that the moment of decision is now.

word_study.meaning: Deaf ones, hear! Cherashim denotes those who are deaf or dumb. The command to deaf ones to hear is paradoxically impossible—yet that is the point.
word_study.significance: The verb shmu (hear) can mean both physical hearing and spiritual understanding/obedience. God is not commanding physical ears to function but spiritual ears to open—the capacity to understand and respond to God's word. The paradox emphasizes that spiritual transformation requires divine grace (God opening the ears) and human willingness (responding to the command).

word_study.meaning: And the blind, look/direct your gaze to see. Ivrim denotes blind ones. Habitu (look) can mean to gaze, to direct attention. The phrase 'to look to see' (habitu lir'ot) suggests that looking is itself the beginning of seeing—attention precedes perception.
word_study.significance: The verb habitu carries implications of deliberate choice: the blind are commanded to 'turn their gaze'—to direct attention to God and His purposes. This is the volitional element: opening oneself to God's light and truth. The Covenant Rendering's 'look, you blind, that you may see' captures this sense of intentional turning toward perception.

word_study.meaning: To see, to perceive, to understand. In biblical Hebrew, sight is not merely physical but epistemological—seeing means knowing and understanding.
word_study.significance: The purpose clause 'that you may see' reveals that the command is not futile but purposeful. The deaf are commanded to hear in order that they may respond; the blind are commanded to look in order that understanding may follow. The commands presume the possibility of transformation through divine power and human cooperation.

cross_references.connection: The Servant Song establishes that the Servant is commissioned to 'open the eyes of the blind' (v. 7) and free captives from darkness. Verse 18 shows Israel as the primary subject needing this spiritual liberation—the Servant is sent to this blind and deaf people.

Later Isaiah addresses 'blind people with eyes' and 'deaf people with ears'—emphasizing that Israel has the capacity for perception but does not use it. The same theme of spiritual insensitivity appears across Isaiah's prophecies.

Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9-10 about a people who 'seeing, do not perceive; hearing, they do not understand.' This connects the theme of spiritual blindness and deafness to Israel's resistance to Jesus' message—showing the continuity of Israel's spiritual condition across centuries.

Modern revelation teaches that those who 'hearken unto my voice' and 'keep my commandments' will receive salvation. The invitation to hear and respond is central to LDS theology of covenant—as in Isaiah 42:18.
Nephi describes his brothers as unable to perceive the meaning of scriptures despite having the words before them. They are spiritually blind and deaf—exactly the condition Isaiah 42:18 addresses.

commentary.historical_context: The command to the deaf and blind would have had both literal and figurative resonance in ancient Israel. Blindness and deafness were real disabilities that affected some individuals. However, the prophetic tradition consistently used these conditions as metaphors for spiritual insensitivity. The figure of the blind person who needs guidance appears frequently in wisdom literature and prophecy as a symbol of those who lack understanding. For exiled Israel, the accusation of blindness and deafness would have been particularly stinging: they claimed to be God's people, yet they could not perceive God's purposes or hear the Servant's message. The command to hear and see is not merely criticism but an urgent call to awakening. The rhetoric suggests that awakening is still possible if Israel will turn its attention and heart toward God.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Throughout the Book of Mormon, prophets command the people to 'hear' and 'awake' (e.g., Jacob 3:1, Alma 5:7, 3 Nephi 9:1). The pattern is consistent: God provides prophets and messages, but the people must be willing to hear and see. The Book of Mormon shows both those who respond ('they did hear,' 'they did believe') and those who do not. Isaiah 42:18 captures this dynamic perfectly: the command is given, but response is contingent on willingness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 58:18-19 teaches that God 'will bring to light all hidden things, secrets of the heart, and will reward every man according to his works.' This relates to the theme of Isaiah 42:18: seeing the truth of God's purposes requires willingness to perceive. Modern revelation emphasizes that truth is available to those who have ears to hear and eyes to see (D&C 101:98).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, initiates are invited to learn and perceive sacred truths about God's plan. The temple experience is, in a sense, an answer to Isaiah 42:18: through covenant participation, individuals' spiritual eyes and ears are opened to understand God's purposes for humanity and creation. The temple teaches what the world cannot see—the continuation of family relationships and the pathway to exaltation.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus declared in Matthew 11:15, 'He that hath ears to hear, let him hear'—echoing Isaiah's command. Jesus consistently called His disciples to perceive deeper truths beneath surface events. In John 9, Jesus heals a blind man and demonstrates that true sight is knowing who Jesus is and perceiving God's purposes—not merely physical vision. The entire Passion narrative can be read through the lens of Isaiah 42:18: those who saw and heard Jesus (the disciples) were sometimes blind and deaf to His purposes (failing to understand that He must die and rise). True sight and hearing come from openness to God's revelation through Christ.
commentary.application: Isaiah 42:18 is directed at every reader who struggles with spiritual perception. Modern disciples are often blind to God's hand in their lives, deaf to the still, small voice, unable to perceive the patterns of covenant and promise that God is weaving. The verse calls for intentional turning: awakening our spiritual senses through scripture study, prayer, and faithful listening. But the verse also carries a warning: the command itself assumes we have some capacity to respond. We are not passive recipients but covenant partners responsible for developing our ability to perceive truth. This means: praying for eyes to see, actively studying scripture, listening to prophetic counsel, attending the temple, and most importantly, being willing to change our understanding when God reveals truth that contradicts our assumptions. The urgency of the command—'Hear,' 'Look'—suggests that moments of spiritual opening are not endless. Now is the time to awaken, to turn our attention toward God, to prepare ourselves to perceive what He is trying to reveal. The blindness Isaiah condemns is not lack of capacity but refusal to use the capacity God has given us. The remedy is not intellectual but volitional: turning toward God and opening ourselves to perception.

text_kjv: Who is blind, but my servant? or deaf, as my messenger that I sent? who is blind as he that is perfect, and blind as the LORD's servant?

commentary.narrative:
This verse pivots dramatically from the glorious description of the Servant in verses 1-4 to a crushing indictment of Israel's actual condition. The rhetorical questions are not gentle—they are devastating irony. Isaiah identifies Israel as God's servant and messenger, yet asks 'who is blind' and 'who is deaf'—expecting the answer: you are. The prophet is not asking genuine questions but making a statement through rhetorical force: the nation entrusted with bringing light to the nations (verse 6) has become the blindest of all peoples.

The use of three designations—'my servant,' 'my messenger,' and 'he that is perfect' (or 'the dedicated one')—emphasizes the sharpness of the irony. These are titles of honor and responsibility. Yet each designation is paired with blindness or deafness. The repetition hammers the point: Israel has failed in every dimension of its calling. This is not a momentary lapse but a fundamental condition—the servant who should see is blind, the messenger who should hear is deaf.

word_study.meaning: Blind, physically or metaphorically unable to perceive. In Isaiah, blindness typically refers to spiritual blindness—inability to recognize God's purposes, signs, or salvation. The root carries the sense of being covered or obscured.
word_study.significance: Throughout Isaiah 40-66, blindness is both judgment and a condition from which the Servant brings deliverance. Here, Israel itself is characterized as blind—unable to perceive the signs of God's deliverance even as it unfolds around them.

word_study.meaning: Deaf, unable to hear. Like blindness, this often functions as spiritual deafness—resistance to God's word, unwillingness to listen to the prophets.
word_study.significance: The pairing of blindness and deafness draws from Isaiah 6:9-10, where God declares that Israel will see but not perceive, hear but not understand. It becomes a leitmotif of judgment: the sensory organs function but the spiritual perception fails.

word_study.meaning: Messenger, angel, one sent. The term denotes both the function (bearing a message) and the status (sent by God). In ANE context, a messenger bore the full authority of the one who sent them.
word_study.significance: Israel is not merely God's servant but His messenger—entrusted with representing His character and will to the nations. The irony intensifies: a messenger who cannot see or hear is useless to the one who sends him.

word_study.meaning: The word carries the sense of 'one who is whole,' 'complete,' or 'dedicated/covenanted.' The Covenant Rendering translates this as 'dedicated one' or 'covenant partner,' emphasizing the relational depth—one who is bound by covenant.
word_study.significance: This term amplifies the irony to its peak. The one most fully committed to God, most completely bound to Him by covenant, is blind. The designation suggests Israel's status as the covenant people—yet that very status makes their blindness more culpable and more tragic.

cross_references.connection: These verses establish the pattern of blindness and deafness as judicial hardening—Israel will see yet not perceive, hear yet not understand. Isaiah 42:19 applies this pattern directly to the servant Israel.
God identifies Israel as 'my servant' and 'the seed of Abraham my friend,' establishing Israel's servant identity. Isaiah 42:19 holds Israel accountable to that very identity by exposing its failure.
Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9-10 to explain why the crowds do not understand His parables. The blindness and deafness Isaiah condemns persists in the rejection of the ultimate Servant.
Paul describes a 'blindness in part' that has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in. This echo of Isaiah's diagnosis applies to both exile and the later apostolic era.
Jesus teaches the Nephites that He fulfilled Isaiah's prophecy concerning the Servant, contrasting His faithfulness with Israel's blindness and deafness.

commentary.historical_context: The prophet addresses Israelites in Babylonian exile (or those facing its threat). The irony would have stung deeply: God had chosen Israel as His instrument for world salvation, yet the nation had repeatedly turned from the covenant. The blindness and deafness were not random—they resulted from centuries of rejecting the prophets. In the ANE worldview, a messenger sent by a king carried that king's authority and reputation. An incompetent or inattentive messenger was a profound insult to the sender. Isaiah uses this cultural logic to amplify Israel's failure: as God's messenger, Israel has brought God shame by refusing to hear His voice or perceive His purposes.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly echoes this theme of Israel's blindness. Nephi warns that the Jews will 'despise the words of the prophets' and 'blind their eyes' (1 Nephi 19:7). Jesus teaches the Nephites that He is the Servant whom the Jews rejected, explicitly connecting their blindness to their rejection of the One Isaiah prophesied about (3 Nephi 16:10-11). The pattern of the covenant people becoming spiritually blind when they reject the Servant is a recurring Book of Mormon typology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 36:2 applies the language of being 'blind' to those who do not receive the restored gospel: 'And thou shalt be ordained under him to preach repentance unto this people...that they may understand that all things which have been given of God of things which are of God, and those which are not of God.' The Lord emphasizes perception and understanding as central to covenant faithfulness, echoing Isaiah's concern with spiritual sight and hearing.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The removal of blindness and deafness is part of the sanctification process in temple covenants. Members covenant to see and hear spiritual truth more clearly. The temple endowment includes imagery of spiritual awakening and enlightenment—the very opposite of the condition Isaiah describes here.

commentary.christological_typology: While Israel is the immediate referent, the verses function typologically. If the nation-servant is blind and deaf, it cannot accomplish its mission of redemption. The Servant-nation's failure points forward to the ultimate Servant—Jesus Christ—who alone perfectly fulfills the role. Christ's opening of the eyes of the blind and the ears of the deaf (as He later does in the Gospels) becomes not merely miracles but the fulfillment of what the servant-nation failed to do. The irony of verse 19 points to the resolution in later Servant Songs: the ultimate Servant will see and hear perfectly and will open the eyes and ears of others.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members can recognize themselves in this passage. Like Israel, we are called to be 'a light to the nations'—to bear witness of Christ to a darkened world. But like Israel, we are vulnerable to spiritual blindness and deafness. We can see scripture and not perceive its message. We can hear prophetic counsel and not truly listen. The verse challenges us to examine whether we are truly receiving the light and truth we claim to follow. Do we see the hand of God in our lives? Do we hear His voice through His servants? Are we 'dedicated' to the covenant while remaining blind to our own need for repentance and growth? The stinging irony Isaiah uses should prompt honest self-examination.

text_kjv: Seeing many things, but thou observest not; opening the ears, but he heareth not.

commentary.narrative:
This verse expands on verse 19 with concrete specificity. It is not that Israel lacks opportunity to see and hear—Israel sees and hears constantly. The problem is that seeing does not translate into perceiving, and hearing does not result in understanding. The shift from 'thou' (addressing Israel directly) to 'he' (describing Israel in third person) creates a subtle distancing effect: the prophet both accuses Israel directly and describes its condition as an observer, emphasizing the tragedy of Israel's spiritual obtuseness.

The term 'observest not' is crucial. The Hebrew shamar (שׁמר) means not merely to see but to guard, keep, protect, or treasure. Israel sees miracles and mighty works but fails to guard them in memory, to keep them as lessons, to treasure them as revelations of God's character. The open ears that do not hear represent willful resistance or spiritual insensitivity. This is not a physical deficiency but a relational failure—Israel has access to God's self-revelation but will not attend to it.

word_study.meaning: To keep, guard, preserve, observe, watch over. The root carries the sense of protecting something valued or remembering something important. In covenant language, to 'keep the commandments' means to treasure and obey them.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes the gap between seeing and observing. Israel has seen—the exodus, Sinai, prophetic signs—but has not guarded or preserved these memories as foundational to faith. The same verb is used in the covenantal formula 'keep my commandments.' Israel's failure to 'observe' what it sees is a failure of covenant remembrance.

word_study.meaning: To see, perceive, understand, experience. The term can mean physical sight or spiritual perception depending on context.
word_study.significance: Here ra'ah denotes physical sight or historical experience—Israel has witnessed God's acts. But seeing without understanding is a theme throughout Isaiah (cf. 6:9-10, 40:21, 42:18).

word_study.meaning: To open (eyes), to make receptive. The term emphasizes the potential for reception and understanding.
word_study.significance: Ironically, Israel's ears are open—the physical capacity is present. Yet the openness does not lead to hearing. This reinforces that the problem is not inability but unwillingness or spiritual obtuseness.

cross_references.connection: The source text for this pattern: 'Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not.' Verse 20 is Isaiah applying this prophetic decree to the contemporary generation.

Moses reminds Israel that although they have 'seen all that the LORD did,' they have not been given 'a heart to perceive, and eyes to see, and ears to hear.' The same diagnostic appears in the covenantal context.
Jesus explains that the parables are given so that some 'seeing see not; and hearing they hear not.' The spiritual blindness and deafness Isaiah condemns persists into the Gospel era.

Nephi's brothers see the vision but do not understand it. Nephi must explain: 'Have ye inquired of the Lord? And did he make known unto you the condition of Jerusalem?' Seeing without understanding is a recurring Book of Mormon theme.

The Lord addresses those who see signs but do not understand: 'Blessed are they...that keep the commandments of God.' Understanding comes through obedience and covenant devotion, not passive observation.

commentary.historical_context: In the context of exile or pre-exile Judah, Israel had experienced centuries of prophetic witness. The nation had seen miraculous deliverance from Egypt, received the law at Sinai, witnessed God's protection through judges and kings, and heard the warnings of prophets from Samuel to Jeremiah. Yet the nation repeatedly cycled through apostasy and repentance. By Isaiah's time, the pattern was clear: Israel had ample evidence of God's faithfulness but lacked the spiritual disposition to treasure and act on it. The phrase 'opening the ears, but he heareth not' reflects the futility the prophets experienced. God provided access to truth, but access is not the same as reception. In ANE culture, a wise person was one who listened to instruction and treasured it. Israel's failure to listen marked it as foolish in the deepest sense.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon emphasizes the importance of not merely seeing miracles but truly understanding and treasuring them. Alma warns the Zoramites that they see the word of God in their synagogues but do not live it (Alma 31:37). The pattern is consistent: seeing without guarding the message leads to spiritual death.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 101:89-90 presents 'a word of wisdom' and notes that some will receive it and some will not: 'in consequence of evils and designs which do and will exist in the hearts of conspiring men.' Understanding requires not just access to truth but a heart willing to 'observe'—to treasure and live what is taught.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment includes instruction and covenant-making designed to help participants truly 'see' and 'hear'—not merely physically but spiritually. The temple is presented as a place where truth is revealed to those who are prepared to receive it. The irony Isaiah describes is that such preparation is often missing.

commentary.christological_typology: The Servant who can truly see and hear (Isaiah 42:1-4, 50:4-9) stands in contrast to Israel's blindness. Jesus demonstrates perfect perception—seeing into hearts, understanding the Father's will completely, hearing the voice of God. His disciples, too, are taught to 'have ears to hear'—a call to spiritual perception that echoes and fulfills what Isaiah demands of Israel. The removal of physical blindness and deafness that Jesus performs (Mark 7:31-37, Matthew 12:22) becomes a sign of His ability to remove spiritual blindness as well.
commentary.application: Do we truly observe what we see in scripture and in life? Reading the Book of Mormon or hearing a General Conference address is not the same as treasuring and guarding the message. This verse should prompt reflection: What spiritual truths have I witnessed or heard that I have not truly 'kept'—have not let shape my life? Modern disciples have unprecedented access to truth through the restored gospel, yet access means little without receptivity. The challenge is to move from passive observation to active engagement—to guard the truths we receive and let them transform us. This requires humility, patience, and willingness to change.

text_kjv: The LORD is well pleased for his righteousness' sake; he will magnify the law, and make it honourable.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks a critical shift. After condemning Israel's blindness and deafness in verses 19-20, the prophet pivots to God's unwavering commitment. Despite Israel's failure, the Lord remains 'well pleased'—or more accurately, the Lord's will is fixed and certain. The 'for his righteousness' sake' clause is crucial: God's magnification of the law does not depend on Israel's obedience. It stems from God's own character, His own tsedeq (righteousness or vindication).

The parallelism of 'magnify the law' and 'make it honourable' suggests that the law is not being changed or abandoned but elevated and vindicated. In the context of Isaiah 40-66, where Israel has failed to keep the law, this verse asserts that the law itself remains glorious and binding. More than that, God will ensure that the law achieves its ultimate purpose—not through Israel's obedience alone but through God's own intervention. This is the voice of a God who does not abandon His covenant even when His people prove unfaithful.

word_study.meaning: To delight in, be pleased with, desire. The verb carries the sense of volition and satisfaction.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'The LORD is well pleased' or 'The LORD desires' establishes God's sovereign will. Unlike humans whose pleasure depends on circumstances, God's delight in His righteous purpose is fixed and absolute. This is not conditional on Israel's response.

word_study.meaning: Righteousness, justice, vindication, right action. In covenant contexts, it often refers to God's faithfulness in upholding His covenant promises.
word_study.significance: God acts 'for His righteousness' sake'—for the vindication of His own name and the fulfillment of His own purposes. This term is central to Isaiah 40-66: God's tsedeqah will be revealed (40:5), will arrive like morning (46:12-13), and will be vindicated through the Servant (53:11).

word_study.meaning: To make great, enlarge, exalt. The term denotes causing something to grow in significance, honor, or power.
word_study.significance: The law will not diminish or become obsolete despite Israel's failure. Rather, God will exalt it—make it greater, cause it to achieve its full purpose. This anticipates the later revelation that the law points toward the Messiah.

word_study.meaning: Mighty, glorious, exalted, honored. The adjective refers to majesty or splendor.
word_study.significance: The law's splendor and majesty will be demonstrated. Despite Israel's blindness, the law's excellence and binding power will be vindicated. This echoes Psalm 119, which celebrates the law's perfection and eternal validity.

cross_references.connection: Later in the same section, Isaiah again promises that God's torah will go forth from Him and His justice will become a light for the peoples. The law's vindication is a future certainty.
The Servant's righteousness (tsedeqah) will vindicate many. God's purpose will prosper in the Servant's hand. This is how the law will be magnified—through the Servant's work.

Paul explains that God's righteousness is demonstrated through Christ's redemption: 'to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins.' God's tsedeqah is vindicated through Christ, who fulfills the law.

Jesus declares He came not to destroy the law but to fulfill it: 'Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law.' The law's honor is secured through its fulfillment in Christ.
The Lord teaches that all things are governed by law and all beings are governed by law. The law's eternal validity and God's commitment to it is a fundamental doctrine.

commentary.historical_context: In the context of exile, Israel faced a theological crisis. If God's law was so important and Israel was God's covenant people, why was Israel exiled and defeated? Verse 21 answers: the law itself remains vindicated and glorious even if Israel has been unfaithful to it. This answers the despair of the exile—God has not repudiated His law or His purpose. Rather, He will ensure that His will is accomplished. In ANE thought, a god's power was demonstrated through the ability to accomplish His purposes despite obstacles. This verse asserts God's absolute sovereignty: He will magnify and honor the law regardless of Israel's current condition.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi emphasizes that although the Jews reject the Messiah, 'the law of Moses shall be fulfilled' (1 Nephi 19:23). The covenant and the law remain valid despite human rejection. The Book of Mormon repeatedly affirms that God's purposes will be accomplished even when Israel apostatizes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:37-38 echoes this verse: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the prophecies and promises which are in them shall all be fulfilled...What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken.' God's word and His law are absolutely secure.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the ultimate magnification and honoring of God's law. Within the temple, covenants are made and the law's deepest meaning is revealed. The Restoration includes the restoration of full temple covenants, which magnifies and exalts the law in ways that go beyond the written word.

commentary.christological_typology: The ultimate magnification of the law occurs through Christ. He is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone that believeth (Romans 10:4). The law points to Him, is fulfilled in Him, and achieves its purpose through Him. Isaiah's promise that God will magnify and honor the law is realized in the Incarnation and the Atonement. The Servant of the following verses will accomplish what the law demands but Israel cannot.
commentary.application: This verse offers profound comfort in the context of personal failure. If you have broken covenants, failed to keep the law, or fallen short of your own standards, this verse teaches that God's purposes and God's law are not invalidated by your failure. God's righteousness and His commitment to His covenant do not depend on your obedience—though your obedience does matter for your own salvation. The verse teaches that we can trust in God's ultimate vindication of His purposes, even when we struggle. More positively, it calls us to honor and magnify the law in our own lives—to treasure it, keep it, and recognize its divine origin. Like Israel, we have been given the law as a covenant people. Our response should be to 'keep' it in both senses: to obey it and to treasure it as a revelation of God's character.

text_kjv: But this is a people robbed and spoiled; they are all of them snared in holes, and they are hid in prison houses: they are for a prey, and none delivereth; for a spoil, and none saith, Restore.

commentary.narrative:
The word 'but' signals a harsh return to Israel's actual condition. Despite the Lord's unwavering commitment (verse 21), Israel itself remains in devastation. The verse catalogs Israel's suffering with vivid, concrete imagery: plundered, looted, trapped in holes, hidden in prison houses. Each image reinforces a sense of helplessness and isolation. The accumulation of images—robbed, spoiled, snared, hid, prey, spoil—creates an almost overwhelming portrait of complete abandonment.

The final phrase is psychologically devastating: 'none saith, Restore.' Israel is not merely suffering; it is undefended. No international power intervenes. No neighboring nation calls for restoration of the exiles. The theological implication hangs unspoken: if even God seems silent, Israel has no hope whatsoever. Yet the verse is addressed to exiles, implying that this catalog of suffering is being read against the promise of verse 21. Paradoxically, verse 22 grounds the need for the salvation about to be announced in verses 23-24. Without understanding the depth of Israel's condition, one cannot grasp the magnitude of God's intervention.

word_study.meaning: To plunder, rob, loot. Bazaz emphasizes taking valuable things; shasis adds the sense of violent stripping.
word_study.significance: The pairing of two terms for plundering emphasizes totality and violence. Israel has not merely lost some possessions but has been stripped of all resources and dignity.

word_study.meaning: Snare or trap; holes or pits. The image is of being caught in hidden traps, unable to escape.
word_study.significance: The term pach is often used metaphorically in Psalms for spiritual entrapment. But here it refers to literal captivity, confinement, the inability to escape.

word_study.meaning: Houses of confinement/prisons; to hide, be hidden. The term kelayim implies places of restraint.
word_study.significance: Israel is not merely confined but hidden away—out of sight, removed from the public eye, as though the world has forgotten them.

word_study.meaning: Plunder, prey, spoil taken by force.
word_study.significance: The term places Israel in the role of the hunted, the victim of predatory powers. Israel has become an object rather than an agent.

word_study.meaning: To return, restore, bring back.
word_study.significance: The absence of anyone saying 'restore' points to the hope of restoration that the Lord alone can provide. The verb shuv becomes central to the prophecy of return and repentance in Isaiah 40-66.

cross_references.connection: A plea from captive Israel: 'Wherefore should the heathen say, Where is their God?...Let the sighing of the prisoner come before thee.' The same experience of being forgotten and undefended.
Describes Jerusalem's fate: 'All that pass by clap their hands at thee...All thine enemies have opened their mouth against thee.' The same isolation and exposure.
Later in the same prophecy, Isaiah promises: 'Shall the prey be taken from the mighty...I will contend with him that contendeth with thee.' God will be Israel's deliverer despite its helplessness.
Alma describes his own spiritual captivity and anguish, isolated in despair. The imagery of being trapped and hidden parallels Isaiah's description of Israel's condition.
The Lord teaches that the wicked will destroy each other, but the righteous will be preserved. Verse 22's portrayal of helplessness contrasts with God's eventual vindication of the righteous.

commentary.historical_context: Verse 22 describes the Babylonian exile vividly. Israelites were deported from Judah, confined in Babylon, their land stripped by Nebuchadnezzar's armies. The phrase 'none saith, Restore' reflects the political isolation of Judah—no ally helped, no nation interceded. In Babylonian thought, exile was equivalent to being 'removed from the land of the living'—not merely a political disaster but a spiritual catastrophe. The exiles would have wondered if God had abandoned them entirely. From the perspective of the exiles in Babylon (or the pre-exile people facing the threat of exile), verse 22 names their worst fear: complete abandonment. Yet the verse is followed by a call to witness and a promise of restoration, suggesting that even in this darkest moment, God's purpose remains intact.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly uses the language of captivity and restoration. Alma speaks of being bound spiritually (Alma 36). Lehi's family flees Jerusalem before its fall, becoming exiles themselves. The pattern of being led away captive is followed by restoration through God's power (Mosiah 7-8). The promise of restoration is central to Book of Mormon theology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 45:26-33 speaks of Israel being 'scattered among all nations' and 'trodden down' until 'the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled.' But this is followed by restoration: 'And they shall see signs and wonders.' The exile is real, but restoration is certain.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the restoration of Israel—the gathering place where covenants are renewed and the exiled return. The language of 'restoration' in verse 22 becomes a type of the gathering of Israel in the latter days, which is central to temple theology in the Restoration.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Himself experienced confinement and abandonment—arrested, imprisoned, tried, and crucified while His disciples fled. His experience parallels and ultimately redeems Israel's experience.
