word_study.significance: God's declaration is not mere speech but the manifestation of God's will and purpose. The verb connects to the prophetic function: God declares future things and brings them to pass.

word_study.meaning: I have saved, delivered, rescued. The hiphil form of yosha means to bring salvation or deliver from danger.
word_study.significance: This verb points to concrete historical acts: the exodus, the crossing of the sea, the victories in conquest, the preservation through judges. Israel has experienced God's salvation repeatedly.

word_study.meaning: I have made known, announced, caused to hear. The hiphil of shama' (to hear) means to cause to be heard or made manifest.
word_study.significance: God's will and purposes have been made known to Israel through prophets, through visible acts, and through covenant instruction. What God has proclaimed has come to pass.

word_study.meaning: Strange, foreign, unfamiliar. Can refer to foreign gods or idols not belonging to Israel's covenant tradition.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'no strange god among you' reflects the ideal of covenant faithfulness: Israel should worship only Yahweh and not invite foreign gods into their worship. This recalls the first commandment.

word_study.meaning: Witnesses, those who testify. The term carries forensic weight: witnesses provide evidence in a trial.
word_study.significance: By the end of the chapter, Israel's role as witnesses has been established multiple times (verses 10, 12). This repetition emphasizes the crucial importance of testimony in God's cosmic trial.

word_study.meaning: God, divine power, the mighty one. Distinct from YHWH (the personal name), elohim encompasses the concept of divinity and authority.
word_study.significance: The use of el (rather than the personal name YHWH) emphasizes God's universal nature and authority. God is not merely Israel's national deity but the divine power over all creation.

cross_references.connection: God reminds Israel of deliverance: 'Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself. Now therefore, if ye will obey my voice indeed, and keep my covenant, then ye shall be a peculiar treasure unto me above all people: for all the earth is mine: And ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests.' Israel's witness role is rooted in deliverance.

Joshua's final address recalls God's acts: 'Now therefore fear the LORD, and serve him in sincerity and in truth: and put away the gods which your fathers served on the other side of the flood, and in Egypt; but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.' The call to exclusive worship and witness.
'Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he hath redeemed from the hand of the enemy.' The redeemed become witnesses through testimony.
'And we have seen and do testify that the Father sent the Son to be the Saviour of the world.' The apostles' testimony in the NT parallels Israel's role in the OT.

'Remember the worth of souls is great in the sight of God...Therefore, dearly beloved brethren, let us cheerfully do all things that lie in our power, and then may we stand still, with the utmost assurance, to see the salvation of God, and for his arm to be revealed.' Members of the Church bear witness to God's salvation.

commentary.historical_context: The historical reference in this verse—'when there was no strange god among you'—is significant for understanding Isaiah's exilic audience. The golden age to which Isaiah points is likely the period of the wilderness wanderings (when Israel had just been freed from Egypt and had not yet encountered Canaanite idolatry) or the early monarchy under David and Solomon (before the divided kingdom and widespread syncretism). However, by the time of Isaiah (eighth century BCE, with the exilic context of Second Isaiah being sixth century), Israel had fallen into idolatry repeatedly. The northern kingdom had been destroyed (722 BCE) and deported by Assyria. Judah itself would soon face Babylonian exile. Isaiah's point is that the period of undivided loyalty to Yahweh—when they had no strange gods and experienced God's favor—was real and verifiable. That history cannot be erased even by current exile. The exiles can point to their ancestors' experiences as evidence of Yahweh's power. This historical memory becomes the foundation of their testimony to the nations.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 9:46, Nephi applies this principle to his own people: 'My beloved brethren, I would that ye should come unto Christ, who is the Holy One of Israel...Behold, he sendeth an invitation unto all men, for the arms of mercy are extended towards them, and he saith: Repent, and come unto me, and ye shall be saved.' The Book of Mormon bears witness to the same God and His same power of salvation. In Mosiah 25:24, the people are reminded: 'And now, because of the covenant which ye have made ye shall be called the children of Mosiah; and as long as ye keep the commandments of the Lord your God ye shall prosper in the land.' Like Israel, Book of Mormon peoples are called to witness through their covenant-keeping.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:29-30 declares: 'For I the Lord cannot look upon sin with the least degree of allowance; Nevertheless, he that repents and doeth the commandments of the Lord shall be forgiven; And he that repents not, from him shall be taken even the light which he has received; for my Spirit shall not always strive with man, saith the Spirit of the Lord.' The pattern of declaration, salvation, and manifestation continues in the Restoration. Doctrine and Covenants 6:9 emphasizes the role of testimony: 'I will tell you in your mind and in your heart, by the Holy Ghost, which shall come upon you and which shall dwell in your heart.' Modern revelation emphasizes that God still declares, saves, and makes things manifest through the Holy Ghost.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the historic acts of God are portrayed through the creation account, the garden, and the subsequent covenants. Participants become part of the continuum of witnesses: they see what God has done, they enter covenant, and they become witnesses to the plan of salvation. The temple's teaching that 'there is no strange god among us' (in the sense that the temple community is devoted exclusively to Christ and His redemptive purpose) continues Isaiah's call to exclusive covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Israel's historical experience of God's deliverance—declared, saved, and made manifest—finds its ultimate fulfillment in the life and ministry of Jesus Christ. Where Israel was saved from Pharaoh and bondage, Christ saves from sin and death. Where God made His power manifest through signs and wonders in the wilderness, Christ made His power manifest through miracles and ultimately through resurrection. The witness role of Israel is assumed by the apostles and disciples of Jesus, who testify to His resurrection and divinity. In John 1:1-18, the Logos (Word) is presented as the agent through whom God has been 'declared' to humanity throughout history, culminating in incarnation. Christ is both God's ultimate declaration, the ultimate savior, and the one through whom God is made manifest to the world. Where ancient Israel testified on the basis of historical memory, the Church testifies on the basis of encounter with the risen Christ.
commentary.application: The structure of verse 12 provides a template for your own testimony. Israel's witness was based on three things: (1) God's declaration—God has spoken truth through prophets and Scripture; (2) God's salvation—Israel had experienced deliverance; (3) God's manifestation—the Lord's power was evident in their lives. You can examine your own testimony through these three lenses. First, what has God declared to you? Through scripture study, through living prophets, through the Spirit? Second, what are the specific instances of salvation or deliverance you have experienced? Answers to prayer, being guided away from harmful paths, experiencing the atonement's power? Third, how has God's power been made manifest in your life and in the world? Miracles, conversions, the growth of the Church? When you bear testimony, you are not being asked to claim perfect understanding or complete righteousness. You are being asked to witness to what you have actually experienced of God's goodness and power. This is powerful testimony—not abstract doctrine but lived reality. Like Israel, your testimony is most credible when you point to specific historical acts of God in your own life and the life of the Church.

text_kjv: Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks a theological turning point in Isaiah's message to exiled Israel. The phrase 'Behold, I am doing a new thing' (hinneni oseh chadashah) announces not merely a repetition of the Exodus deliverance but something qualitatively unprecedented. The Dead Sea Scrolls confirm this reading was unchanged from antiquity, underscoring its foundational importance. God is not simply repeating past redemptive acts; He is initiating something that transcends historical precedent and reaches into eschatological fulfillment.

The verb 'springs forth' (titsmach) uses the language of organic growth—a plant pushing through soil, visible to those with eyes to see. This is not abstract or hidden but perceptible to the discerning. The Babylonian exiles, blinded by their circumstances (42:18–20), are challenged: 'Do you not perceive it?' God's new work is already germinating in history; the question is whether Israel possesses spiritual sight. The second half reverses the harshness of the wilderness wandering: God will provide 'a way in the wilderness' and 'rivers in the desert.' Where the original exodus saw water struck from rock through Moses' intercession, this new exodus flows supernaturally in the wasteland itself.

For Isaiah's first audience in Babylon, this was a radical promise of return. But The Covenant Rendering's note on the Hebrew chadashah ('new thing') flags something profound: this language trajectory continues into the New Testament, where Paul speaks of 'a new creation' (2 Corinthians 5:17) and John's vision culminates in 'a new heaven and a new earth' (Revelation 21:5). The 'new thing' is not confined to the sixth-century return; it is eschatological, pointing to a transformation that touches all creation.

word_study.meaning: Something novel, unprecedented, qualitatively different from what came before. The root חדש (hadash) emphasizes newness not merely as temporal succession but as creative originality. In Isaiah's context, it signals that God's next act of redemption will transcend the patterns of the past.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering highlights that chadashah carries eschatological weight, not merely historical renewal. Israel's return from Babylon is the immediate referent, but the language opens toward the ultimate new creation. This term becomes christologically charged: Jesus Christ is the embodiment of God's new work (2 Corinthians 5:17).

word_study.meaning: To sprout, germinate, grow—language of plant life breaking through soil. The root emphasizes organic, visible emergence. The imperfect tense suggests continuous action: the new thing is actively springing forth, not merely promised for the future.
word_study.significance: This imagery inverts despair into hope. Exiles in Babylon experienced only desolation. Isaiah insists that God's redemptive work is already visible in history, like a seed pushing through earth. The challenge—'do you not perceive it?'—indicts spiritual blindness.

word_study.meaning: Path, road, journey. In exodus narratives, derech signifies the route of deliverance. Here it emphasizes that God provides not merely escape but a clear, marked pathway through hostile terrain.
word_study.significance: The wilderness (midbar) was the testing ground of the first exodus (40 years of wandering). Now God promises to make the wilderness navigable, transforming the place of trial into a thoroughfare of redemption.

word_study.meaning: Streams, rivers—the plural emphasizes abundance. In a desert (yeshimon), rivers are life-giving, impossible without divine intervention. The plural suggests not mere survival but abundance.
word_study.significance: This reverses the wilderness narrative. Where Israel once thirsted at Marah and Massah (Exodus 15:23–25; 17:1–7), God now causes waters to flow supernaturally. The abundance foreshadows the messianic age when 'the desert shall rejoice and blossom as the rose' (Isaiah 35:1).

cross_references.connection: Immediately preceding this passage, God indicts Israel's spiritual blindness: 'Hearing, [you] hear not; seeing, [you] see not.' Verse 19's challenge—'Do you not perceive it?'—directly confronts this blindness, asserting that the new thing is perceptible to those who will see.

The original exodus narrative records Israel's thirst in the wilderness and God's provision of water. Isaiah 43:19 reconfigures this: no longer must Israel search desperately for water; God will cause rivers to flow in the desert, transforming desperation into abundance.

Isaiah's vision of messianic restoration: 'The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.' Isaiah 43:19 foreshadows this eschatological transformation, where the wasteland becomes habitable and fertile.

Paul applies Isaiah's 'new thing' language to Christ: 'If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature.' The Covenant Rendering notes that chadashah trajectory continues into NT theology of new creation in Christ.

John's vision of ultimate redemption echoes Isaiah's 'new thing': 'Behold, I make all things new.' The eschatological horizon of Isaiah 43:19 finds its ultimate fulfillment in the eternal restoration of all things.

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah addresses Israel in exile (or preparing for exile) in Babylon, c. 587–539 BCE. The wilderness is not merely poetic imagery: the journey home from Babylon to Judea crossed the Syrian desert, a genuinely hostile terrain requiring water and provisions. Ancient Near Eastern literature sometimes depicts gods providing for travelers (e.g., divine provision in Ugaritic texts), but Isaiah's assertion that God will transform the desert itself—making rivers flow supernaturally—exceeds typical ancient religious expectations. The Babylonian context is crucial: Israel's gods appeared powerless; their temple lay in ruins. Isaiah's declaration that Yahweh will do 'a new thing' is an act of radical faith, asserting that the God of Israel is not defeated but actively engaged in history.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon echoes Isaiah's 'new thing' language in prophetic vision. When Nephi sees Christ's ministry and the establishment of His church, he witnesses the emergence of 'a new thing' among the nations (1 Nephi 13:5–9). The trajectory from Isaiah's new exodus to Christ's new covenant finds typological expression in the Nephite covenant community.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:24–25 echoes this passage: 'I am making a way for my people... that they may escape the enemy.' The Doctrine and Covenants applies Isaiah's promise of a cleared pathway to the Restoration, positioning the saints as heirs of Israel's redemptive promises. The 'new thing' becomes the restored Church of Jesus Christ.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The imagery of water flowing in the desert resonates with temple symbolism: the waters of life (Ezekiel 47:1–12; Revelation 22:1–2) emanate from the sanctuary. Israel's return journey and ultimate redemption are temple-centered—God's dwelling place is restored, and from it flows life and provision.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 43:19 prefigures Christ as the embodiment of God's 'new thing.' Just as God promises to accomplish something unprecedented in the wilderness, Christ inaugurates 'a new covenant' (Luke 22:20), calling into being 'a new creation' (2 Corinthians 5:17). The pathway through the wilderness that God provides prefigures Christ as 'the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6). The rivers in the desert anticipate the 'living water' that Jesus offers (John 4:10–14; 7:38–39), which flows from the pierced side of the crucified Savior (John 19:34) and sustains the redeemed eternally.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members live between the promise and its fulfillment. Just as Isaiah challenged exiled Israel to perceive God's 'new thing' already germinating in history, we are invited to recognize Christ's ongoing redemptive work. The question 'Do you not perceive it?' confronts our own spiritual blindness: Can we see evidence of God's hand in our personal histories, in the Church, in world events? The imagery of a way through the wilderness and rivers in the desert speaks directly to trials: God does not promise to remove deserts from our path, but to make them navigable and even fruitful. When facing spiritually arid seasons—loss, uncertainty, disillusionment—this verse invites us to trust that God is doing something new, something we may not yet comprehend. The challenge is to develop spiritual sight: to recognize the signs of God's work, to trust His unprecedented promises, and to drink from the waters He provides in our own wildernesses.

text_kjv: The beast of the field shall honour me, the dragons and the owls: because I give waters in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert, to give drink to my people, my chosen.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 20 extends the cosmic significance of God's new thing: creation itself will respond in honor to God's redemptive acts. The enumeration of desert creatures—'beasts of the field,' 'jackals,' 'ostriches'—is not merely poetic embellishment but a profound theological claim. In ancient Near Eastern thought, the wilderness belonged to chaos, to forces beyond human (and divine) control. Isaiah insists that even creatures of desolation will honor God when redemption flows through the wasteland.

The grammatical structure is significant: God gives waters in the wilderness 'in order that' (le + infinitive: lehashkot) He may give drink to His chosen people. The purpose clause makes clear that creation's transformation serves a redemptive end—the sustenance of God's covenant community. This is not nature worship or pantheism but covenantal theology: God's redemptive work extends to all creation, but the focal point remains His people, ammi bechiri ('my chosen people'). The phrase echoes Isaiah 42:1, where the Servant is described as 'my chosen one,' creating a subtle connection: the Servant's redemptive work will result in the renewal of all things, with God's people at the center.

For exiles facing the Syrian desert, this was psychologically revolutionary. They did not fear divine impotence; they feared abandonment—that their God had relinquished them to chaos and death. Isaiah insists that even the beasts of the wasteland will be conscripted into God's redemptive narrative. When water flows impossibly in the desert, even jackals and ostriches—creatures that normally flee from human habitation—will pause and honor the God who makes such provision. The verse invokes a moment of cosmic alignment: all creation, from the most wild to the most civilized, will acknowledge God's power through His redemptive act.

word_study.meaning: Wild animals, creatures of open terrain. The term emphasizes creatures untamed by human control, associated with wilderness, danger, and the outer boundaries of civilization.
word_study.significance: By asserting that even wild beasts will 'honor' God, Isaiah claims that God's redemptive power encompasses all creation, not merely human society. Nothing escapes God's sovereignty.

word_study.meaning: Jackals or possibly serpents/dragons. The term denotes creatures of desolation, often associated in biblical literature with ruin and abandonment (e.g., Isaiah 13:22; Psalm 44:19). The KJV renders it 'dragons,' capturing the sense of otherworldliness.
word_study.significance: Jackals are scavengers of empty places. Their presence in a location signals desolation. By declaring that jackals will 'honor' God, Isaiah transforms the symbol of desolation into a witness of redemption. The desert becomes not a place of death but of witness.

word_study.meaning: The ostrich, a large desert bird known for speed and for inhabiting arid regions where few other creatures survive. The phrase 'daughters of the ostrich' may emphasize flocks or communities of ostriches.
word_study.significance: Ostriches are adapted to desert life and avoid human settlement. Their presence marks the deep wilderness. The Covenant Rendering's use of 'ostriches' rather than KJV's 'owls' better captures the Hebrew and the creature's association with genuine, uninhabited wasteland. Even these creatures will honor God.

word_study.meaning: My chosen one/people. The singular can function collectively ('my chosen people'). The root bachir means to select or choose, emphasizing God's deliberate election. The possessive suffix—'my chosen'—indicates intimate covenant relationship.
word_study.significance: This term echoes 42:1, where the Servant is introduced as God's 'chosen one.' By using the same term for both the Servant and the people, Isaiah suggests that the Servant's redemptive work and the people's election are inseparable. The people are chosen; the Servant accomplishes their redemption.

cross_references.connection: God introduces the Servant as 'my chosen one, in whom my soul delights.' The identical term (bechir) for both the Servant and God's people creates a theological link: the Servant is chosen to accomplish redemption for the chosen people.

In a prophetic oracle against Babylon, Isaiah describes desolate Babylon as a haunt of 'owls' (likely the same creature, ya'anah) and 'jackals.' The imagery of desert creatures marking abandonment is inverted in 43:20: those same creatures will honor God when He redeems His people from Babylon.

The psalmist laments: 'Thou hast sore broken us in the place of jackals.' The place of jackals signifies desolation and divine judgment. Isaiah 43:20 reclaims this imagery: the place of jackals becomes the place where God is honored for His redemptive acts.

Paul echoes Isaiah's vision of cosmic redemption: 'The creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption.' Isaiah 43:20 anticipates this NT theology of universal reconciliation, where all creation participates in God's redemptive work.

Modern revelation affirms that 'all things' belong to God and that He 'made them for the benefit of man.' Isaiah 43:20's vision of creatures honoring God through sustenance provided to God's people resonates with this LDS understanding of creation's purpose in God's redemptive economy.

commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near Eastern worldview divided reality into zones: the city (human order), the cultivated field (managed nature), and the wilderness (chaos, inhabited by demons and dangerous creatures). The desert between Babylon and Judea represented the ultimate chaos—vast, waterless, filled with bandits and wild animals. No ancient reader would have expected wild creatures to 'honor' a god; they embodied forces hostile to human survival. Isaiah's claim is therefore radical: when God acts redemptively, even the chaos-realm responds. Jackals and ostriches, which contemporary travelers would have feared or fled from, become witnesses to God's power. This inverts not only Near Eastern geography but also Near Eastern theology, which typically confined divine action to civilization and cult.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains Messianic visions of creation's transformation (2 Nephi 8 quotes Isaiah 51–52; 3 Nephi records Christ's teachings that even 'the very beasts of the forest shall glorify me'—see 3 Nephi 20:16). The vision of creation honoring God culminates in Christ's millennial reign, when even predatory animals will lie down together (Isaiah 11:6–9, quoted in D&C 101:24–26).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:24–26 portrays Christ's future redemptive act: 'I shall command the great deep to dry up its waters; And the mountains shall tremble, and their refuges shall become desolate.' The restoration of all things will cause creation itself to respond. Isaiah 43:20 is foundational to this LDS eschatology.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the axis mundi—the point where heaven and earth meet. Isaiah 43:20 suggests that redemption radiates from God's redemptive act outward to encompass all creation. The temple theology of Latter-day Saints affirms that ultimate redemption will restore all creation to harmony with God's will.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 43:20 foreshadows Christ as the one through whom all creation is reconciled to God. Colossians 1:20 declares that Christ has reconciled 'all things' through His 'blood, by means of the cross.' Just as water flowing in the desert causes all creatures to honor God, Christ's redemptive power draws all things toward ultimate harmony with God. The Servant's work encompasses not merely Israel's return but the transformation of creation itself. In a subordinate sense, the provision of 'rivers in the desert' for God's people prefigures the 'living water' that Christ gives, which satisfies both physical and spiritual thirst.
commentary.application: This verse invites us to perceive the cosmic scope of God's redemptive work. When we experience God's provision in our personal 'deserts'—times of spiritual drought, loneliness, or material lack—we participate in a drama that encompasses all creation. The verse challenges a privatized spirituality: our redemption is not merely personal but cosmic. It matters not only for us but for creation itself. Practically, this means cultivating a sacramental view of nature: recognizing that God's hand is visible in provision, in unexpected mercy, in the very resources that sustain life. The imagery of creatures 'honoring' God suggests that gratitude is the natural response to God's provision. When we receive God's 'rivers in the desert'—unexpected help, surprising grace, provision that defies explanation—we join even the jackals and ostriches in honoring Him. The verse also speaks to environmental stewardship: because all creation is drawn into God's redemptive purposes, we have a sacred obligation to care for creation as witnesses to God's glory.

text_kjv: This people have I formed for myself; they shall shew forth my praise.

commentary.narrative:
This verse distills Israel's theological purpose into crystalline clarity: God has deliberately shaped a people for one primary end—to declare His praise. The Hebrew yatsarti li ('I formed for myself') uses the potter's verb, evoking the image of God as a craftsman deliberately shaping clay (see Isaiah 29:16; 45:9; Jeremiah 18:4–6). This is not arbitrary creation but purposeful design. The nation exists not for self-aggrandizement, wealth, or military power but to be a vehicle of God's self-revelation and glory.

The shift in tense is important. Verse 19 declares 'I am doing a new thing' (present). Verse 21 grounds this new act in God's original purpose: this is the people God 'formed'—an act completed in the past. God is not changing His purpose for Israel but rather fulfilling it through a new act of redemption. Exile has not negated the covenant; rather, return from exile will enable Israel to fulfill its original calling. The exiles might have despaired that their captivity meant rejection, that they were no longer God's people. Isaiah insists: you are still the people God deliberately shaped; now I will restore you so that you can again declare my praise.

The phrase 'show forth my praise' (yesapperu tehillati) carries the sense of narrative proclamation—not merely singing hymns but narrating God's deeds, recounting His mighty acts. Israel's vocation is prophetic: to be a living testimony to God's redemptive power. Every restored exile becomes a witness. The very fact of their return becomes a story to tell, a praise that echoes throughout the nations. This is why Isaiah emphasizes that the new thing will be perceptible (v.19): the redemption will be so evident that Israel cannot help but proclaim it, and through Israel's proclamation, the nations will hear of God's power.

word_study.meaning: To form, fashion, shape—especially used of a potter shaping clay on the wheel. The root emphasizes intentionality and craft: the potter envisions the final form and deliberately shapes matter to achieve it. In theological usage, it describes God's deliberate creation of His people.
word_study.significance: By using the potter's verb, Isaiah emphasizes that Israel's existence is not accidental but purposeful. God did not stumble upon Israel; He deliberately shaped them for a specific calling. This verb appears in Isaiah's critique of idols (29:16) and God's response to human presumption (45:9–10), creating a resonance: just as God has authority over the clay, He has authority to reform and restore Israel.

word_study.meaning: Praise, a song of praise. The root hillel means to shine, to make bright, to glorify. Tehillah is both the act of praising and, in plural form (tehillim), the Book of Psalms. It encompasses both formal hymnic praise and the recounting of God's deeds.
word_study.significance: Israel's primary calling is to make God's glory visible, 'bright,' known among the nations. This is not peripheral to Israel's purpose but central. The Book of Psalms (tehillim) was Israel's book of praise; the nation itself becomes a living psalm, a proclamation of God's greatness.

word_study.meaning: To number, count, tell, recount, narrate. The root saphar has both mathematical and narrative dimensions: to count events, to tell stories. In prophetic literature, it often means to announce or proclaim.
word_study.significance: Israel's praise is not merely emotional but narrative: it consists of recounting what God has done. The restored exiles will tell their story—how God sustained them in captivity, how He broke their chains, how He cleared a path through the desert. Through this narrative, God's glory becomes known.

cross_references.connection: Peter applies this verse directly to the Church: 'But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light.' The LDS understanding of the Church as spiritual Israel inherits this calling from Isaiah.

Isaiah uses the potter metaphor to critique human presumption: 'Surely your turning of things upside down shall be esteemed as the potter's clay.' Here in 43:21, the same verb (yatsar) emphasizes God's rightful authority to shape Israel for redemptive purposes.

Moses reminds Israel of their election: 'For thou art an holy people unto the LORD thy God... because the LORD loved thee.' Isaiah 43:21 echoes this covenantal election, but adds the explicit purpose: they are formed 'to show forth His praise.'

A psalm of thanksgiving: 'Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise... For the LORD is good.' Psalm 100 exemplifies the 'showing forth of praise' that Isaiah declares to be Israel's purpose. Israel as a nation is to embody what the psalmist exhorts: perpetual praise.

King Benjamin declares that God 'has created you, and for this very purpose he has kept you alive.' This Book of Mormon passage applies Isaiah's theology of purpose-driven creation directly: God sustains us in order that we might serve His purposes.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, a nation's survival often depended on political power, military might, or economic resources. Israel, by contrast, claimed that its very reason for existence was theological: to bear witness to the invisible God. This was countercultural. In Babylon, surrounded by temples dedicated to Marduk and other gods with visible manifestations and political power, Israel's priests and prophets would have faced the question: What is the point of a nation exiled, militarily defeated, whose God is invisible? Isaiah's answer: This is precisely why you exist—to proclaim that your invisible God is greater than all visible powers, that He sustains you despite empire, that He will restore you and through your restoration, the nations will know His name.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 15:14–16, Nephi is shown that his descendants (the Nephites) will become 'a branch of the house of Israel' and that 'they shall be a remnant.' This remnant will eventually 'show forth the praises' of the Lord through the covenant community established by Christ. The verse anticipates the role of the Book of Mormon itself: a record that 'shows forth the praises' of God to a latter-day Israel.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 115:4 identifies the Church as 'the only true and living church upon the face of the whole earth.' Like Isaiah's Israel, the Restoration community is formed for a specific purpose: 'that this people might be established in this land, to prepare the way for the fulness of my gospel' (D&C 20:21). The Church, like Israel, exists to 'show forth' God's praise through testimony and the proclamation of His work.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, members covenant to 'give their lives... to the service of God.' This is the enacted form of what Isaiah 43:21 describes: a people deliberately shaped to declare God's glory through covenant action and witness. The temple endowment itself teaches Israel's role as a 'kingdom of priests' (Exodus 19:6), commissioned to bear witness to God's purposes.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 43:21 foreshadows the Church as the body of Christ, formed through Christ's redemptive work to praise God and proclaim His glory. Just as Israel was shaped to witness to God's power, the Church is called to proclaim Christ and His Atonement (1 Peter 2:9, as noted above). In a more direct typology, Christ Himself embodies the ultimate fulfillment of this verse: His entire life was an act of showing forth God's praise. His redemptive work is the supreme 'new thing' (v.19), and through His Church, this redemption continues to be proclaimed throughout the world.
commentary.application:
This verse cuts to the heart of individual and communal purpose. Every covenant member inherits Israel's calling: to declare God's praise through word and deed. This is not an optional vocation but the defining purpose of our existence. The verse invites us to ask: Am I deliberately shaped by God for a specific purpose? How do I 'show forth' God's praise in my daily life? The answer is not confined to formal testimony-bearing (though that is included) but encompasses how we live: Do our choices reflect God's glory? Do our relationships show forth His love? Does our resilience in trials witness to His sustaining power?

In the context of exile—Isaiah's historical setting and a metaphor for our own spiritual trials—this verse is profoundly comforting. Hardship does not negate our purpose; it can deepen it. The exiles would not have been able to 'show forth' God's deliverance had they never been in captivity. Our trials become testimonies. Our redemptions become narratives of praise. The Latter-day Saint understanding of personal revelation deepens this further: each member can discern specific ways God has shaped them (yatsar) for purposes known to God alone. Your particular gifts, experiences, and challenges are not random; they are part of God's deliberate design to make His glory visible through your life.

text_kjv: But thou hast not called upon me, O Jacob; but thou hast been weary of me, O Israel.

commentary.narrative:
The tone shifts abruptly. After declaring Israel's purpose and God's new redemptive act, Isaiah now levels an indictment: Israel has failed in their fundamental calling. The conjunction 'but' (vav) signals a sharp reversal—not a contradiction of what came before but a specification of Israel's failure. This verse does not negate God's purpose for Israel (v.21) but rather explains why redemption and restoration are necessary: Israel has abandoned their calling.

The verb 'called upon' (qarah) means to invoke, to summon in prayer, to cry out for help. Israel 'has not called upon me'—not because they lacked ability but because they chose not to. In exile, surrounded by Babylonian religion and culture, the exiles may have turned to other gods or ceased seeking the God of their ancestors. Isaiah charges them with neglect of prayer, with ceasing to invoke the covenant God. More cutting still is the second accusation: 'you have been weary of me' (yaga'ta bi). The word yaga'a means to grow tired, to be exhausted. Israel grew tired of God—tired of waiting for deliverance, tired of trusting in an invisible God while Babylon's gods seemed powerful and immediate.

The irony is devastating. In Isaiah 40:28, God declared that He 'shall not faint, neither be weary' (lo' yiga'). God does not grow weary; He sustains all things with infinite power and patience. Yet Israel—the people whom God 'formed for myself' (v.21)—grew weary of God. The roles are inverted. God waits patiently; Israel becomes impatient. God sustains; Israel faints. This is not merely doctrinal irony but relational heartbreak: the covenant people have ceased to call upon their covenant God.

word_study.meaning: To call, invoke, summon, cry out. In prayer contexts, it means to call upon God, to invoke Him by name, to seek His attention and aid. The perfect tense ('you have not called') suggests a completed state of non-calling.
word_study.significance: Prayer is the relational fabric of covenant. To cease calling upon God is to sever that relationship. The verb captures not merely intellectual assent but relational action. Israel's sin is not primarily doctrinal but relational: they stopped seeking God.

word_study.meaning: To grow tired, be exhausted, labor in vain. The perfect form (yaga'ta) indicates a state of weariness that has set in. The verb can suggest not merely tiredness but futility—the sense that effort is pointless.
word_study.significance: By accusing Israel of being 'weary' of God, Isaiah inverts the expected pattern. In a healthy covenant, the human party should trust that God will sustain them until rest comes. Instead, Israel grew tired of trusting God. The verb appears again in verse 23–24, creating a wordplay: God did not 'weary' Israel with ritual demands (v.23), yet Israel 'wearied' God with sin (v.24).

cross_references.connection: Just three chapters earlier, Isaiah proclaimed: 'Hast thou not known? ... the everlasting God... shall not faint, neither be weary.' Isaiah 43:22 forms a tragic counterpoint: God does not weary, but Israel does. This creates theological irony that makes the charge in verse 22 especially cutting.

Jeremiah recalls an earlier time when Israel 'followedst me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown.' By contrast, in Isaiah's time, Israel has ceased to follow and call upon God. Jeremiah provides historical depth to Isaiah's accusation—this is not Israel's original character but their current failing.

The psalmist declares: 'When thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, LORD, will I seek.' This represents the proper covenant response—to seek God when He calls. Isaiah 43:22 indicts Israel for the opposite: they neither sought God's face nor called upon Him.

After the crucifixion and resurrection, Christ appears to the Nephites and laments: 'How oft have I gathered you as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!' This echoes Isaiah's lament: God reaches out; the people refuse to call upon Him.

commentary.historical_context: In exile, Israel faced a genuine spiritual crisis. The temple was destroyed; cultic worship was impossible. Synagogal prayer was beginning to develop, but it was not yet the robust institution it would later become. Some exiles likely assimilated to Babylonian religion, finding it more immediately compelling than devotion to an invisible, apparently defeated God. Others maintained their faith but may have despaired that God had abandoned them. Isaiah's accusation reflects a real historical possibility: that in the early exilic period, some of Israel ceased calling upon the God of their ancestors. The term 'weary of me' captures the spiritual exhaustion of exile—the temptation to give up on a God who seemed powerless to help.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains multiple instances of this pattern: when Israel ceases to call upon God (ceases to pray, seek revelation, repent), they fall into spiritual darkness. Alma 32:28–42 describes the growth of faith through spiritual experiment and continued calling upon God; the opposite—ceasing to pray, growing weary in well-doing—leads to apostasy (see also Alma 4:10–12).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 58:29 counsels: 'Let those commandments which I have given concerning these things be heeded and my church be not broken up upon the earth because of transgression.' The pattern Isaiah identifies—Israel's failure to call upon God—is precisely what D&C warns against: if the covenant people cease to seek God through prayer and revelation, the covenant is broken.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is fundamentally a house of prayer. To cease calling upon God is to abandon the temple's purpose. Modern Latter-day Saints are counseled to frequent the temple, to engage in prayer within its walls, and to call upon God there. Isaiah 43:22 warns of the spiritual peril of ceasing to do so.

commentary.christological_typology: Prophetically, this verse anticipates Israel's rejection of Christ. In John 1:11, the Evangelist writes: 'He came unto his own, and his own received him not.' Christ is God's ultimate call upon Israel to 'call upon' Him, to trust Him, to follow Him. Israel's failure to do so in Isaiah's time prefigures their failure in Christ's time. Yet Christ Himself, as the Servant of the Lord, never ceased to call upon God the Father (Gethsemane, the cross), embodying the true covenant response that Israel failed to give.
commentary.application:
This verse addresses the spiritual peril of prayerlessness and the danger of growing weary in devotion. For modern covenant members, it invites honest self-examination: Are we regularly calling upon God through prayer? Or have we grown 'weary' of seeking Him? This can happen gradually—not through a sudden abandonment of faith but through the slow erosion of prayer, scriptural study, and spiritual practice. The demands of work, family, and secular life can leave us exhausted, tempted to defer our spiritual seeking until 'we have more time.' Isaiah's indictment warns of the danger in this pattern.

But the verse also hints at God's response. Though Israel ceased calling upon Him, God did not cease reaching out (as the verses that follow will make clear). The indictment is part of a redemptive narrative: God charges Israel with their failure not to condemn them beyond hope but to call them back. The question 'Have you called upon me?' is simultaneously an invitation: 'Call upon me now.' The verse invites us to ask where our devotion has lapsed and to restore it, to remember that we covenant each week to 'always remember him,' and to honor that covenant through consistent prayer and seeking of His face.

text_kjv: Thou hast not brought me the small cattle of thy burnt offerings; neither hast thou honoured me with thy sacrifices. I have not caused thee to serve with an offering, nor wearied thee with incense.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 23 continues the indictment but introduces an unexpected turn: God clarifies the nature of Israel's failure. The first half charges Israel with not bringing sacrifices ('sheep for burnt offerings') and not honoring God through sacrifice. In the cultic world of ancient Israel, sacrifice was the primary mode of worship. To withhold sacrifice was to withhold worship itself. Yet the second half of the verse contains a surprising affirmation: God has not 'wearied' Israel with excessive ritual demands.

This creates a crucial theological distinction. The verse does not charge Israel with failing to perform an impossible standard of sacrifice. Rather, God asserts that the requirements were reasonable, not burdensome. The word 'wearied' (hoga'tika) picks up the root from verse 22 ('you have been weary of me'), creating a semantic bridge: Israel grew weary of God, yet God did not weary Israel with ritual demands. The irony is that Israel was weary without cause, without justification. God's requirements were not oppressive. This exonerates God and accentuates Israel's culpability: they cannot claim they were overwhelmed by divine demands.

In the context of exile, this is highly significant. The exiles could not perform Temple sacrifice—the Temple was destroyed. Yet God's complaint is not about the absence of sacrifice (which was impossible) but about Israel's prior failure to 'call upon' God (v.22) and to honor Him with devotion. The verse suggests that the real issue is not external compliance with ritual but internal relationship. God would rather have a people who call upon Him in prayer and devotion than a people who mechanically perform sacrifices. This anticipates later prophetic critique (Amos 5:21–24; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6–8) that external sacrifice without internal devotion is empty. Isaiah's theology aligns with this: Israel's primary sin is not ritual failure but relational failure—ceasing to call upon God, growing weary of Him.

word_study.meaning: A whole burnt offering, an offering in which the entire animal is consumed on the altar. The root alah means to ascend, and the offering was so named because it ascended to God in smoke. It was the most common sacrifice in the Temple and symbolized complete dedication to God.
word_study.significance: By withholding whole burnt offerings, Israel withheld the primary symbol of total devotion. Yet God's point is that this was not a new, unexpected demand—it was Israel's ancient covenant obligation.

word_study.meaning: To honor, show respect, glorify. The root kabed means heavy or weighty; to honor something is to ascribe weight or significance to it. In cultic contexts, honoring God meant treating Him as supreme through sacrifice and devotion.
word_study.significance: Failure to bring sacrifice is more than ritual neglect; it is a failure to honor God, to ascribe significance to Him. This suggests that the real sin is spiritual—a loss of God's priority in Israel's life.

word_study.meaning: To serve, work, labor, perform service. In cultic contexts, it refers to priestly service in the Temple. The word can also mean to be enslaved or to undergo labor.
word_study.significance: God says 'I have not caused thee to serve with an offering'—literally, to labor in ritualistic service. The word carries a note of heaviness, as if to say: I have not burdened you with laborious demands. This softens God's indictment: Israel's failure was not due to an oppressive burden but to their own neglect.

word_study.meaning: To weary, tire, exhaust. This is the same root as 'yaga'ta' (you have been weary) in verse 22, creating a wordplay. God is saying: I did not weary you, yet you grew weary of me.
word_study.significance: The repetition of the weary-root creates an ironic contrast. The Covenant Rendering makes this wordplay clear: Israel wearied while God did not weary them. This is a rhetorical masterpiece—Israel's complaint that God was too demanding is answered by God's assertion that He was not demanding at all.

word_study.meaning: Frankincense, an aromatic resin burned as incense in worship. It was imported, expensive, and symbolized the preciousness of worship. Incense burned before the Lord produced fragrant smoke that symbolized prayers rising to heaven.
word_study.significance: Incense was a luxury offering, a sign of devotion that required economic sacrifice. By saying 'I have not wearied you with frankincense,' God asserts that He did not demand excessive expenditure or burdensome ritual. Yet Israel still withheld even this reasonable offering.

cross_references.connection: Samuel rebukes King Saul: 'Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice.' This verse anticipates Isaiah's theology: God values internal obedience and devotion over external ritual compliance.

Amos delivers a similar prophetic indictment: 'I hate, I despise your feast days, and I will not smell in your solemn assemblies... But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.' Like Isaiah, Amos critiques mechanical sacrifice divorced from genuine devotion and righteousness.

Hosea records God's indictment: 'For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.' This verse directly parallels Isaiah 43:23, emphasizing that relational knowledge of God supersedes ritual observance.

In modern revelation, God distinguishes between temporal law and spiritual law: 'And again, I say unto you, that every man who is obliged to provide for his own family, let him provide.' God's laws are not oppressive but reasonable. Isaiah 43:23's assertion that God has not made unreasonable demands resonates with the LDS understanding of divine law as enabling rather than enslaving.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, sacrifice was the central act of worship. Without the Temple, exiles could not perform these rituals. Some scholars suggest that this very impossibility drove the development of prayer and Torah study as substitutes for sacrifice—a shift that would profoundly shape Judaism. Isaiah 43:23 does not mock sacrifice but contextualizes it: the real failure is not the absence of sacrifice (which circumstances make impossible) but the prior abandonment of prayer and devotion. In Babylonian context, gods were often portrayed as requiring elaborate, even oppressive ritual service. Isaiah's God, by contrast, asserts that His requirements are reasonable and that the failure is not excessive demand but human refusal to seek Him.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 22:23–25, Nephi teaches that the Lord 'doth not command in all things that which is contrary to the nature of things,' and that He does not 'command that which is not good.' The Book of Mormon echoes Isaiah's theology: God's laws are not designed to burden but to bless. Nephi further teaches that faithfulness to God's reasonable commandments is the path to redemption.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 58:26–29 outlines God's law as enabling and life-giving, not oppressive: 'Wherefore, I command you to relax your minds concerning the affairs of this life... And let those commandments which I have given concerning these things be heeded.' Modern revelation affirms that God's commandments are designed to free us from excessive worry, not to burden us with impossible demands.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the Latter-day Saint temple, the language of sacrifice and offering takes on new meaning. The temple represents the fulfillment of Old Testament sacrifice through Christ's Atonement. Modern members are invited to make 'a covenant, even that of sacrifice' in the temple—but this is not the sacrifice of animals but of time, devotion, and covenant-keeping. Isaiah 43:23's principle stands: God values the internal offering of our hearts more than external ritualism.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 43:23 foreshadows Christ as the ultimate fulfillment of sacrifice. In Hebrews 10:5–10, the author declares that Christ came saying, 'Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not... then said I, Lo, I come to do thy will, O God.' Christ offers Himself—the only sacrifice that fully satisfies God's requirements and transforms the entire sacrificial system. The internal devotion emphasized in Isaiah 43:23 finds its perfect exemplar in Christ's unqualified surrender of His will to the Father. Through Christ, external sacrifice is internalized: the sacrifice God desires is a 'broken and contrite heart' (Psalm 51:17), which Christ embodied perfectly.
commentary.application:
This verse diagnoses a spiritual disease: the substitution of external compliance for internal devotion. For modern covenant members, it invites self-examination: Do I 'go through the motions' of religious practice without genuine seeking of God? Am I present physically at church but absent spiritually? Do I pray mechanically without real connection to God? Conversely, the verse offers profound comfort: God does not demand the impossible. The requirements of discipleship are not oppressively burdensome. God does not expect perfect performance or superhuman sacrifice; He asks for sincere seeking, honest prayer, and devoted hearts.

The verse also challenges a common spiritual temptation: the assumption that God is perpetually demanding, that we can never do enough to satisfy Him. Isaiah's response is clear: God has not wearied you with demands. Your weariness comes not from God's impossibly high standards but from your own disconnection from Him. If you feel spiritually exhausted by religious practice, the issue may not be that God asks too much, but that you have lost touch with the relational core of discipleship—prayer, seeking, genuine love for God. The remedy is not to intensify external performance but to restore internal devotion through honest prayer and reconnection with God's presence.

text_kjv: Thou hast bought me no sweet cane with money, neither hast thou filled me with the fat of thy sacrifices: but thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 24 completes the indictment with a stunning rhetorical inversion that constitutes one of the most remarkable anthropomorphisms in the Hebrew Bible. The verse begins with a specific complaint—Israel has not brought 'sweet cane' (aromatic reeds used in incense and perfume) or provided the 'fat of your sacrifices.' These are luxury offerings, signs of devotion and expense. Yet the verse pivots to something far more serious: Israel has made God 'serve' (he'evadtani) with their sins and 'wearied' Him with their iniquities.

The verb he'evadtani ('you have made me serve') uses the same root as 'eved (slave, servant). Israel, who should be God's servants, has inverted the relationship: they have enslaved God, forcing Him to serve them by bearing the weight of their sins. This is theologically audacious. God cannot literally be enslaved or forced into service, yet the poetic language captures a profound relational truth: sin burdens God. The God who 'shall not faint, neither be weary' (Isaiah 40:28) declares Himself wearied—not by the demands of sustaining creation but by the burden of Israel's iniquities.

This inversion reframes the entire discussion of verses 22–24. Israel complained (or Isaiah suggests they might complain) that God's demands were oppressive. God responds: I did not weary you with ritual demands (v.23), but you have wearied me with your sins (v.24). The roles are reversed. The real weight, the real burden, lies not on Israel obeying God but on God bearing the consequences of Israel's disobedience. This anticipates the Servant passages (especially Isaiah 53), where the Servant bears the iniquities of the people. Here, God Himself declares that He bears the weight of Israel's sin. It is a statement of divine sorrow and burden that only Calvary could fully answer.

word_study.meaning: Cane or reed; also fragrant wood. Keseph means silver or money. Sweet cane was an aromatic substance, likely imported, used in incense and ointments (see Exodus 30:23). The phrase 'sweet cane with money' emphasizes an offering requiring economic sacrifice.
word_study.significance: Sweet cane was a luxury item, a sign of devotion that required expenditure. Israel's failure to bring it is emblematic of withholding the best, the most costly offerings.

word_study.meaning: You have enslaved me, made me serve, subjected me to servitude. The root avad means both to work/serve and to be enslaved. By using this verb with God as the object, Isaiah creates a shocking reversal: humans enslaving God.
word_study.significance: This is one of the boldest theological statements in the Hebrew Bible. The verb transforms our understanding of sin: it is not merely rule-breaking but a relational reversal where the creature subjects the Creator to servitude. The Covenant Rendering captures this by rendering it 'burdened': Israel has burdened God with sin.

word_study.meaning: You have wearied me, exhausted me, tired me out. This repeats the root from verses 22–23, creating a powerful wordplay: Israel grew weary of God (v.22), God did not weary Israel with demands (v.23), but Israel has wearied God with iniquities (v.24).
word_study.significance: The wordplay is unmissable in Hebrew: yaga'ta bi ('you wearied of me'), lo' hoga'ticha ('I did not weary you'), hoga'tani ('you wearied me'). This creates a theological narrative in miniature: God remains constant while Israel fails, and the consequence is that God, though inexhaustible in sustaining creation, bears the weight of human sin.

word_study.meaning: Iniquities, wrongdoings, perversities, distortions. The root avan means to be crooked or twisted. Avonot captures not merely sins (violations of law) but the deep moral deformity that sin represents—a twisting away from God's truth.
word_study.significance: By using 'iniquities' rather than mere 'sins,' Isaiah emphasizes that Israel's problem is not accidental failure but deep moral perversity. Yet God bears even this—the weight of Israel's twisted rebellion.

cross_references.connection: The Servant passage: 'He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities.' Isaiah 43:24 anticipates the Servant's burden-bearing: God's statement that Israel has 'wearied me with your iniquities' finds its redemptive answer in the Servant who bears those iniquities willingly.

David's confession: 'Have mercy upon me, O God... For I acknowledge my transgressions... Against thee, thee only, have I sinned.' Like Isaiah 43:24, the psalmist recognizes that sin is fundamentally a burden placed upon God, a wound in the relationship with the divine.

The voice of Zion: 'Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow.' This reflects the relational pain that Isaiah 43:24 articulates: God's sorrow at bearing the weight of Israel's sin.

John echoes the Isaianic theology: 'If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves... But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins.' The acknowledgment that God bears our sins and the call to confess them both resonate with Isaiah 43:24's indictment and implication of forgiveness.

Christ speaks: 'Therefore I command you to repent... that you may not bring down wrath upon yourselves... I, the Lord, have suffered the pain of all men... Which suffering caused myself... to tremble because of pain.' This Restoration passage applies Isaiah 43:24's theology to Christ: He takes upon Himself the weight of human sin.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, gods were often depicted as demanding tribute, sacrifice, and service from humans. The relationship was transactional: humans served gods; gods provided protection and blessing. Israel's conception was similar but carried a covenant dimension: the relationship was mutual obligation. Yet Isaiah inverts even this: it is not God demanding service but God bearing human burden. This reflects the mature prophetic understanding that sin is fundamentally relational—it damages the covenant bond and places weight upon God's heart. The language is remarkably personal, suggesting that God experiences emotional pain at Israel's unfaithfulness. This anthropomorphic language was bold in its time and remains so: it asserts that God is not remote or indifferent but genuinely affected by human sin.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 7:11–12, Alma teaches that Christ 'shall go forth, suffering pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind; and this that the word might be fulfilled which saith he will take upon him the sins of his people.' The Book of Mormon applies Isaiah 43:24's principle: the burden of human sin is borne by God through Christ. Just as Isaiah declares that God has wearied Himself bearing Israel's iniquities, the Atonement shows how Christ takes that burden upon Himself.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:15–18 is perhaps the most direct modern revelation application of Isaiah 43:24. Christ Himself states: 'I, the Lord, have suffered the pain of all men, that all men might repent and come unto me.' The Restoration makes explicit what Isaiah implies: God, through Christ, suffers the weight of human sin. This is not passive victimhood but active love—Christ willingly bears what we have made Him bear.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony emphasizes the burden of sin and the necessity of repentance. The principle of Isaiah 43:24—that sin burdens God and must be addressed—underlies the temple's call to reconciliation and covenant-renewal. Members who understand this passage more deeply recognize that the Atonement, central to temple theology, is God's answer to the unbearable weight of human iniquity.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 43:24 is perhaps the most powerful pre-Christian witness to the Atonement. By declaring that God is wearied by Israel's iniquities, Isaiah articulates a fundamental truth: sin cannot be forgiven costlessly; it must be borne by someone. Christ is the one who bears this weight. In His passion, Christ takes upon Himself the iniquities Isaiah speaks of. The 'weariness' Isaiah attributes to God becomes the anguish of Gethsemane and Calvary. Just as God declares He has been burdened and enslaved by Israel's sins, Christ voluntarily allows Himself to be bound, mocked, and crucified—taking upon Himself what humans have burdened God with. The redemptive arc moves from indictment (vv.22–24) to grace: though Israel has wearied God with iniquities, God's response is not judgment but redemption through the Servant who bears those iniquities.
commentary.application:
This verse pierces the comfortable assumption that sin is a private matter or a mere violation of abstract law. Isaiah asserts that sin burdens God—it affects the heart and will of the Almighty. This inverts how we typically think about sin: we imagine that we are primarily harmed by our own wrongdoing, or that God is distant and unaffected. Isaiah insists: your sin burdens God. You have wearied Him.

This is a call to profound repentance. Repentance is not merely 'feeling sorry' or 'doing better next time.' It is recognizing that our rebellion has burdened the God who loves us, that we have made Him 'serve' in the sense of bearing consequences we should bear ourselves. For Latter-day Saints, this connects directly to the Atonement: Christ took upon Himself the burden that Isaiah declares—the weight of our iniquities. To understand this verse deeply is to recognize that every act of repentance honors Christ's sacrifice, acknowledging that He bore what we made God bear.

Practically, this verse invites us to ask: What iniquities am I burdening God with? Where am I refusing to repent? The question is not meant to induce shame but to motivate gratitude and change. Because God has been burdened by our sins, and because Christ has taken that burden upon Himself, we are invited to lay down the burden of unredeemed sin and walk in the light of forgiveness. The verse concludes the indictment section; the verses that follow will bring redemption. But this verse ensures that when redemption comes, we understand its cost and value it accordingly.

text_kjv: I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.

commentary.narrative:
After the devastating indictment of verses 22-24—where God revealed that Israel had not called upon Him, had grown weary of Him, and had instead burdened Him with their sins—this verse arrives as an astonishing pivot. One expects judgment, condemnation, and rejection. Instead, God declares not only that He will forgive but that the initiative belongs entirely to Him. The doubled 'I, I am He' (anokhi anokhi) is emphatic beyond measure in Hebrew, shifting the entire focus from Israel's failure to God's sovereign character. This is not conditional forgiveness contingent on Israel's repentance or worthiness; it is declarative, absolute, and grounded in God's own purposes ('for my own sake'—lema'ani). The verb 'blots out' (mocheh) is visceral: it means to wipe away completely, as one wipes a dish clean or erases a written record. God does not merely overlook sin; He annihilates its very record.

The second clause—'I will not remember thy sins'—is theologically critical. This is not human forgetfulness; it is a sovereign decision to treat sin as non-existent in the record of judgment. In the Ancient Near Eastern legal context, 'remembering' means calling upon, invoking, or executing judgment. To 'not remember' is to remove from the docket of accountability. The Covenant Rendering captures the power: the doubled pronoun 'I, I am He' insists that forgiveness flows from God's initiative alone, not from human merit or effort. This declaration anticipates the language of the new covenant in Jeremiah 31:34 ('I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more') and grounds the theology of grace that permeates the New Testament.

For an Israelite audience in exile, this verse offered radical hope. They had failed their covenant obligations; their leadership had led them astray. Yet God declares that the grounds for forgiveness rest not on their restoration but on His character. This is the heart of Isaiah 40-55: Israel's restoration is grounded in God's redemptive purpose, not Israel's merit. The 'for my own sake' motif appears throughout Isaiah 48 and echoes God's covenant commitment made at Sinai and renewed through the patriarchs. God's name, reputation, and purpose are at stake in Israel's restoration, and that stake is sufficient to move Him to forgive.

word_study.meaning: A doubled first-person pronoun for emphatic insistence—'I myself, I alone.' This construction appears elsewhere in Isaiah (41:4, 46:4, 48:12) and signals God's exclusive agency and authority. The repetition moves beyond simple emphasis into the realm of self-identification and uniqueness.
word_study.significance: The doubling underscores that forgiveness is God's unilateral action, not a negotiated settlement. In covenant language, it emphasizes that God alone has the power and prerogative to restore the covenant relationship.

word_study.meaning: To wipe, erase, or obliterate completely. The verb is used for wiping a dish clean (2 Kings 21:13) or erasing a written record. In the Exodus narrative, it describes God's threat to blot out Israel's name from His book (Exodus 32:32-33). Here, it is applied to the complete annihilation of the record of sin.
word_study.significance: The term conveys total removal, not mere concealment. Sin is not hidden or set aside; it is erased from the record of accountability. This differs from 'covering' sin (kaphar) and emphasizes the completeness of divine forgiveness.

word_study.meaning: For my own sake, for my own purpose or benefit. This preposition-noun construction indicates the motivation or ground for an action. Throughout Isaiah 48, God repeatedly acts 'for my name's sake' (lema'an shemi), grounding all restoration in His character and covenant commitment.
word_study.significance: This phrase distinguishes grace from merely pragmatic mercy. God does not forgive because Israel deserves it, has repented sufficiently, or has offered adequate compensation. He forgives because His own character, reputation, and covenant commitment require it. This is grace at its most radical.

word_study.meaning: I will not remember, invoke, or recall. In legal and covenantal contexts, 'remembering' means to call upon or enforce. To 'not remember' is a sovereign decision to strike from the record of judgment.
word_study.significance: This is not divine amnesia but judicial amnesia—a formal decision to treat the sin as if it had not been recorded. It echoes the formula of acquittal in ancient legal proceedings and parallels Jeremiah 31:34's new covenant language.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah 43:25 is the foundation for Jeremiah's new covenant promise: 'I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.' The language is nearly identical, and both verses ground forgiveness in God's sovereign decision rather than human merit.

God repeats this motif: 'For my name's sake will I defer mine anger, and for my praise will I refrain for thee, that I cut thee not off.' The same 'for my own sake' reasoning justifies both restraint and restoration.

When Moses intercedes for Israel after the golden calf, he asks God to blot him out of God's book if Israel is not forgiven. Here, God promises to do the opposite: to blot out Israel's transgressions from His record.

The New Testament explicitly quotes Jeremiah 31:34 and applies it to the new covenant through Christ: 'I will be merciful to their unrighteousness, and their sins and their iniquities will I remember no more.' Isaiah 43:25 is the Old Testament precedent for this radical grace.

These verses immediately preceding v. 25 detail Israel's complete failure: they have not called upon God, have grown weary of Him, and have burdened Him with their sins. V. 25's promise of forgiveness is all the more stunning against this backdrop of comprehensive unfaithfulness.

commentary.historical_context: The exile to Babylon (586 BCE onwards) created a crisis of covenant faith for Israel. Had God abandoned the covenant? Were the promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob void? Had Israel's sin severed the relationship permanently? In this context, Isaiah 40-55 was composed to reassure the exilic community that despite their failure and Babylon's apparent dominance, God's purposes remained unchanged. The historical background includes the fall of Jerusalem, the destruction of the Temple, and the transport of the Jewish elite to Mesopotamia. The Babylonian Empire was culturally and religiously dominant, with powerful civic religions and impressive monuments. Israel's God seemed defeated, His Temple in ruins. Isaiah 43:25 directly challenges this narrative: God's commitment to Israel is not contingent on their performance but on His own character. This would have been heard as radical counter-testimony to the apparent triumph of Babylon's gods and the apparent failure of Israel's covenant.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes God's grace flowing from His character rather than human merit. Alma 22:14 captures this dynamic: 'O God, have mercy upon me, and wipe away my sins that I may be clean.' The emphasis on complete forgiveness ('wipe away') echoes mocheh. Jacob 4:7 declares that God 'desireth the hearts of the children of men'—His motivation flows from covenant purpose, not human worthiness. The Nephite experience of repeated cycles of covenant-breaking and divine forgiveness (Mosiah, Alma) illustrates the principle that God's forgiveness is grounded in His character and redemptive purposes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 58:42 applies this principle directly to modern saints: 'Behold, he who has repented of his sins, the same is forgiven, and I, the Lord, remember them no more.' The structure mirrors Isaiah 43:25: God ('I, the Lord') forgives and 'remembers them no more.' This is reiterated in D&C 64:10, where God commands the Saints to forgive 'as I have forgiven you.' The restoration principle is that forgiveness in the covenant community flows from God's example—His willingness to erase the record of sin becomes the model for covenant relationships.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ordinances of washing and anointing carry forward this imagery of erasure and cleansing. The 'blotting out' of sin is liturgically enacted through purification rituals. The garment worn after these ordinances represents the covering of sin and the fresh covenant standing. In the endowment, God's willingness to establish covenant despite humanity's weakness is portrayed through the narrative arc from the fall to exaltation. The theme of God's grace grounding the entire structure—not human perfection—is central to temple theology.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 43:25 anticipates Christ's redemptive work in multiple dimensions. The verb 'blots out' (mocheh) previews Christ as the one who bears away sin completely—not covering it but removing it. The motivation 'for my own sake' (lema'ani) reflects Christ's submission to the Father's will and redemptive purposes. Christ is the ultimate expression of God's unilateral grace: 'I, I am He' becomes incarnate in the Son who says, 'The Father and I are one.' The promise to 'not remember' sin finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ's sacrifice, which provides the legal ground for God to treat sin as if it had never been recorded. In Hebrews 10:17, this verse is explicitly applied to Christ's once-for-all sacrifice: 'Their sins and iniquities will I remember no more.'
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 43:25 dismantles the false theology that God's forgiveness must be earned through perfect repentance, sufficient restitution, or adequate suffering. It teaches that forgiveness is God's sovereign gift, grounded in His character and covenant commitment, not in the measure of human performance. This has profound implications for personal discipleship: it means that when we genuinely repent, God does not keep a ledger of remaining debts or residual judgment. The record is blotted out. It also means that God's restoration of a fallen member is not contingent on that member's complete self-restoration; God acts 'for His own sake,' to fulfill His own redemptive purposes. For those struggling with shame, scrupulosity, or the sense that they have sinned 'too much' for God to forgive, this verse is a direct word: God's forgiveness is not proportional to human merit but to His character. The practical application is learning to accept God's forgiveness as a gift rather than a negotiated settlement, and extending that same radical forgiveness to others in the community of faith.

text_kjv: Put me in remembrance: let us plead together: declare thou, that thou mayest be justified.

commentary.narrative:
This verse shifts to courtroom language, invoking the legal imagery that frames much of Isaiah 40-55. God invites Israel to make their case: 'Put me in remembrance'—remind me, bring forward your evidence, make your argument in court. 'Let us plead together'—let us take this to trial, argue it out before the judge. 'Declare thou, that thou mayest be justified'—present your case and let's see if you can prove yourself innocent. The invitation appears to offer Israel equal standing: a genuine opportunity to defend itself against the charges. Yet this verse carries profound irony, which only becomes apparent when read in sequence with verses 22-25.

Verse 22-24 has already established that Israel has no defense: they did not call upon God, they grew weary of Him, they burdened Him with their sins. There is no hidden case that will vindicate Israel, no evidence that will prove Israel innocent. Israel cannot be justified on its own merits. The Covenant Rendering makes the irony clearer: 'Set forth your case, that you may be proved right.' The conditional clause 'that you may be proved right' is not a promise; it is a challenge. God is essentially saying, 'Go ahead—present your case and see if it proves you innocent.' But we know from the preceding verses that it won't. Israel stands convicted.

Yet this verse is preceded by verse 25's stunning declaration of forgiveness, which means that the legal proceeding is conducted in a courtroom where the verdict has already been rendered in Israel's favor—before the case is even argued. This is the paradox of grace: Israel is simultaneously guilty and acquitted, condemned and forgiven. The courtroom language serves not to determine the outcome but to dramatize the gracious absurdity of God's decision to restore Israel despite Israel's complete inability to justify itself. God is not trying Israel; God is inviting Israel to see the futility of self-justification and to accept forgiveness as a gift.

word_study.meaning: Remind me, bring to my remembrance, call to mind. The verb zakhar (to remember) in the causative form means to cause someone to remember or to invoke their memory. In legal contexts, it means to submit evidence or to make a case.
word_study.significance: The legal resonance is critical: to 'put God in remembrance' in a trial context is to present evidence that should influence the verdict. The irony is that Israel has no evidence that will prove innocence.

word_study.meaning: Let us judge together, argue together, plead the case together. The verb shaphat means to judge or render judgment; the reflexive form (niphal) means to argue, dispute, or bring a lawsuit. Yachad means together, simultaneously.
word_study.significance: This formulation suggests equal standing in the courtroom—both parties presenting their cases to a judge. But it is rhetorical: God, as the judge, already knows the outcome. The 'together' emphasizes that Israel is not excluded from the process; God invites Israel into it, even though the verdict is predetermined by grace.

word_study.meaning: You declare, you recount, you set forth. The verb sapphar means to recount, narrate, or describe. In legal contexts, it means to present one's case or account.
word_study.significance: The emphasis falls on Israel: 'You declare.' God is not declaring Israel's innocence; God invites Israel to do so. The burden of proof, rhetorically, is on Israel—a burden it cannot meet.

word_study.meaning: In order that you may be justified, so that you may be pronounced righteous. Tzedek means righteousness or rightness; the niphal form titzdaq means to be justified, vindicated, or proved right. Lema'an indicates purpose or result.
word_study.significance: The conditional structure ('in order that you may be justified') makes justification contingent on Israel's case. But Israel cannot be justified by its works—only by God's grace. The verse thus sets up the paradox that unifies chapters 40-66: Israel is justified not by proving itself righteous but by receiving God's declaration of righteousness.

cross_references.connection: These verses immediately preceding v. 26 establish the charges against Israel: they did not call upon God, grew weary of Him, and burdened Him with their sins. V. 26's invitation to plead is ironic in light of this indictment.
