This comprehensive scope is crucial: Israel need not negotiate which sins are 'big enough' to be forgiven.

word_study.meaning: Return, turn back, come back. The verb shuvah is repentance's core word—a turning from one direction to another, a change of direction and allegiance.
word_study.significance: The call to return *follows* the promise of redemption, making it an invitation grounded in grace rather than a condition to be met. Israel can return precisely because God has removed the obstacles to return.

word_study.meaning: I have redeemed, ransomed, bought back. The verb ga'al carries the sense of a kinsman-redeemer who buys back what was lost or enslaved, restoring it to the family.
word_study.significance: God acts as Israel's kinsman-redeemer—the one who pays the price to restore Israel from captivity and restore it to the covenant family. This is not a distant divine act but an intimate, familial redemption.

cross_references.connection: 'I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.' Isaiah 43:25 uses the same verb (mocheh, blot out) and reinforces that God's act of erasure is grounded in His own character, not in Israel's worthiness.

'He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.' The prophet uses similar imagery—sins cast away and destroyed—as the basis for Israel's hope.

'As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.' The psalmist echoes Isaiah's theme of complete removal of sin, using spatial imagery (east and west, infinite separation) where Isaiah uses meteorological imagery (cloud dissipation).

'By this ye may know if a man repenteth of his sins—behold, he will confess them and forsake them. And now, verily, I say unto you, I the Lord forgive sins, and am merciful unto those who confess their sins before me and ask forgiveness.' The D&C parallels Isaiah's theology: God's forgiveness is real and complete, but it works in concert with human repentance (confession and forsaking).

'But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin... If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.' John echoes Isaiah's promise of comprehensive forgiveness grounded in Christ's redemptive act.

commentary.historical_context: The historical setting is crucial: this verse addresses Israel in Babylonian exile, some 50–60 years after the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BCE. Israel's experience would have been one of profound displacement and shame—the temple was destroyed, the city lay in ruins, and Israel's covenant identity seemed shattered. The question would be acute: Has God abandoned Israel? Is the covenant broken? Can Israel ever return? Isaiah 44:22 is God's answer: *Yes*, the covenant is still valid. Your sins—including the national sins that led to exile—are blotted out. You are still My servant, still redeemed. The Babylonian context is important because it shows that this promise is not made to a righteous people but to a people in exile under judgment. The erasure of sin is not a reward for good behavior; it is God's sovereign act of grace, offered to Israel when Israel is farthest from deserving it.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 4:25-27: 'My God hath been my support; he, by the hand of his holy prophet, brought us out of the land of Jerusalem, and hath kept and preserved me that I should not perish... I know that the Lord will make a way for me to accomplish the words which he hath spoken unto me.' Nephi echoes Isaiah's theology that God's redemptive act precedes and enables return. Similarly, Alma 36:17-21 describes Alma's conversion as a moment when he suddenly grasps that the Lord had redeemed him—and the recognition of redemption immediately produces the desire to return to God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:41: 'He comprehendeth all things, and all things are before him, and all things are round about him; and he is above all things, and in all things, and is through all things, and is round about all things.' God's redemptive power is comprehensive and total—it encompasses all times, all places, all sins. This principle underlies Isaiah's promise that God has blotted out transgressions and sins completely. Also, D&C 19:15-18 (Christ's atonement): 'Therefore I command you to repent... And again, I command you to repent, lest I smite you... Therefore, I gave unto them commandments, not of myself, but that all men everywhere must repent, or they can in nowise inherit the kingdom of God.' The imperative to repent (return) is grounded in the prior reality of Christ's redemptive atonement.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The sacrament ceremony annually renews the member's covenant of redemption and repentance. The bread and water, taken in remembrance of Christ's body and blood, signify the complete remission of sins offered through His atonement—directly echoing Isaiah 44:22. The member partakes not because she has earned forgiveness through her own righteousness, but because God's redemptive act is offered unconditionally. The call to 'always remember him and keep his commandments' (D&C 20:77) follows the same logic as Isaiah 44:22: the call to return follows and is grounded in the prior act of redemption.

commentary.christological_typology: The verse is preeminently Christological. The one who 'redeems' (ga'al) is the kinsman-redeemer, and in the restored gospel, this is Christ—the one who buys back humanity from sin and death through His atonement. The blotting out of sins is the central work of Christ's redemption: 'I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly' (John 10:10). The call to 'return unto me' becomes in the New Testament the call to come unto Christ: 'Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest' (Matthew 11:28). The pattern—redemption first, then the invitation to return—is the pattern of the gospel: 'While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us' (Romans 5:8). We do not earn redemption through repentance; redemption is offered to us, and through it we are enabled to repent and return.
commentary.application: This verse is perhaps the most gospel-centered text in Isaiah, and its application to modern covenant life is transformative. The sequence matters: (1) God has blotted out your transgressions—not conditionally, not provisionally, but as a completed act. Your rebellion, your failures, your shame—all are erased. (2) Because this is true, the call to return is not a demand but an invitation, grounded in grace. You can return not because you have earned the right, but because God has removed the obstacle. The modern application involves three movements: First, *believe the promise*. Many members live in the shadow of past sin, believing that they are still under the cloud of judgment. Isaiah's promise is that the cloud is *gone*, dissolved like mist. Second, *respond to the invitation*. The call to 'return unto me' is active—it requires turning, realignment, a change of direction. But this turning is not grim obligation; it is joyful response to an act of grace. Third, *live from the reality of redemption*. Covenant life is not about earning God's favor (which is impossible) but about inhabiting the reality of already-given redemption. The knowledge that God has blotted out your sins is not a comfort to be accessed occasionally; it is the foundation of daily spiritual confidence.

text_kjv: Sing, O ye heavens; for the LORD hath done it: shout, ye lower parts of the earth: break forth into singing, ye mountains, O forest, and every tree therein: for the LORD hath redeemed Jacob, and glorified himself in Israel.

commentary.narrative:
The promise of redemption in verse 22 is so cosmic in scope that it demands cosmic response. Verse 23 is a hymn of universal praise—the whole creation is called to celebrate God's redemptive act. This is not metaphorical poetry; it is Isaiah's vision of what *should* happen when God redeems His people: all creation responds in joy. The imperative mood—'Sing!', 'Shout!', 'Break forth!'—is vigorous and demanding. The heavens are summoned to sing; the lower parts of the earth (the depths, the underworld) are called to shout; the mountains are invited to break forth in song. The forest and every tree join the chorus. Creation is not a silent backdrop to redemption; it is a participant in the celebration.

This is extraordinary theology. In most ancient Near Eastern literature, redemption is a transaction between a god and a specific people. But Isaiah envisions something different: when God redeems His people, the entire cosmos recognizes and celebrates it. The reason is given in the final clause: 'for the LORD hath redeemed Jacob, and glorified himself in Israel.' The redemption of Jacob (Israel) is not a parochial event; it is an act that glorifies God *in the sight of all creation*. God's glory—His character, His power, His faithfulness—is *revealed* through His covenant love for Israel. In redeeming Israel, God glorifies Himself; and when creation perceives this glory, it cannot help but break into song.

The progression from heavens to depths to mountains to forests to individual trees is a comprehensive enumeration of creation—from the heights to the depths, from the great powers of nature to the humble trees. None are excluded from the call to praise. This is Isaiah's vision of the restorative power of God's redemption: when God acts to save His people, the entire cosmos is restored to its proper function, which is to witness and celebrate the glory of God.

word_study.meaning: To sing, to shout for joy, to break into jubilation. The verb carries intense emotional force—it is not quiet singing but exuberant celebration.
word_study.significance: The verb ranan appears often in the Psalms for the joy of the redeemed (Psalm 65:13: 'The pastures are clothed with flocks; the valleys also are covered over with corn; they shout for joy, they also sing.' Here creation itself rejoices because God's redemptive and providential care is visible in the harvest).

word_study.meaning: The heavens, the sky, the realm above the earth. In biblical cosmology, the heavens are the dwelling place of God and the realm of the divine.
word_study.significance: The summons to the heavens to sing is a summons to the realm closest to God to initiate the cosmic praise. If heaven sings, all other creation will follow.

word_study.meaning: The depths of the earth, the underworld, the subterranean realm. This is not hell or the place of the dead, but the hidden depths of the earth.
word_study.significance: By summoning both the heights (heavens) and the depths (earth), Isaiah envisions redemption as an act that encompasses all dimensions of creation, unifying the cosmos in praise. Nothing is outside the scope of God's redemptive reach and nothing is exempt from the call to praise.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'let the mountains burst forth into singing.' The verb patzach means to break through, to burst out, to erupt. It conveys the irrepressible nature of the joy—the mountains cannot contain their celebration; they must break forth into song.
word_study.significance: This is Isaiah's most exuberant image: the mountains—solid, immovable, massive—break forth into song. If the mountains sing, if the forest and every tree join in, then redemption has touched the deepest, most material realities of creation.

word_study.meaning: Redeemed, ransomed, bought back. The verb is the same used in verse 22—it emphasizes that redemption is a real, completed transaction, not a promise or a hope.
word_study.significance: The repetition of ga'al (redeemed) in both verse 22 and verse 23 anchors the cosmic praise in historical reality. This is not abstract celebration but celebration of a concrete act: God has redeemed Jacob from exile and captivity.

word_study.meaning: He has glorified Himself, made His glory manifest, revealed His honor. The reflexive form suggests that God's glory is revealed *through* the redemptive act itself—God does not need external praise to be glorious, but the redemption of Israel is the means by which His glory becomes visible to all creation.
word_study.significance: This is a crucial theological point: God's glory is inseparable from His covenant faithfulness. To glorify God is to participate in recognizing and celebrating His faithfulness to His people. Creation's praise is not flattery but recognition of reality—God is revealed as glorious precisely in His redemptive acts.

cross_references.connection: 'Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad; let the sea roar, and the fulness thereof; Let the field be joyful, and all that is therein: then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice, Before the LORD: for he cometh, for he cometh to judge the earth.' Psalm 96 echoes Isaiah's vision of cosmic praise in the context of God's coming judgment and salvation—all creation rejoices when God acts.

'For ye shall go out with joy, and be led forth with peace: the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.' Isaiah develops this theme further in chapter 55, showing that the cosmic joy in response to redemption becomes the experience of the redeemed themselves—they go out with joy as creation itself celebrates.

'For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now... And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption.' Paul applies Isaiah's vision to the eschatological future: all creation groans in anticipation of redemption, waiting for the full manifestation of God's glory.

'And I beheld, and I heard the voice of many angels round about the throne... Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing... Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, be unto him that sitteth upon the throne.' Revelation's vision of cosmic praise echoes Isaiah's theme—all creation celebrates the redemptive act of the Lamb.

'And the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness comprehendeth it not; nevertheless, the day shall come when you shall comprehend even God, being quickened in him and by him. Then shall ye know that ye have seen me, that I am, and that I am the true light.' The revelation emphasizes that all creation, in recognizing God's light and redemptive power, comes to understand and praise His nature and glory.

commentary.historical_context: This verse must be read against the backdrop of the Babylonian exile. Israel is in captivity, and the peoples of the ancient world have witnessed Israel's defeat and humiliation. In the ancient Near East, military defeat was read as theological defeat—the gods of the conquered people were understood to be weaker than the gods of the conqueror. Therefore, for Israel to be redeemed, for God to act on Israel's behalf, would be an act that vindicated God's glory *before all the nations*. Isaiah's call for cosmic praise reflects this: when God redeems Israel from exile, it is not a secret act but a public vindication. The heavens and the earth—in the view of all the nations—will witness and celebrate God's redemptive power. The vision is theologically revolutionary: it locates the meaning of Israel's redemption not in Israel's own experience alone, but in its implications for the entire cosmos and all creation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 19:18: 'And as Isaiah spake concerning the restoration of the Jews, or in other words, the restoration of the house of Israel.' Nephi emphasizes that Isaiah's vision of Israel's redemption extends beyond the immediate historical event to include a cosmic dimension—the restoration of all things. Also, 2 Nephi 9:13: 'O how great the holiness of our God! For he knoweth all things, and there is not anything save he knows it.' The cosmic scope of Isaiah's vision—that all creation recognizes and celebrates redemption—is grounded in God's omniscience and omnipotence, themes the Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:23-24: 'And now, after the many testimonies which have been given of him, this is the testimony, last of all, which we give of him: That he lives! For we saw him, even on the right hand of God; and we heard the voice bearing record that he is the Only Begotten of the Father.' The Restoration emphasizes that the ultimate redemption is the manifestation and vindication of Christ's glory before all creation. Similarly, D&C 88:88: 'And by the power of my Spirit will I make known unto you the thoughts and intents of the hearts of all men.' God's redemptive power is intimately connected to His ability to know and be present throughout all creation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony celebrates the restoration of covenant relationship in language reminiscent of Isaiah 44:23. The celestial room represents the restored creation—a place of light, beauty, and wholeness—where God's glory is manifest. The movement through the temple symbolically traces the restoration of humanity and creation itself from the fall to redemption. The call to praise God in the temple is a response similar to that called for in Isaiah 44:23—the recognition that God's redemptive act touches all of creation and calls forth universal praise.

commentary.christological_typology: The redemption of Jacob, which calls forth cosmic praise, finds its ultimate fulfillment in the redemption of all humanity through Christ's atonement. Christ's redemptive act is not merely for a particular people at a particular time; it is cosmic in scope and eternal in significance. Revelation 5 presents the ultimate fulfillment of Isaiah 44:23: all of heaven and earth join in praise of the Lamb who was slain. The redemption Christ accomplishes is so comprehensive that it transforms not merely individual souls but the entire cosmos. The 'glory of God' revealed through Israel's redemption is fully and finally revealed through Christ—'the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ' (2 Corinthians 4:6).
commentary.application: For modern readers, Isaiah 44:23 offers at least two applications: First, it invites us to participate in cosmic praise. When we recognize and celebrate God's redemptive acts—in history, in scripture, in our own lives—we join creation in its proper function, which is to witness and glorify God. The passage suggests that praise is not merely an emotional response but a cosmically significant act; when we praise God for redemption, we align ourselves with the purpose of all creation. Second, it reminds us that our individual redemption is not isolated. We are part of a vast, created cosmos, and our redemption—our turning back to God—is a note in a symphony of cosmic restoration. This knowledge has practical implications: it means that our covenant faithfulness matters not only to ourselves but to the whole creation. We are part of God's restoration project. The passage also invites us to expand our vision of what God is doing. He is not merely forgiving us individually; He is redeeming all things, and in that vast project of restoration, we have a particular and precious place.

text_kjv: Thus saith the LORD, thy redeemer, and he that formed thee from the womb, I am the LORD that maketh all things; that stretcheth forth the heavens alone; that spreadeth abroad the earth by myself;

commentary.narrative:
The final verse of this section (vv. 21–24 form a unified promise) anchors Israel's redemption and restoration in the ultimate theological truth: God is the sole Creator. There is no other. In doing so, Isaiah repudiates every claim of polytheism and, implicitly, every claim of the idols condemned in verses 9–20. The verse is structured as a series of divine self-identifications, each expanding the scope of God's power and authority. God is identified as 'thy redeemer' (go'alekha—the kinsman-redeemer), 'and he that formed thee from the womb' (yatzarti mibaten—the one who shaped you from the beginning). These are personal, relational titles that locate God as intimately involved in Israel's history and identity.

But then the focus shifts to the cosmic: 'I am the LORD that maketh all things' (ani YHWH oseh kol). The phrase 'all things' is comprehensive—everything that exists is made by God. There is no realm, no aspect of reality, outside God's creative power. The declaration immediately addresses the ancient Near Eastern mythological context: unlike the Babylonian creation accounts, where multiple deities collaborate in creation and where chaos-powers must be subdued, the biblical creation is the work of a single God. He needs no assistant, no collaborator.

The two final phrases—'that stretcheth forth the heavens alone' (noteh shamayim levaddi) and 'that spreadeth abroad the earth by myself' (roqa ha'aretz me'itti)—are emphatic about divine solitude and power. The words 'alone' (levaddi) and 'by myself' (me'itti) are not synonymous but complementary: they stress from different angles that no other being participated in creation. This is not a statement of power in isolation but a statement of power *without equal*. God's creative act requires no delegated authority, no council of gods, no subjugation of opposing forces.

The theological point is revolutionary: If God alone created all things, then God alone is worthy of worship, and any worship given to created things (idols, which are the work of human hands) is fundamentally confused. Moreover, if God is the sole Creator of all things, then God's creative power extends to Israel's redemption as well. The same God who stretched out the heavens is capable of erasing transgressions and sins (v. 22) and redeeming Israel from exile. The verse concludes (in the KJV) with apparent incompleteness—'by myself' is not followed by a predicate—but this is the design: the statement stands open, waiting to be completed by the implications the reader will draw. God has created all things, and the God who did this is the one who redeems you.

word_study.meaning: Redeemer, kinsman-redeemer, the one who restores. In Israelite law, the go'el was a family member who had the responsibility and right to restore what had been lost (land, family honor, a slave member of the family).
word_study.significance: The title 'redeemer' applied to God suggests that God stands in a familial relationship to Israel—not distant and remote, but intimately committed to restoring what has been lost. God is not a cosmic force but a covenant partner with personal investment in Israel's restoration.

word_study.meaning: I formed you from the womb. The verb yatzar (to form, to shape) is used of a potter at the wheel; the phrase 'from the womb' suggests that God's forming of Israel began at the very beginning of Israel's existence as a people.
word_study.significance: This echoes language used elsewhere of individual birth and formation, but here it is applied to a nation. Israel's formation as a people is not accidental or evolutionary but is the result of God's direct, intentional shaping from the beginning. The implication is that Israel cannot be undone or abandoned: to reject Israel would be for God to reject His own formative work.

word_study.meaning: Makes all things. The verb osah (to make, to do) is comprehensive; kol (all) excludes nothing.
word_study.significance: This phrase positions God's redemptive work within His larger creative sovereignty. The same power that called all things into existence is at work redeeming Israel. Moreover, it rules out any dualism or competition with other powers: God makes all things, which means nothing can resist His will or exist outside His dominion.

word_study.meaning: Stretches out the heavens alone. The verb natah means to stretch, to extend, to pitch (as a tent). 'Alone' (levaddi) is emphatic: no other being stretched out the heavens.
word_study.significance: This language is used throughout Isaiah (40:22: 'It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth... that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain') and echoes Genesis 1. The stretching of the heavens is God's primary creative act—the establishment of the cosmos itself. To stretch the heavens 'alone' is to claim ultimate creative authority.

word_study.term_english: spreadeth abroad the earth by myself
word_study.meaning: Spreads out the earth by myself. The verb raqa means to spread out, to hammer out (as metal), to flatten. 'By myself' (me'itti) again emphasizes solitary action.
word_study.significance: If stretching the heavens is the primary act of cosmic creation, spreading out the earth is the second—the establishment of the habitable realm. The phrase 'by myself' (me'itti) differs slightly from 'alone' (levaddi) in the previous phrase, but both serve to rule out any shared creative authority. God's creative work is His work alone; it requires no council, no assistant, no opposing force to be overcome.

cross_references.connection: 'It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in: That bringeth the princes to nothing; he maketh the judges of the earth as vanity.' This passage uses nearly identical language and context: God's creative power over the heavens and earth establishes the basis for God's power over all nations and rulers.
'In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.' Isaiah's language of creation echoes and reinforces Genesis's opening declaration: all creative authority rests with the God of Israel.

'Unto thee it was shewed, that thou mightest know that the LORD he is God; there is none else beside him.' Moses repeats the same monotheistic affirmation that Isaiah makes: there is no God but the LORD. This fundamental covenant principle is what Isaiah invokes against idolatry.

'He hath made the earth by his power, he hath established the world by his wisdom, and hath stretched out the heavens by his discretion... Shall any of the gods of the nations deliver them? for my God... is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name.' Jeremiah echoes Isaiah's language of creation and uses it to affirm that the God who created all things is the one who redeems Israel.

'And the light and the Redeemer of the world... I, the Lord God, am without variableness, neither shadow of changing.' The restored revelation affirms the same principle: the Creator (who is also the Redeemer, Christ) is unchanging and without peer in power. Creation and redemption flow from the same divine source.

commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near Eastern context is crucial for understanding the polemical force of this verse. In Babylonian mythology (the Enuma Elish), creation is the result of violent conflict: the god Marduk defeats the chaos-power Tiamat and creates the world from her corpse. Multiple gods are involved; Marduk emerges as supreme only by defeating his rivals. The entire mythological framework assumes that creation is a struggle involving multiple divine beings. Isaiah's statement—that the LORD 'alone' stretches out the heavens and spreads out the earth 'by myself'—directly contradicts this polytheistic cosmology. Moreover, during the Babylonian exile, Israel would have been exposed to Babylonian creation mythology and the religious claims of Babylonian priests that Marduk (and therefore Babylon) was supreme in the cosmos. Isaiah's affirmation that the God of Israel—not Marduk, not any Babylonian deity—is the sole Creator and therefore the sole God worthy of worship is a countercultural assertion of faith during exile. The exiled community would have heard this verse as a radical reorientation: *The God of your fathers is not defeated; He is the God who created everything, including the Babylonian gods' supposed power. Return to Him.*

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 2:14: 'Wherefore, by the law no flesh is justified; by the law men are cut off... Wherefore, redemption cometh in and through the Holy Messiah; for he is full of grace and truth.' The Book of Mormon emphasizes that the Creator God is also the Redeemer God—the same divine Being who created all things is the one who redeems humanity. Also, 1 Nephi 17:36: 'Yea, and he also said that it should be the last sign that should be given unto the nations of the earth, therefore, lord, how can we disbelieve?' Nephi treats the creation of all things as evidence of God's power to accomplish redemption—the same logic Isaiah employs.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 131:7-8: 'There is a law, irrevocably decreed in heaven before the foundations of this world, upon which all blessings are predicated... And when we obtain any blessing from God, it is by obedience to that law upon which it is predicated.' The principle of divine order and law underlying creation is the same principle underlying redemption. God's creative act and God's redemptive act both flow from the same eternal divine nature. Also, D&C 75:3-4: 'For behold, the field is white already to harvest; therefore, whoso desireth to reap let him thrust in his sickle with his might, and reap while the day lasts, that he may treasure up for his soul everlasting light.' God's redemptive work parallels His creative work—both require divine power working in harmony with human response.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The creation room or garden room in the temple represents the cosmos as created by God—a place of order, beauty, and divine intention. The temple teaching emphasizes that God is the Creator and that humanity's role is to participate in God's creative and redemptive purposes within that created order. The progression through the temple symbolically rehearses creation and restoration, affirming the same God is at work in both.

commentary.christological_typology: In the New Testament and in the restored gospel, Jesus is identified as the one through whom all things were created: 'All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made' (John 1:3). The creator power affirmed here for God in Isaiah 44:24 is applied to Christ, who is revealed as God. Moreover, Christ is both Creator and Redeemer—He who made all things redeems all things. Colossians 1:15-17 states: 'Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature: For by him were all things created... And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.' The assertion that creation and redemption flow from the same divine source finds its fullest expression in Christ, who is 'the Redeemer of the world' and the one through whom God 'maketh all things.'
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 44:24 anchors faith in several essential truths: First, *God is absolutely sovereign*. He created all things without assistance or opposition. This means no force in the universe can ultimately thwart God's purposes or violate His covenants. When Israel (or we) doubt God's power to deliver on His promises, we doubt the very God who created the cosmos. Second, *the God who redeems is the God who created*. Our redemption is not a secondary work, delegated to a minor deity or dependent on our own efforts. It is the work of the one who spoke all things into existence. This should inspire absolute confidence. Third, *creation and covenant are inseparable*. The God who shaped Israel 'from the womb' (v. 24) is the same God who 'formed thee' (v. 21) and will not forget you (v. 21). God's creative power is not abstract but is focused on the restoration and redemption of His covenant people. The practical application is this: when facing circumstances that seem overwhelming, when doubting whether God can deliver, remember Isaiah 44:24. The God who created all things is your Redeemer. All things—including your impossible circumstances—are within the scope of divine creative power. The covenant with you is backed by the same authority that stretched out the heavens.

text_kjv: That frustrateth the tokens of the liars, and maketh diviners mad; that turneth wise men backward, and maketh their knowledge foolish;

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 44:25 presents a stark contrast to the preceding verses about God's power over creation and covenant. Here the prophet turns his attention to the intellectual pretenders of Babylon—those who claimed rival authority through divination, augury, and false wisdom. The verse is structured in two parallel movements: God frustrates the 'signs of liars' and makes 'fools of diviners,' then 'turns wise men back' and makes 'their knowledge foolish.' This is not merely theoretical; it reflects the crisis of credibility facing Judahite exiles who had been surrounded by Babylonian priests and wise men confidently proclaiming their own gods' power and the permanence of exile.

The Hebrew terms matter here. Baddim (liars, literally 'empty talkers') refers to false prophets and charlatans. Qosemim (diviners) were the professional class of those who read omens from birds, animal entrails, and celestial signs—a respected profession in Mesopotamian religion and political counsel. Chakhamim (wise men) were the scribal and intellectual elite. By lumping all three categories together and declaring their knowledge 'foolish' (yiskol), Isaiah is mounting a comprehensive assault on Babylon's entire knowledge establishment. The God who 'gives understanding to the universe' (40:28) exposes as fraudulent all competing claims to cosmic knowledge.

This verse serves a psychological and spiritual purpose for the exiles: it provides intellectual permission to doubt their oppressors' certainties. If the mighty Babylonian wise men and diviners are exposed as fools, then their proclamations about the futility of return are equally suspect. God's word stands; theirs crumbles. The Covenant Rendering captures this force by using 'frustrates' and 'makes fools of'—verbs of active divine intervention—emphasizing that God doesn't merely ignore these rivals but actively unmasks them.

word_study.meaning: to break, negate, annul, frustrate. From the root פרר (parar). The term suggests undoing something that was established or breaking apart something that was whole. In legal contexts, it can mean to abrogate a covenant.
word_study.significance: The choice of mefer rather than a simple 'ignores' shows God actively dismantles the claims of liars. Their 'signs'—the outward manifestations they point to as proof of divine favor—are not merely questioned but rendered null and void. This echoes covenant language: what the liars have built (their reputation, their claims) God breaks apart.

word_study.meaning: signs, wonders, miracles, omens. Often used for divine demonstrations of power (as in the plagues of Egypt), but also for signs of prediction or cosmic portents. In the Mesopotamian context, otot were the empirical data that augurs interpreted.
word_study.significance: The liars produce 'signs'—they point to phenomena and claim them as evidence of their gods' power or their own divinatory accuracy. Isaiah declares these signs fraudulent and negated. This is theologically significant: true signs come from the true God and cannot be counterfeited indefinitely.

word_study.meaning: liars, empty talkers, those who speak vanity or emptiness. From bad (empty, vain). The root suggests speech that is hollow, without substance or foundation.
word_study.significance: Baddim is not primarily a moral judgment but an epistemic one: their words have no foundation, no reality behind them. They speak, but what they say refers to nothing real. This prepares the ground for v. 26, where God's word—by contrast—confirms reality and brings it into being.

word_study.term_english: maketh diviners mad / makes fools of diviners
word_study.meaning: makes mad, makes foolish, causes to act like a fool. From הלל (halal), related to הלל (hilul, profaning, or the sense of acting without sense or restraint). Can mean to drive mad, to render senseless.
word_study.significance: The qosemim—the professional diviners whom Babylonian kings consulted for every decision—are made 'mad' in their own enterprise. Their skill becomes useless; their calculations yield nonsense. The irony is sharp: those who claimed to read the cosmic order are rendered unable to perceive reality.

word_study.meaning: turns wise men back/behind. Achor means 'backward, behind, the reverse direction.' Meshiv means 'turns back, returns.' The phrase suggests reversal, undoing progress, forcing retreat.
word_study.significance: The wisdom of Babylon's intellectual elite—their hard-won knowledge—is reversed, undone, made to run backward. In the context of exile, where the wise men had proclaimed the futility of hope for return, this verse says their 'wisdom' will be shown to have led them backward, away from truth. Only God's word moves forward (55:11).

word_study.meaning: their knowledge, their understanding, their discernment. From ידע (yada, to know). Refers to intellectual comprehension and awareness.
word_study.significance: The term dattam parallels chakhamim (wise men)—the verse is not attacking wisdom itself but false wisdom. The wise men's knowledge, which they confidently applied to political and theological matters, is declared 'foolish' (yiskol). Only knowledge rooted in fear of God (Proverbs 1:7) is true knowledge.

cross_references.connection: Earlier in this section, God's absolute sovereignty over creation and history is established; v. 25 applies that sovereignty to the exposure of false wisdom and diviners who claim competing knowledge.

Paul applies similar logic in the New Testament: 'the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men.' God's undoing of human wisdom recurs in the covenant tradition.

When Babylonian diviners and wise men cannot interpret Nebuchadnezzar's dream, Daniel proves their futility. Isaiah 44:25 prophetically frames this recurring pattern of Babylon's intellectual bankruptcy before God's true prophet.
Jeremiah warns the exiles not to listen to false prophets and diviners in Babylon. Isaiah 44:25 provides the theological foundation: these figures are already exposed and powerless in God's sight.

Modern revelation confirms that false traditions and wisdom will be brought to naught when God's word goes forth. 'Behold, I am God; give heed to my word, which is quick and powerful, sharper than a two-edged sword.'

commentary.historical_context: Babylon in the 6th century BC was renowned throughout the ancient world for its diviners, augurs, and scribal wisdom. The Babylonian priest-scholars—holders of cuneiform learning, mathematical astronomy, and religious authority—were the equivalent of modern intellectuals and scientists. They served the king's council, predicted celestial events, and offered ritual justifications for political decisions. For Jewish exiles, surrounded by this confident intellectual apparatus, it would have been psychologically devastating to hear daily that their God had failed, that return was impossible, and that Babylon's gods reigned supreme. Isaiah 44:25 cuts through this by pronouncing the Babylonian wise men frauds—not through counter-argument but through prophetic declaration. The irony deepened when Cyrus the Persian, from outside the Babylonian system entirely, conquered the city (539 BC) and issued the decree allowing Jewish return. The very 'signs' the Babylonian diviners had read—perhaps omens of Babylon's eternal dominion—were falsified by history itself.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 13:26-29, Nephi sees the corruption of the true record by 'great and abominable church.' Just as Isaiah exposes false Babylonian wisdom, the Book of Mormon exposés false teachings that obscure the truth. The pattern is consistent: God's word stands; human philosophies are made foolish.
restoration_lens.dc_connections:
D&C 93:36-37 teaches that truth is knowledge of things as they are, were, and will be. By contrast, the liars and diviners of Isaiah 44:25 speak falsehoods—they do not know things as they truly are. The revelation directly inverts the false wisdom Isaiah condemns: 'And truth is knowledge of things as they are, as they were, and as they are to come.'

D&C 1:24 and D&C 35:19 both stress that God's word 'shall not pass away, but shall all be fulfilled.' This echoes Isaiah 40:8 (part of this week's reading) and reinforces v. 25's message: God's declarations stand; empty human wisdom crumbles.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The exposure of false counsel parallels the temple's role as a place where true knowledge and covenant understanding are restored. Just as Isaiah promises that God will confirm His servant's word (v. 26), the temple confirms and makes real the covenants God has made with His people. False wisdom (Babylon's diviners) operates in darkness and confusion; true wisdom (covenantal knowledge) operates in light and clarity (Doctrine and Covenants 88:11).

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 44:25 previews Christ's ultimate exposure of false wisdom. In the Gospels, Jesus repeatedly confounds the scribes and Pharisees, showing their interpretations of the law to be empty shells that miss the kingdom. His crucifixion appears as 'foolishness' to worldly wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:18), yet proves to be the apex of divine wisdom. Christ embodies the principle here: He is the Word that stands, the one through whom all false claims to authority are ultimately undone.
commentary.application: For modern readers, v. 25 invites critical thinking about competing claims to knowledge and authority in our own time. Scientific claims, political certainties, popular philosophies—all are here implicitly tested against the question: Is this word from God, or is it from the 'liars' of our age? The verse does not attack learning itself but false confidences that exclude God. A covenant member should ask: Where do I place ultimate authority? Do I test teachings against the word of God, or do I absorb the unquestioned 'wisdom' of the world around me? The verse also provides comfort when facing an intellectual establishment (academic, professional, cultural) that seems arrayed against faith. If the proud Babylonian wise men were exposed as fools before God, so too will the proud philosophies of every age.

text_kjv: That confirmeth the word of his servant, and performeth the counsel of his messengers; that saith to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be inhabited; and to the cities of Judah, Ye shall be built, and I will raise up the decayed places thereof:

commentary.narrative:
Verse 26 marks the great reversal. Having exposed the empty words of Babylon's wise men in v. 25, Isaiah now declares what God's words accomplish: they are confirmed and fulfilled. The parallelism is exact and intentional—the false prophets' words are frustrated (v. 25); God's servant's words are confirmed (v. 26). The 'servant' here is most naturally read as the prophet Isaiah himself, the vessel through whom these promises come. But beyond the prophet, the servant language will expand in chapters 49-53 to encompass the Suffering Servant, the Messiah. For now, the focus is on the immediate fulfillment: Jerusalem will be inhabited; Judah's cities will be rebuilt; the ruins of exile will be raised up.

The promise is intensely concrete and practical. Exile had left cities in ruins—not metaphorically but literally. The ruined sites (chorvot) were tangible evidence that God had abandoned His people. To promise that these ruins would be raised up (yaqumetm) was to promise that the exile itself would be reversed, that life would return. The Dead Sea Scrolls confirm the MT reading here without variant; both ancient witnesses affirm that this promise stood unchanged in the tradition. The parallelism between 'word of His servant' and 'counsel of His messengers' (plural) suggests both the singular prophet and the broader prophetic tradition—all true prophecy originates in God and will be fulfilled.

This verse must be read against the despair of the exile. After 586 BC, when Jerusalem's walls were breached and the Temple destroyed, survivors scattered, and the best and brightest deported to Babylon, the psychological impact was catastrophic. The exiles might well have asked: 'Has God abandoned His promises? Is His word now null and void, like the shattered Temple itself?' Isaiah 44:26 answers: No. The ruins will be raised up. The word that seemed to have failed will be confirmed. True prophecy, spoken through God's servant, will be fulfilled in history. The promise is not merely spiritual comfort; it is a historical commitment that Judah will see its cities rebuilt, its people restored, and its covenant relationship renewed.

word_study.meaning: raises up, establishes, confirms, fulfills. From קוּם (qum, to rise, stand, establish). Can mean to fulfill a promise, to establish a covenant, or literally to erect or raise something.
word_study.significance: Meqim is the opposite of mefer (v. 25). Where God 'breaks/frustrates' the signs of liars, He 'raises up/confirms' the word of His servant. The term suggests both stability (establishing something firmly) and action (causing it to stand, be fulfilled). It is actively generative, not passive.

word_study.meaning: The word/utterance of His servant. Devar can mean word, utterance, thing, matter, or event. Eved (servant) in Isaiah has multiple referents: the prophet, the nation Israel, and ultimately the Suffering Servant (Messiah). Here it most immediately refers to the prophet.
word_study.significance: The 'word' of God's servant is not the servant's own invention but God's word channeled through the servant. This establishes the prophetic office: the prophet is not a free agent but a vessel through whom God speaks. By confirming the servant's word, God confirms the prophetic word as His own.

word_study.meaning: fulfills, completes, pays, performs. From שׁלם (shalom, to complete, pay, make whole). The term implies bringing something to its intended completion or end.
word_study.significance: Yashlem suggests that God doesn't merely acknowledge prophecy but brings it to completion. The 'counsel of His messengers' is not left hanging or partial but fully realized. In covenant language, this is fulfillment—God completes what He has promised.

word_study.meaning: The counsel/plan of His messengers (or angels). Atzah means counsel, plan, purpose. Malak (messenger) can refer to human prophets or heavenly messengers (angels). The plural 'messengers' suggests a broader prophetic tradition.
word_study.significance: The parallelism with 'word of His servant' (singular) followed by 'counsel of His messengers' (plural) may suggest that individual prophets (servants) speak as part of a larger divine counsel that transcends any single person. All true prophecy participates in God's unified purpose.

word_study.meaning: shall be inhabited, shall be lived in, shall sit. From יָשַׁב (yasab, to sit, dwell, inhabit). Tusab is passive: the city will receive inhabitants, will be lived in.
word_study.significance: The promise is not abstract but demographic. It is not enough for ruins to be stone; they must be lived in by people. This reflects the covenant concern with land, seed, and covenant—all three were threatened by exile. To promise that Jerusalem will be inhabited is to promise the restoration of the covenantal community.

word_study.meaning: Her ruins, her desolate places. From חֲרֵב (charev, to be desolate, devastated). Chorvot (plural of chorev) specifically refers to ruins left after destruction—broken walls, empty city sites.
word_study.significance: The choice to mention 'ruins' rather than merely 'cities' is theologically important. The exiles could see the ruins of Jerusalem (either in memory or in reports). To promise that chorvot themselves would be raised up is to promise that the visible evidence of judgment and destruction would be reversed. The ruins are not left as monuments to defeat but transformed into signs of restoration.

cross_references.connection: Earlier in this section, Isaiah declares 'the word of our God shall stand for ever.' Verse 26 applies that principle specifically: God's word through His servant will stand and be fulfilled even as exile seems to contradict it.

Jeremiah is called 'to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant.' Isaiah 44:26 parallels this—the prophet is empowered with words that build and restore, confirming the prophetic office across traditions.

The historical fulfillment of Isaiah 44:26: Cyrus's decree (538 BC) allows the Jews to return and rebuild Jerusalem and the Temple. 'The LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia.' History confirms the prophet's word.

The Lord tells the Prophet Joseph Smith, 'Wherefore, meaning the church, thou shalt give heed unto all his words and commandments which he shall give unto you as he receiveth them, walking in all holiness before me.' Like Isaiah's servant, the Lord's prophet's word is to be confirmed and fulfilled.
The Book of Mormon teaches that the Lord's words will be 'established according to his will.' The principle of confirmed divine word recurs throughout the covenant restoration.

commentary.historical_context: The historical specificity of Isaiah 44:26 is remarkable. The promise of Jerusalem's habitation and the rebuilding of Judah's cities was not fulfilled immediately. The exiles returned in waves: first under Cyrus's decree (539 BC), beginning reconstruction of the Temple (completed by 516 BC); then again under Ezra and Nehemiah in the 5th century BC, when the city walls were rebuilt. The 'ruins' (chorvot) that Isaiah references would have been the literal debris of the 586 BC destruction—collapsed walls, burned buildings, streets overgrown. Archaeological evidence from Jerusalem shows extensive fire destruction from the Babylonian siege. Isaiah's promise, made during the exile itself, predicts not merely the end of exile but the physical restoration of the city. This was a radical claim in its context: the Babylonian empire seemed permanent and all-conquering. Claiming that its captive cities would be rebuilt and inhabited was a political and religious statement of extraordinary boldness. The fulfillment through Cyrus (whom v. 28 names) proved the word of God's servant true.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 25:19-23, Nephi prophesies concerning the destruction and scattering of Israel, but also promises restoration: 'But behold, I say unto you that the Lord God shall remember all those who have been broken off, whomsoever they are of the house of Israel.' Isaiah 44:26 provides the scriptural foundation for this Restored covenant principle: God's servant speaks promises of restoration that will be fulfilled.
restoration_lens.dc_connections:
D&C 45:59-61 teaches that the earth will be renewed and prepared for the Millennium, with all things restored. Isaiah 44:26's promise of raising up ruins connects to this larger Restoration theology: the final ruin will be the earth itself, which will be made new. Interim restorations (Jerusalem, Judah) are type and shadow of the ultimate restoration.

D&C 29:24 states, 'That every man may act in doctrine and principle pertaining to futurity, according to the moral agency which I have given unto him, that every man may be accountable for his own sins in the day of judgment.' The fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy depended on Cyrus exercising his moral agency (v. 28); God's word stands, but human agency participates in its fulfillment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The rebuilding of Jerusalem's Temple is an explicit part of this verse's promise. In the Restoration, the temple is the central place where God's covenant with His people is renewed and confirmed. Just as Isaiah's promise included the restoration of the Temple (Ezra 3-6), the Restoration of the gospel includes the temple as the place where God's word and covenant are confirmed in ordinance form. The promise to 'raise up' ruins (v. 26) is paralleled in the Restoration by the 'raising up' of the Church and kingdom from a broken, scattered state (D&C 27:13).

commentary.christological_typology: The 'servant' whose word is confirmed in v. 26 ultimately points to the Servant of Isaiah 49-53, who is Christ. Just as the servant-prophet's word is confirmed through historical events (the return from exile), so Christ's redemptive work is confirmed through historical resurrection and the establishment of His kingdom. The promise structure—word spoken in darkness, then fulfilled in light—mirrors Christ's death and resurrection. And just as Isaiah's servant's word brings restoration (Jerusalem rebuilt), Christ's work brings ultimate restoration (all things made new).
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, v. 26 teaches the power of God's spoken word through His servants. When a prophet speaks a promise—even if circumstances seem to contradict it—the promise stands in God's sight and will be fulfilled according to His timeline, not ours. This provides enormous comfort during seasons of trial or apparent divine silence. It also establishes the fundamental LDS principle of ongoing revelation: the Lord speaks through His servants, and those words are not mere opinions but are confirmed by God Himself. The verse also invites personal application: if we are God's servants, speaking His word and doing His work, our efforts—however small they seem amid ruins and desolation—will be confirmed and fulfilled. We are not laboring in vain.

text_kjv: That saith to the deep, Be dry, and I will dry up thy rivers:

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 44:27 takes an abrupt leap from the historical promise of Jerusalem's rebuilding to cosmic and mythological language. God addresses the 'deep' (tsulah)—the primordial waters—and commands them to dry up. This verse operates on multiple levels simultaneously. First, it invokes the language of creation (Genesis 1:2, where the Spirit of God moves upon the 'deep'). Second, it echoes the Exodus narrative (the parting of the Red Sea). Third, it may contain a historical allusion to Cyrus's military engineering at Babylon. All three levels enrich the meaning.

The 'deep' (tsulah in Hebrew) is not merely physical water but carries mythological weight in ancient Near Eastern thought. The Babylonian creation myth (Enuma Elish) describes the defeated deep (Tiamat) out of which the cosmos is ordered. By having God command the deep to be dry, Isaiah asserts that the God of Israel has absolute dominion over the primordial forces that pagan cosmologies feared. He does not negotiate with them or sacrifice to appease them; He commands them to obey. The drying of rivers (naharoteykha) continues this theme of absolute dominion.

Historically, the verse likely alludes to Cyrus's military strategy. When Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BC, one account (Herodotus and others) suggests his forces diverted the Euphrates River, allowing soldiers to enter the city along the riverbed. By framing this as God's command to the waters, Isaiah claims that even the engineering feat that will liberate the exiles is actually God's orchestration. The waters obey God, not Cyrus; Cyrus is merely the instrument. This is a crucial theological move: it prevents the exiles from mistaking Cyrus's power for ultimate power. All things—even the waters, even the rivers—respond to God's word.

The verse sits between the historical promise (v. 26) and the naming of Cyrus (v. 28), creating a theological framework: Before Cyrus acts, before history unfolds, God has already commanded the waters. The causality runs from God's word to history, not from history to God's vindication. Isaiah's prophecy precedes and transcends the events it describes.

word_study.meaning: The deep, the abyss, the depths of water. Related to the Aramaic ṣulā and carrying cosmic significance in the ancient Near East. In Genesis 1:2, the Hebrew tehom (deep) is the primordial chaos waters. Tsulah is a more poetic variant emphasizing the unfathomable depths.
word_study.significance: By addressing the 'deep' as something that responds to God's command, Isaiah reframes the cosmological fear present in exile theology. The exiles had been living under Babylonian dominion, which had its own cosmic mythology centered on the struggle against primordial chaos. Isaiah declares that the true God—not the Babylonian deities—rules over chaos itself. The deep obeys His voice.

word_study.meaning: Be desolate, become dry, be laid waste. From חָרַב (charav, to become desolate, dry up). When applied to water, it means to evaporate, disappear, be dried up.
word_study.significance: The imperative form (chorvabi) is striking: it is a command, not a request. God does not negotiate with the deep; He orders it. The waters have no choice but to obey. This contrasts sharply with pagan mythologies where cosmic forces must be managed or appeased. Here, they respond instantaneously to God's decree.

word_study.term_english: dry up / I will dry up
word_study.meaning: I will dry up, I will make desolate. From אָבֵש (avesh, to dry up, wither). The 'I' here is emphatic: it is God Himself who dries up the rivers, both by command to the deep and by active agent. The repetition (deep is commanded to be dry; rivers are actively dried up) creates a dual assurance.
word_study.significance: The combination of imperative (command to the deep) and future promise (God's personal action drying the rivers) presents redundancy that is emphatic rather than repetitive. Both the waters respond to command, and God actively ensures the drying. No obstacle remains; all means will be available for the liberation.

word_study.meaning: Your rivers (with possessive suffix 'your,' addressed to the deep/chaos itself). Nahar means river, stream, watercourse. The possessive suggests that the rivers belong to the deep; they are extensions of chaotic waters.
word_study.significance: In the Mesopotamian context, rivers were sacred and dangerous. The Euphrates defined Babylon's identity and security. By promising to dry up rivers, Isaiah issues a radical claim: the very geographic features that define Babylon's power are subject to God's command. For the exiles, this would mean: your captors' security is not secure; their stronghold can be breached.

cross_references.connection: The primordial 'deep' (tehom) over which God's Spirit moved in creation is here commanded again by God's voice. Isaiah frames the coming liberation as a new creation, a reversal of chaos into order.

God divides the Red Sea, allowing Israel to pass through on dry ground. Isaiah 44:27 echoes this deliverance: just as God dried the sea for the exodus, He will dry rivers for the return from exile. The pattern of watery liberation repeats.

Later in Isaiah, the poet explicitly connects the drying of the sea in exodus to the expected salvation: 'Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD... Art thou not it that hath dried the sea, the waters of the great deep?' The cosmic language of v. 27 is elaborated here.

The psalmist recalls God's power over the sea and rivers as a sign of divine kingship and salvation: 'God is my King of old... Thou didst divide the sea by thy strength... Thou driedst up mighty rivers.' Isaiah stands in this covenant tradition.

Modern revelation speaks of the Lord's power over the elements: 'Whatsoever you ask the Father in my name it shall be given, that is expedient for you.' The principle of divine command over creation recurs in Restoration theology.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thought, rivers and the sea were sites of danger and power. The Euphrates River defined Babylon itself; the city stood on its banks and relied on it for defense, agriculture, and transport. To suggest that God could simply dry it up was to claim dominion over Babylon's very foundation. Herodotus and other ancient historians record that when Cyrus conquered Babylon (539 BC), his forces diverted the Euphrates River, allowing soldiers to wade into the city along the riverbed. Whether this account is historically accurate in its details is debated by modern scholars, but the symbolic import is clear: what seemed an impenetrable barrier became a pathway for liberation. The prophecy in Isaiah 44:27, likely composed before Cyrus's rise, predicts this very scenario in mythic language. For the exiles, the point would have been both spiritual and practical: the obstacles that seemed to trap them (geography, Babylonian power, cosmic forces aligned against them) would be overcome. God's word would remake the landscape itself.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 19:10-12, Nephi quotes Isaiah and discusses the deliverance of Israel in the latter days. The pattern of waters being overcome (Red Sea, rivers dried up) prefigures the spiritual waters of the covenant being restored. In Nephi's vision (1 Nephi 11-14), the waters represent temptations and trials that are overcome through Christ.
restoration_lens.dc_connections:
D&C 61:14 teaches that 'the waters shall obey my voice as at the Red Sea.' This is a direct application of Isaiah 44:27 to Latter-day Saint context. The Lord asserts His dominion over the elements just as He did in antiquity. The principle is cosmological: creation obeys the Creator's voice.

D&C 109:55 (part of the Kirtland Temple dedication) emphasizes that all elements will obey God's law. Verse 27 establishes the scriptural foundation for this: rivers and waters respond to divine command.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The waters of the temple—the baptismal font, the washing, the covenantal waters—represent both chaos that must be overcome and renewal. Isaiah 44:27 theologically frames baptism: the waters obey God's voice, not the power of sin or death. In temple ordinances, water becomes the medium of cleansing and new life, not a barrier. The drying of rivers (v. 27) leads to passage to new land (v. 26 and v. 28); temple covenants lead to exaltation in the celestial kingdom.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's power over water is demonstrated repeatedly in the Gospels: He walks on water (Matthew 14:22-27), stills the storm (Mark 4:35-41), and turns water into wine (John 2:1-11). Each event is a claim that the risen Christ possesses the same dominion over creation that the Father does. The principle in Isaiah 44:27—that obstacles are dissolved before God's word—culminates in Christ, whose resurrection proves that even death (the ultimate 'deep') is conquered. The drying of rivers becomes, in typology, the drying of the tears of suffering and the passing through waters of judgment to resurrection life.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, v. 27 invites confidence that obstacles that seem insurmountable will be overcome by God's power. The 'rivers' blocking the way forward might be personal, financial, social, or spiritual. The promise is that God's word stands over all barriers. This verse also teaches trust in divine timing: God does not wait until the river is already dry to command it; He speaks the command in advance, knowing the waters will obey. In personal trials, this suggests that God's assurance often precedes visible evidence of deliverance. Secondly, the verse establishes that creation itself is on God's side. The universe is not indifferent to our covenants or sufferings; it is structured to respond to God's voice. This reframes how we understand obstacles: they are not violations of natural law but opportunities for God's power to manifest through the natural order. Finally, the verse teaches that liberation comes not through human engineering alone but through alignment with God's purposes. Cyrus's diversion of the river (if historical) succeeds because God has already commanded the waters. Our own efforts succeed when aligned with God's word and purposes.

text_kjv: That saith of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure: even saying to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be built; and to the temple, Thy foundation shall be laid.
text_kjv_alt: That saith of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure: even saying to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be built; and to the temple, Thy foundation shall be laid.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 44:28 is arguably the most remarkable prophetic statement in all of Isaiah—and perhaps in all of Scripture. Here, by name, God identifies Cyrus, the Persian emperor who will conquer Babylon and liberate the Jewish exiles, more than a century before his birth. The text presents this as God speaking: 'That saith of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure.' Not only does God name Cyrus; He calls him 'my shepherd'—a title previously reserved for David and for God Himself (Psalm 23:1). And He promises that Cyrus will fulfill God's purposes: the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the laying of the Temple's foundation.

The identification of Cyrus by name is nearly unique in biblical prophecy. Specific human names named before birth are rare; the most famous examples are John the Baptist (Luke 1:13) and Jesus Himself (Isaiah 7:14, though His personal name is not explicitly given in that verse). That Cyrus is named over a century in advance suggests that the prophecy operates at multiple levels: it is both predictive and theological. The prediction proves God's omniscience and trustworthiness to those living in exile; the theology emphasizes that even pagan rulers serve God's purposes for His covenant people.

The title 'my shepherd' (ro'i in Hebrew) is loaded with significance. In ancient Near Eastern royal ideology, the shepherd was the common metaphor for a wise and protective ruler. But in Israel's covenant tradition, only David and his descendants—anointed by God, in direct relationship with Him—received this title (2 Samuel 5:2). By applying it to Cyrus, Isaiah is making a radical theological statement: this Persian pagan king, who does not worship the God of Israel and has no covenant with Israel, nevertheless serves as God's instrument and executes God's will. He is, in effect, God's shepherd for this moment in history. The Covenant Rendering captures this by maintaining 'my shepherd'—the possessive is crucial. It is not that Cyrus thinks of himself as shepherd; God calls him that.

The specific promises attached to Cyrus's reign are historical and verifiable: Jerusalem will be built (rebuilt after the exile), and the Temple's foundation will be laid. In 538 BC, Cyrus issued the decree recorded in Ezra 1:1-4, allowing the Jews to return and rebuild the Temple. By 520 BC, work on the Temple had begun in earnest (Ezra 5:2). By 516 BC, the Temple was completed and dedicated (Ezra 6:14-15). Isaiah's prophecy was fulfilled in detail. The Dead Sea Scrolls confirm the MT reading without variant; 1QIsaᵃ preserves 'my shepherd' (ro'i) exactly as it appears in later manuscripts, showing that this remarkable name has stood unchanged through more than two millennia of transmission.

word_study.term_english: saith of Cyrus / says of Cyrus
word_study.meaning: 'He who says of Cyrus' or 'He who speaks concerning Cyrus.' The article on 'omer (the one saying) indicates that God is the speaker. Koresh is the Hebrew transliteration of the Persian Kurush (Cyrus).
word_study.significance: The use of the article ('the one saying') maintains the pattern from vv. 25-27: God is the agent who acts, speaks, and commands. This verse continues that divine assertion of sovereignty. But now, for the first time in Scripture, a pagan ruler is named directly by God as the instrument of His purposes.

word_study.meaning: Cyrus (Kurush in Persian), the second ruler of the Persian Achaemenid Empire, reigned c. 559-530 BC. His reign was marked by the conquest of the Median, Lydian, and Babylonian empires and the reorganization of Persian imperial policy to allow subject peoples considerable religious and cultural autonomy.
word_study.significance: This is the first mention of Cyrus by name in Scripture. Scholars debate whether Isaiah of the 8th century BC wrote this verse or whether it comes from a later prophetic tradition (Second Isaiah, c. 6th century BC). The prophetic literature itself does not mark the transition; the text as received attributes all of Isaiah to the prophet of that name. For our purposes, the theological significance is what matters: God's purposes are so comprehensive that even the rise of a pagan empire is orchestrated according to His design.

word_study.meaning: My shepherd. From רָעָה (ra'ah, to shepherd, tend, pasture). The shepherd metaphor was common in the ancient Near East for rulers. It denoted care, protection, leadership, and provision. In Israel, it was applied to David (2 Samuel 5:2), God Himself (Psalm 23:1), and the Messiah (Ezekiel 34:23).
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that the shepherd title for rulers is common in ANE culture, but for Cyrus—a non-Israelite, non-monotheist—to receive it from the God of Israel is extraordinary. It suggests that the category of 'shepherd' is broader than the Davidic covenant; God may raise up shepherds for His people from unexpected sources. Historically, Cyrus's policy of allowing return and religious reconstruction was remarkably beneficent for the time; he earned the designation through his actual care for the exiles.

word_study.term_english: perform all my pleasure / fulfill all my purpose
word_study.meaning: And all my pleasure/purpose he will fulfill. Chephetz means desire, pleasure, purpose, delight. Yashlem (from shalom, to complete) means to fulfill, complete, accomplish. The phrase means that Cyrus will accomplish everything God intends.
word_study.significance: The term 'all my pleasure' is strong: it suggests that Cyrus's entire reign, or at least his actions toward the exiles, are orchestrated to fulfill God's will. Cyrus is not acting independently; he is an instrument through which God accomplishes His purposes. This is a stunning claim about divine sovereignty over pagan rulers.

word_study.meaning: Shall be founded, shall have its foundation laid. From יָסַד (yasad, to establish, found, lay a foundation). The passive form suggests that the foundation is laid by someone (God, through Cyrus's decree), not by the Temple itself.
word_study.significance: The specific promise about the Temple's foundation is historically precise. When the exiles returned under Cyrus's decree, the first major act was the laying of the Temple's foundation (Ezra 3:10-13). The promise is not merely spiritual (a temple in the heart) but material and architectural (an actual Temple with a literal foundation).

cross_references.connection: The historical fulfillment of Isaiah 44:28: 'Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom... Let him go up to Jerusalem... and let him build the house of the LORD.' Cyrus's decree directly fulfills the prophecy.

David is called 'shepherd' by Israel: 'Also in time past, when Saul was king over us, thou wast he that leddest out and broughtest in Israel: and the LORD said to thee, Thou shalt feed my people Israel, and thou shalt be captain over Israel.' The shepherd title establishes David's covenant role; Isaiah extends it to Cyrus for a specific historical moment.
'The LORD is my shepherd.' The shepherd language applied to God Himself establishes the tradition into which Cyrus is now placed, though as a servant-instrument rather than as the ultimate Shepherd.

The next chapter continues the Cyrus oracle: 'Thus saith the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden, to subdue nations before him.' Cyrus is here called 'my anointed' (mashiach), another title normally reserved for Davidic kings and the Messiah. The extraordinary language continues and escalates.

Jeremiah prophesies to the exiles that 'After seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place.' Isaiah and Jeremiah speak in concert: the exile has a set duration, and God will accomplish restoration through specific historical means (Cyrus).

Modern revelation speaks of God's purposes being accomplished through various instruments: 'But let all things be done in order.' The principle that God works through history and through instruments (even unexpected ones) recurs in Restoration theology.

commentary.historical_context:
Cyrus II, known as Cyrus the Great, ruled the Persian Achaemenid Empire from approximately 559-530 BC. His reign was marked by unprecedented imperial expansion and a revolutionary change in imperial policy: instead of destroying or assimilating conquered peoples, Cyrus allowed them to maintain their religions, languages, and cultures under Persian rule. This policy was materially beneficial for Jewish exiles and is reflected in the positive portrayal of Cyrus in biblical and Jewish sources (notably Ezra and the Jewish historian Josephus). The famous 'Cyrus Cylinder' (discovered in Babylon and now housed in the British Museum) records Cyrus's policy of repatriating peoples and restoring temples, though it does not specifically mention the Jews.

When Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BC, he inherited control of the Babylonian Empire, including the Jewish exiles deported there in 586 BC (and subsequent deportations). Cyrus's decree in Ezra 1:1-4 is historically plausible and is corroborated by his broader imperial policy. Jewish exiles did begin returning, and the Temple was eventually rebuilt (completed 516 BC), though the process was slow and faced obstacles (Ezra 4-6).

The naming of Cyrus in Isaiah 44:28 raises the famous 'Deutero-Isaiah' scholarly question: Did Isaiah of the 8th century BC write this, or was it added by a later prophetic voice during or after the exile (6th century BC)? Traditional LDS teaching attributes all of Isaiah to Isaiah ben Amoz; modern scholarship is divided. For purposes of this commentary, the text as canonized is what matters, and it presents these verses as Isaiah's prophecy, extending God's sovereignty backward from exile conditions to the court of an eighth-century king (where Cyrus would have been unknown) and forward to the Persian conquest (which would not occur for 150+ years).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 25:19-24, Nephi sees the coming salvation and speaks of it in language parallel to Isaiah. Like Cyrus, Nephi recognizes that the purposes of God will be fulfilled through means that may be unexpected or come from unexpected quarters. In 1 Nephi 13:37, the book speaks of God's word being 'established according to his will.' Just as Cyrus, though unaware of his role, fulfills God's will, so do many who are brought into the Lord's purposes unknowingly.
restoration_lens.dc_connections:
D&C 1:38 teaches, 'Whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.' The principle of Isaiah 44:28 is applied here: God accomplishes His purposes through various instruments. Cyrus is an instrument of God's voice, even though he does not recognize God's claim upon him.

D&C 50:24 teaches that 'all things unto me are spiritual.' This suggests that Cyrus's political actions (decreeing return, enabling Temple rebuilding) are spiritual events—part of God's grand design for covenant restoration. The material and the spiritual are unified in God's purposes.

D&C 38:27 states, 'I, the Lord, have decreed to lift up as a light unto the world.' God elevates instruments and figures to accomplish His purposes. Cyrus is 'lifted up' as a light (shepherd) for the exiles, though unknowingly.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Verse 28 explicitly promises that the Temple's foundation will be laid under Cyrus's reign. In Restoration theology, the temple is central to covenant relationship. The promise that the Temple will be built (through Cyrus's decree, fulfilled through returned exiles' labor) typologically points to the 'raising up' of temples in the Latter-day Restoration as signs that the covenant has been renewed. Just as Isaiah promises physical Temple reconstruction, modern revelation promises multiple temples (D&C 124:39-42) as witnesses to God's ongoing covenant with His people. The temple promised in Isaiah 44:28 becomes real in Ezra 6:14-15; temples promised in modern revelation are becoming real through the work of the Church.

commentary.christological_typology: The figure of Cyrus prefigures Christ in important ways, though the typology is inverse in some respects. Like Christ, Cyrus is named by God before his historical appearance; both are chosen instruments through whom God's purposes are accomplished. But where Cyrus is a pagan ruler used for a specific historical task, Christ is the eternal Son, who accomplishes redemption. However, both reveal a principle: God's purposes are so comprehensive that even those who do not consciously know God are ordained to serve His designs. Christ's ultimate shepherd-role—mentioned in John 10:14 ('I am the good shepherd') and Psalm 23 (applied to God)—surpasses the provisional shepherding of Cyrus. Where Cyrus led to physical return from exile, Christ leads to spiritual return from sin and death. The promise that Cyrus would lay the Temple's foundation is a type of Christ, who is Himself the 'Temple of the Holy Ghost' (John 2:19-21) and whose resurrection establishes the foundation for all covenant relationship.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, Isaiah 44:28 teaches several powerful principles. First, it demonstrates God's comprehensive knowledge of history and His ability to orchestrate events according to His purposes, regardless of whether human actors are aware of their role. This invites trust in difficult circumstances: the Lord sees the end from the beginning and is orchestrating events toward His purposes, even when we cannot perceive it. Second, the verse expands our understanding of how God works in the world. He does not only work through the faithful and covenant-aware; He works through 'unlikely' instruments (Cyrus, a pagan king) to accomplish His purposes for His people. This should humble us and expand our vision of God's power and wisdom. Third, the specific promise regarding the Temple should sharpen our covenant commitment. Just as the exiles' return and the Temple's reconstruction were the fulfillment of God's promise, so the restoration of temples in the Latter-day work is the fulfillment of God's covenant in our time. We live in an era when temples are being rebuilt and multiplied (President Nelson's temple initiative), which is itself a fulfillment of the principle established in Isaiah 44:28. Finally, the verse invites us to reflect on what our role might be in God's larger purposes. We may never know the full extent of how our faith and obedience contribute to God's grand design, but we are invited to be—like Cyrus, though we may be more aware than he was—instruments through which God's purposes are accomplished.
