text_kjv: Thus saith the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden, to subdue nations before him; and I will loose the loins of kings, to open before him the two leaved gates; and the gates shall not be shut;

commentary.narrative:
This verse opens with one of the most extraordinary theological claims in the Hebrew Bible: God calls Cyrus II of Persia by the title 'anointed' (mashiach)—the same word that will later designate the Messiah himself. This is the only instance in all of Scripture where a non-Israelite, a pagan ruler who never knew Israel's God, receives this sacred designation. The historical context is the Babylonian exile (586–539 BCE); Cyrus's conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE allowed the Jewish exiles to return home and rebuild the Temple. Isaiah 45 announces this deliverance not as the work of a human liberator alone, but as the execution of God's sovereign plan. God 'grasps' Cyrus's right hand—an image of intimate guidance and empowerment—to accomplish what no human power could: the subjugation of nations and the 'loosing of loins' (a poetic way of describing the disarming and dismaying of kings).

The KJV's 'loose the loins of kings' reflects the Hebrew metaphor mathnei melachim (literally 'loins of kings'), which in ancient Near Eastern language represents the strength, dignity, and military readiness of rulers. When loins are 'loosed,' a king is stripped of power and confidence. The image shifts to 'gates of brass' in the next clause—a reference to Babylon's famous bronze gates, which Herodotus describes as impregnable. The theological claim is audacious: God uses a foreign monarch, unaware of his role in Israel's redemption, to accomplish divine purposes.

word_study.meaning: One who has been anointed with oil; set apart for a sacred office or role. The root is from the verb mashach ('to anoint'). In Israel's tradition, kings (1 Samuel 16:12-13), priests (Exodus 29:7), and the promised messianic king (Daniel 9:25) receive this anointing. The word's semantic range includes royalty, priestly office, and eventually the eschatological deliverer—the Messiah.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that applying mashiach to Cyrus is 'a deliberate theological claim that God's purposes operate through foreign rulers.' This challenges any notion that God works only through Israel's covenant people. The application to a pagan emperor anticipates the New Testament revelation that God's purposes transcend ethnic and religious boundaries. In the Restoration, this principle expands: the Lord works through nations and individuals of all backgrounds to accomplish His eternal designs (see D&C 101:80, where nations are instruments in God's hand).

word_study.meaning: To grasp, seize, or hold firmly by the right hand; the verb hechezaqti is the perfect form of chazaq, meaning 'to strengthen, make firm, or take hold of.' The phrase describes concrete physical action—God taking Cyrus by the right hand—but also spiritual empowerment and guidance.
word_study.significance: The Translator Notes of The Covenant Rendering point out this is 'the same language used for God leading Israel' (see Isaiah 41:13: 'I will help thee'). The right hand is the place of power and honor in ancient Near Eastern convention. God's grasp of Cyrus's hand is not accidental or incidental; it is the deliberate seizure of a ruler by divine intention to accomplish redemption.

word_study.meaning: To tread down, trample, or subjugate; the verb rad carries the sense of military conquest and the domination of enemies beneath one's feet. Goyim means 'nations' (non-Israelite peoples).
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes Cyrus's role as a military conqueror whose victories are ordained by God. This is not Cyrus's personal ambition but the execution of a divine plan. The nations before him—including Babylon—will be subdued as part of God's design to restore Israel.

word_study.term_english: loose the loins / strip of armor
word_study.meaning: Loins; in ancient Near Eastern metaphor, the loins represent strength, courage, virility, and military readiness. To 'loose' or 'strip' the loins is to deprive someone of power and confidence. The Covenant Rendering renders this as 'strip kings of their armor,' which captures the sense of disarming and humbling.
word_study.significance: This poetic language conveys psychological and military defeat. Kings who face Cyrus will lose not only their fortifications but their very confidence and authority. The metaphor is visceral—it describes the inner dissolution of enemy power before it is outwardly conquered.

cross_references.connection: Earlier in the same prophecy, Isaiah announces the rise of a righteous figure from the east who will conquer nations; these verses provide the first hint that this figure is Cyrus, whom God has 'raised up in righteousness.'
In the verse immediately preceding this chapter, Cyrus is explicitly named as the Lord's 'shepherd' who will perform His pleasure and decree the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the Temple.
The historical fulfillment: Cyrus's decree allowing the Jews to return and rebuild the Temple, confirming Isaiah's prophecy.
The historical record of Cyrus's proclamation granting the exiles permission to return—the realization of Isaiah's prophecy in actual history.
Modern revelation teaches that the Lord uses nations and their leaders, even those who know Him not, as instruments to accomplish His purposes in the latter days.

commentary.historical_context:
Cyrus II of Persia (c. 590–530 BCE) was the founder of the Achaemenid Empire and one of antiquity's most celebrated rulers. In 539 BCE, his armies conquered Babylon without a siege—a remarkable feat attributed in ancient sources to either sabotage or Cyrus's military genius. The Nabonidus Chronicle records that Babylon's gates were opened and its king captured without major bloodshed. This historical victory opened the way for the Jewish exiles, held in Babylon for nearly fifty years (586–539 BCE), to return to Judah and rebuild the Temple.

The Covenant Rendering's translator notes reference Herodotus's account of Babylon's hundred bronze gates—massive fortifications that seemed impregnable. Cyrus's conquest of these gates without their being 'shut against him' (as v. 1 states) would have seemed miraculous to observers. In the ancient Near East, the 'loosing of loins' was a common metaphor in Assyrian and Egyptian royal inscriptions to describe the terror and defeat of enemy kings. Isaiah employs this language to describe Cyrus's effect on the kings of the world—they lose their strength and confidence before him.

Theologically, the calling of Cyrus as God's 'anointed' is unique in the Hebrew Bible. No pagan ruler—not Pharaoh, not Nebuchadnezzar, not any king of the nations—is given this title. It reflects a profound shift in Isaiah's theology: God's purposes are not confined to Israel's covenant structures but operate through world history and secular powers. This would have been shocking to exiles who might have expected salvation to come through a restored Davidic king or a priest from Israel's own ranks.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon reinforces this principle that God works through various peoples and nations. Nephi learns that the Lord's purposes 'shall be brought to pass' regardless of who opposes them (2 Nephi 27:11). The principle that God uses gentile nations to accomplish His purposes appears in Nephi's vision of the Gentiles serving the seed of Nephi (1 Nephi 13:12-19). In Alma 37:6-7, Alma teaches that small means accomplish great things when directed by the Lord—a principle that applies to Cyrus, who was small in God's eyes but mighty in accomplishing redemption.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:80 directly applies Isaiah's principle to the latter-day context: 'I have suffered the affliction to come upon them, wherewith they have been afflicted, in consequence of their transgressions; but I will soften the hearts of those to whom I send him, that he may desire the welfare of the Zion of my God.' This teaches that God prepares the hearts of national leaders—even those outside the covenant—to accomplish His purposes. D&C 58:20-22 similarly teaches that the Lord works through the laws of the land. The principle of Isaiah 45:1 is that God ordains the rise and fall of nations to serve His eternal design.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Cyrus's role in allowing the rebuilding of the Second Temple makes him, in a sense, a type or shadow of one who facilitates sacred restoration. The physical temple in Jerusalem was restored through a gentile ruler's decree—anticipating the spiritual temple in the heart that the Lord builds in His covenant people. The anointing of Cyrus parallels the anointing of kings and priests in Israel's temple tradition, suggesting that God's anointing extends beyond Israel's borders and into the world.

commentary.christological_typology: While Cyrus is explicitly called 'anointed' (mashiach), he is clearly not the Messiah in the ultimate sense—he does not know God, nor does he come to redeem Israel from sin. However, he functions as a type of messianic agent: one anointed by God to accomplish liberation, to break down barriers (the gates of Babylon), to restore the exiles, and to enable the rebuilding of God's house. The Messiah will ultimately accomplish what Cyrus shadows in type: breaking the gates of death, leading the spiritually captive to freedom, and restoring God's people. In this sense, Cyrus's 'anointing' foreshadows the Anointed One (the Messiah) whose anointing will be eternal and whose purposes will be redemptive not for one nation but for all humanity.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 45:1 teaches a humbling truth: God's purposes are larger than our understanding, and He often accomplishes His work through unexpected and unconventional means. We may expect salvation to come through the visible structures of the Church, through prophets and apostles, through familiar channels—and it does. But God also works through history, through political changes, through people who do not know His name. This invites us to trust in Providence rather than control, to see God's hand in world events even when they appear secular or driven by human ambition alone. It also challenges any notion of tribal religion: God's covenant is not bound by ethnicity or national identity. His purposes transcend all human boundaries. For Latter-day Saints, this principle undergirds the doctrine of restoration—God raises up instruments in many places and times to accomplish His eternal design, and we are called to discern His hand and cooperate with it.

text_kjv: I will go before thee, and make the crooked places straight: I will break in pieces the gates of brass, and cut in sunder the bars of iron:

commentary.narrative:
God now declares His personal leadership of Cyrus's military campaign, promising to level obstacles and demolish fortifications. The verse employs metaphors of roadmaking and gatekeeping that would resonate powerfully with exiles who had walked the long, hard roads of captivity. The language shifts from declaration about Cyrus to address to him: 'I will go before thee'—God positions Himself as the vanguard of Cyrus's forces, removing impediments and enabling conquest.

The Covenant Rendering translates verse 2b as 'I will level the mountains,' which is more precise than the KJV's 'make the crooked places straight.' The Hebrew word hadurim (or horim) refers to swellings, rough terrain, or mountains—geographical obstacles that would impede an army's advance. God promises to remove all physical obstacles between Cyrus and his objective. The 'gates of brass' and 'bars of iron' are not merely poetic: they reference actual Babylon, whose fortifications were legendary in the ancient world. The Translator Notes cite Herodotus's description of Babylon's hundred bronze gates—engineering marvels that seemed impregnable. Yet God promises to 'shatter' (ashshaber, from shabar, 'break in pieces') these gates and 'cut through' (agaddea, from gadad, 'cut') the iron bars.

This verse functions both literally and symbolically. On the literal level, it predicts Cyrus's conquest of Babylon without a traditional siege. On the symbolic level, it reassures the exiles that every barrier between them and home will be removed by divine intervention. The passage addresses Cyrus in the second person but is heard by the exiles—reminding them that their deliverance is not dependent on their own strength or on Cyrus's personal sympathy toward them, but on God's active removal of every obstacle.

word_study.meaning: To go before, precede, lead from the front. The verb form here is 'I will go' (lelech), emphasizing active movement ahead of someone. The preposition l'faneyim means 'before your face,' i.e., in front of you.
word_study.significance: In ancient warfare and sacred narrative, the leader or the divine force goes before the army to ensure victory and safe passage. God promises to be Cyrus's vanguard—a remarkable statement that the God of Israel leads the Persian emperor's armies. This echoes language used for God leading Israel through the wilderness (Exodus 13:21: 'And the LORD went before them').

word_study.meaning: Yashar: to make straight, level, or smooth. Hadurim: swellings, rugged places, mountains, or rough terrain. The verb ayasher means 'I will make level.' Together they describe the flattening of landscape—the removal of geographical obstacles.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures this more precisely as 'I will level the mountains.' This echoes the later language of John the Baptist (Luke 3:5): 'Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low'—language applied in the New Testament to the preparation of the way of the Lord. The principle is that God removes obstacles before His chosen instruments.

word_study.meaning: To break, shatter, or smash into pieces. The verb carries the sense of violent destruction, not mere opening. The bronze gates will not be simply opened but destroyed.
word_study.significance: This is not a surrender or a treaty but a conquest. The gates that were symbols of Babylon's strength and security are violently destroyed. For the exiles, this destruction is liberation—the shattering of the barriers that held them captive.

word_study.meaning: To cut, sever, or divide. The verb gadad specifically refers to cutting or slicing through something, as in cutting leather or wood. Here it is applied to iron bars—gates' reinforcement.
word_study.significance: The verb choice emphasizes the destruction of the structural reinforcement that made the gates impregnable. Iron bars were the strongest defensive technology of the ancient world. God's power transcends all human military engineering.

cross_references.connection: God went before Israel in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night during the exodus; similarly, God promises to go before Cyrus, establishing a parallel between Israel's liberation from Egypt and the exiles' liberation from Babylon.

Earlier in Isaiah, the voice in the wilderness promises to 'make the rough places plain' and 'level the mountains'—the same language applied here to Cyrus's path, unifying the redemptive narrative across Isaiah 40-45.

John the Baptist quotes this Isaianic language ('valleys shall be filled, mountains brought low') as preparation for the Messiah's coming—applying the principle of obstacle removal to spiritual salvation.

God recalls making a way through the sea and breaking down the chariots and horses of Pharaoh; the same God now promises to break down the gates of Babylon—establishing continuity in God's redemptive action.
In latter-day revelation, the Lord teaches that He will go before the faithful to 'smooth down the rough places' of their path—applying Isaiah's principle to individual disciples.

commentary.historical_context:
The historical conquest of Babylon by Cyrus in 539 BCE is one of antiquity's most significant military achievements. Ancient sources describe Babylon as surrounded by massive walls and bronze gates, seemingly impregnable. Yet Cyrus captured the city without a traditional siege. The Nabonidus Chronicle records that the city's gates were opened without battle, possibly due to internal sabotage or the king's absence (Nabonidus had withdrawn to Tema). Herodotus, writing later, reports that Cyrus's troops diverted the Euphrates River that ran through Babylon, allowing them to enter the city through lowered water gates.

Whether by engineering, strategy, or internal collapse, Cyrus's conquest of Babylon appeared to the ancient world as impossible made possible—a fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy that the 'gates of brass' would be shattered. For the Jewish exiles in Babylon, this conquest meant the collapse of their captor and the opening of the road home. The Covenant Rendering's reference to 'mountains' being leveled also reflects the ancient practice of road-making for armies—the construction of ramps and the flattening of terrain to enable rapid troop movement. The Persians were renowned for their road systems (the 'Royal Road' connected Susa to Sardis), so the promise that 'mountains will be leveled' before Cyrus was culturally intelligible to the exiles.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon employs similar language of obstacle-removal and the preparation of the way. In 1 Nephi 17:7-8, the Lord provides Nephi with ore to make a ship and commands him to make bellows—removing the obstacles to his family's deliverance. In Alma 37:4-6, Alma teaches Helaman that the 'small means' the Lord provides will be magnified 'in bringing about the salvation of his people'—a principle that applies to Cyrus, whose conquest opens the way for Israel's redemption. The Nephite prophets also teach that God prepares the way for His people's deliverance through both miraculous and natural means.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:33 applies this Isaianic principle directly to modern disciples: 'Wherefore, the Lord will have mercy upon you, for he shall go before your face. He shall be on your right hand and on your left, and his Spirit shall be in your hearts, and his angels round about you, to bear you up.' This teaches that the principle of God going before His people and removing obstacles is not unique to ancient Israel or Cyrus but applies to the Restoration and to individual covenant members. D&C 109:24-26 similarly promises that the Lord will 'go before' the faithful and 'cause the rough places to be made smooth.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The removal of obstacles before Cyrus can be understood as the removal of barriers between the exiles and the Temple—the center of Israel's covenant worship. Cyrus's conquest enables not just the physical return of exiles but the restoration of the Temple itself. In latter-day perspective, this prefigures the building of temples as centers of covenant relationship with God. The principle that God 'goes before' His people to enable them to build temples and engage in sacred ordinances is central to Restoration theology.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 2 prefigures the Messiah's role in breaking down the barriers between God and humanity. Christ is the ultimate gateway-breaker: He breaks down the iron gates of death (the bars that imprisoned humanity in mortality and sin) and makes straight the crooked path that separated sinful mortals from holy God. The mountain-leveling language also echoes Christ's teaching that faith can remove mountains (Matthew 17:20)—faith in Christ removes the spiritual obstacles that prevent covenant relationship with God. The Messiah goes before His people as both vanguard and Savior, removing every obstacle to redemption.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 2 invites trust in God's active removal of obstacles in our paths toward redemption and spiritual growth. We often face barriers—internal doubts, external opposition, unforeseen challenges—that seem as impenetrable as Babylon's bronze gates. The promise of Isaiah 45:2 is that God does not merely encourage us to overcome these barriers ourselves; He actively goes before us to remove them. This does not mean we become passive, but it means we trust that God's power and foresight exceed any obstacle we perceive. The verse also teaches the principle of preparation: before we can reach our spiritual destination, God often removes barriers we cannot see or remove ourselves. In covenant life, this might mean that family members become more receptive to the gospel, that financial circumstances improve to allow us to serve, or that understanding deepens where confusion reigned. The Lord goes before, and we follow in faith.

text_kjv: And I will give thee the treasures of darkness, and hidden riches of secret places, that thou mayest know that I, the LORD, which call thee by thy name, am the God of Israel.

commentary.narrative:
Having removed obstacles, God now promises Cyrus wealth—'treasures of darkness' and 'hidden riches of secret places.' This verse shifts from military conquest to economic reward, suggesting that Cyrus will not merely defeat Babylon but will possess its legendary wealth. Babylon was famed throughout the ancient world for its accumulated treasures, stored in vaults beneath temples and palaces. The phrase 'treasures of darkness' likely refers to underground vaults where wealth was kept in darkness, away from thieves. These riches would naturally fall to Cyrus upon his conquest of the city.

But the verse's purpose is not primarily to promise Cyrus personal enrichment. The theological purpose is stated in the phrase 'that thou mayest know that I, the LORD'—the treasures serve a revelatory function. God gives Cyrus wealth so that he will recognize that it is God, not chance or his own military prowess, who has accomplished his victories. The phrase 'call thee by thy name' emphasizes personal relationship: God knows Cyrus individually and calls him specifically to his role. The phrase 'am the God of Israel' clarifies that this God is not Marduk (Babylon's chief deity) but the God of the covenant people. Cyrus will come to know—intellectually and perhaps spiritually—that the power behind his throne belongs to Israel's God.

This is remarkable theology: God reveals Himself to a pagan ruler not through Scripture or covenant but through historical events and the gift of wealth. The Translator Notes emphasize that 'God reveals Himself through history, not just through Scripture.' Cyrus's education in the nature of the true God comes through his own experience of inexplicable prosperity and miraculous conquest. The promise is that even without Cyrus's conscious faith or prior knowledge, his experiences will testify to the reality of Israel's God.

word_study.meaning: Treasures or storehouses in darkness; the word otzrot means vaults, storehouses, or treasuries. Choshekh means darkness, which in context refers to underground chambers, secret vaults, or hidden places where wealth was stored away from light and thieves. This is not darkness of evil but of hiddenness.
word_study.significance: The phrase evokes Babylon's legendary underground wealth. Wealthy temples and palaces stored precious metals, jewels, and tribute in underground vaults. The phrase also carries theological weight: riches hidden from the world are revealed and given by God's hand. In the Restoration, this principle appears in D&C 89:19, where the Lord promises health and 'treasures of knowledge' to the obedient.

word_study.meaning: Hidden or concealed riches; matmunim means things that are buried or hidden, and mistarim means things that are concealed or secret. The phrase emphasizes both the hiddenness and the great value of these riches.
word_study.significance: These are not just riches but carefully concealed riches—treasures guarded in secret places, requiring conquest to access. The doubling of the phrase (treasures of darkness and hidden riches) emphasizes the magnitude and the mysteriously providential nature of what Cyrus will gain.

word_study.meaning: To call by name; the verb kara means 'to call' or 'to proclaim,' and beshimcha means 'by your name' or 'in your name.' To call someone by name in Hebrew implies personal knowledge, recognition, and often a commissioning for a specific purpose.
word_study.significance: God's calling of Cyrus by name establishes a personal relationship despite Cyrus not knowing God in return. The Covenant Rendering notes that this phrase 'uses the same language used for God calling Israel by name (Isaiah 43:1).' It suggests that God's relationship with Cyrus, while different from the covenant relationship with Israel, is nonetheless personal and specific. God knows Cyrus not as a generic pagan ruler but as an individual called for a particular historical purpose.

word_study.meaning: In order that, so that; this is a purpose clause. Teda is 'you will know.' The phrase indicates that the giving of treasures is not merely an act of generosity but an act designed to bring about knowledge or recognition.
word_study.significance: The purpose of Cyrus's enrichment is not his personal pleasure but his coming to knowledge of God. This reflects a principle throughout the Abrahamic religions: God acts in history to reveal Himself and to bring about recognition of His sovereignty. The accumulation of evidence (military victory, inexplicable prosperity, the fulfillment of prophecy) is meant to produce faith or at least acknowledgment.

cross_references.connection: God calls Israel by name, assuring them of His love and protection; similarly, God calls Cyrus by name, extending personal knowledge and commission beyond the covenant people.
God declares that He has 'raised up one from the north, and he shall come; from the rising of the sun shall he call upon my name'—Cyrus again, whom God raises up and calls for His purposes.
Jeremiah prophesies that Nebuchadnezzar is God's 'servant' and that his son will also serve Him; God uses foreign rulers as instruments, paralleling Isaiah's claim about Cyrus.

The Lord teaches that all riches and treasures belong to Him and are held in trust for the obedient; the principle that wealth is a gift from God for a redemptive purpose appears in latter-day revelation.
Wisdom is compared to hidden treasures that must be sought; similarly, knowledge of the true God is presented as hidden treasure revealed through Cyrus's experience.

commentary.historical_context:
Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar and his successors accumulated legendary wealth. The city's temples—especially the temple of Marduk—held vast treasures of gold, silver, and precious stones, accumulated from tribute and taxation across the Babylonian Empire. Ancient sources describe treasure vaults beneath temples and palaces, protected by guards and secrecy. When Cyrus conquered Babylon, he would have gained access to these royal treasuries. The Translator Notes note that 'treasures of darkness refer to Babylon's legendary wealth stored in underground vaults.'

Historically, Cyrus was known for his clemency toward conquered peoples and his respect for local religions and temples. Rather than looting temples and destroying religious structures, he often allowed them to continue functioning and even provided resources for their maintenance. The paradox is that while Cyrus showed respect for Babylonian temples, the wealth accumulated in those temples ultimately came under his control. For the Jewish exiles, this meant that Cyrus's access to Babylon's treasures indirectly facilitated their own liberation—he had the resources to support their return journey and the rebuilding of the Temple. The promise of 'treasures' also reflects the ancient Near Eastern practice of spoils of war: victorious armies took portable wealth from conquered cities.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains several passages about hidden treasures. In Alma 37:3-6, Alma discusses the liahona, a divine instrument that guides the righteous, comparing it to a record 'that hath been kept with care.' The principle is that God hides precious things and reveals them to the faithful. In Helaman 3:14-15, the Lord provides increase and prosperity to those who turn to Him. The promise of 'treasures of darkness' being revealed echoes the Nephite experience of material blessings accompanying spiritual covenant-keeping.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 89:18-21 applies the principle of God's provision and treasure-giving to the latter-day context: the Lord promises 'wisdom and great treasures of knowledge, even hidden treasures' to those who obey His law. D&C 38:39 teaches that 'seek not for riches but for wisdom, and behold, the mysteries of God shall be unfolded unto you.' This indicates that in Restoration theology, the greatest treasures are spiritual—wisdom and knowledge of God—though temporal means may also be granted. The principle that God gives wealth as a means of bringing about knowledge and covenant is central to latter-day economic ethics.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The treasures of Babylon that will fall to Cyrus will ultimately be used to support the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem. The wealth of the nations comes into service of God's covenant purposes. In Restoration temple theology, the principle appears in D&C 109:73, where the Lord promises that 'the wealth of the Gentiles shall be consecrated unto thy people, the children of Jacob.' The physical wealth of nations serves the spiritual and physical restoration of the covenant people.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 3 foreshadows Christ as the one who possesses and dispenses the ultimate treasures. In Matthew 6:19-21, Christ teaches that the 'treasures of heaven' are where the heart should be fixed. In Colossians 2:3, Paul writes that in Christ 'are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.' Christ is the hidden treasure (Matthew 13:44-46)—the pearl of great price for which all else is surrendered. As Cyrus receives treasures of darkness to know God, so believers receive the treasures of Christ (justification, redemption, wisdom) through faith in Him. The purpose clause—'that thou mayest know'—also applies to Christ: we receive His grace 'that we might know' Him (John 17:3) and come to eternal life.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 3 teaches that God's provision of material blessings has a spiritual purpose: to draw us toward knowledge and worship of Him. Prosperity is not an end in itself but a means to recognizing God's hand and surrendering to His will. The verse also invites reflection on how God makes known His reality and power through events in our lives. We may experience unexpected opportunities, surprising reversals of fortune, or providential circumstances—what seem like fortunate coincidences—that in fact reveal God's active involvement in our affairs. Like Cyrus, we may gradually come to know God through our experience of His providence, even before we fully understand or commit to Him. The application for the faithful is more direct: when God blesses us with temporal means, we are to recognize these as gifts meant to expand our knowledge of Him and our ability to serve His purposes. Hoarding treasures for ourselves alone violates the purpose God has in giving them; using them to build Zion, support the Church and temple, and care for others fulfills their intended meaning.

text_kjv: For Jacob my servant's sake, and Israel mine elect, I have even called thee by thy name: I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me.

commentary.narrative:
This verse pivots the focus from Cyrus back to Israel, clarifying that every promise made to Cyrus serves ultimately the purpose of redeeming Jacob (Israel). God calls Cyrus not because of Cyrus's merit or faith but 'for Jacob my servant's sake'—the covenant people are the ultimate beneficiaries and the ultimate reason for Cyrus's rise to power. The verse reinforces the astonishing theological claim: God gives Cyrus a title of honor ('I have surnamed thee') precisely to accomplish the deliverance of a people Cyrus does not know and a God Cyrus has never encountered. This is predestination of a peculiar sort: God ordains a foreign ruler for the sake of a covenant people, without requiring that ruler's conscious knowledge of or belief in God.

The phrase 'Jacob my servant' echoes Israel's ancient name and the patriarchal covenant. 'Israel mine elect' employs the language of election and chosenness. These are the names and titles of covenant relationship—terms that define Israel's identity as God's chosen, redeemed people. Cyrus, by contrast, is not named in terms of covenant or election but is honored with a title for his instrumental role. The tension is profound: the elect nation (Israel) will be redeemed by a non-elect foreign ruler (Cyrus) who serves God unknowingly. The Translator Notes emphasize that 'God's anointed does not know God,' and yet God's purposes are accomplished through him. This challenges any theology that makes divine purposes dependent on human knowledge or faith; God is free to work through whatever means He chooses to accomplish His covenant purposes.

word_study.meaning: Servant; one who serves or is in service to another. The term carries both the sense of human slavery and of voluntary service or administrative office. In covenant theology, 'servant of the Lord' (eved YHWH) becomes a title of honor—Moses, Joshua, Job, and the prophets are all called 'servants of the Lord.'
word_study.significance: Jacob/Israel is God's servant—a relationship of covenant obligation and intimate connection. The same word is not applied to Cyrus; Cyrus is not a covenant servant but an instrument of God's will. This distinction is crucial: Israel's relationship with God is covenantal and eternal; Cyrus's role is instrumental and temporary. The designation 'servant' also echoes the Suffering Servant passages (Isaiah 42-53) and points forward to Christ as the ultimate Servant of the Lord.

word_study.meaning: Chosen, elect, selected; from the verb bachar, meaning 'to choose' or 'to select.' The elect are those chosen by God for a specific relationship or purpose. In covenant theology, Israel is God's chosen people, selected not for their strength or goodness but for God's own purposes.
word_study.significance: The term 'elect' (bachir) defines Israel's election—the foundational act by which God chose them as His covenant people. This election is not earned but given. The contrast with Cyrus is implicit: Cyrus is not elect but is called to serve the purposes of the elect nation. This establishes a hierarchy of purpose: God's covenant people are the center; foreign rulers are instrumental to that center.

word_study.meaning: To give a name, surname, or title; the verb kanna (or qanah) means 'to name' or 'to call.' The prefix a suggests 'I give you'—'I give you a title' or 'I give you a name.' The Covenant Rendering translates this as 'I give you a title of honor.'
word_study.significance: God's naming or renaming of Cyrus establishes a personal, deliberate relationship. Throughout Scripture, God renames people to mark a new identity or calling (Abram to Abraham, Simon to Peter). Here, God gives Cyrus a title of honor—not necessarily a new name but a designation that elevates his status. The honor given is instrumental: Cyrus is honored in order to accomplish God's purposes through him.

word_study.term_english: though thou hast not known me
word_study.meaning: And you have not known me; the verb yada (to know) in biblical Hebrew carries the sense of intimate, experiential knowledge—knowing by relationship and encounter, not merely intellectual awareness. The negative form ('you have not known') indicates that Cyrus has not experienced or entered into relationship with God.
word_study.significance: This phrase is the chapter's most theologically provocative statement, according to the Translator Notes. It establishes that God's anointed, God's chosen instrument for redemption, does not know God. This shatters any notion that God works only through those who have faith, knowledge, or covenant relationship with Him. It opens the possibility that God's purposes transcend human knowledge, consciousness, and intention. This principle has profound implications for how we understand Providence: God works through secular history, through unknowing agents, through nations and leaders who have no faith.

cross_references.connection: God reminds Israel, 'Thou whom I have taken from the ends of the earth...and said unto thee, Thou art my servant; I have chosen thee'—establishing the foundational covenant election that verse 4 here reaffirms.
God declares Israel to be 'my peculiar treasure...a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation'—the election and covenant status that Cyrus is called to serve and restore.
Paul argues that God's purposes are not bound by human worthiness or knowledge; God is free to raise up vessels for His purposes—a principle that applies directly to Cyrus and echoes Isaiah 45:4.

In the Doctrine and Covenants, the Lord declares that He will 'take upon him the form of man...and go forth to battle against the enemies of his people'—the principle that God accomplishes His covenant purposes through willing and unwilling instruments.
God calls Israel by name, assuring them, 'Thou art mine'—establishing the intimate covenant relationship that is the purpose behind all God's dealings with Cyrus.

commentary.historical_context:
The historical reality behind verse 4 is that Cyrus's conquest of Babylon and his subsequent decree allowing the Jewish exiles to return home was not driven by any faith in or knowledge of Israel's God. Cyrus was a Zoroastrian, worshiping Ahura Mazda. His policy of religious tolerance and his support for the rebuilding of temples and religious centers were consistent with his general approach to conquered peoples and their religions—he sought stability and loyalty by respecting local customs and religious practices. The Cyrus Cylinder, discovered in the nineteenth century and now in the British Museum, records Cyrus's own account of his conquest of Babylon and his restoration of various temples and religions. There is no mention of Israel's God or any special relationship with the Jewish people.

Yet historically, Cyrus did decree the return of the exiles and provided resources for the rebuilding of the Temple. Second Chronicles 36:22-23 and Ezra 1:1-4 record this decree. The Jewish exiles experienced this as miraculous divine intervention—the God of Israel had moved the heart of a pagan emperor to accomplish their redemption. From Cyrus's perspective, he was simply following his policy of religious tolerance and empire-building. From God's perspective, He was using Cyrus's ambitions and character to accomplish redemptive purposes. This is the paradox of divine Providence: God works through human agents according to their own will and motivation, yet accomplishes purposes those agents do not consciously intend.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains parallel examples of God using unknowing agents to accomplish His purposes. In 1 Nephi 2:24, Nephi prophesies that the Lamanites will be an instrument 'to stir up [the Nephites] in remembrance'—the Lamanites do not know they are fulfilling God's purposes. In Helaman 6:35-36, the Lord sends forth the wicked to accomplish His purposes among the righteous, 'that [the righteous] may distinguish between the righteous and the wicked.' The principle is that God uses all agents, willing and unwilling, knowing and unknowing, to accomplish His covenant designs.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:58-59 teaches that God works through His 'chosen vessels' but also through circumstances and events beyond individuals' control or knowledge. D&C 101:79-81 teaches that the Lord 'shall exalt the righteous' and 'bring down the wicked' and uses nations and their leaders as instruments: 'I have raised up you up as a lamb for the slaughter; and now, therefore, hark unto the voice of him that speaketh.' The principle that God uses nations and their leaders without their conscious knowledge of His purposes is central to latter-day understanding of Providence and history.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Verse 4 emphasizes that Cyrus's rise and his granting of permission for the Temple's rebuilding are entirely for the sake of Israel's covenant restoration. The Temple is the center of Israel's covenant relationship with God, and Cyrus's instrumental role is to restore the conditions for Temple worship and sacrifice. In Restoration theology, this principle extends to the building of modern temples: all historical events and providential circumstances that enable temple building and covenant ordinances are ordered by God for the sake of His covenant people's redemption and exaltation.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 4 foreshadows Christ as the one ultimately elected and beloved for the sake of all who will inherit salvation. Christ is God's 'servant' and God's 'elect' (1 Peter 2:4-6 applies Old Testament election language to Christ). However, unlike Cyrus, Christ knows the Father perfectly (John 1:1-3, John 10:30) and comes consciously to accomplish redemption. The principle of verse 4—that God ordains and uses individuals for the sake of the covenant people—finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ, who gives Himself for the redemption of His chosen people (Ephesians 1:3-14). Where Cyrus is an unknowing instrument, Christ is the conscious, willing, and eternally willing Savior.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 4 teaches a liberating and humbling truth: God's purposes for our redemption transcend our personal worthiness or knowledge. We do not need to be perfect or fully knowledgeable to be beneficiaries of God's grace. God works through history, through events we may not understand, through people and circumstances we may not control, all for the sake of His covenant people's ultimate redemption and exaltation. It also teaches us to recognize God's hand in seemingly secular or irreligious events and peoples. A political change, an economic opportunity, a historical accident—any of these may be God's way of advancing His covenant purposes. We are called not to be passive observers but to recognize and cooperate with God's purposes as they unfold in our lives and in history. We should also reflect on the implications: if God uses Cyrus, unknowingly, for Israel's sake, then we should examine whether we are cooperating with God's purposes consciously, through faith and covenant, or whether we are being used according to our natural inclinations without recognizing God's hand. The covenant invitation is to move from being an unknowing instrument (like Cyrus) to being a conscious, willing partner in God's redemptive design.

text_kjv: I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me: I girded thee, and thou hast not known me.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 5 shifts from the particular claim about Cyrus to a universal theological declaration: monotheism absolute and uncompromising. God asserts, 'I am the LORD, and there is none else'—a statement that eliminates any rival deity or co-equal power. This is the first of the chapter's monotheistic declarations (see also verse 6), and it appears in the context of God's working through Cyrus, suggesting that the universal God who alone exists uses particular human agents to accomplish universal purposes. The phrase 'I girded thee' uses military language: to 'gird' someone is to outfit them with armor or weapons, to prepare them for war. God is not merely guiding Cyrus but actively equipping him with the military and material resources necessary to conquer nations and subdue kings.

The repetition of 'thou hast not known me' reinforces the previous verse's point: the monotheistic God of Israel, the only God who exists, accomplishes His purposes through Cyrus without Cyrus's conscious knowledge or faith. This creates a striking paradox: the one true God, who is jealously guarded against idolatry and who demands exclusive devotion from His covenant people, works through an agent who worships other gods (Ahura Mazda in the Zoroastrian tradition) and has no knowledge of Israel's God. For the exiles hearing this prophecy, the message is that their God is so powerful, so absolute in His sovereignty, that He can use even pagan rulers to accomplish redemption. Nothing—no human knowledge, no human intention, no human faith—is necessary for God to accomplish His purposes. God is free, and His freedom is manifest in working through unconventional and unexpected means.

word_study.meaning: I am the LORD; the declaration of God's identity and name. YHWH (the Tetragrammaton, traditionally transliterated as Yahweh) is the divine name revealed to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14), the most sacred and personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible. The first-person declaration 'I am YHWH' (ani YHWH) is a formula of self-identification and assertion of authority.
word_study.significance: The declaration 'I am the LORD' (ani YHWH) appears with particular frequency in Isaiah, especially in Isaiah 40-55 (the 'Second Isaiah'). It is a claim to ultimate reality and power. In the context of Cyrus and Persian religion, the declaration is defiant: it asserts that the God of Israel alone is real and powerful, in direct contradiction to the Zoroastrian faith of Cyrus's empire. This was revolutionary theology in the exilic context: the exiles' God was not diminished by captivity or defeat but remains the sole, absolute reality.

word_study.term_english: there is none else / there is no other
word_study.meaning: And there is no other; the phrase ve'ein od occurs multiple times in Isaiah 45 (vv. 1, 5, 6, 14) and asserts absolute monotheism. The phrase eliminates all alternatives: no rival deity, no co-equal power, no alternative source of being or authority.
word_study.significance: This is one of the clearest statements of monotheism in the Hebrew Bible. It goes beyond saying that God is greater than other gods (which would allow other gods to exist); it asserts that other gods do not exist at all. In the exilic context, when the exiles were surrounded by pagan religions and might have wondered whether their God had been defeated, this declaration reasserts the absolute sovereignty and reality of Israel's God. In later theology, this verse becomes foundational to Jewish monotheism and influences Christian theology through the Shema ('Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord'; Deuteronomy 6:4).

word_study.term_english: there is no God beside me
word_study.meaning: There is no God besides me; the phrase asserts that no deity exists apart from or alongside Israel's God. Elohim is the Hebrew word for God(s), used for the God of Israel but also for pagan deities. The phrase is maximally exclusive.
word_study.significance: The repetition of the monotheistic claim (v. 5a and 5b, and again in v. 6) emphasizes its centrality to the theological message. For a people in exile, surrounded by powerful pagan religions and magnificent temples, the claim that their God alone is real and powerful is an act of faith and a challenge to cultural despair. The exiles must trust not in visible power or architectural grandeur but in the reality of an invisible, transcendent God who alone exists and has purposes that transcend the visible political landscape.

word_study.meaning: To gird, encircle, or arm; the verb azar means to wrap or fasten a belt or garment, but in military contexts it means to arm or equip for battle. To 'gird one's loins' is to prepare oneself for action. The verb here is transitive: God girds Cyrus, equips him for conquest.
word_study.significance: The military language emphasizes that God is not merely an abstract, transcendent being but an active agent in history who equips particular rulers for particular tasks. God provides Cyrus with the material, military, and political resources necessary to conquer Babylon. For the exiles, the message is that their redemption will come through concrete, historical means—through a ruler's military might placed at God's service. This bridges the abstract (monotheistic theology) and the concrete (historical event and military conquest).

cross_references.connection: The Shema, Judaism's foundational monotheistic declaration: 'Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God is one LORD'; Isaiah 45:5 provides theological grounds for this exclusive monotheism.
God declares, 'I am God, and there is none like me'—a restatement of the monotheistic claim, suggesting its centrality to the book's theology.

Paul writes, 'We know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one'—applying Isaiah's monotheism to early Christian theology and the problem of pagan religion in Corinth.
The Lord declares, 'There is no God beside me'—the exact phrase from Isaiah, establishing continuity between Old Testament monotheism and Restoration theology.
In the preceding chapter, God asserts, 'Is there a God beside me? yea, there is no God; I know not any'—the same monotheistic claim that sets up the revelation about Cyrus.

commentary.historical_context:
The exilic period (586–539 BCE) was a theological crisis for the Jewish people. The destruction of the Jerusalem Temple, the exile of the royal line and the priesthood, the apparent abandonment of Jerusalem by God—all raised the question of whether Israel's God was real, powerful, or still interested in His covenant people. The religions of the exile—Babylonian polytheism with its magnificent temples and its pantheon of gods, and later Zoroastrianism with its cosmic dualism—offered alternative frameworks for understanding reality and divine power.

Isaiah 45:5's assertion that Israel's God alone exists, and that there is no God besides Him, was therefore not a philosophically abstract claim but a radical assertion of faith and a challenge to cultural despair. It claimed that the visible power of Babylon's gods and temples was illusory; the invisible God of Israel alone was real. This would be reinforced by the historical event: Cyrus, despite worshiping other gods, would be used by Israel's God to bring about liberation. The Dead Sea Scrolls confirm that this text circulated without emendation in the pre-Christian period—the audacious claim about Cyrus and monotheism stood as written. The theological claim was not softened or revised; it became stronger and more uncompromising.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon reinforces monotheism while acknowledging the reality of evil spiritual opposition. In Alma 11:26-28, Zeezrom is taught by Amulek that 'there could be no Christ' if 'there should be more Gods than one'—asserting that monotheism is essential to Christian theology. In 1 Nephi 13:37, Christ is described as the 'mediator of the new covenant' through whom the Father works—all divine purposes flow through the one God and His Christ. The principle of Isaiah 45:5—that God alone exists and acts—is affirmed throughout the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 20:37 directly quotes Isaiah 45:5: 'There is no God beside me.' The Doctrine and Covenants also teaches that God is 'infinite and eternal...a personage of spirit' (D&C 130:22) and that He exercises dominion over all things through His works. D&C 76:1-24 describes the vision of the degrees of glory, emphasizing that God's purposes encompass all creation and all souls—none can escape His authority. The restoration principle is that monotheism is not merely philosophical but practical: there is one source of authority and redemption, and that authority is vested in God and His Christ.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Verse 5's assertion that there is 'no God beside me' establishes the theological foundation for temple worship: the temple is the place where the one true God is worshipped, where His covenant is renewed, where His presence is particularly manifest. The monotheistic claim eliminates syncretism or the mixing of other religious practices with covenant worship. In Restoration temple theology, the temple is the place of exclusive covenant with the one God through the mediation of Jesus Christ. All other sources of religious authority and power are subordinate to or irrelevant beside this.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 5 establishes the theological framework for understanding Christ: If there is only one God, then Christ must be understood as the full expression of God's power and purposes in human form (Hebrews 1:1-3). The 'girding' or equipping of Cyrus for his work foreshadows Christ being 'girded' or equipped with the Holy Spirit without measure (John 3:34) to accomplish redemption. Christ is the ultimate agent through whom God works, the one who makes known the invisible God (John 1:18) and through whom all things are accomplished (Colossians 1:16-17). The monotheistic claim ensures that Christ is not a separate or co-equal deity but the perfect revelation and instrument of the one God.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 5 provides profound comfort and challenge. The comfort is that there is one God, one source of ultimate reality and authority, and that God is absolute and eternal in His power. We are not at the mercy of multiple competing spiritual forces or uncertain divine intentions; there is one will, one purpose, one God directing history and our individual lives. The challenge is to trust in this God's sovereignty even when we do not understand His methods or timeline. Like Cyrus, we may be used by God in ways we do not fully comprehend. We may fulfill divine purposes without knowing it, or we may be called to cooperate consciously with God's will even when the path is unclear. The verse invites us to examine our trust: Do we believe that the Lord 'is' (that He truly exists and is present), or do we live as though other powers (wealth, status, human relationships, worldly success) are as real and influential as God? The monotheistic claim is an invitation to radical faith: to see through all the apparent competing powers in the world and recognize one God working all things toward His purposes of redemption and covenant. Our role is to recognize and align ourselves with those purposes.

text_kjv: That they may know from the rising of the sun, and from the west, that there is none beside me. I am the LORD, and there is none else.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 6 concludes the chapter's first section with an expansion of the monotheistic claim to universal scope. Where verse 5 asserted that God is absolute and alone, verse 6 adds the purpose: 'that they may know'—the entire world, from east to west, from sunrise to sunset, will come to knowledge of the one God. The phrase 'from the rising of the sun, and from the west' uses geographical extremes to indicate the entire inhabited world. In ancient Near Eastern perspective, the rising sun (east) and the setting sun (west) represented the farthest reaches of the known world. Herodotus used similar language to describe the extent of the Persian Empire under Cyrus. The Translator Notes emphasize the scope: 'The scope is universal: from east (mizrach-shemesh, 'sunrise') to west (ma'aravah, 'sunset') — the entire inhabited world.'

The purpose of Cyrus's victories and of God's working through history is not merely the liberation of one exiled people, though that is included. The ultimate purpose is that all humanity comes to know that the God of Israel alone is real and powerful. This is a staggering claim in the exilic context: a small exiled community, seemingly defeated and powerless, believes that their God will ultimately be recognized by all nations. The theological scope is universal and eschatological—it points toward the day when all creation acknowledges the one God. The verse does not specify how this knowledge will come about (through direct revelation, through historical events, through missionary activity, through judgment). It simply asserts that this is God's ultimate purpose, and that Cyrus's role in history, though limited and particular, serves this universal and eternal end.
commentary.christological_typology: Verse 6 points to Christ as the one through whom the knowledge of the one God is universally revealed. Christ declares, 'I and my Father are one' (John 10:30), making known the unity of the Godhead. In John 1:1-18, Christ is identified as 'the Word,' through whom 'all things were made.' The universal revelation of God—from east to west, to all nations—is accomplished through Christ's atonement and the restoration of all things through Him. Revelation 5:13 describes the ultimate fulfillment: 'Every creature which is in heaven, and on the earth, and under the earth, and such as are in the sea, and all that are in them, heard I saying, Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, be unto him that sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb for ever and ever'—the universal acknowledgment of the one God through Christ.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains passages with similar universal scope. In 2 Nephi 27:14, Isaiah's prophecy is quoted: 'My work shall proceed, and my word shall be fulfilled'—and in the context, this prophecy encompasses 'all nations.' In 3 Nephi 16:4, Christ promises that the Gentiles will 'know that [the Father] will repent of his threatenings which he hath made unto them.' The principle that God's ultimate purposes are universal—extending to all nations and peoples—is central to Book of Mormon theology and the doctrine of the restoration.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 133:58-59 applies Isaiah's principle directly to the latter-day context: 'And it shall be said at the coming of the Lord: Who is ready and willing to come forth to plant the Lord's kingdom? I, the Lord, am willing to make these things known unto all flesh; for I am no respecter of persons.' This teaches that God's ultimate purpose is the universal revelation of His will and purposes to all humanity. D&C 128:22 teaches that 'the invisible world shall come forth, and then shall all the exposed and hidden things appear before the bar of God'—the ultimate universal revelation of truth. The restoration principle is that God's purposes encompass all people, all nations, and all dispensations.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Verse 6's promise that 'all may know' that God alone is God is fulfilled in the temple, the place where the fullness of God's covenant is revealed and made available to all who enter. In Restoration theology, the temple is the place where the knowledge of God is most fully communicated. Isaiah 2:2-3 (quoted in D&C 110:16) prophesies that 'the mountain of the Lord's house shall be established...and all nations shall flow unto it.' The universal knowledge promised in Isaiah 45:6 finds its fulfillment in the spread of temples throughout the world in the latter days, making available to all people the ordinances and covenants through which genuine knowledge of God is obtained.

word_study.meaning: In order that, so that...they may know; this is a purpose clause indicating God's intentional design. Yede'u is the third-person plural form of yada ('to know'), referring to people generally or all humanity coming to knowledge.
word_study.significance: The purpose clause indicates that all God's actions in history—raising up Cyrus, accomplishing the exiles' return, demonstrating His power through conquest—are directed toward bringing humanity to knowledge of the true God. Knowledge (yada) in biblical Hebrew is not merely intellectual acknowledgment but involves recognition, relationship, and sometimes obedience. The knowledge intended here is a global acknowledgment of God's sole reality and power.

word_study.term_english: from the rising of the sun / from sunrise
word_study.meaning: From the rising of the sun; mizrach is 'east' or 'rising,' and shemesh is 'sun.' The phrase describes the easternmost point, the direction of sunrise, representing the farthest visible reach of the world in one direction.
word_study.significance: In ancient Near Eastern geography and theology, the rising sun symbolized renewal, appearance, and the farthest visible reach. The phrase establishes the eastern boundary of the known world. The theological implication is that God's knowledge and recognition will reach even to the farthest and most visible extremities of creation.

word_study.meaning: From the west; ma'aravah means 'west' or the direction of the setting sun. The phrase represents the western boundary of the known world.
word_study.significance: The pairing of east and west (sunrise and sunset) represents the entire habitable world from extremity to extremity. In ancient cosmology, this encompassed the known world—from the Atlantic in the west to the edges of Asia in the east. The theological claim is that God's sovereignty and the knowledge of His sole reality extend to all corners of the known world. The Translator Notes note that this 'universal' scope—from east to west—encompasses 'the entire inhabited world.'

word_study.term_english: there is none beside me / there is no other
word_study.term_original: אֶפֶס בִּלְעָדַי / אֵין עוֹד (efes bil'adai / ein od)
word_study.meaning: Nothing besides me / there is no other; efes means 'naught, nothing, or nothingness,' and bil'adai means 'beside me, apart from me.' The phrase combines two forms of negation: efes ('nothing/nothingness') and ein ('there is not'). The Covenant Rendering captures this as 'there is none besides me.'
word_study.significance: The repetition of the monotheistic claim (fifth occurrence in Isaiah 45: vv. 1, 5, 6, and more to come) emphasizes its absolute centrality. The use of both efes and ein underscores the exclusivity: not only are there no rival gods, but the very concept of a god besides the Lord is nothingness, non-existent. This is the strongest possible assertion of monotheism—not that God is greater than other gods, but that other gods are literally nothing.

cross_references.connection: Earlier Isaiah declares the Lord will make known future events 'from the east'; the principle of universal revelation of God's purposes through historical events is established in the preceding chapters.

In the New Testament apocalypse, 'every eye shall see him'—the principle that all humanity will eventually recognize and acknowledge God's reality and authority is applied to Christ's return and the eschaton.
Paul writes that 'at the name of Jesus every knee should bow...and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord'—the universal acknowledgment of God's authority through Christ.

The Lord declares, 'Verily, verily, I say unto you, that when I give a commandment to any of the sons of men to do a work unto my name...he shall be upheld by the virtue of my word'—the principle that God's purposes extend universally through all the world.

John writes, 'Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be'—the principle that God's ultimate purposes extend beyond current visibility to a universal future revelation.

commentary.historical_context:
The historical context of verse 6 is still the exilic period (586–539 BCE) and the liberation promised through Cyrus. But the theological scope extends far beyond the particular historical event. The verse speaks of a universal knowledge of the one God that will eventually encompass all nations. In the ancient Near Eastern context, this would have seemed like an absurd boast from a defeated, exiled people. Babylon was the superpower; its gods and temples were magnificent; Marduk was worshiped throughout the empire. Yet Isaiah claims that the God of Israel, whose temple lay in ruins and whose people were captives, alone was real and would eventually be acknowledged by all nations.

Historically, this did not occur in the way a literal reading might suggest. The world did not convert to Judaism or to the worship of the God of Israel. However, the principle underlying the verse—that God's purposes extend beyond the particular to the universal—proved prophetically true in the spread of monotheistic religions (Judaism, Christianity, Islam) that claim descent from or are influenced by the God revealed to Israel. The Jewish return from exile, enabled by Cyrus, preserved the Torah and the covenant tradition, which became foundational to Christianity and Islam. In that sense, the God of Israel did eventually become known to the world, though through unexpected means and centuries of historical development. The verse's scope—universal and eschatological—suggests that the full realization of this knowledge may still be future, in the eschaton when all creation recognizes the one God.
commentary.application:
For modern covenant members, verse 6 extends the application beyond the particular to the universal. We live in the latter days, in which the restoration of the gospel is occurring. The promise of verse 6—that all people 'from the rising of the sun...to the west' will come to know that there is no God beside the Lord—becomes our mission and our vision. We are called to be part of the mechanism through which this universal knowledge spreads. The work of missionary activity, of temple building, of family history work that extends covenant blessings across generations and nations, all participate in fulfilling this verse.

But the application is also personal and spiritual. We are invited to move from ignorance or nominal belief to genuine knowledge of God. The purpose clause—'that they may know'—is not merely about intellectual understanding but about experiential knowledge of God's reality and presence in our lives. As we engage in temple worship, in scripture study, in prayer and revelation, we come to know God in the way Isaiah intends: not as an abstract theological principle but as a living reality who directs our lives and history. And as we come to know God in this way, we become instruments through whom that knowledge spreads. The promise is that ultimately all creation will acknowledge the one God—and we are called to participate in and hasten that day through our faithfulness, our witness, and our work.

text_kjv: I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil: I the LORD do all these things.

commentary.narrative:
This verse stands as one of Scripture's most direct assertions of God's absolute sovereignty over all events and conditions. Isaiah presents Yahweh as the sole cause of both light and darkness, peace and calamity — a bold theological claim in the context of ancient Near Eastern dualism. The verse is likely a conscious rebuttal to the Persian Zoroastrian worldview that dominated the exilic environment, which posited two competing deities: Ahura Mazda (god of light and good) and Angra Mainyu (god of darkness and evil). Isaiah's declaration insists there is no such duality — one God orchestrates the full spectrum of human experience.

The word choice matters profoundly. The verb bara (create), used exclusively for God's creative acts in Genesis 1, appears twice here—applied to both darkness and to calamity. This elevates these conditions to the status of divine creative work, not accidents or failures in God's plan. The pairing of shalom (peace, well-being) with ra (calamity, adversity) is not about moral evil—it is about the experiential conditions of human existence. God does not create sin, but He does order the circumstances of life, whether favorable or adverse. As The Covenant Rendering notes, ra in this context means 'calamity' rather than 'evil,' because the parallel structure indicates opposition between favorable and unfavorable circumstances, not between good and evil as moral categories.

This assertion comes at a crucial moment in the exile. Cyrus is about to be named as God's instrument (verse 1), and some Israelites might wonder: Can God truly use a foreign king? Can He guarantee deliverance? This verse answers with cosmic scope—if the Lord controls light itself, darkness itself, and all the conditions of existence, then directing the rise of Cyrus is well within His power. The exiles are called to trust a God whose sovereignty is absolute and unrivaled.

word_study.meaning: to form, shape, fashion (especially as a potter shapes clay). Carries the sense of deliberate craftsmanship and intelligent design.
word_study.significance: Used for God's formative work throughout Isaiah. The present participle form suggests ongoing, continuous work—God is always forming, shaping His creation.

word_study.meaning: light, illumination, clarity. In Hebrew thought, light is not merely physical but carries metaphorical weight: knowledge, truth, God's presence, salvation.
word_study.significance: The fundamental cosmic opposite to darkness. Isaiah uses light imagery throughout to represent God's revelation and redemptive work.

word_study.meaning: to create ex nihilo, to bring into being from nothing. Used exclusively of God's creative acts in the Hebrew Bible.
word_study.significance: Appears twice in this verse—with 'darkness' and with 'calamity.' This verb, reserved for divine creation, emphasizes that these are not accidents or failures but part of God's purposeful order.

word_study.meaning: peace, completeness, well-being, wholeness, harmony. Not merely absence of conflict but fullness of right relationship.
word_study.significance: In Isaiah's vision, shalom is the ultimate human condition that God creates. It encompasses physical safety, spiritual wholeness, and justice.

word_study.meaning: evil, calamity, disaster, adversity. The semantic range spans moral wickedness and experiential misfortune; context determines which sense applies.
word_study.significance: Paired with 'peace,' ra here denotes unfavorable circumstances and conditions rather than moral evil. The verse asserts God's control over the conditions of human existence, both favorable and adverse. This is not theodicy about sin but about God's sovereignty over circumstances.

word_study.meaning: The personal name of God, derived from the verb 'to be.' Emphasizes God's eternal, self-existent nature and relational presence with His covenant people.
word_study.significance: The use of the divine name here is emphatic—after describing cosmic acts, Isaiah declares that it is Yahweh, Israel's covenant God, who does all these things. This personalizes divine sovereignty within the covenant relationship.

cross_references.connection: The original act of forming light and darkness at creation; Isaiah echoes Genesis to assert that the God who made light at the beginning still controls all cosmic conditions.
Another prophetic assertion of God's total causality: 'Shall there be evil in a city, and the LORD hath not done it?' — the same theological principle applied to calamity.
A suffering exile cries out: 'Out of the mouth of the most High proceedeth not evil and good?' — questioning whether God ordains both, a tension Isaiah resolves by affirming divine sovereignty.
Job's wife urges him to curse God, but he asks: 'Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?' — the same principle tested in the crucible of personal suffering.
Lehi is guided by the Lord into the wilderness; the Book of Mormon illustrates that God directs circumstances (favorable and adverse) for covenant purposes.

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah 45 was composed during or immediately after the Babylonian exile (c. 550 BCE), when Cyrus of Persia was rising to power. The exiled Israelites lived in a thoroughly dualistic religious environment shaped by Zoroastrian thought. Zoroastrianism, the state religion of the Persian Empire, taught that the universe is a cosmic battle between Ahura Mazda (god of light, truth, and goodness) and Angra Mainyu or Ahriman (god of darkness, lies, and evil). Neither is omnipotent; the outcome of history hangs in balance. This worldview profoundly shaped the cultural and intellectual context of exile. Isaiah's declaration—that one God, Yahweh, forms both light and darkness, both peace and calamity—is a direct theological challenge to this dualism. It reasserts monotheism in a dualistic environment. For exiles tempted to adopt Persian religious categories, this verse insists: there is only one ultimate power, and it is the God of Abraham, not a divided cosmos of competing deities.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 2:2, Lehi receives revelation about leading his family into the wilderness—the Lord directs both the blessing (guidance, protection) and the adversity (privation, hardship). Nephi later affirms (1 Nephi 2:24) that the Lord permits suffering to accomplish His purposes. This echoes Isaiah 45:7's principle that God orchestrates both favorable and adverse conditions for redemptive ends.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:12-13 teaches that 'the light which is in all things' emanates from God and orders the cosmos. D&C 29:34-35 affirms that God permits opposition in all things—'by reason of transgression cometh the fall, which fall bringeth death, and inasmuch as ye were born into the world by water, and blood, and the spirit, which I have made, and so became of dust a temporal body, nevertheless ye are still my sons and my daughters.' God's sovereignty encompasses both creation and the conditions of mortality.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The imagery of God forming and creating connects to the temple as the place where God's creative power and redemptive design are made manifest. The covenants of the temple affirm that God's purposes—including both trials and blessings—are part of His eternal design for exaltation.

commentary.christological_typology: While this verse does not directly typify Christ, it establishes the theological framework that allows Christ's redemption to work. If God were not sovereign over all conditions—if darkness or calamity were outside His control—then evil could thwart the plan of salvation. But Isaiah's assertion that Yahweh controls all things sets the stage for the Suffering Servant passages (Isaiah 52-53), where Christ's redemptive work unfolds within God's omniscient and omnipotent design. The apparent defeat of the cross is, within God's sovereignty, the means of universal redemption.
commentary.application: This verse invites modern believers to surrender the illusion of control and accept that God's sovereignty extends over all circumstances—not just the pleasant ones. When life brings adversity, injustice, illness, or loss, this verse does not excuse God from responsibility nor does it make Him the author of sin; rather, it asserts that even adverse circumstances are held within God's purposes and can be redeemed. For members of the Church, this becomes an invitation to faith: if God can direct Cyrus, a foreign king, to accomplish His purposes (as the chapter declares), then He can direct the circumstances of your life toward your ultimate exaltation. The test is whether you will trust that the 'calamity' you experience is not outside God's design but part of it.

text_kjv: Drop down, ye heavens, from above, and let the skies pour down righteousness: let the earth open, and let them bring forth salvation, and let righteousness spring up together; I the LORD have created it.

commentary.narrative:
After asserting God's absolute sovereignty over cosmic conditions (verse 7), Isaiah now shifts to a prophetic prayer or proclamation calling heaven and earth to cooperate in bringing forth salvation and righteousness. This verse envisions a saturated cosmos—heavens raining down tsedeq (righteousness), earth opening to receive and sprout yesha (salvation). The imagery is agricultural and participatory: both heaven and earth are called to active collaboration in God's redemptive work. This is not passive waiting but a summons to creation itself to witness and participate in salvation.

The parallelism is elegant and precise. 'Heavens drop down' and 'skies pour down righteousness' establish the divine supply from above. 'Earth open' and 'salvation spring forth' establish the human/earthly response—the earth receives what heaven pours and produces growth. Righteousness (tsedeq/tsedaqah) appears twice, framing the passage, which suggests it is the comprehensive condition of God's redemptive order. Salvation (yesha) is what springs from the earth when heaven has watered it. The doubled appearance of righteousness also echoes Isaiah's theme: salvation is not cheap grace but the triumph of God's justice and right order.

The final clause—'I the LORD have created it'—reaffirms that this cosmic cooperation, this rain of righteousness, this sprouting of salvation, is not beyond God's creative power or intention. The exiles are being prepared to understand that the coming of Cyrus, the restoration of Jerusalem, the redemption from captivity—all of this is woven into God's cosmic plan and creative purpose. Verse 8 is not merely poetic; it is a proclamation that redemption is emerging from the very fabric of creation itself.

word_study.meaning: to drip, trickle, rain down. A verb suggesting gentle but continuous flow—not violent flooding but steady, life-giving moisture.
word_study.significance: The choice conveys that righteousness comes not as destructive catastrophe but as life-sustaining provision, like rain on parched soil. This sets the tone for the cosmic redemption Isaiah envisions.

word_study.meaning: shamayim = the vast expanse above, the realm of God's throne; shechaqim = clouds, the visible dome of sky. Together they represent the full cosmic height from which blessing flows.
word_study.significance: The doubled invocation of 'heavens' and 'skies' emphasizes the totality of heaven's participation. This is not a limited or partial blessing but one that engages the entire upper cosmos.

word_study.meaning: righteousness, justice, right order, vindication. In Hebrew, tsedeq/tsedaqah encompasses both moral uprightness and the triumph of justice—the setting right of what is wrong.
word_study.significance: In Isaiah's vision, righteousness is not merely an ethical quality but a cosmic force—it can rain from heaven and sprout from earth. It is the substance of salvation itself, the full restoration of right relationship between God, humanity, and creation.

word_study.meaning: to open, split open, be receptive. The earth is summoned to open itself—not passively, but as an active receptivity.
word_study.significance: The earth's opening is not mere geological event but theological posture—creation yielding itself to receive and express the redemptive purposes of God.

word_study.meaning: salvation, deliverance, victory, safety. Often used in Isaiah for God's specific acts of rescue and restoration, not merely spiritual abstraction but historical deliverance.
word_study.significance: That salvation 'springs forth' from the earth suggests it is not imposed from outside but grows naturally from the redeemed soil—the exiles will experience restoration not as foreign intrusion but as the natural fruit of God's creative work.

word_study.meaning: to cause to sprout, make grow, bring forth vegetation. Used for agricultural growth and metaphorically for the flowering of redemptive reality.
